2-chronicles-1:1:1.summary: Solomon sits on David’s throne and “his kingdom was firmly prepared,” the Kings parallel to his growing strong.
2-chronicles-1:1:1.why: Parallel account of Solomon’s secure reign.

2-chronicles-1:1:2.summary: “The Lord was with Joseph” shares the formula of God’s presence but concerns another person.

2-chronicles-1:1:3.summary: “God is with you” said of Abraham shares only the presence formula.

2-chronicles-1:1:4.summary: God’s “I will be with you” to Moses shares only the presence theme.

2-chronicles-1:1:5.summary: The shown text reports only Shimei’s execution, with nothing on Solomon’s strength or God’s presence.

2-chronicles-1:1:6.summary: God tells David “I was with you” and made his name great, the presence and greatness now given Solomon.
2-chronicles-1:1:6.why: Shows the promise continuing to David’s son.

2-chronicles-1:1:7.summary: “The Lord was with Joseph” repeats the presence formula only.

2-chronicles-1:1:8.summary: God “highly exalted” Christ, only a general parallel to God making Solomon great.
2-chronicles-1:1:8.why: Typological theme of God exalting His king.

2-chronicles-1:1:9.summary: Christ’s “I am with you” shares only the theme of divine presence.

2-chronicles-1:2:1.summary: Lists “ancestral rulers, commanders of thousands and hundreds,” the same officials Solomon addresses.

2-chronicles-1:2:3.summary: David consults “commanders of thousands and of hundreds” before moving the ark, as Solomon gathers them for worship.

2-chronicles-1:2:2.summary: Mentions “ancestral rulers” of priests and Levites, a shared title only.

2-chronicles-1:2:4.summary: David “assembled all Israel” for the ark, a general parallel to Solomon addressing all Israel.

2-chronicles-1:2:5.summary: David addresses “the whole assembly” about Solomon, a loose parallel.
2-chronicles-1:2:5.why: Similar royal address to the assembly.

2-chronicles-1:2:6.summary: Josiah gathers elders and all the people to the Lord’s house; a general pattern only.

2-chronicles-1:2:7.summary: Dividing priestly “rulers of ancestral houses” shares only a title with Solomon’s address.

2-chronicles-1:2:8.summary: The king, rulers, and assembly taking counsel on Passover loosely parallels Solomon with his leaders.

2-chronicles-1:2:9.summary: Hezekiah gathers the city’s rulers to go to the Lord’s house, a general parallel.
2-chronicles-1:2:9.why: Similar king leading rulers to worship.

2-chronicles-1:2:10.summary: “Rulers of the Levites’ ancestral houses” shares a title only.

2-chronicles-1:3:1.summary: The Lord’s tent stood “at Bama in Gabaon,” the same high place Solomon visits.

2-chronicles-1:3:2.summary: Kings narrates Solomon going to Gibeon’s high place to sacrifice and the night vision, the same event; truncated.

2-chronicles-1:3:3.summary: Calls Moses the “servant of the Lord,” matching only the epithet.

2-chronicles-1:3:4.summary: Moses is instructed to make the tabernacle, the tent he made in the wilderness; long range truncated.
2-chronicles-1:3:4.why: Origin of the tent at Gibeon.

2-chronicles-1:3:5.summary: Names the “Tent of Testimony,” the same tent, but no shared event.

2-chronicles-1:3:6.summary: Moses is told to erect “the Tent of Testimony,” the tent later at Gabaon.
2-chronicles-1:3:6.why: Origin of the Tent of Testimony.

2-chronicles-1:3:7.summary: Making the tent’s ten curtains relates loosely to the tent Moses made.

2-chronicles-1:3:8.summary: Glory filling “the Tent of Testimony” names the same tent but no shared event.

2-chronicles-1:4:3.summary: David “prepared the place for God’s ark, and made a tent for it,” as the source states.

2-chronicles-1:4:0.summary: David goes to bring up “the ark of God,” the same transfer referred to.
2-chronicles-1:4:0.why: Parallel account of the ark’s journey.

2-chronicles-1:4:1.summary: The ark is set “inside the tent David had pitched for it,” the same tent.
2-chronicles-1:4:1.why: Narrates the ark placed in David’s tent.

2-chronicles-1:4:2.summary: Chronicles narrates all Israel bringing up the ark with music, the same transfer.
2-chronicles-1:4:2.why: Parallel account of the ark’s ascent.

2-chronicles-1:4:5.summary: David brings God’s ark “from the city of Jarim,” the same Kariathiarim.
2-chronicles-1:4:5.why: Origin point of the ark’s transfer.

2-chronicles-1:4:6.summary: The psalm recalls seeking a dwelling for the Lord and finding the ark “in the plains of the forest.”
2-chronicles-1:4:6.why: Poetic memory of the ark’s transfer.

2-chronicles-1:5:0.summary: “Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur” is the same craftsman as Beseleel son of Ouriou son of Or.

2-chronicles-1:5:1.summary: Narrates making “the bronze altar” and its utensils, the same altar at Gabaon.

2-chronicles-1:5:2.summary: Instructions for the altar overlaid with bronze describe the same bronze altar; truncated.

2-chronicles-1:5:3.summary: The genealogy “Or begot Uri, and Uri begot Bezalel” matches the source’s lineage.

2-chronicles-1:5:4.summary: The ark was not “sought” since Saul, while Solomon “sought out” the altar; a loose verbal echo.
2-chronicles-1:5:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-1:6:1.summary: Solomon’s massive temple sacrifices are a different occasion, sharing only lavish offerings.
2-chronicles-1:6:1.why: Shows Solomon’s pattern of lavish worship.

2-chronicles-1:6:2.summary: David offers “a thousand” calves, rams, and lambs, echoing the thousandfold offering on another occasion.

2-chronicles-1:6:3.summary: Isaiah says no offering is enough for God; only “whole burnt offering” is shared.

2-chronicles-1:7:0.summary: “Ask, and it will be given” shares the invitation to ask God.

2-chronicles-1:7:1.summary: Confidence that God grants what is asked according to His will is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-1:7:2.summary: The promise that the Father gives what is asked is only a thematic echo.

2-chronicles-1:7:3.summary: Trusting God rather than one’s own wisdom shares no specific link with God’s offer.

2-chronicles-1:7:5.summary: Jesus’ “What do you want Me to do for you?” resembles God’s open offer to Solomon.
2-chronicles-1:7:5.why: Similar open offer to a petitioner.

2-chronicles-1:7:6.summary: Jesus asks the same open question, but the disciples request glory, unlike Solomon’s request.
2-chronicles-1:7:6.why: Contrasts requests for glory and wisdom.

2-chronicles-1:8:0.summary: God chose Solomon “to seat him upon the throne,” the kingship Solomon acknowledges.

2-chronicles-1:8:1.summary: “The holy and sure blessings of David” relates loosely to God’s mercy to David.
2-chronicles-1:8:1.why: Prophetic recall of God’s favour to David.

2-chronicles-1:8:2.summary: God shows “mercy to His anointed, to David and his descendants,” matching Solomon’s words.
2-chronicles-1:8:2.why: David’s own praise of that mercy.

2-chronicles-1:8:3.summary: God recounts making David king and giving him Saul’s house, a general parallel of God’s favour.

2-chronicles-1:8:4.summary: God recalls taking David from the sheepfold to rule, part of His favour, but without mercy wording.

2-chronicles-1:8:5.summary: “My truth and My mercy will be with him” describes the mercy to David Solomon recalls; truncated.
2-chronicles-1:8:5.why: Psalm on God’s mercy to David.

2-chronicles-1:8:6.summary: “Solomon sat upon the throne of David his father,” the kingship in David’s place.

2-chronicles-1:8:7.summary: “Thy mercy toward me is great” shares wording but concerns personal rescue.

2-chronicles-1:8:8.summary: The psalm recalls the “mercies” God swore to David, the mercy Solomon cites.

2-chronicles-1:9:0.summary: God’s promise of seed like “the sand of the earth” stands behind a people numerous as “the dust of the earth.”

2-chronicles-1:9:1.summary: Nathan’s promise of David’s seed and throne is the word Solomon asks God to confirm.

2-chronicles-1:9:2.summary: The Lord swore to David to set his offspring on his throne, the promise Solomon invokes.
2-chronicles-1:9:2.why: Poetic form of the Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-1:9:3.summary: God’s oath that David’s seed and throne will remain for ever underlies Solomon’s plea.
2-chronicles-1:9:3.why: Poetic form of the Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-1:9:4.summary: Seed “as the sand upon the shore” shares the numerous-people theme only.

2-chronicles-1:9:6.summary: Balaam asks who can count Jacob’s seed, loosely matching a countless people.

2-chronicles-1:9:7.summary: Chronicles’ promise to raise David’s offspring and establish his throne is the word Solomon asks God to confirm.

2-chronicles-1:9:8.summary: David prays, “let Thy word … be made secure for ever,” as Solomon asks God to confirm His word.

2-chronicles-1:9:9.summary: God says Solomon will build His house and his kingdom be set upright for ever.

2-chronicles-1:9:10.summary: David prays, “confirm for ever the word Thou hast spoken,” the same plea for confirmation.

2-chronicles-1:10:1.summary: James urges those lacking “wisdom” to ask God, as Solomon asks for wisdom.
2-chronicles-1:10:1.why: New Testament teaching on asking for wisdom.

2-chronicles-1:10:2.summary: “The Lord gives wisdom” and understanding is a general parallel to Solomon’s request.
2-chronicles-1:10:2.why: Shows God as the source of wisdom.

2-chronicles-1:10:4.summary: Praise of wisdom as worth more than gold shares only the general value of wisdom.
2-chronicles-1:10:4.why: Shows why wisdom is worth asking for.

2-chronicles-1:10:5.summary: David “led Israel out and brought them in” as shepherd-ruler, the leadership idiom Solomon uses.

2-chronicles-1:10:6.summary: The plea “Give me understanding” matches Solomon’s request, but to keep God’s law, not to rule.

2-chronicles-1:10:7.summary: “Give me understanding” echoes Solomon’s request, but for learning commandments.

2-chronicles-1:10:8.summary: Sufficiency from God is a loose parallel to Solomon’s sense of inadequacy.

2-chronicles-1:10:9.summary: A leader “who will go out before them and come in” uses the same leadership idiom.
2-chronicles-1:10:9.why: Shared idiom of leading God’s people.

2-chronicles-1:10:10.summary: Moses can no longer “go in and come out,” sharing the leadership idiom in another setting.

2-chronicles-1:10:11.summary: “Who is sufficient for these things?” loosely echoes “who can judge this great people?”
2-chronicles-1:10:11.why: Similar sense of inadequacy for a task.

2-chronicles-1:10:12.summary: Solomon’s voice in Wisdom says “I prayed, and understanding was given me,” recalling this prayer.

2-chronicles-1:10:13.summary: Solomon’s prayer in Wisdom asks God to send wisdom to work at his side, echoing this request.

2-chronicles-1:11:0.summary: Describes “the wisdom from above,” only a general theme of God-given wisdom.

2-chronicles-1:11:1.summary: The Saints text speaks of swallowing a hair and eating, with nothing about the heart or wisdom.
2-chronicles-1:11:1.why: Greek wording removes the heart link.

2-chronicles-1:11:2.summary: God looks at the heart, loosely matching God noting what came into Solomon’s heart.
2-chronicles-1:11:2.why: Theme of God seeing the heart.

2-chronicles-1:11:3.summary: Asks who is “wise and understanding,” a general wisdom theme.

2-chronicles-1:11:4.summary: Israel sees “God’s discernment was within him to carry out justice,” fulfilling the request to judge.

2-chronicles-1:11:5.summary: God examines hearts and loves righteousness, a loose link to Solomon’s heart’s request.
2-chronicles-1:11:5.why: Theme of God weighing the heart.

2-chronicles-1:11:7.summary: Ananias’s deceit “in your heart” shares only the heart phrase.

2-chronicles-1:11:8.summary: God tells David “Because it came into your heart” to build, the same divine commendation formula.
2-chronicles-1:11:8.why: Parallel divine approval of a royal intention.

2-chronicles-1:11:9.summary: A general proverb on wisdom and folly has no specific tie to Solomon’s request.

2-chronicles-1:11:10.summary: David says “It came upon my heart to build,” a loose echo of what came into Solomon’s heart.

2-chronicles-1:11:11.summary: God’s word judging the heart’s thoughts shares no specific link with God’s answer to Solomon.

2-chronicles-1:12:0.summary: God gives “wisdom” to the one who asks; Solomon receives wisdom from God, but James speaks generally of prayer, not Solomon.
2-chronicles-1:12:0.why: Frames Solomon's gift as an instance of God's generous giving.

2-chronicles-1:12:1.summary: Solomon became greater than all kings “in both wealth and wisdom,” fulfilling the promise of wisdom, wealth, and unmatched glory.
2-chronicles-1:12:1.why: Shows the promise of 1:12 fulfilled later in Solomon's reign.

2-chronicles-1:12:2.summary: Seeking God's kingdom first and having “all these things” added loosely mirrors Solomon receiving wealth he did not ask for.
2-chronicles-1:12:2.why: Offers a New Testament principle echoing Solomon's added blessings.

2-chronicles-1:12:3.summary: God able to do more than “all we ask” loosely parallels God granting Solomon wealth and glory beyond his request.
2-chronicles-1:12:3.why: General theme of God's surpassing generosity.

2-chronicles-1:12:4.summary: The Lord gave Solomon “glory” such as no king before him had, matching the promise that none like him existed among kings before.
2-chronicles-1:12:4.why: Confirms the unmatched royal glory promised to Solomon.

2-chronicles-1:12:5.summary: The Preacher “surpassed everyone who was before me” while his “wisdom” remained, echoing Solomon's unrivaled wisdom and greatness.
2-chronicles-1:12:5.why: Solomonic voice reflecting on the promised wisdom and greatness.

2-chronicles-1:13:0.summary: Both name the high place in Gabaon where the Tent of Testimony stood, Solomon going there and returning to Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-1:13:0.why: Frames the start and end of Solomon's Gabaon visit.

2-chronicles-1:13:1.summary: Describes Solomon's peaceful rule over Judah and Israel; the source only notes that he reigned over Israel.
2-chronicles-1:13:1.why: Gives a general picture of Solomon's reign.

2-chronicles-1:14:0.summary: Kings' summary of Solomon's chariot horses and “twelve thousand horsemen” parallels the same figure here.
2-chronicles-1:14:0.why: Parallel record of Solomon's cavalry in Kings.

2-chronicles-1:14:3.summary: Repeats Solomon's “twelve thousand horsemen” stationed “in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.”
2-chronicles-1:14:3.why: Chronicles repeats the same summary near the end of Solomon's reign.

2-chronicles-1:14:2.summary: Lists Solomon's building of “all the chariot cities” and horsemen's cities, the same cities where his chariots were kept.
2-chronicles-1:14:2.why: Identifies the chariot cities mentioned here.

2-chronicles-1:14:4.summary: Solomon's gold spears share only the theme of royal wealth, not chariots or horsemen.
2-chronicles-1:14:4.why: No specific link to Solomon's chariot force.

2-chronicles-1:14:5.summary: The law says the king “shall not multiply horses” or return the people to Egypt, while Solomon amasses chariots and horsemen.
2-chronicles-1:14:5.why: Sets Solomon's military buildup against the law for kings.

2-chronicles-1:15:0.summary: Nearly identical wording: gold and silver in Jerusalem “like stones,” cedars as plentiful as “sycamores in the plain.”
2-chronicles-1:15:0.why: Chronicles repeats this summary of Solomon's wealth.

2-chronicles-1:15:1.summary: Promised exchange of lesser materials for gold and silver loosely echoes precious metals made common like stones.
2-chronicles-1:15:1.why: Prophetic image of abundance recalling Solomonic wealth.

2-chronicles-1:15:2.summary: Pairs “sycamores and cedars” and “stones,” but as a boast of rebuilding, not Solomon's abundance.
2-chronicles-1:15:2.why: Shared stock pairing of sycamore and cedar.

2-chronicles-1:15:3.summary: God's promise of “wealth, possessions, and glory” is fulfilled in the abundance of gold, silver, and cedar.
2-chronicles-1:15:3.why: Links the promise to its immediate fulfillment.

2-chronicles-1:15:4.summary: Greek wording speaks of a mound, rock, and torrents of Ophir; it lacks the gold-like-dust image the label assumes.
2-chronicles-1:15:4.why: The Greek text does not carry the abundance image.

2-chronicles-1:15:5.summary: Only the incidental word “sycamore” is shared; Amos describes his occupation.

2-chronicles-1:16:0.summary: Solomon's horses came “out of Egypt,” the same trade reported again in chapter 9.
2-chronicles-1:16:0.why: Parallel notice of Solomon's horse trade.

2-chronicles-1:17:0.summary: Jehu's continuing in Jeroboam's sins has no link to Solomon's chariot and horse trade.

2-chronicles-1:18:1.summary: God's promise that David's son “will build a house for My name” and have a kingdom, now resolved upon by Solomon.
2-chronicles-1:18:1.why: Shows Solomon acting on the promise given to David.

2-chronicles-1:18:2.summary: Records Solomon building “his own house,” the royal house he resolved to build here.
2-chronicles-1:18:2.why: Shows the second house actually built.

2-chronicles-1:18:3.summary: The chosen place where God sets “His name” anticipates a house for the Lord's name, but without naming the temple.
2-chronicles-1:18:3.why: Background in the law for a house for God's name.

2-chronicles-1:18:4.summary: The place chosen “for His name” to be called upon loosely anticipates the house for the Lord's name.

2-chronicles-1:18:5.summary: David's desire “to build a house for My name” is the plan Solomon now resolves to carry out.
2-chronicles-1:18:5.why: Connects Solomon's resolve to David's original intention.

2-chronicles-1:18:6.summary: Solomon finished “the Lord's house, the king's house,” completing both houses he resolved to build.
2-chronicles-1:18:6.why: Shows the completion of both building projects.

2-chronicles-1:18:7.summary: Only the word “name” is shared; the verse warns about fearing the Lord's name, not building a house.

2-chronicles-1:18:8.summary: Solomon declares “I have built the house for the name of the Lord,” fulfilling the resolve stated here.
2-chronicles-1:18:8.why: Shows the resolve brought to completion.

2-chronicles-1:18:9.summary: Only the words “name” and “kingdom” overlap; the Lord's Prayer has no link to Solomon's building plans.

2-chronicles-1:10:3.summary: Proverbs 4:7 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-1:10:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-1:10:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-2:1:0.summary: The same seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand quarrymen, and three thousand six hundred overseers.

2-chronicles-2:2:1.summary: Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar to build David’s house, exactly what Solomon recalls.

2-chronicles-2:2:2.summary: Kings’ parallel of Solomon’s message to Hiram about building the Lord’s house (truncated).
2-chronicles-2:2:2.why: Parallel account of the same correspondence.

2-chronicles-2:3:0.summary: Aaron burns incense “morning by morning,” the incense rite Solomon’s house will continue.

2-chronicles-2:3:1.summary: Bread of the Presence set “continually” corresponds to the “continual presentation.”

2-chronicles-2:3:2.summary: Solomon resolved to build a house for the Lord’s name, which he now announces to Chiram.

2-chronicles-2:3:3.summary: David desired to build a house for God’s name, which Solomon his son now builds.

2-chronicles-2:3:5.summary: Sabbaths and the feasts of the Lord listed in Leviticus are the occasions named for temple offerings (truncated).

2-chronicles-2:3:6.summary: Solomon’s dedication sacrifices fulfill the purpose of offerings in the house, but differ from the regular schedule.

2-chronicles-2:3:7.summary: Loaves set before the Lord “continually” on the Sabbath as “an everlasting covenant” match the continual presentation and everlasting obligation.

2-chronicles-2:3:8.summary: The “continual” whole burnt offering morning and evening is the offering Solomon names.

2-chronicles-2:4:1.summary: “Who is like Thee among the gods” affirms God’s superiority over the gods.

2-chronicles-2:4:2.summary: “Our Lord is above all the gods” closely matches “our God is greater than all the gods.”

2-chronicles-2:4:3.summary: “The work is great, for the building is for the Lord God” parallels the great house for a great God.

2-chronicles-2:4:4.summary: God as “King of those who reign” is a general sovereignty parallel.

2-chronicles-2:4:6.summary: “The house I am building is great and glorious” repeats the same claim in context.

2-chronicles-2:4:7.summary: “Great is the Lord” generally supports God’s greatness.

2-chronicles-2:4:8.summary: “There is none like Thee among gods” matches God’s superiority over all gods.

2-chronicles-2:4:9.summary: The “lofty house” later astonishes passersby in its ruin, contrasting with the great house being built.

2-chronicles-2:4:10.summary: Ornaments made into abominations have no specific link to building a great house for God.

2-chronicles-2:5:0.summary: “Heaven and the heaven of heaven will not suffice for Thee” matches the same confession at the dedication.
2-chronicles-2:5:0.why: Solomon repeats the idea at dedication.

2-chronicles-2:5:2.summary: “What sort of house will you build for Me?” echoes the question of who can build God a house.
2-chronicles-2:5:2.why: God cannot be contained by a house.

2-chronicles-2:5:3.summary: Stephen quotes “What kind of house will you build for Me,” echoing God’s transcendence over the temple.
2-chronicles-2:5:3.why: New Testament use of the theme.

2-chronicles-2:5:4.summary: David’s “Who am I” before God parallels Solomon’s humble “Who am I to build Him a house?”

2-chronicles-2:5:5.summary: The place God chooses for His name and offerings is background to the house for burning incense.

2-chronicles-2:5:6.summary: Moses’ “Who am I” shares the humble question in a different task.

2-chronicles-2:5:7.summary: David’s “Who am I, and who are my people,” in the temple offering context, parallels Solomon’s humility.
2-chronicles-2:5:7.why: Humility about giving for the temple.

2-chronicles-2:5:8.summary: “Who can judge this great people?” shares Solomon’s rhetorical humility.

2-chronicles-2:5:9.summary: Bringing offerings to the place chosen for God’s name is general background.

2-chronicles-2:5:10.summary: Offering at the chosen place is general background to the temple’s purpose.

2-chronicles-2:5:11.summary: Paul as “the very least of all saints” shares only the humility theme.

2-chronicles-2:5:12.summary: “Who is sufficient for these things?” shares the rhetorical sense of inadequacy.

2-chronicles-2:5:13.summary: The chosen place for God’s name and offerings is general background.

2-chronicles-2:6:1.summary: Bezaleel filled with wisdom to work in gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, scarlet parallels the skilled craftsman requested.

2-chronicles-2:6:2.summary: Chiram answers by sending the wise craftsman skilled in exactly these metals and colors.

2-chronicles-2:6:3.summary: The Greek-based Saints wording of Isaiah 28:29 does not carry wisdom from the Lord as the label assumes.

2-chronicles-2:6:4.summary: Foreigners building and kings serving loosely parallel a Tyrian king sending builders.

2-chronicles-2:6:5.summary: Hiram, a Tyrian’s son filled with skill and knowledge, is the craftsman sent.

2-chronicles-2:6:6.summary: Being disciplined by God’s judgment in the Saints text has no link to skilled craftsmen.

2-chronicles-2:7:1.summary: Solomon’s and Chiram’s servants bring pinewood for the Lord’s house, the cooperation requested here.

2-chronicles-2:7:2.summary: Hiram’s ship brings wood, related to the timber trade but not Lebanon cutting.

2-chronicles-2:8:0.summary: The “lofty house” becoming an object of astonishment contrasts with the great, glorious house being built.

2-chronicles-2:8:1.summary: “The house I am building is great” repeats the same claim in context.

2-chronicles-2:8:2.summary: The “lofty house” later astonishes passersby, contrasting with its glorious construction.

2-chronicles-2:9:1.summary: Royal provision of kors of wheat, wine, and oil for temple work resembles Solomon’s provisions.

2-chronicles-2:9:2.summary: “The worker is worthy of his pay” generally supports paying workers.

2-chronicles-2:9:3.summary: Paying what is owed is a general principle.

2-chronicles-2:9:4.summary: The Saints text of the sea’s brim gives no liquid measure, so the label’s measurement link is absent.
2-chronicles-2:9:4.why: Shown text lacks the shared element.

2-chronicles-2:9:5.summary: Basin capacity “forty choes by measure” is only an incidental unit, unrelated to wages in kind.

2-chronicles-2:10:0.summary: “Because the Lord your God loved Israel … He made you king over them” closely echoes Chiram’s words.
2-chronicles-2:10:0.why: Foreign ruler’s recognition of God’s love in Solomon.

2-chronicles-2:10:2.summary: The blessed king of Psalm 72 loosely parallels a foreign king blessing Solomon’s appointment.

2-chronicles-2:10:3.summary: “The Lord loved you” and chose Israel underlies Chiram’s statement that the Lord loves His people.
2-chronicles-2:10:3.why: Foundation of God’s love for Israel.

2-chronicles-2:11:3.summary: “The living God, who made heaven and earth” shares the creator formula.

2-chronicles-2:11:4.summary: “Who made heaven and earth” shares the creator formula.

2-chronicles-2:11:8.summary: “God made heaven and earth” is the origin of the creator formula Chiram uses.

2-chronicles-2:11:0.summary: The heavens established by the Lord’s word shares the creator theme.

2-chronicles-2:11:1.summary: “Blessed be the God” shares the blessing formula only.

2-chronicles-2:11:2.summary: God as creator of all things shares the creator theme.

2-chronicles-2:11:5.summary: The Lord founding earth and heavens shares the creator theme.

2-chronicles-2:11:6.summary: God grants Solomon “wisdom and understanding,” which Chiram praises in the “wise son, skilled in understanding.”

2-chronicles-2:11:7.summary: “The One who made heaven and earth” shares the creator formula.

2-chronicles-2:11:9.summary: “Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel” matches Chiram’s blessing formula.

2-chronicles-2:11:10.summary: “Who created heaven … and the earth” shares the creator formula.

2-chronicles-2:11:11.summary: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel” is word-for-word Chiram’s opening.

2-chronicles-2:11:12.summary: Solomon’s plan for “a house for the Lord’s name and a house for his kingdom” matches Chiram’s words.

2-chronicles-2:11:14.summary: David’s assembly blessing the Lord shares the act of blessing God.

2-chronicles-2:11:15.summary: All things created in heaven and earth shares the creator theme.

2-chronicles-2:11:17.summary: God who made the heavens “with understanding” loosely links creation and understanding.

2-chronicles-2:11:18.summary: “Who made heaven and earth” shares the creator formula.

2-chronicles-2:11:19.summary: Groaning until bone clings to flesh has no link to Chiram’s blessing.

2-chronicles-2:12:0.summary: Chiram makes the bronze vessels for the Lord’s house, the same craftsman sent here.

2-chronicles-2:13:2.summary: Bezaleel’s skill in gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, and scarlet parallels Chiram’s listed skills.

2-chronicles-2:13:1.summary: Hiram from Tyre, a widow’s son whose father was “a Tyrian man,” is the same craftsman, with a differing tribe.
2-chronicles-2:13:1.why: Kings parallel; note Naphtali versus Dan.

2-chronicles-2:14:1.summary: Solomon gives Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat and oil, the provisions requested.

2-chronicles-2:15:0.summary: Mentions Joppa as a boundary only geographically.

2-chronicles-2:15:2.summary: Cedar from Lebanon brought “to the sea at Joppa” for the second temple mirrors Solomon’s arrangement.
2-chronicles-2:15:2.why: Repeated timber route for the temple.

2-chronicles-2:15:3.summary: All things coming into being through the Word has no link to timber rafts to Joppa.

2-chronicles-2:15:4.summary: Peter staying at Joppa beside the sea shares only the place name.

2-chronicles-2:15:5.summary: Tabitha in Joppa shares only the place name.

2-chronicles-2:16:1.summary: The same labor force of seventy thousand, eighty thousand, and three thousand six hundred drawn from the foreigners counted.

2-chronicles-2:16:2.summary: Kings lists the same seventy thousand burden-bearers, eighty thousand stonecutters, and 3,600 overseers.
2-chronicles-2:16:2.why: Kings parallel of the labor force.

2-chronicles-2:16:3.summary: Remaining non-Israelite peoples brought under tribute explain the resident foreigners Solomon conscripted.

2-chronicles-2:16:4.summary: Kings parallel: remaining Hittites, Amorites, and others subjected to Solomon’s levy.
2-chronicles-2:16:4.why: Kings parallel identifying the foreign laborers.

2-chronicles-2:17:0.summary: Both verses give Solomon’s same labor figures: seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand quarrymen, and three thousand six hundred overseers.
2-chronicles-2:17:0.why: Repeats the census of Solomon’s temple workforce.

2-chronicles-2:4:5.summary: Jeremiah 10:6 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-2:4:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-2:4:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-2:11:13.summary: Jeremiah 10:10 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-2:11:13.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-2:11:13.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-3:1:0.summary: The angel directs David to build an altar “at the threshing floor of Orna the Jebusite”—the very site of the temple.

2-chronicles-3:1:5.summary: David acquires “the threshing floor of Orna the Jebusite” to build an altar; the site where Solomon builds.
2-chronicles-3:1:5.why: Story of how the site was obtained.

2-chronicles-3:1:1.summary: “In the mountain the Lord appeared” echoes “where the Lord appeared”; the Greek here lacks a shared Moriah name to tie the sites explicitly.
2-chronicles-3:1:1.why: Traditional link of Abraham’s mountain and temple mount.

2-chronicles-3:1:2.summary: Greek reads “the high land”, not Moriah, so the Moriah/“Amoria” link assumed by the label is not carried by the shown text.
2-chronicles-3:1:2.why: Greek wording drops the Moriah name.

2-chronicles-3:1:3.summary: David declares the threshing-floor site “the house of the Lord God”; identifies the place David prepared.

2-chronicles-3:1:4.summary: Kings’ account of Solomon building the Lord’s house; parallel to Chronicles’ building narrative.
2-chronicles-3:1:4.why: Parallel account of the temple’s construction.

2-chronicles-3:2:0.summary: Same date: “in the fourth year, in the second month” of Solomon’s reign.

2-chronicles-3:3:0.summary: David gives Solomon the pattern of the temple and its measures; background to the measurements Solomon followed.

2-chronicles-3:4:0.summary: “Solomon’s Portico” in the later temple; associated by name with Solomon’s porch, not the same structure.
2-chronicles-3:4:0.why: Later use of Solomon’s name for a portico.

2-chronicles-3:4:1.summary: Jesus walks in “Solomon’s Portico”; name association only, a later structure.

2-chronicles-3:4:2.summary: People gather at “the portico called Solomon’s”; name association only.

2-chronicles-3:5:0.summary: Solomon lines the house’s walls with cedar timbers; parallel to paneling the great house with cedar.

2-chronicles-3:5:1.summary: “He covered the whole house with gold”; parallel to gilding with pure gold.

2-chronicles-3:6:0.summary: New Jerusalem adorned with “every precious stone” and pure gold; thematic echo of a gem-adorned house.
2-chronicles-3:6:0.why: Heavenly city as fulfillment of temple splendor.

2-chronicles-3:6:1.summary: Restored Zion built with precious stones; general gem-adornment image.

2-chronicles-3:6:3.summary: People gave stones “to the storerooms of the Lord’s house”; source of the precious stones used.

2-chronicles-3:7:0.summary: Solomon covered the sanctuary and “the whole house with gold”; parallel gilding account.

2-chronicles-3:7:1.summary: Tabernacle curtains made “with cherubim”; tabernacle precedent for cherubim decoration.

2-chronicles-3:7:2.summary: Ornaments turned into images of abominations; no real link to gilding and cherubim.

2-chronicles-3:7:4.summary: Tabernacle posts overlaid with gold; general gold-overlay precedent.

2-chronicles-3:8:2.summary: Twenty cubits made “into the Holy of Holies”; parallel account of the same room.

2-chronicles-3:8:0.summary: Veil divides the Holy Place from “the Holy of Holies”; tabernacle precedent.
2-chronicles-3:8:0.why: Tabernacle precedent for the inner room.

2-chronicles-3:8:1.summary: A tent “called the Holy of Holies”; names the same kind of room.
2-chronicles-3:8:1.why: New Testament reflection on the inner room.

2-chronicles-3:8:4.summary: Entry into “the holy places” by Jesus’ blood; typological reflection.
2-chronicles-3:8:4.why: Christological fulfillment of the inner sanctuary.

2-chronicles-3:8:5.summary: The earlier sanctuary as “a figure” with sacrifices; no specific link to building the Holy of Holies.

2-chronicles-3:9:0.summary: David’s pattern included “its upper rooms”; matches the gilded upper room.

2-chronicles-3:10:1.summary: “Make two cherubim” of gold; precedent for the two cherubim in the Holy of Holies.

2-chronicles-3:13:0.summary: Tabernacle cherubim spread wings with faces “toward one another”; contrasts with faces “toward the house.”

2-chronicles-3:14:0.summary: “Behind the second curtain” the Holy of Holies; general reference to such a curtain.

2-chronicles-3:14:1.summary: “The veil of the sanctuary was torn”; the successor of this curtain, torn at Christ’s death.
2-chronicles-3:14:1.why: Shows the curtain’s significance in Christ.

2-chronicles-3:14:2.summary: Way inaugurated “through the curtain—that is, His flesh”; typological reading of the curtain.

2-chronicles-3:15:0.summary: Solomon’s two pillars, “thirty-five cubits high” with five-cubit cornices; same pillars and same measurements.

2-chronicles-3:16:1.summary: Gold in front of the inner sanctuary; only loosely related to the serseroth and pomegranates.
2-chronicles-3:16:1.why: Partial overlap on the inner sanctuary.

2-chronicles-3:17:0.summary: Solomon set up two named pillars (Iachoum and Boaz); same pillars, here translated as Establishment and Strength.

2-chronicles-4:1:0.summary: The same “bronze altar” before the Lord’s house proved too small at the dedication.
2-chronicles-4:1:0.why: Shows the altar in use at the dedication.

2-chronicles-4:1:1.summary: Ezekiel’s visionary altar is given in cubit measurements, but it is a different altar.

2-chronicles-4:1:2.summary: Ahaz moves “the bronze altar” that stood before the Lord’s house, the altar Solomon made.
2-chronicles-4:1:2.why: Later history of the same altar.

2-chronicles-4:1:3.summary: Beseleel’s tabernacle “bronze altar” is the predecessor, not the altar Solomon made.
2-chronicles-4:1:3.why: Tabernacle precedent for the bronze altar.

2-chronicles-4:1:4.summary: Solomon offers burnt offerings on “the altar he built for the Lord,” the same altar.
2-chronicles-4:1:4.why: Shows Solomon’s altar in regular use.

2-chronicles-4:1:6.summary: Solomon stands before “the Lord’s altar” at the dedication; the altar is mentioned only incidentally.
2-chronicles-4:1:6.why: Altar as setting for Solomon’s prayer.

2-chronicles-4:2:0.summary: The Saints text of Zechariah 13:1 speaks only of places opened in David’s house, with no water or cleansing link.
2-chronicles-4:2:0.why: Greek wording lacks the fountain image.

2-chronicles-4:2:2.summary: The tabernacle’s “bronze basin” for priestly washing is the forerunner of Solomon’s cast sea.
2-chronicles-4:2:2.why: Tabernacle precedent for the washing vessel.

2-chronicles-4:2:3.summary: “Washing of regeneration” links only typologically to the sea, whose washing purpose is not stated in this verse.

2-chronicles-4:2:4.summary: Washing robes in the Lamb’s blood has no specific link to the sea’s measurements.

2-chronicles-4:3:0.summary: An ox not muzzled while threshing shares only an animal word with the cast calves.

2-chronicles-4:3:1.summary: A living creature “like a calf” shares only the word with the cast calf figures.

2-chronicles-4:3:2.summary: Ezekiel’s creatures with a “calf’s face” share only the animal image with the cast calves.

2-chronicles-4:4:0.summary: Calves facing four directions has no real link to preaching to the whole world.

2-chronicles-4:4:1.summary: Twelve foundations of apostles share only the number twelve with the twelve calves.

2-chronicles-4:4:2.summary: Proclamation to all nations has no link beyond allegorizing the four directions.

2-chronicles-4:4:3.summary: Paul’s calling to Gentiles has no real connection to the calves under the sea.

2-chronicles-4:4:4.summary: Building the Church on the rock has no specific link to the sea resting on calves.

2-chronicles-4:4:5.summary: The Great Commission to all nations has no specific link to calves facing four directions.

2-chronicles-4:4:6.summary: The foundation of apostles and prophets has no real link to the sea’s supporting calves.

2-chronicles-4:6:2.summary: “Wash me” for cleansing from sin relates only generally to the temple’s washing basins.

2-chronicles-4:6:3.summary: Hiram’s summary of cauldrons and bowls belongs to the parallel temple-furnishings account but does not mention the basins.

2-chronicles-4:6:4.summary: The Saints text of Ezekiel 40:38 lists chambers and porches only, without the washing of offerings.
2-chronicles-4:6:4.why: Greek wording lacks the washing link.

2-chronicles-4:6:5.summary: Priests “wash the entrails and the feet with water” for the whole burnt offering, the very rinsing the basins served.
2-chronicles-4:6:5.why: Explains what was washed in the basins.

2-chronicles-4:6:6.summary: Earthly copies cleansed by sacrifices relates generally to temple purification.
2-chronicles-4:6:6.why: Hebrews on the meaning of ritual cleansing.

2-chronicles-4:6:7.summary: “You washed yourselves clean” shares only a general washing theme.

2-chronicles-4:6:8.summary: The law to “wash the entrails and the feet with water” for burnt offerings matches the basins’ purpose.
2-chronicles-4:6:8.why: Explains what was washed in the basins.

2-chronicles-4:6:9.summary: Robes washed in the Lamb’s blood shares only a general washing image.

2-chronicles-4:6:10.summary: Aaron and his sons are washed with water, the priestly washing for which the sea was provided.

2-chronicles-4:6:11.summary: Christ’s blood cleansing conscience relates only generally to ritual washing.
2-chronicles-4:6:11.why: Hebrews contrasts ritual and inner cleansing.

2-chronicles-4:6:12.summary: Jesus’ blood “cleanses us from every sin” shares only a general cleansing theme.

2-chronicles-4:6:13.summary: Describes the same cast “sea” that this verse says was for the priests to wash in.

2-chronicles-4:6:14.summary: Freed from sins and made “priests” relates loosely to priestly washing.

2-chronicles-4:7:1.summary: The tabernacle’s gold “lampstand” is the ordinance the ten golden lampstands follow.

2-chronicles-4:7:2.summary: “Light of the world” shares only the idea of light with the lampstands.

2-chronicles-4:7:3.summary: David’s pattern for the house’s courts and chambers is general background, not the lampstands themselves.

2-chronicles-4:7:4.summary: Zechariah’s lampstand with olive trees on right and left shares imagery but is a vision.

2-chronicles-4:7:5.summary: David gave Solomon “the weight of the lampstands and of the lamps” for these same lampstands.

2-chronicles-4:7:6.summary: Seven “golden lampstands” as churches shares the image symbolically.

2-chronicles-4:7:7.summary: David’s written pattern from the Lord relates generally to making things “according to their ordinance.”

2-chronicles-4:7:8.summary: Making everything “according to the pattern” relates generally to the lampstands’ prescribed form.

2-chronicles-4:7:9.summary: Zechariah’s “lampstand entirely of gold” shares imagery but is a visionary lampstand.

2-chronicles-4:7:10.summary: A lamp placed on a lampstand in a house has no specific link to the temple lampstands.

2-chronicles-4:8:0.summary: Kings lists Solomon placing “the gold table” in the Lord’s house in the parallel furnishings account.

2-chronicles-4:8:1.summary: The tabernacle’s gold “table” is the model for Solomon’s golden tables.

2-chronicles-4:8:2.summary: “The Lord’s table” in Corinth has no specific link to Solomon’s ten tables.

2-chronicles-4:8:3.summary: Isaiah’s feast for the nations shares no specific element with the temple tables and bowls.

2-chronicles-4:8:4.summary: Malachi’s “Lord’s table” polluted relates to altar service, not the tables Solomon made.

2-chronicles-4:8:5.summary: Cauldrons becoming like “bowls before the altar” shares the temple bowls image only.

2-chronicles-4:8:6.summary: Priests approaching “My table” relates generally to temple service.

2-chronicles-4:8:7.summary: Beseleel made “the table of presentation of pure gold,” the tabernacle forerunner of Solomon’s tables.

2-chronicles-4:8:8.summary: The bowls and gold vessels taken by the chief guard relate to the later fate of temple vessels.
2-chronicles-4:8:8.why: Later fate of the temple vessels.

2-chronicles-4:8:9.summary: Antiochus strips “the table of presentation” and “bowls” of the second temple, a later analogous loss.

2-chronicles-4:9:1.summary: Manasseh builds altars “in the two courts of the Lord’s house,” the courts Solomon made.
2-chronicles-4:9:1.why: Later desecration of the same courts.

2-chronicles-4:9:2.summary: Kings describes construction around “the great court,” the same court.

2-chronicles-4:11:1.summary: Introduces the bronze craftsman (Hiram) who “did all the works” for Solomon, the same Chiram.

2-chronicles-4:12:1.summary: Describes the same “two pillars” and their capitals placed before the house.

2-chronicles-4:13:0.summary: Kings describes “two rows of bronze pomegranates interwoven as a net” on the capitals.

2-chronicles-4:13:1.summary: Jeremiah counts the “pomegranates around the net” on the pillars destroyed by Babylon.
2-chronicles-4:13:1.why: Later account of the same pomegranates.

2-chronicles-4:13:2.summary: Gold “pomegranates, with bells between them” on the priest’s robe echoes the bells and pomegranates here.

2-chronicles-4:13:4.summary: An “orchard of pomegranates” is a love image unrelated to the temple pillars.

2-chronicles-4:16:0.summary: Huram sends “Chiram, my father,” the same craftsman who made these vessels.

2-chronicles-4:16:1.summary: Chiram “made the meat hooks” and finished all the work for Solomon, the same summary.

2-chronicles-4:16:2.summary: David weighs out metal for “meat hooks” and bowls, but in gold; related planning only.

2-chronicles-4:16:3.summary: Solomon brought Hiram from Tyre, a bronze craftsman who “did all the works,” the same Chiram.

2-chronicles-4:16:4.summary: The “meat hook” and “cauldron” at Shiloh share the utensil names only.
2-chronicles-4:16:4.why: Shows how such utensils were used.

2-chronicles-4:16:6.summary: “Cauldrons in the Lord’s house” made holy shares the vessel image only.

2-chronicles-4:16:7.summary: The tabernacle altar’s bowls, meat forks and firepan were all “of bronze,” as Solomon’s were.

2-chronicles-4:16:8.summary: Beseleel made the altar’s utensils and “bronze meat forks,” the tabernacle counterpart.

2-chronicles-4:18:1.summary: The bronze of Solomon’s pillars, sea and calves was “beyond weighing,” the same abundance.

2-chronicles-4:18:2.summary: David prepared “bronze in abundance, beyond weighing,” the supply Solomon used.

2-chronicles-4:18:3.summary: David prepared bronze and iron “beyond weighing because there is so much.”

2-chronicles-4:19:17.summary: David gave the weight for “the tables of presentation, each golden table.”

2-chronicles-4:19:0.summary: The heavenly “golden altar” before God echoes the temple’s golden altar symbolically.

2-chronicles-4:19:1.summary: The shown text mentions only anointing oil and incense; the incense altar in the truncated range is not shown.

2-chronicles-4:19:2.summary: “All the vessels of God’s house” were carried to Babylon, the fate of these vessels.
2-chronicles-4:19:2.why: Later fate of the same vessels.

2-chronicles-4:19:3.summary: Cyrus returns “the vessels of the Lord’s house” taken by Nebuchadnezzar.

2-chronicles-4:19:4.summary: Records the making of the same ten tables and golden bowls.

2-chronicles-4:19:5.summary: Nebuchadnezzar takes “the desirable vessels of the Lord’s house” to Babylon.
2-chronicles-4:19:5.why: Later fate of the same vessels.

2-chronicles-4:19:6.summary: Belshazzar drinks from “the gold and silver vessels of God’s house” brought from Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-4:19:7.summary: The tabernacle incense altar overlaid “with pure gold” is the model for the golden altar.
2-chronicles-4:19:7.why: Tabernacle precedent for the golden altar.

2-chronicles-4:19:10.summary: The chief guard takes the temple’s gold lampstands, bowls and vessels, the fate of Solomon’s furnishings.

2-chronicles-4:19:11.summary: Uzziah burns incense on “the incense altar,” the golden altar, but the story is about his trespass.
2-chronicles-4:19:11.why: Later episode at the same altar.

2-chronicles-4:19:12.summary: Daniel rebukes use of “the vessels of the living God’s house,” a later reference to temple vessels.

2-chronicles-4:19:13.summary: Twelve loaves set “on the pure table before the Lord” explain the bread of presentation.
2-chronicles-4:19:13.why: Law of the bread of presentation.

2-chronicles-4:19:14.summary: The Chaldeans carry off the bowls, gold and silver vessels of the Lord’s house.

2-chronicles-4:19:15.summary: The heavenly “golden altar” with incense echoes the temple’s golden altar symbolically.

2-chronicles-4:19:16.summary: A promise to return “the vessels of the Lord’s house” relates to their later fate.

2-chronicles-4:19:18.summary: Nebuchadnezzar cuts apart “all the gold vessels Solomon king of Israel had made.”

2-chronicles-4:19:19.summary: Antiochus strips the second temple’s “table of presentation,” an analogous later loss.

2-chronicles-4:19:20.summary: The Maccabees make new vessels and bring in the incense altar and table, restoring similar furnishings.

2-chronicles-4:20:0.summary: The lampstand “of pure gold” and its lamps in the tabernacle is the ordinance followed here.

2-chronicles-4:20:1.summary: The same golden lampstands made “according to their ordinance.”
2-chronicles-4:20:1.why: Earlier mention of the same lampstands.

2-chronicles-4:20:2.summary: Mentions “the inner sanctuary” (dabir) only in passing, in describing side chambers.

2-chronicles-4:20:3.summary: The ark brought into “the inner sanctuary,” the dabir before which the lamps stood.
2-chronicles-4:20:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-4:20:4.summary: The Greek-based “holy temple” lacks the inner-sanctuary term the label assumes; only lifting hands in prayer.

2-chronicles-4:20:6.summary: Solomon builds “the inner sanctuary into the Holy of Holies,” the dabir named here.

2-chronicles-4:21:0.summary: Carved cherubim and palm trees on walls share nothing with the gold tongs, lamps and fire pans.

2-chronicles-4:21:2.summary: Carved “spreading petals” on walls do not match this Saints verse, which lists tongs, lamps and fire pans.
2-chronicles-4:21:2.why: Greek wording lacks the flower link.

2-chronicles-4:21:3.summary: The tabernacle lampstand’s pure-gold fittings model these golden lamps and utensils (range truncated).

2-chronicles-4:21:4.summary: The sea’s “lily” rim does not match this Saints verse, which lacks the flower ornament.
2-chronicles-4:21:4.why: Greek wording lacks the flower link.

2-chronicles-4:22:0.summary: The Saints verse speaks of the golden inner doors, not the utensils taken by Babylon.

2-chronicles-4:22:1.summary: Gold lamps and tongs do not appear in this Saints verse, which concerns the inner doors.

2-chronicles-4:22:3.summary: Bronze bowls and meat forks have no link to this Saints verse about the golden doors.

2-chronicles-4:22:4.summary: Mentions “doors” and gold vessels for the Lord’s house, but in a later funding regulation.

2-chronicles-4:22:5.summary: Kings describes the doors at “the entrance of the inner sanctuary” covered with gold.
2-chronicles-4:22:5.why: Kings parallel for the golden doors.

2-chronicles-4:3:3.summary: Ezekiel 10:14 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-4:3:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-4:3:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-4:21:1.summary: Exodus 37:20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-4:21:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-4:21:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-4:21:5.summary: 1 Kings 6:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-4:21:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-4:21:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-5:1:1.summary: Salomoth guards “the treasuries of the holy things that King David” consecrated.

2-chronicles-5:1:2.summary: “King David dedicated these to the Lord, with the silver and gold,” the holy things Solomon brought in.
2-chronicles-5:1:2.why: Origin of David’s dedicated silver and gold.

2-chronicles-5:1:3.summary: David prepared gold and silver “for the Lord’s house,” which Solomon deposits.

2-chronicles-5:2:5.summary: David charges the Levites to “bring up the ark” to its prepared place, the earlier stage of the ark’s journey.
2-chronicles-5:2:5.why: Earlier transfer of the ark by David.

2-chronicles-5:2:6.summary: David and “Israel’s elders” go “to bring up the ark of the Lord’s covenant,” the same phrasing as Solomon’s assembly.
2-chronicles-5:2:6.why: Earlier transfer of the ark to Zion.

2-chronicles-5:2:11.summary: “The ark of the Lord’s covenant” leads Israel in the wilderness; shared title only.

2-chronicles-5:2:0.summary: David brought the ark up “to the city of David,” from which Solomon now brings it.
2-chronicles-5:2:0.why: How the ark reached David’s city.

2-chronicles-5:2:1.summary: David had brought God’s ark to a tent in Jerusalem, where it stayed until Solomon moved it.

2-chronicles-5:2:2.summary: The singers and trumpeting priests belong to the same ceremony of bringing the ark into the temple.
2-chronicles-5:2:2.why: Same event, later in the narrative.

2-chronicles-5:2:4.summary: The Lord loving “the gates of Zion” relates generally to Zion as the ark’s home.

2-chronicles-5:2:7.summary: Zion as God’s “holy mountain” relates only generally to David’s city.

2-chronicles-5:2:8.summary: “The stronghold of Zion, which is the city of David” matches the same identification.

2-chronicles-5:2:9.summary: “Ancestral rulers” of priests and Levites shares only a leadership term.

2-chronicles-5:2:10.summary: “Ancestral rulers” who consecrated treasures share only a leadership term.

2-chronicles-5:2:12.summary: God’s ark set in the tent David pitched, the place from which Solomon brings it up.

2-chronicles-5:2:13.summary: “Ancestral rulers of the priests and Levites” shares only a leadership term.

2-chronicles-5:2:14.summary: The preceding verse on finishing the house and storing David’s gifts sets the scene but shares no specific element.

2-chronicles-5:2:15.summary: The Lord choosing Zion as His dwelling relates generally to the ark’s move.

2-chronicles-5:2:16.summary: Moses’ words when the ark rested share only the ark with Solomon’s assembly.

2-chronicles-5:2:17.summary: “David assembled in Jerusalem all Israel’s rulers,” a matching royal assembly formula.

2-chronicles-5:3:1.summary: Solomon kept “the feast” with all Israel, ending on the “seventh month,” the same occasion.
2-chronicles-5:3:1.why: Completes the account of the same feast.

2-chronicles-5:3:2.summary: The Feast of Tents in “this seventh month” is the feast being kept.

2-chronicles-5:4:4.summary: Levites purify themselves “to bring up the ark of Israel’s God,” as Levites carry it here.
2-chronicles-5:4:4.why: Precedent for Levites carrying the ark.

2-chronicles-5:4:0.summary: Priests “lifted up the ark of the covenant” at the Jordan, a general precedent for bearing the ark.

2-chronicles-5:4:2.summary: The sons of Kohath are assigned “to carry” the holy things, the law behind Levites taking up the ark.

2-chronicles-5:4:3.summary: Continues the same procession: the priests bring the ark to the Holy of Holies.

2-chronicles-5:4:5.summary: The Saints text shows only Joshua going in to the priests, with no mention of the ark.

2-chronicles-5:4:6.summary: “No one may lift God’s ark except the Levites,” the rule obeyed here.
2-chronicles-5:4:6.why: Rule that Levites carry the ark.

2-chronicles-5:5:0.summary: God’s “Tent of Testimony” at Gabaon is the tent now brought up with the ark.

2-chronicles-5:5:2.summary: Kings parallel: the priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary.
2-chronicles-5:5:2.why: Kings account of the same event.

2-chronicles-5:6:0.summary: Sacrifices of “a calf and a lamb” accompany David’s ark procession, as calves and sheep do here.

2-chronicles-5:6:1.summary: Offerings presented when God’s ark was set in David’s tent parallel the sacrifices before the ark.

2-chronicles-5:6:2.summary: David’s abundant sacrifices of calves and lambs relate to the theme of abundant offerings only.

2-chronicles-5:7:0.summary: “Rise, Lord, to Thy rest, Thou and the ark” celebrates the ark reaching its resting place.

2-chronicles-5:7:1.summary: The gold cherubim “sheltering…with their wings” above the ark parallel the cherubim’s wings here.

2-chronicles-5:7:2.summary: Describes the two cherubim in the inner sanctuary whose wings the ark rests beneath.

2-chronicles-5:7:4.summary: Hebrews describes “the ark of the covenant” with “cherubim of glory overshadowing” it.
2-chronicles-5:7:4.why: New Testament reflection on the ark.

2-chronicles-5:7:5.summary: Shares only the term “dabir,” before which the lampstands stood.

2-chronicles-5:8:0.summary: The ark’s gold-overlaid “carrying poles” are the poles the cherubim cover.

2-chronicles-5:8:1.summary: A covering over the ark with its “carrying poles” in transit is a loose parallel to the cherubim covering.

2-chronicles-5:8:2.summary: Gold rings made for the ark’s “carrying poles” explain the poles mentioned here.

2-chronicles-5:10:0.summary: Hebrews lists “the tablets of the covenant” in the ark along with the manna jar and Aaron’s rod.

2-chronicles-5:10:2.summary: Solomon placed the ark “in which is the Lord’s covenant that He made with Israel.”
2-chronicles-5:10:2.why: Solomon’s own description of the ark.

2-chronicles-5:10:3.summary: The covenant ratified with blood relates to the covenant the tablets embodied, but no tablets or ark appear.

2-chronicles-5:10:4.summary: “Keep My covenant” relates generally to the covenant at Sinai.

2-chronicles-5:10:5.summary: Moses shatters “the two tablets”; these are the first tablets, not those placed in the ark.

2-chronicles-5:10:6.summary: The covenant made with the fathers when brought “out of Egypt’s land” is contrasted with a new covenant.
2-chronicles-5:10:6.why: Contrasts the old and new covenants.

2-chronicles-5:10:7.summary: Israel entering the covenant in Moab relates only generally to the covenant at Choreb.

2-chronicles-5:10:8.summary: Refers to “the covenant which He made with them in Horeb,” the same covenant.

2-chronicles-5:10:9.summary: Moses carries “the two tablets of the testimony” from the mountain.

2-chronicles-5:10:10.summary: Moses “put them into the ark,” the testimonies that remain in the ark here.
2-chronicles-5:10:10.why: When the tablets entered the ark.

2-chronicles-5:10:11.summary: Hebrews quotes the covenant made with the fathers “to lead them out of the land of Egypt,” contrasting a new covenant.
2-chronicles-5:10:11.why: Contrasts the old and new covenants.

2-chronicles-5:10:12.summary: God gives Moses “the two tablets of the testimony” on Sinai.

2-chronicles-5:10:13.summary: Moses hews “two tablets of stone like the first,” the second tablets that went into the ark.

2-chronicles-5:11:0.summary: Josiah arranges priests “by your courses,” whereas here they served without regard to courses.

2-chronicles-5:11:1.summary: Hezekiah tells Levites to purify themselves and the holy places; general priestly sanctification theme.

2-chronicles-5:11:2.summary: Purity for the holy places at Hezekiah’s Passover relates only generally.

2-chronicles-5:11:3.summary: Job purifying his sons has no specific link to the priests’ sanctification.

2-chronicles-5:11:4.summary: Levites “purified themselves” to cleanse the Lord’s house; general sanctification theme.

2-chronicles-5:11:5.summary: Priests slow to purify themselves under Hezekiah contrasts loosely with all priests sanctified here.

2-chronicles-5:11:6.summary: David’s divisions of Aaron’s sons are the “courses” the priests here set aside.

2-chronicles-5:11:7.summary: Purifying the people before Sinai is a general sanctification parallel.

2-chronicles-5:11:8.summary: Priests and Levites “purified themselves” for Hezekiah’s Passover; general theme.

2-chronicles-5:11:9.summary: Moses consecrates the people before Sinai; general sanctification before God’s appearing.

2-chronicles-5:12:0.summary: Priests “sounded trumpets before God’s ark” in David’s procession, as priests trumpet here.
2-chronicles-5:12:0.why: Earlier priestly trumpeting before the ark.

2-chronicles-5:12:1.summary: Four thousand praising with instruments David made relates generally to Levitical music.

2-chronicles-5:12:2.summary: Introduces “Heman the psalm singer,” one of the singers named here.

2-chronicles-5:12:3.summary: Levites with instruments and priests sounding trumpets at the dedication, “For His mercy endures for ever.”

2-chronicles-5:12:4.summary: Introduces “Asaph son of Barachia,” one of the singers named here.

2-chronicles-5:12:5.summary: The law of silver trumpets is general background for priestly trumpeting.

2-chronicles-5:12:6.summary: Levites stationed “with cymbals, nablas, and kinyras,” the same instrument triad.

2-chronicles-5:12:7.summary: The bride’s “fine linen” shares only the fabric with the singers’ robes.

2-chronicles-5:12:8.summary: Aiman and Idithon with “trumpets and cymbals” praising the Lord, the same musicians.

2-chronicles-5:12:9.summary: David’s ark procession with cymbals and trumpets is a general parallel.
2-chronicles-5:12:9.why: Music at an earlier ark procession.

2-chronicles-5:12:11.summary: Aiman, Asaph and Aithan appointed with cymbals as psalm singers.

2-chronicles-5:12:12.summary: The shown psalm verse has no musician names or instruments; any superscription link is not shown.

2-chronicles-5:12:13.summary: Musicians in a festal procession relate generally to temple music.

2-chronicles-5:12:14.summary: Levites and psalm singers “in a fine-linen robe” carrying the ark, as here.

2-chronicles-5:12:15.summary: Priests with trumpets and Asaph’s sons with cymbals sing “His mercy…endures for ever” at the second temple’s founding.

2-chronicles-5:12:16.summary: Praise on psaltery and lyre relates generally to the instruments here.

2-chronicles-5:12:17.summary: A psalm attributed to Asaph links only by the singer’s name.

2-chronicles-5:12:18.summary: The shown psalm verse is a lament with no musicians or instruments; any Heman superscription is not shown.

2-chronicles-5:12:19.summary: Praise with trumpet, psaltery and “cymbals” relates generally to the instruments.

2-chronicles-5:12:20.summary: Angels clothed in linen share only the fabric with the singers.

2-chronicles-5:12:21.summary: Praise with tambourine and psaltery is a general musical-worship parallel.

2-chronicles-5:12:22.summary: Asaph sounds cymbals and priests sound trumpets “before the ark of God’s covenant.”

2-chronicles-5:12:23.summary: Priests blowing trumpets before the ark at Jericho is a loose parallel.

2-chronicles-5:12:24.summary: Levites standing to praise morning and evening relates generally to their duty.

2-chronicles-5:13:9.summary: “Give thanks unto the Lord, for it is good, for His mercy endures for ever” is the same refrain.

2-chronicles-5:13:0.summary: “For it is good, for His mercy…endures for ever” sung at the second temple’s founding.
2-chronicles-5:13:0.why: Same refrain at the rebuilt temple.

2-chronicles-5:13:1.summary: The Lord’s glory on the house and the cry “For it is good, for His mercy endures for ever.”
2-chronicles-5:13:1.why: Same glory and refrain at dedication.

2-chronicles-5:13:2.summary: Jeremiah foresees voices saying “Give thanks…for the Lord is good; His mercy is for ever” in the Lord’s house.
2-chronicles-5:13:2.why: Prophetic echo of the temple refrain.

2-chronicles-5:13:3.summary: Watchmen raising their voice “together” relates loosely to unified praise.

2-chronicles-5:13:4.summary: Heavenly worship with lyres and many voices is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-5:13:6.summary: “His mercy is for ever” echoes the refrain sung at the dedication.

2-chronicles-5:13:7.summary: Shouting to God with thanksgiving and psalms is a general praise parallel.

2-chronicles-5:13:8.summary: Jehoshaphat’s singers say “Give thanks to the Lord, for His mercy is for ever.”

2-chronicles-5:13:10.summary: Musicians and assemblies blessing God is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-5:13:11.summary: Believers “of one heart and soul” relates loosely to the singers’ one voice.

2-chronicles-5:13:12.summary: The Greek-based text says “another heart,” not one heart, so the unity link the label assumes is absent.

2-chronicles-5:13:13.summary: The cloud covered the tent and it “was filled with the glory of the Lord,” as the temple is here.

2-chronicles-5:13:14.summary: Glorifying God “with one accord and one mouth” relates loosely to one voice of praise.

2-chronicles-5:13:15.summary: A psalm for thanksgiving calling all to shout to the Lord; general praise theme.

2-chronicles-5:13:16.summary: The Maccabees sing “For it is good, for His mercy is for ever,” the same refrain.

2-chronicles-5:13:17.summary: Psalm singers praising with their voices amid a great sound is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-5:14:2.summary: Isaiah sees the house “full of His glory” and filled with smoke.

2-chronicles-5:14:3.summary: “The priests could not enter…because the Lord’s glory had filled the house.”

2-chronicles-5:14:4.summary: The temple filled with smoke from God’s glory so that “no one was able to enter.”
2-chronicles-5:14:4.why: Heavenly echo of the glory cloud.

2-chronicles-5:14:5.summary: “The cloud filled the house” with the Lord’s glory, as at the dedication.

2-chronicles-5:14:6.summary: God dwelling in “unapproachable light” relates generally to the priests being unable to stand.

2-chronicles-6:1:0.summary: Moses entered “the thick darkness where God was.”
2-chronicles-6:1:0.why: Sinai background of God in darkness.

2-chronicles-6:1:1.summary: God “made darkness His hiding place,” with dark clouds as His tent.
2-chronicles-6:1:1.why: Poetic image of God in darkness.

2-chronicles-6:1:2.summary: The Lord says “I will appear in a cloud above the propitiatory cover,” His presence over the ark.

2-chronicles-6:1:4.summary: “Clouds are the dust of His feet” is a general image of God and clouds.

2-chronicles-6:1:5.summary: Hebrews recalls Sinai’s “gloom and darkness,” a general allusion.

2-chronicles-6:1:6.summary: The mountain burned “with darkness, gloom” at God’s presence on Sinai.
2-chronicles-6:1:6.why: Sinai background of God in darkness.

2-chronicles-6:1:7.summary: God’s glory in the cloud covering Sinai parallels God dwelling in cloud and darkness.

2-chronicles-6:1:8.summary: “Cloud and gloom surround Him” matches God dwelling in thick darkness.
2-chronicles-6:1:8.why: Poetic image of God in darkness.

2-chronicles-6:2:0.summary: Solomon is “building a house for the name of the Lord my God, to consecrate it to Him.”

2-chronicles-6:2:1.summary: God promised David’s son “shall build Me a house,” now fulfilled.

2-chronicles-6:2:2.summary: Seeking “a dwelling for the God of Jacob” relates generally to the house for dwelling.

2-chronicles-6:2:3.summary: “He will build a house for My name,” the promise Solomon fulfills.

2-chronicles-6:2:4.summary: “He will build Me a house for My name,” the promise Solomon fulfills.

2-chronicles-6:2:5.summary: Christ’s tent “not made by hands” contrasts generally with the built house.

2-chronicles-6:2:6.summary: God’s tabernacle “with men,” where He shall dwell, echoes the theme of God dwelling.

2-chronicles-6:2:7.summary: Worship neither on this mountain “nor in Jerusalem” contrasts with the house built for God.

2-chronicles-6:2:8.summary: David urges Solomon to finish the work of the Lord’s house; general background.

2-chronicles-6:2:9.summary: “This is My rest for age upon age; here I will dwell” matches a house for dwelling throughout the ages.

2-chronicles-6:2:10.summary: The Lord “who dwells in Jerusalem” relates generally to God’s dwelling.

2-chronicles-6:2:11.summary: God said “Solomon your son will build My house,” fulfilled here.

2-chronicles-6:3:1.summary: A crowd standing on the shore shares only the idea of a standing assembly.

2-chronicles-6:3:2.summary: Joshua “blessed them,” a general leader’s blessing.

2-chronicles-6:3:3.summary: The priestly blessing is a general background for blessing Israel.

2-chronicles-6:3:4.summary: Solomon “blessed the whole assembly of Israel” at the dedication, in the Kings account.

2-chronicles-6:3:5.summary: All the people stood while Esdras blessed the Lord; general assembly parallel.

2-chronicles-6:3:6.summary: The king and people worshiping after offerings shares no specific element with Solomon blessing the assembly.

2-chronicles-6:3:7.summary: David “blessed the people in the Lord’s name” after installing the ark; similar royal blessing.

2-chronicles-6:3:8.summary: Jesus lifted His hands “and blessed them”; general blessing parallel.

2-chronicles-6:4:0.summary: “Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel” matches Solomon’s opening blessing.

2-chronicles-6:4:1.summary: Christ’s words not passing away relates generally to God fulfilling His word.

2-chronicles-6:4:2.summary: Ends “Blessed is God” and praises the God of Israel; general praise.

2-chronicles-6:4:3.summary: The promise “He shall build Me a house” is the word spoken to David now fulfilled.

2-chronicles-6:4:4.summary: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel” for fulfilling what “He spoke through the mouth” of prophets.

2-chronicles-6:4:5.summary: Thanks for God magnifying His utterance relates generally to fulfilled promise.

2-chronicles-6:4:6.summary: David: “Blessed art Thou, O Lord, the God of Israel,” the same formula before the assembly.

2-chronicles-6:4:7.summary: A call to sing to God shares no specific element with blessing God for a fulfilled promise.

2-chronicles-6:4:8.why: Christian use of the blessing formula.

2-chronicles-6:4:9.summary: The assembly blesses the Lord at David’s urging; general parallel.

2-chronicles-6:4:10.summary: “Blessed be the Lord, Israel’s God” is the same formula.

2-chronicles-6:5:0.summary: The Lord choosing Saul relates loosely to choosing a leader.

2-chronicles-6:5:1.summary: Promise of David’s lasting house relates generally to the Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-6:5:2.summary: God’s name “called over Thy city” relates generally to a city for His name.

2-chronicles-6:5:3.summary: Altars “in every place where I name My name” is the background for a chosen place for His name.
2-chronicles-6:5:3.why: Law of the place of God’s name.

2-chronicles-6:5:5.summary: “The place which the Lord your God shall choose in one of your tribes, to set His name there.”

2-chronicles-6:5:6.summary: “The place which the Lord your God shall choose for His name” matches the choice described.

2-chronicles-6:5:7.summary: The Lord appointing a ruler “over His people” relates loosely to choosing a leader.

2-chronicles-6:5:8.summary: “My name is upon him” of the angel shares only the word name.

2-chronicles-6:5:9.summary: God has not dwelt in a house “from the day I brought the sons of Israel up from Egypt.”

2-chronicles-6:5:10.summary: Saul’s rejection for divination has no specific link to God choosing no city or leader.

2-chronicles-6:6:0.summary: “The Lord chose Zion” as His dwelling, matching God choosing Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-6:6:0.why: Psalm on the choice of Zion.

2-chronicles-6:6:1.summary: David says the Lord “chose me…to be king over Israel.”
2-chronicles-6:6:1.why: David’s own account of his choosing.

2-chronicles-6:6:2.summary: Jerusalem is “the city the Lord chose from all the tribes…to name His name there.”
2-chronicles-6:6:2.why: Same formula of the chosen city.

2-chronicles-6:6:3.summary: God “chose Judah’s tribe, Mount Zion” and “chose David His servant.”

2-chronicles-6:6:4.summary: Praise in “our God’s city” relates generally to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-6:6:5.summary: God “raised a chosen one” and found David His servant.
2-chronicles-6:6:5.why: Psalm on the choice of David.

2-chronicles-6:6:6.summary: “The Lord founded Zion” relates generally to choosing Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-6:6:7.summary: God sends Samuel to Jesse because He has seen one of his sons “to reign for Me.”

2-chronicles-6:7:0.summary: David contrasts his cedar house with the ark beneath skins, the start of his building wish.
2-chronicles-6:7:0.why: Origin of David’s desire to build.

2-chronicles-6:7:1.summary: David “could not build a house for the name of the Lord,” Solomon tells Hiram.
2-chronicles-6:7:1.why: Explains why David did not build.

2-chronicles-6:7:2.summary: David: “it came upon my soul to build a house for the name of the Lord God.”

2-chronicles-6:7:3.summary: David tells Nathan of his cedar house while the ark is in a tent; Nathan approves his heart’s plan.
2-chronicles-6:7:3.why: Origin of David’s desire to build.

2-chronicles-6:7:4.summary: David: “It came upon my heart to build a house of rest for the ark.”

2-chronicles-6:8:1.summary: “She did what she could” relates loosely to God approving a good intention.

2-chronicles-6:8:2.summary: “If the readiness is present, it is acceptable” relates loosely to God approving David’s intent.

2-chronicles-6:9:1.summary: “You shall not build Me a house,” the same refusal to David.

2-chronicles-6:9:2.summary: David’s seed “from your own body” will “build Me a house for My name.”

2-chronicles-6:10:0.summary: Life as a passing shadow has no specific link to Solomon succeeding David.

2-chronicles-6:10:1.summary: God “chose Solomon my son to seat him upon the throne,” fulfilled here.

2-chronicles-6:10:2.summary: God promises to raise David’s offspring and prepare his kingdom, fulfilled in Solomon.

2-chronicles-6:10:3.summary: God placed “Thy servant in place of my father David” on his throne.

2-chronicles-6:10:4.summary: “Solomon sat upon the throne of David his father.”

2-chronicles-6:10:5.summary: Generations passing has no specific link to Solomon’s succession.

2-chronicles-6:10:6.summary: Leaving toil to a successor shares no specific element with God’s fulfilled promise.

2-chronicles-6:10:7.summary: Solomon grew strong over his kingdom; general account of his reign.

2-chronicles-6:10:8.summary: “Solomon sat on the throne of his father David.”

2-chronicles-6:11:5.summary: The ark held “the tablets of the covenant” from when the Lord made a covenant with Israel.
2-chronicles-6:11:5.why: Kings parallel on the ark’s contents.

2-chronicles-6:11:0.summary: The ark contained the two tablets of the covenant made with Israel’s sons.
2-chronicles-6:11:0.why: Explains the covenant in the ark.

2-chronicles-6:11:1.summary: The priests brought “the ark of the Lord’s covenant to its place,” where Solomon says he placed it.

2-chronicles-6:11:2.summary: Moses put the testimonies into the ark, the covenant it holds.
2-chronicles-6:11:2.why: When the covenant entered the ark.

2-chronicles-6:11:4.summary: “The ark of the covenant” holding “the tablets of the covenant.”
2-chronicles-6:11:4.why: New Testament reflection on the ark.

2-chronicles-6:12:0.summary: Isaiah’s call to fear the Lord and trust His name shares nothing specific with Solomon standing at the altar spreading his hands.
2-chronicles-6:12:0.why: No real connection to the scene.

2-chronicles-6:12:1.summary: The psalmist will “lift my hands” in God’s name, a general parallel to Solomon’s prayer gesture.
2-chronicles-6:12:1.why: Shows lifted hands as a common prayer posture.

2-chronicles-6:12:2.summary: Moses “spread out his hands to the Lord” in intercession, the same gesture Solomon uses before the altar.
2-chronicles-6:12:2.why: Classic precedent for the outspread-hands prayer posture.

2-chronicles-6:12:3.summary: Zophar urges turning hands upward toward God, loosely echoing Solomon’s outstretched hands.
2-chronicles-6:12:3.why: General image of hands raised to God.

2-chronicles-6:12:4.summary: “I spread out my hands unto Thee” repeats the very gesture described of Solomon.
2-chronicles-6:12:4.why: Same verbal image of prayer with outspread hands.

2-chronicles-6:12:5.summary: The psalmist lifts his hands “toward Thy holy temple,” matching prayer with hands directed toward God’s house.
2-chronicles-6:12:5.why: Links hand-raised prayer specifically to the temple.

2-chronicles-6:12:7.summary: Josiah, like Solomon, stands before the Lord in the temple leading the whole people, though the act is covenant-making, not prayer.
2-chronicles-6:12:7.why: Royal leadership of worship in the temple.

2-chronicles-6:12:8.summary: Worship “in His holy courtyard” overlaps only generally with Solomon’s prayer in the temple court.

2-chronicles-6:12:9.summary: “The lifting of my hands” as an evening sacrifice parallels prayer with raised hands, without specific connection.
2-chronicles-6:12:9.why: Frames raised hands as an offering of prayer.

2-chronicles-6:12:10.summary: Joash stands by the pillar before the people, a loose royal-position parallel; the source mentions no pillar.
2-chronicles-6:12:10.why: Only a king standing before the assembly in common.

2-chronicles-6:12:11.summary: Ethiopia hastening “its hand toward God” is a loose hand-toward-God image unrelated to Solomon’s prayer.

2-chronicles-6:12:12.summary: Paul’s call to pray “lifting holy hands” shares the prayer gesture in general terms.
2-chronicles-6:12:12.why: Shows the gesture carried into Christian prayer.

2-chronicles-6:13:1.summary: Esdras stands on a raised wooden platform before the assembly, comparable to Solomon’s bronze platform.
2-chronicles-6:13:1.why: Leaders addressing Israel from a raised stand.

2-chronicles-6:13:2.summary: Ezra bends “upon my knees” and stretches “out my hands toward the Lord,” the same kneeling, outstretched posture as Solomon.
2-chronicles-6:13:2.why: Close parallel of kneeling prayer with outstretched hands.

2-chronicles-6:13:3.summary: The call to “bow down and fall before Him” matches prostrate worship only generally.

2-chronicles-6:13:4.summary: Daniel prays toward Jerusalem falling on his face; posture and devotion are only loosely parallel to Solomon’s kneeling.
2-chronicles-6:13:4.why: Shows later prayer oriented toward the temple city.

2-chronicles-6:13:5.summary: Believers “knelt on the beach and prayed,” sharing only the kneeling posture.

2-chronicles-6:13:6.summary: The “great court” built with bronze-covered doors is the temple court where Solomon set his bronze base.
2-chronicles-6:13:6.why: Identifies the court where Solomon prayed.

2-chronicles-6:13:7.summary: Describes the construction of the inner court, possibly the same area, but with no mention of the platform or prayer.

2-chronicles-6:13:8.summary: Describes the walls of “the great court,” related to the temple courts only as background.

2-chronicles-6:13:9.summary: Jesus “knelt down, and prayed,” a general kneeling-prayer parallel.

2-chronicles-6:13:10.summary: Paul “knelt down with them all and prayed,” sharing only the kneeling posture before a group.

2-chronicles-6:14:0.summary: “Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord?” matches Solomon’s confession that “there is no god like Thee.”
2-chronicles-6:14:0.why: Incomparability of God, from the Song of the Sea.

2-chronicles-6:14:1.summary: God “keeps covenant and mercy” for those who love Him, the exact phrase in Solomon’s prayer.

2-chronicles-6:14:2.summary: Nehemiah addresses God who “dost keep the covenant and mercy,” reusing Solomon’s formula.
2-chronicles-6:14:2.why: Later prayer echoing the same formula.

2-chronicles-6:14:3.summary: “Lord, God of powers, who is like Thee?” parallels Solomon’s statement of God’s incomparability.

2-chronicles-6:14:4.summary: No one “in clouds” or among sons of God compares to the Lord, matching “no god like Thee in heaven.”

2-chronicles-6:14:5.summary: God says “I will keep My mercy for him, and My covenant is faithful,” the covenant-and-mercy pairing tied to David.
2-chronicles-6:14:5.why: Davidic covenant framed with keeping mercy.

2-chronicles-6:14:6.summary: God remembering mercy toward Israel His servant overlaps generally with covenant mercy.
2-chronicles-6:14:6.why: General theme of God’s covenant mercy.

2-chronicles-6:14:7.summary: Paul’s call to “walk worthily of God” shares only the walking metaphor.
2-chronicles-6:14:7.why: Loose echo of walking before God.

2-chronicles-6:14:9.summary: David leads the whole assembly in blessing God, a general setting parallel to Solomon’s prayer before the assembly.

2-chronicles-6:14:10.summary: The Lord is God “in heaven above and upon earth beneath; there is none beside Him,” matching “in heaven or on earth.”

2-chronicles-6:14:11.summary: Zechariah and Elizabeth “walking blamelessly” before God, a general parallel to walking before Him wholeheartedly.
2-chronicles-6:14:11.why: Example of faithful walking before God.

2-chronicles-6:14:13.summary: In this Greek-based reading Enoch “pleased God”; the “walked with God” wording the label assumes is absent.
2-chronicles-6:14:13.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.
2-chronicles-6:14:13.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-6:14:14.summary: Elijah addresses the “Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel,” sharing only the form of address.

2-chronicles-6:14:15.summary: God’s mercy upon those who fear Him overlaps generally with mercy for faithful servants.
