2-chronicles-7:20:10.summary: God will “remove that nation” if it does not return; shares removal language for other nations.

2-chronicles-7:20:11.summary: God will pluck out and remove the wicked from his dwelling; individual judgment, loose link.

2-chronicles-7:20:12.summary: God speaks to remove and destroy a nation; general judgment wording.

2-chronicles-7:20:13.summary: Jews become “an object of mockery” to enemies; loose link to becoming a byword.

2-chronicles-7:20:14.summary: Jude’s uprooted fruitless trees describe false teachers; no link to the temple and land judgment.

2-chronicles-7:21:0.summary: Passers-by ask “Why did the Lord act this way toward this great city?” and are answered: they abandoned the covenant.

2-chronicles-7:21:1.summary: “Everyone passing through it” will be appalled at the ruined city, echoing the astonished passers-by.

2-chronicles-7:21:2.summary: “Why did the Lord speak all these evils against us?” answered by fathers abandoning Him for foreign gods.

2-chronicles-7:21:3.summary: “Everyone passing through Babylon will look gloomy”; same formula applied to Babylon.

2-chronicles-7:21:4.summary: Everyone passing Idumea will hiss; the passer-by formula used for Edom.

2-chronicles-7:21:5.summary: God gave Judah over to “terror… and hissing”; a partial fulfillment of the astonishment.

2-chronicles-7:21:6.summary: “For what reason has the Lord our God done all these things to us?” answered by serving foreign gods.

2-chronicles-7:21:8.summary: “Why have these things happened to me?” answered by great injustice; similar question form.

2-chronicles-7:21:9.summary: Jeconiah cast out like a useless vessel has no direct link to passers-by questioning the house’s ruin.

2-chronicles-7:21:10.summary: “Why has the Lord done thus unto this land?” answered: they forsook the covenant and served other gods.

2-chronicles-7:22:0.summary: Jerusalem’s ruin attributed to prophets’ and priests’ sins; explains calamity but not by idolatry.

2-chronicles-7:22:1.summary: God brought “great calamities upon us” in Jerusalem as He had spoken, confirming the threatened calamity.

2-chronicles-7:22:2.summary: The Lord fulfilled His words from ancient days in Jerusalem’s fall; general fulfillment theme.

2-chronicles-7:22:3.summary: “They forsook the Lord, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt” and served other gods.
2-chronicles-7:22:3.why: Same charge in nearly same words.

2-chronicles-7:22:4.summary: Recognizing God did not act in vain against Jerusalem; loose justification of judgment.

2-chronicles-7:22:5.summary: Judgment “because they abandoned Me” and sacrificed to foreign gods, the same reason.

2-chronicles-7:22:6.summary: The Chaldean king brought against Judah is the calamity that fulfilled this warning.

2-chronicles-7:22:7.summary: Israel scattered for idols and uncleanness, profaning God’s name among nations; related but different framing.

2-chronicles-7:6:6.summary: Joshua 6:4 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-7:6:6.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-7:6:6.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-7:18:1.summary: Jeremiah 33:20–21 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-7:18:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-7:18:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-7:18:5.summary: Jeremiah 33:25–26 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-7:18:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-7:18:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-7:20:5.summary: 1 Kings 14:15 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-7:20:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-7:20:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-8:3:0.summary: Mentions Hadadezer king of Zobah, Solomon’s adversary from that region; place link only, not the conquest.

2-chronicles-8:3:1.summary: “The entrance into Hamath” as Israel’s boundary relates to Aimath, but not Soba or the campaign.

2-chronicles-8:3:3.summary: David struck Hadadezer “king of Zobah,” the earlier conquest of the same region.

2-chronicles-8:3:4.summary: Spies went as far as “Ephaath” (Hamath); place-name link only.

2-chronicles-8:4:0.summary: The 1 Kings list (Greek numbering) records Solomon’s building of Gezer, Upper Beth-horon and the chariot cities, parallel to Chronicles’ building list; Thedmor itself is not in the shown truncated text.
2-chronicles-8:4:0.why: Kings’ version of Solomon’s fortification program.

2-chronicles-8:5:0.summary: Both name the building of Upper and Lower “Baithoron.”
2-chronicles-8:5:0.why: Earlier founding of the same twin towns.

2-chronicles-8:5:1.summary: Asa likewise builds cities with “walls,” “gates, and bars,” the same fortification formula.
2-chronicles-8:5:1.why: Shows a later king repeating Solomon’s fortifying.

2-chronicles-8:5:2.summary: Lower Beth-horon appears as a boundary point of Ephraim, the same town Solomon fortified.

2-chronicles-8:5:3.summary: Upper Beth-horon is named on Ephraim’s border, the same town Solomon fortified.

2-chronicles-8:6:0.summary: Ecclesiastes’ “whatever my eyes asked for” loosely echoes Solomon building “everything Solomon desired”; the link is thematic only.
2-chronicles-8:6:0.why: Reflective view on royal ambition and works.

2-chronicles-8:6:1.summary: Both mention Solomon’s “chariot cities” and horsemen stationed there.
2-chronicles-8:6:1.why: Details what the chariot cities held.

2-chronicles-8:6:3.summary: A house built with timber from “Lebanon’s forest” loosely relates to Solomon building in Lebanon.
2-chronicles-8:6:3.why: Possible example of Solomon’s Lebanon projects.

2-chronicles-8:6:4.summary: The Song’s poetic call “Come from Lebanon” shares only the place name.

2-chronicles-8:6:5.summary: The preceding verse in the same list of Solomon’s “fortified cities” he built.
2-chronicles-8:6:5.why: Immediate context of the building list.

2-chronicles-8:6:6.summary: Solomon’s chariots and horsemen left in “the chariot cities” and with the king in Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-8:6:7.summary: Jehoshaphat also built “fortified cities,” a general royal building parallel.

2-chronicles-8:6:8.summary: The Greek list reads Alkatha, Begethon, Gebeelan; Baalath does not appear, so the place link is lost.
2-chronicles-8:6:8.why: No shared place in the Saints text.

2-chronicles-8:6:9.summary: “I built houses for myself” echoes Solomon’s building generally.

2-chronicles-8:7:0.summary: The same list of peoples—Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites—whom Israel was to dispossess.

2-chronicles-8:7:1.summary: The promise to Abram lists the same nations—Hittites, Perizzites, Amorites, Hivites, Jebusites.
2-chronicles-8:7:1.why: Links remnant peoples to the land promise.

2-chronicles-8:8:0.summary: Canaanites not destroyed remained in the land “to this day,” as Solomon’s tributary peoples.

2-chronicles-8:8:2.summary: Solomon’s officer Adoniram was “over the tributes,” the system imposed on the remnant peoples.

2-chronicles-8:8:3.summary: Tribes did not remove the Jebusites and others, who dwelt among Israel “to this day.”
2-chronicles-8:8:3.why: Shows how the remnant peoples remained.

2-chronicles-8:8:4.summary: Kings records a levy from “all Israel,” in tension with Chronicles’ claim that only foreigners were conscripted.
2-chronicles-8:8:4.why: Raises the question of Israelite labor.

2-chronicles-8:8:5.summary: Israel made the Canaanites subject to them “but did not utterly destroy them.”
2-chronicles-8:8:5.why: Precedent for subjecting rather than destroying.

2-chronicles-8:8:6.summary: The psalm recalls that Israel “did not destroy the nations,” the same remnant situation.
2-chronicles-8:8:6.why: Theological comment on the failure to exterminate.

2-chronicles-8:8:7.summary: Solomon assigns resident foreigners as burden bearers and quarrymen, the same foreign labor force.

2-chronicles-8:9:0.summary: Paul’s free woman/slave woman allegory has no real tie to Solomon’s labor policy.

2-chronicles-8:9:1.summary: Israel as a “royal priesthood” shares no specific element with Solomon’s exempting Israelites from servitude.

2-chronicles-8:9:2.summary: The law forbids making an Israelite brother serve as a household slave while permitting slaves from the nations.

2-chronicles-8:9:3.summary: The king will take Israel’s sons for “chariots,” “horsemen,” and as “commanders,” the roles named here.
2-chronicles-8:9:3.why: Samuel’s warning fulfilled in Solomon’s army.

2-chronicles-8:9:4.summary: The free “Jerusalem above” shares nothing specific with this verse.

2-chronicles-8:10:0.summary: Solomon’s “taskmasters over the people,” the same supervisory staff, numbered differently.

2-chronicles-8:10:2.summary: The Greek Kings parallel lists officials “over Solomon’s works” as overseers of the people.
2-chronicles-8:10:2.why: Kings’ version with a different count.

2-chronicles-8:11:0.summary: Pharaoh’s daughter was brought into the City of David until Solomon finished building.

2-chronicles-8:11:1.summary: Kings describes the separate “house for Pharaoh’s daughter” that Solomon built.
2-chronicles-8:11:1.why: Describes the house she moved into.

2-chronicles-8:11:3.summary: The “holy mountain” of the Transfiguration shares only the word holy.

2-chronicles-8:11:4.summary: God’s presence makes the place “sanctified,” loosely matching holiness where the ark entered.

2-chronicles-8:11:5.summary: “The place where you stand is holy” echoes the place where the ark entered being holy.

2-chronicles-8:11:6.summary: A judgment oracle mentioning “holy places” has no specific link.

2-chronicles-8:12:1.summary: Solomon’s Portico in John has no link; the Saints verse speaks of the altar “opposite the sanctuary,” not a porch.
2-chronicles-8:12:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-8:12:2.summary: Temple vessel weights share nothing specific with Solomon’s burnt offerings.

2-chronicles-8:12:3.summary: Priests weeping at the “altar’s platform” share only the word altar.

2-chronicles-8:12:4.summary: The area “between the porches and the altar” relates loosely to the altar’s location before the sanctuary.

2-chronicles-8:12:5.summary: Asa “renewed the Lord’s altar before the Lord’s sanctuary,” the same altar position.

2-chronicles-8:13:1.summary: Moses’ command of a daily continual offering underlies offering “according to each day’s requirement.”

2-chronicles-8:13:2.summary: Ezekiel’s ruler offers on Sabbaths and new moons, a general parallel to the festival calendar.

2-chronicles-8:13:3.summary: The ruler provides burnt offerings at festivals, new moons and Sabbaths, matching Solomon’s role.

2-chronicles-8:13:4.summary: “Three times a year”: the feasts of unleavened bread, harvest and completion.
2-chronicles-8:13:4.why: Mosaic source of the three feasts.

2-chronicles-8:13:5.summary: Solomon offered burnt offerings “three” times a year on the altar he built.

2-chronicles-8:13:6.summary: Leviticus sets out the Sabbath and appointed feasts that Solomon observed “as Moses commanded.”

2-chronicles-8:14:0.summary: A list of gatekeepers relates generally to the gatekeepers in their divisions.

2-chronicles-8:14:1.summary: Priests “in their divisions” and Levites stationed over the service, echoing Solomon’s arrangement.

2-chronicles-8:14:2.summary: Praise with the songs of “David the man of God,” the same title.

2-chronicles-8:14:3.summary: Levites praise “by the command of David the man of God,” division facing division.

2-chronicles-8:14:4.summary: Priests at their station and Levites in their divisions by the king’s command.

2-chronicles-8:14:5.summary: David’s written pattern given to Solomon loosely underlies “David’s ordinance.”

2-chronicles-8:14:7.summary: At the dedication priests served “without being arranged by their courses,” contrasting with the divisions set here.

2-chronicles-8:14:8.summary: Zechariah serves “in the order of his division,” the same priestly system much later.

2-chronicles-8:14:9.summary: An unnamed “man of God” at Bethel shares only the title.

2-chronicles-8:14:10.summary: Moses is called “the man of God,” the same title applied to David.

2-chronicles-8:14:11.summary: Priests and Levites posted “at the gates” relates generally to gate duties.

2-chronicles-8:14:12.summary: Hezekiah arranged divisions of priests and Levites to praise and minister at the gates.

2-chronicles-8:14:13.summary: David has the Levites appoint singers and gatekeepers, the origin of David’s ordinance.

2-chronicles-8:14:14.summary: David’s inspiration oracle shares no specific element.

2-chronicles-8:14:15.summary: Those David appointed over the singers took places “according to their prescribed order.”

2-chronicles-8:14:16.summary: Paul’s summary of David’s kingship has no link to temple divisions.

2-chronicles-8:14:17.summary: David appointed Levites to minister and praise before the ark.

2-chronicles-8:14:18.summary: David’s death and decay share nothing with the ordinance.

2-chronicles-8:14:19.summary: Zechariah of “the division of Abijah” reflects the priestly divisions.

2-chronicles-8:14:20.summary: Idithon’s sons “at the gate” with instruments loosely parallels gatekeepers and Levites.

2-chronicles-8:15:0.summary: Levites over holy vessels and supplies relates generally to temple stewardship.

2-chronicles-8:15:1.summary: Israel did all “as the Lord commanded Moses,” a general theme of exact obedience.

2-chronicles-8:15:2.summary: Judah carried out the “king’s” ordinance, a general echo of not transgressing the king’s commands.

2-chronicles-8:15:3.summary: Solomon placed consecrated things “in the treasuries of the Lord’s house.”

2-chronicles-8:15:4.summary: Levites were “over the treasuries of the Lord’s house,” the treasury arrangement mentioned.

2-chronicles-8:16:0.summary: “They prepared the stones and timber,” the preparation of the work.

2-chronicles-8:16:1.summary: The house built of prepared stones relates generally to the work being prepared.

2-chronicles-8:17:0.summary: Ailoth (Ailath) is rebuilt and restored to Judah.

2-chronicles-8:17:1.summary: Ailon and Ezion-geber are named on Israel’s route past Seir.

2-chronicles-8:17:2.summary: Ailath taken by Syria and occupied by Idumeans.

2-chronicles-8:17:4.summary: Jehoshaphat’s ship for gold from Sophir was wrecked at Ezion-geber.
2-chronicles-8:17:4.why: Later failed venture at the port.

2-chronicles-8:17:6.summary: Israel camped at Ezion-geber during the wilderness journey.

2-chronicles-8:18:0.summary: Solomon’s and Chiram’s servants brought gold from Souphir.

2-chronicles-8:18:1.summary: Solomon’s yearly gold income relates generally to gold brought from Sophira.

2-chronicles-8:18:3.summary: “I also gathered silver and gold” echoes Solomon’s acquisition of gold.

2-chronicles-8:18:4.summary: Solomon’s ship sailed with Hiram’s ships, bringing gold.

2-chronicles-9:1:0.summary: Jesus cites the queen who “came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom.”
2-chronicles-9:1:0.why: New Testament use of the visit.

2-chronicles-9:1:1.summary: Jesus recalls the queen of the south coming “to hear the wisdom of Solomon.”
2-chronicles-9:1:1.why: New Testament use of the visit.

2-chronicles-9:1:3.summary: The queen of Saba gives gold, spices and precious stones.

2-chronicles-9:1:4.summary: Camels coming “from Saba, bringing gold,” the same image of tribute.

2-chronicles-9:1:5.summary: The table of nations names Seba and Sheba, possible origins of the queen’s land.

2-chronicles-9:1:6.summary: Sheba appears in Shem’s line, possible background to Saba.

2-chronicles-9:1:7.summary: Hannah “pouring out my soul” loosely echoes speaking about everything in her soul.

2-chronicles-9:1:8.summary: Proverbs mentions understanding “riddles,” the queen’s test.

2-chronicles-9:1:9.summary: God’s promise of wisdom and wealth beyond all kings is what the queen comes to test.

2-chronicles-9:1:10.summary: Jesus speaking in parables has no specific tie to the queen’s riddles.

2-chronicles-9:1:11.summary: “I will open my riddle” shares the word riddle.

2-chronicles-9:1:12.summary: “Arabia’s gold” given to the king loosely parallels gold brought by the queen.

2-chronicles-9:1:13.summary: Magi offer gold and frankincense, a general parallel of foreign gift-bearers.

2-chronicles-9:1:14.summary: The saying about the heart’s abundance has no link.

2-chronicles-9:1:15.summary: Mysteries of the kingdom share nothing specific.

2-chronicles-9:1:16.summary: Pouring out a plea to God has no real connection.

2-chronicles-9:1:17.summary: Solomon made “exceedingly great” explains his fame generally.

2-chronicles-9:1:18.summary: Solomon was “wiser than all people,” the reputation that drew the queen.

2-chronicles-9:1:19.summary: “I will utter riddles” shares the riddle motif.

2-chronicles-9:1:20.summary: Jokshan’s son Sheba, possible ancestry of the queen’s people.

2-chronicles-9:1:21.summary: “Kings of the Arabians and Saba will bring gifts” echoes the queen of Saba’s gifts.

2-chronicles-9:2:0.summary: Jesus “explained everything” privately, echoing Solomon explaining all questions.

2-chronicles-9:2:1.summary: Asking God for wisdom has no specific link to Solomon answering the queen.

2-chronicles-9:2:2.summary: Jesus “made known to you everything” loosely parallels Solomon withholding nothing.

2-chronicles-9:2:3.summary: “All the treasures of wisdom” hidden in Christ, a general wisdom theme.

2-chronicles-9:2:4.summary: The Lord gave Solomon “very great wisdom,” the source of his answers.

2-chronicles-9:2:5.summary: Parables for outsiders share nothing specific.

2-chronicles-9:2:6.summary: The penetrating word of God has no link.

2-chronicles-9:2:7.summary: God gives Solomon “a discerning and wise heart” unmatched before or after.

2-chronicles-9:2:8.summary: Walking with the wise relates loosely to the queen consulting Solomon.

2-chronicles-9:2:9.summary: Deep waters of words share nothing specific.

2-chronicles-9:3:0.summary: Solomon building the Lord’s house may be the “house he had built” she saw.

2-chronicles-9:3:1.summary: The temple “King Solomon built” loosely relates to the house the queen saw.

2-chronicles-9:3:2.summary: Kings’ parallel: Solomon “explained all her matters to her.”

2-chronicles-9:3:3.summary: Barnabas seeing God’s grace shares only the verb saw.

2-chronicles-9:4:0.summary: A master serving watchful slaves has no link to Solomon’s court.

2-chronicles-9:4:1.summary: “My spirit is spent” depends on the Hebrew idiom; the Saints text says “she was beside herself.”
2-chronicles-9:4:1.why: Link lost in the Greek wording.

2-chronicles-9:4:2.summary: Ahaz’s altering of the royal entrance assumes the Hebrew “ascent”; the Saints text has burnt offerings.
2-chronicles-9:4:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-9:4:3.summary: Ezekiel’s ruler eating at the gate shares no specific element.

2-chronicles-9:4:4.summary: The ruler’s burnt offerings at the gate loosely parallel the king’s offerings in the Lord’s house.

2-chronicles-9:4:5.summary: The king’s gate of the Levites shares nothing specific with the Saints wording.

2-chronicles-9:4:6.summary: John falling “as dead” at the vision loosely matches the queen being overwhelmed.

2-chronicles-9:4:7.summary: Solomon’s daily provisions of flour, cattle and game describe “the food of the tables.”

2-chronicles-9:4:8.summary: The Song’s lovesick plea has no link.

2-chronicles-9:4:9.summary: Wisdom’s invitation to bread and wine shares only food words.

2-chronicles-9:4:10.summary: Nehemiah as the king’s cupbearer reflects the court office of wine-pourers.

2-chronicles-9:4:11.summary: Athaliah seeing the king at his station shares only incidental wording.

2-chronicles-9:4:12.summary: Eating Christ’s flesh has no link to Solomon’s tables.

2-chronicles-9:4:13.summary: Christ dining with the believer has no specific link.

2-chronicles-9:4:15.summary: Daniel with “no breath left” loosely matches the queen being beside herself.
2-chronicles-9:4:15.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-9:4:16.summary: The soul failing with longing for salvation has no real link.

2-chronicles-9:6:0.summary: Solomon “wiser than all people” supports the queen’s verdict on his wisdom.

2-chronicles-9:6:2.summary: The bride’s praise of her beloved has no link to the queen’s speech.

2-chronicles-9:6:3.summary: The queen’s preceding words: “The report I heard … was true.”

2-chronicles-10:11:3.summary: Authority over “scorpions” as enemies shares only an incidental word.

2-chronicles-10:11:4.summary: Locusts given authority like scorpions shares only an incidental word.

2-chronicles-10:11:5.summary: Making a yoke “exceedingly heavy” echoes the heavy yoke, but concerns Babylon.

2-chronicles-10:11:6.summary: Pharaoh demands the same bricks without straw, a ruler increasing the burden.

2-chronicles-10:11:7.summary: Christ's gentle “yoke” and rest contrasts with Rehoboam's promise of a heavier yoke.

2-chronicles-10:11:8.summary: Pharaoh answers Israel's plea by ordering “Let these men's tasks be heavier,” as Rehoboam answers the people's plea by adding to their yoke.
2-chronicles-10:11:8.why: Casts Rehoboam's reply in the mold of Pharaoh's oppression.

2-chronicles-10:11:9.summary: God's call to “release the crushed” and loosen bonds contrasts with Rehoboam's harsher yoke.
2-chronicles-10:11:9.why: Contrasts God's will with oppressive rule.

2-chronicles-10:11:10.summary: Locusts with “tails like scorpions” that harm people share only the scorpion image of painful punishment.
2-chronicles-10:11:10.why: Shared image of the scorpion's sting.

2-chronicles-10:11:11.summary: Samuel warns the people will “cry out because of the king” they chose, realized in Rehoboam's oppressive threat.
2-chronicles-10:11:11.why: Shows Samuel's warning about kingship coming true.

2-chronicles-10:12:0.summary: Rehoboam told them to go away “for three days” and return, the instruction they now fulfill.
2-chronicles-10:12:0.why: Links the request to its fulfillment in the narrative.

2-chronicles-10:13:0.summary: Nabal answers David's servants rudely, a similar harsh reply, but otherwise unrelated.
2-chronicles-10:13:0.why: Another example of a harsh answer.

2-chronicles-10:13:1.summary: Joseph as lord of the land “spoke harshly,” sharing only the wording of a harsh reply.

2-chronicles-10:13:2.summary: Pharaoh's harsh dismissal of Moses loosely parallels a ruler's harsh answer.

2-chronicles-10:13:3.summary: Ahab heeds the elders' advice, contrasting with Rehoboam's abandoning the elders' counsel (range truncated).
2-chronicles-10:13:3.why: Contrasts a king who heeded elders.

2-chronicles-10:13:4.summary: Joseph “spoke harshly” to his brothers, sharing wording but not situation.

2-chronicles-10:13:5.summary: A son who falls short of a father's discipline loosely fits rejecting his father's counselors.

2-chronicles-10:13:6.summary: Same narrative: Rehoboam “abandoned the elders' counsel,” stated again here.
2-chronicles-10:13:6.why: Repeats the decisive choice within the scene.

2-chronicles-10:13:7.summary: “A painful word stirs up anger,” exactly what Rehoboam's harsh answer does to Israel.
2-chronicles-10:13:7.why: Proverbial lens on Rehoboam's harsh reply.

2-chronicles-10:13:8.summary: Sirach calls Rehoboam “deficient in understanding,” who made the people revolt “through his counsel.”
2-chronicles-10:13:8.why: Later Scripture's verdict on this very decision.

2-chronicles-10:14:6.summary: Rehoboam repeats the young men's words nearly verbatim: “I will add to your yoke” and “scorpions.”
2-chronicles-10:14:6.why: Shows Rehoboam adopting their counsel word for word.

2-chronicles-10:14:0.summary: Righteous versus impious reasonings loosely contrasts the two counsels.

2-chronicles-10:14:1.summary: Darius's officials' decree about prayer has no link to Rehoboam's harsh reply.

2-chronicles-10:14:2.summary: Earthly, ambitious wisdom produces disorder and fights, loosely like the young men's counsel leading to division (range truncated).

2-chronicles-10:14:3.summary: Faction and battle leading to want loosely anticipates the division that follows.

2-chronicles-10:14:4.summary: A patient person is better than one “high in spirit,” loosely fitting Rehoboam's arrogant answer.

2-chronicles-10:14:5.summary: After his father died, Ahaziah followed counselors “to destroy him,” a close pattern of a young king ruined by bad counsel.
2-chronicles-10:14:5.why: Another Judahite king undone by bad advisers.

2-chronicles-10:14:7.summary: Woe to a city whose king is young loosely fits Rehoboam following young men's counsel.

2-chronicles-10:14:8.summary: Solomon's worry whether his heir “will be wise or foolish” loosely anticipates Rehoboam, though he is not named.
2-chronicles-10:14:8.why: Solomonic reflection apt to Rehoboam's folly.

2-chronicles-10:15:0.summary: Ahijah the Shilonite's prophecy to Jeroboam of the torn kingdom is the word the Lord now establishes (range truncated).

2-chronicles-10:15:1.summary: Eli's sons “would not listen” because the Lord resolved to judge them, as Rehoboam does not listen through a reversal from God.
2-chronicles-10:15:1.why: Shows divine purpose behind refusal to listen.

2-chronicles-10:15:2.summary: Amaziah's refusal to heed counsel is tied to God's purpose to destroy him; the closest divine-cause verse is truncated.
2-chronicles-10:15:2.why: Similar pattern of God working through a king's stubbornness.

2-chronicles-10:15:3.summary: Events occur by “God's determined purpose,” a general theme of divine sovereignty over human choices.
2-chronicles-10:15:3.why: General theme of providence through human acts.

2-chronicles-10:15:4.summary: The Lord arranges Ahab's deception to bring his fall, loosely like God's reversal behind Rehoboam's refusal.
2-chronicles-10:15:4.why: God working through flawed royal decisions.

2-chronicles-10:15:5.summary: The Lord tells Rehoboam the split “has come from Me,” confirming the same divine reversal.
2-chronicles-10:15:5.why: Confirms the division was God's doing.

2-chronicles-10:15:6.summary: The Lord sends a spirit of wandering on Egypt's leaders, loosely like God's hand in bad decisions.

2-chronicles-10:15:7.summary: Samson's parents did not know “this was from the Lord,” a similar hidden divine purpose in a human choice.
2-chronicles-10:15:7.why: Divine purpose hidden in human decisions.

2-chronicles-10:15:9.summary: God's purpose determined beforehand loosely parallels God establishing His word.

2-chronicles-10:15:10.summary: Unbelief happens so a prophet's “word” might be fulfilled, a general fulfillment pattern.

2-chronicles-10:15:11.summary: Names “Achia the Selonite” and “Jeroboam son of Nabat” together, the same prophet and recipient.
2-chronicles-10:15:11.why: Identifies the prophet's record concerning Jeroboam.

2-chronicles-10:15:12.summary: Disobeying God's words leads to sudden collapse, loosely like the kingdom's split.
2-chronicles-10:15:12.why: General theme of disobedience and collapse.

2-chronicles-10:15:13.summary: Only a general Scripture-fulfillment formula is shared; the crucifixion details have no link.

2-chronicles-10:15:14.summary: Only the fulfillment formula is shared; casting lots for garments has no link.

2-chronicles-10:15:15.summary: The Lord hardened Sihon's spirit to bring about His purpose, loosely like the reversal from God here.
2-chronicles-10:15:15.why: God's hand behind a king's refusal.

2-chronicles-10:16:0.summary: Sheba's cry, “no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse's son… to your tents, Israel,” closely matches Israel's words here.

2-chronicles-10:16:1.summary: Summarizes the outcome: Israel “rejected allegiance to David's house,” the result of this outcry.
2-chronicles-10:16:1.why: States the lasting result of the revolt.

2-chronicles-10:16:2.summary: Jesus as “the Root and the offspring of David” contrasts with Israel's rejection of David's house.
2-chronicles-10:16:2.why: Points to the Davidic line's ultimate vindication.

2-chronicles-10:16:3.summary: A child's endless rule “upon the throne of David” contrasts with the shrinking Davidic kingdom.
2-chronicles-10:16:3.why: Messianic hope for a restored Davidic throne.

2-chronicles-10:16:4.summary: Many disciples went back and no longer followed, loosely like Israel abandoning its king.

2-chronicles-10:16:5.summary: “Each went to his own house” is an incidental verbal echo of going home, with no real link.

2-chronicles-10:16:6.summary: Christ reigning until enemies are subdued has no specific link to Israel's revolt.

2-chronicles-10:16:7.summary: Doeg's report mentions “Jesse's son” only as a name for David; no link to the revolt.

2-chronicles-10:16:8.summary: Those who “did not want me to reign over them” loosely parallels rejecting the Davidic king.
2-chronicles-10:16:8.why: Parable of rejecting a rightful king.

2-chronicles-10:16:9.summary: A shoot from “the root of Jesse” offers hope after the people reject Jesse's son's house.

2-chronicles-10:16:10.summary: Israel showing no loyalty to Gideon's household loosely parallels rejecting David's house.
2-chronicles-10:16:10.why: Another case of ingratitude to a ruling house.

2-chronicles-10:16:11.summary: God will not take the whole kingdom but leaves one scepter “because of David,” explaining why Judah remains after the split.
2-chronicles-10:16:11.why: Explains the limits of the division.

2-chronicles-10:16:13.summary: God's oath to seat David's descendant on his throne loosely contrasts with the revolt against David's house.
2-chronicles-10:16:13.why: Points to the enduring Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-10:16:14.summary: A future David ruling as “one shepherd over all” contrasts with the division of Israel from David's house.
2-chronicles-10:16:14.why: Prophetic hope of reunion under David.

2-chronicles-10:16:16.summary: Saul's insult using “Jesse's son” shares only a name for David.

2-chronicles-10:16:17.summary: The hearts of Israel's men going after Absalom loosely parallels Israel turning from David's house.
2-chronicles-10:16:17.why: Earlier defection of Israel from David.

2-chronicles-10:16:18.summary: Saul's question about “Jesse's son” missing a meal shares only the phrase.

2-chronicles-10:16:21.summary: Human thought acknowledging God has no link to Israel's revolt in this Greek wording.

2-chronicles-10:16:22.summary: Promise that David's son's throne will stand “for ever” stands in tension with the revolt.

2-chronicles-10:16:24.summary: God prepares “a lamp” for David's anointed, loosely relevant to preserving David's house.

2-chronicles-10:16:25.summary: Saul's speech about what “Jesse's son” could give shares only the phrase.

2-chronicles-10:16:26.summary: God will take the kingdom “from his son's hand” and give Jeroboam ten scepters, fulfilled in this revolt (range truncated).
2-chronicles-10:16:26.why: Supplies the prophecy behind the split.

2-chronicles-10:16:27.summary: God's unfailing mercy and lasting throne for David's house loosely frame its survival despite the revolt.

2-chronicles-10:16:28.summary: David enduring Shimei's curses has no specific link to the northern revolt.

2-chronicles-10:16:30.summary: Saul's accusation about “Jesse's son” shares only the phrase.

2-chronicles-10:16:31.summary: Jesus given “the throne of His father David” to reign forever contrasts with David's house losing Israel.
2-chronicles-10:16:31.why: Messianic restoration of the Davidic throne.

2-chronicles-10:16:32.summary: Citizens saying “We do not want this man to reign over us” loosely parallels rejecting Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-10:17:0.summary: Solomon's son keeps “the two scepters” for David's sake, matching Rehoboam ruling only those in Judah's cities.

2-chronicles-10:17:2.summary: Rehoboam assembles Judah and Benjamin, the remnant he still rules, to try to recover Israel.
2-chronicles-10:17:2.why: Shows what Rehoboam's reduced kingdom did next.

2-chronicles-10:18:1.summary: “Adoniram son of Ephra was over the tributes,” the same official stoned here.

2-chronicles-10:18:3.summary: Zechariah's stoning by Joash's command shares only the act of stoning.

2-chronicles-10:19:0.summary: The people's cry “What share have we in David” leads directly to Israel's rejection of David's house.

2-chronicles-10:19:1.summary: Shares only the phrase “this day” about Israel's guilt; no link to the northern revolt.

2-chronicles-10:19:2.summary: Shares only the formula “to this day” about Jordan stones.

2-chronicles-10:19:3.summary: Shares only the formula “to this day” about the ark's poles.

2-chronicles-10:19:4.summary: If David's sons “abandon My law,” discipline follows, loosely explaining the loss of Israel.

2-chronicles-10:19:6.summary: Abijah recounts how Jeroboam “withdrew from his lord” and opposed Rehoboam, despite God's covenant with David's house.
2-chronicles-10:19:6.why: Judah's later interpretation of the revolt.

2-chronicles-10:19:7.summary: “Israel was apart from David's house, and they made Jeroboam … king,” describing the same lasting separation.

2-chronicles-11:1:1.summary: A king “is not saved through a great force,” loosely commenting on Rehoboam's large army.

2-chronicles-11:1:3.summary: The Lord “nullifies the counsels of rulers,” loosely fitting the halting of Rehoboam's war plan.

2-chronicles-11:4:14.summary: Cain slaughtering his brother illustrates the evil of kin violence, loosely related.

2-chronicles-11:14:3.summary: Lists Levitical cities in Ephraim and other tribes, the northern holdings they left (range truncated).

2-chronicles-11:14:4.summary: Tithe laws have no specific link to the Levites' flight from Jeroboam.

2-chronicles-11:14:5.summary: Lists Levitical cities like Sychem in Ephraim, the holdings abandoned (range truncated).

2-chronicles-11:14:6.summary: Defines the Levites' ministry and support, loosely relevant to their being barred from ministering (range truncated).

2-chronicles-11:14:7.summary: Jeroboam appointed priests of high places “from some of the people,” replacing the expelled Levites.

2-chronicles-11:15:0.summary: Jeroboam made “two golden heifers,” the calves named here.

2-chronicles-11:15:1.summary: Sacrificing to new gods loosely parallels Jeroboam's false worship; the Greek source speaks of “vain things,” not demons.

2-chronicles-11:15:2.summary: Jeroboam “appointed priests of high places,” matching his appointing priests for the high places here.

2-chronicles-11:15:5.summary: Aaron's cast “calf” hailed as gods who brought Israel from Egypt is the model for Jeroboam's calves (range truncated).
2-chronicles-11:15:5.why: Links Jeroboam's calves to the golden-calf sin.

2-chronicles-11:15:6.summary: Moses confesses that the people made “gods of gold,” loosely related to Jeroboam's calves.

2-chronicles-11:15:7.summary: Demonic spirits gathering kings for war have no link to Jeroboam's priests and calves.

2-chronicles-11:15:8.summary: Israel makes cast images and mentions calves, loosely condemning the northern calf cult.

2-chronicles-11:15:9.summary: “Rub away your calf, Samaria”: Hosea condemns the northern calf that led people astray.

2-chronicles-11:15:10.summary: Departing to teachings of demons has no specific link in this Greek-based wording.

2-chronicles-11:15:11.summary: Israel “made a calf at Horeb,” recalling the earlier calf sin that Jeroboam repeats.

2-chronicles-11:15:12.summary: Sacrifice to demons is not in the Greek-based source, which speaks of idols and vain things.
2-chronicles-11:15:12.why: Greek wording does not carry the demon link.

2-chronicles-11:16:0.summary: “Many from Israel joined” Asa when they saw the Lord was with him, the same movement of faithful northerners to Judah.
2-chronicles-11:16:0.why: Shows a recurring migration of the faithful southward.

2-chronicles-11:16:1.summary: Bringing gifts to worship in the Lord's courts loosely fits coming to Jerusalem to sacrifice.
2-chronicles-11:16:1.why: General theme of worship at the sanctuary.

2-chronicles-11:16:2.summary: Men from Aser, Manasse, and Zaboulon “came to Jerusalem,” another case of northerners coming to worship there.
2-chronicles-11:16:2.why: Shows the recurring northern pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-11:16:3.summary: Urges worship at the Lord's tabernacle rather than a rival altar, loosely like leaving Jeroboam's shrines.

2-chronicles-11:16:4.summary: “My heart is ready” shares only the word heart.

2-chronicles-11:16:5.summary: Offer sacrifices only at the place the Lord chooses, the principle behind going to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-11:16:6.summary: Pilgrims with ascents in their heart going to Zion loosely fits devout northerners coming to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-11:16:7.summary: Darius's grief over Daniel has no link to seeking the Lord in Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-11:16:8.summary: Moses' charge to heed his words shares only the idea of the heart.

2-chronicles-11:16:9.summary: Not attaching the heart to wealth has no link to seeking the Lord.

2-chronicles-11:16:10.summary: David designates Jerusalem's altar for Israel's burnt offerings, the place they came to sacrifice.

2-chronicles-11:16:11.summary: Bringing sacrifices to the chosen place for His name, the principle behind coming to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-11:16:12.summary: God withholding the spirit has no link to the faithful seeking the Lord.

2-chronicles-11:16:13.summary: “Set your hearts upon your ways” shares only the word heart.

2-chronicles-11:16:14.summary: Remaining with the Lord “with steadfast purpose of heart” loosely fits those who gave their heart to seek Him.

2-chronicles-11:16:15.summary: Ignoring the Lord's word about livestock has no link here.

2-chronicles-11:16:16.summary: Seek the chosen place and bring sacrifices there, the principle behind coming to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-11:16:17.summary: Priests feeding on the people's sins has no link to devout worshippers.

2-chronicles-11:16:18.summary: Northerners from Ephraim and Manasse have hearts “directed to seek the Lord, the God of their fathers,” matching this verse's wording.
2-chronicles-11:16:18.why: Same northern devotion to Jerusalem worship.

2-chronicles-11:16:19.summary: Returning to the Lord with all the heart and serving Him alone loosely fits the devout migrants.

2-chronicles-11:16:20.summary: “Give your hearts and your souls to seek the Lord” closely echoes those “who gave their heart to seek the Lord.”

2-chronicles-11:17:1.summary: Faith that lasts “only a short time” loosely fits Rehoboam's three years of faithfulness.

2-chronicles-11:17:2.summary: God's condition to “walk before Me as David your father did,” the standard Rehoboam meets for three years.

2-chronicles-11:17:3.summary: Solomon's strong, God-blessed beginning loosely parallels walking in Solomon's ways (range truncated).
2-chronicles-11:17:3.why: Shows Solomon's ways at their best.

2-chronicles-11:17:4.summary: Solomon's ordered worship by David's commands illustrates the ways of David and Solomon (range truncated).
2-chronicles-11:17:4.why: Shows what following David's ways meant.

2-chronicles-11:17:5.summary: Judah's mercy passing “like morning dew” loosely fits Rehoboam's brief faithfulness.

2-chronicles-11:18:0.summary: Eliab, Jesse's son, appears before Samuel; the same Eliab whose daughter Rehoboam married.

2-chronicles-11:18:1.summary: “Eliab, one of David's brethren,” the same son of Jesse named here.

2-chronicles-11:20:3.summary: Abiou son of Rehoboam's mother was “Maacah daughter of Absalom,” the same wife and son.

2-chronicles-11:20:0.summary: Names Abijah's mother as Maacah, though here “daughter of Ouriel from Gabaon,” a variant lineage.
2-chronicles-11:20:0.why: Shows a variant tradition of Maacah's parentage.

2-chronicles-11:20:1.summary: Rehoboam loved “Maacah daughter of Absalom” more than all his wives, the same marriage.

2-chronicles-11:20:2.summary: “Abijah his son became king,” the same son born to Maacah.

2-chronicles-11:20:4.summary: “Rehoboam begot Abijah” in Christ's genealogy, the same son born here.
2-chronicles-11:20:4.why: Places Abijah in the messianic line.

2-chronicles-11:21:0.summary: Solomon's many wives and concubines turned his heart, loosely paralleling Rehoboam's large harem.
2-chronicles-11:21:0.why: Shows the inherited pattern of many wives.

2-chronicles-11:21:1.summary: Gideon's many wives and seventy sons loosely parallel Rehoboam's many wives and children.
2-chronicles-11:21:1.why: Another leader with a large family.

2-chronicles-11:21:2.summary: The law says the king “shall not multiply wives,” yet Rehoboam has eighteen wives and thirty concubines.
2-chronicles-11:21:2.why: Sets Rehoboam's harem against the law for kings.

2-chronicles-11:21:3.summary: Lists Absalom, son of David by Maacah, identifying the Absalom whose daughter Rehoboam married.

2-chronicles-11:21:4.summary: David took more wives and concubines and had more sons and daughters, a similar royal pattern.

2-chronicles-11:21:5.summary: Among many queens and concubines one is uniquely loved, loosely like Maacah's favored place.
2-chronicles-11:21:5.why: Image of one favored among many.

2-chronicles-11:21:6.summary: Rehoboam “requested many wives,” the same household described here.

2-chronicles-11:21:7.summary: Names Absalom among David's sons, identifying Maacah's father (range truncated).

2-chronicles-11:22:0.summary: The law forbids favoring the loved wife's son over the firstborn, while Rehoboam elevates the son of his beloved Maacah.
2-chronicles-11:22:0.why: Raises the law on inheritance and favoritism.

2-chronicles-11:22:1.summary: David publicly designates Solomon as chosen successor, a loosely similar royal designation.
2-chronicles-11:22:1.why: Pattern of a king naming his heir.

2-chronicles-11:22:2.summary: Firstborn rights pass from Reuben and a leader comes from Judah, loosely about preferring a younger son.
2-chronicles-11:22:2.why: Theme of leadership not by birth order.

2-chronicles-11:23:0.summary: Rehoboam's earlier foolish counsel contrasts with his later consolidation; the shown range is truncated and only shows the folly.
2-chronicles-11:23:0.why: Contrasts his early folly with later management.

2-chronicles-11:23:1.summary: The Greek source says he “grew greater,” not that he acted prudently, so the link to the prudent steward fails.
2-chronicles-11:23:1.why: Greek wording does not carry the label's link.

2-chronicles-11:23:2.summary: Abraham gives his other sons gifts and sends them away; the Greek source does not clearly describe dispersing sons.
2-chronicles-11:23:2.why: Loose pattern of providing for non-heir sons.

2-chronicles-11:23:3.summary: Jehoshaphat gave his sons gifts and “walled cities in Judah” but the kingdom to one son, a close pattern.

2-chronicles-11:23:4.summary: Adonijah's self-promotion shows rivalry among princes, loosely relevant to managing royal sons.

2-chronicles-11:6:1.summary: 1 Samuel 17:12 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-11:6:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-11:6:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-11:15:4.summary: 1 Kings 14:9 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-11:15:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-11:15:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-11:18:2.summary: 1 Samuel 17:28 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-11:18:2.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-11:18:2.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-11:18:3.summary: 1 Samuel 17:13 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-11:18:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-11:18:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-12:1:0.summary: Rehoboam's kingdom was strengthened “for three years,” the establishment after which he abandoned the law.
2-chronicles-12:1:0.why: Shows the strength that preceded his apostasy.

2-chronicles-12:1:1.summary: “Rehoboam became strong in Jerusalem and reigned,” restating his established kingdom.
2-chronicles-12:1:1.why: Same narrative of Rehoboam's secured reign.

2-chronicles-12:1:2.summary: Uzziah “grew strong” and then his heart was lifted up and he acted unjustly, the same strength-then-apostasy pattern.
2-chronicles-12:1:2.why: Shows a recurring pattern in Judah's kings.

2-chronicles-12:1:5.summary: “You forsook God who begat you” loosely parallels abandoning the Lord's commandments.

2-chronicles-12:1:6.summary: Ephraim assigning ordinances to Baal has no specific link to Rehoboam in this Greek wording.

2-chronicles-12:1:7.summary: Filled to fullness, hearts lifted up, “they forgot Me,” loosely the pattern of security leading to apostasy.

2-chronicles-12:1:8.summary: Jacob grew fat and “forsook God who made him,” the pattern of prosperity followed by apostasy.

2-chronicles-12:1:9.summary: Addresses “all Judah and Benjamin,” the people later called “all Israel” who abandon the commandments with Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-12:1:10.summary: Walking in wicked kings' counsels brings destruction, loosely like Judah's apostasy.

2-chronicles-12:1:11.summary: Moses warns that when settled and prosperous they may “fail to keep His commandments” and forget the Lord, exactly what happens here (range truncated).

2-chronicles-12:1:12.summary: Calamity comes “because they abandoned the Lord,” loosely anticipating Sousakim's invasion.

2-chronicles-12:1:13.summary: Warning not to forget the Lord once filled, loosely the pattern of Rehoboam's apostasy.
2-chronicles-12:1:13.why: Warning against forgetting God in prosperity.

2-chronicles-12:1:14.summary: Judah's rulers acting wrongly and facing judgment, loosely related.

2-chronicles-12:1:15.summary: People who say “We will not be ruled” loosely parallels abandoning the commandments.

2-chronicles-12:1:16.summary: “Judah also did not keep the commandments,” a general later summary of the same failure.

2-chronicles-12:2:0.summary: “Shishak king of Egypt,” who sheltered Jeroboam, is the same king (Sousakim) who now attacks Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-12:2:1.summary: God's warning that if they “abandon My ordinances” He will remove them is enacted in the invasion for sin.
2-chronicles-12:2:1.why: Shows the covenant warning beginning to take effect.

2-chronicles-12:2:2.summary: Israel forsook the Lord and was handed to plunderers, the same sin-and-invasion pattern in general.
2-chronicles-12:2:2.why: Recurring pattern of judgment through enemies.

2-chronicles-12:2:3.summary: A foreign king comes against Jerusalem because of Judah's unfaithfulness, a later and fuller instance (range truncated).
2-chronicles-12:2:3.why: Final instance of the same pattern.

2-chronicles-12:2:4.summary: Calamities came “because you … sinned against the Lord,” a general parallel.
2-chronicles-12:2:4.why: General link between sin and disaster.

2-chronicles-12:2:6.summary: David warns Solomon “if you forsake Him, He will forsake you,” the principle behind the invasion for Judah's sin.
2-chronicles-12:2:6.why: States the principle applied to Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-12:2:7.summary: Rebellion turns God to hostility against His people, loosely like the invasion as judgment.

2-chronicles-12:2:8.summary: Israel provoked God and was humbled, yet He heard them, loosely matching sin, invasion, and later repentance.
2-chronicles-12:2:8.why: Pattern of sin, affliction, and mercy.

2-chronicles-12:2:9.summary: Lament over ended joy has no specific link to Sousakim's invasion.

2-chronicles-12:2:10.summary: “Your apostasy will discipline you,” a general principle fitting the invasion.
2-chronicles-12:2:10.why: Theme of sin bringing its own discipline.

2-chronicles-12:2:11.summary: God gave the rebellious people “into the hand of those oppressing them,” a general summary of the pattern.
2-chronicles-12:2:11.why: Recurring pattern of judgment and rescue.

2-chronicles-12:3:0.summary: Nahum names Ethiopia, Egypt and “Libyans” as Egypt’s allies, the same African peoples who march with Sousakim’s Egyptian host.
2-chronicles-12:3:0.why: Shows Libyans and Ethiopians as Egypt’s standing allies.

2-chronicles-12:3:2.summary: Daniel places “Libyans and Ethiopians” in the “multitude” of a conqueror controlling Egypt, echoing Sousakim’s multitude of Libyans and Ethiopians.
2-chronicles-12:3:2.why: Same allied peoples in an Egyptian-linked army.

2-chronicles-12:3:3.summary: The table of nations lists Cush, Mizraim and Put; the shown text never names Ethiopians, Egypt or Libyans, so the link rests on name identification.
2-chronicles-12:3:3.why: Background on the peoples’ origins only.

2-chronicles-12:3:4.summary: Libyans appear among a mixed company falling by the sword, but only one people overlaps and the Egyptian setting is implicit in the shown text.
2-chronicles-12:3:4.why: Libyans as part of Egypt’s coalition.

2-chronicles-12:3:5.summary: Both describe a vast mounted host, but Revelation’s visionary cavalry has no historical link to Sousakim’s army.
2-chronicles-12:3:5.why: General image of an overwhelming army.

2-chronicles-12:3:6.summary: Midian’s invaders, like Sousakim’s host, are “beyond numbering,” but the shared phrase describes different invasions.
2-chronicles-12:3:6.why: Shared picture of a countless invading horde.

2-chronicles-12:3:7.summary: Egypt and Ethiopia are named as Israel’s ransom, unrelated to an Egyptian army invading Judah.

2-chronicles-12:3:8.summary: Sisera’s nine hundred chariots parallel only loosely the chariot count of Sousakim’s force.
2-chronicles-12:3:8.why: Another enemy chariot army against Israel.

2-chronicles-12:3:9.summary: The foreigners come with chariots, horsemen and countless people, a similar but separate description of an invading force.

2-chronicles-12:3:10.summary: David’s defeat of Syrian chariots and horsemen shares only military counts with Sousakim’s army.

2-chronicles-12:3:11.summary: Zare the Ethiopian later invades Judah with a huge force and chariots, a close Chronicler counterpart to Sousakim’s Ethiopian-laden host.
2-chronicles-12:3:11.why: Second African invasion in Chronicles for comparison.

2-chronicles-12:3:12.summary: The Lord strikes the Ethiopians before Judah, a later defeat of the same kind of foe, not this invasion.

2-chronicles-12:4:1.summary: Assyria’s great force comes to Jerusalem, a similar invasion pattern but a different king and event.
2-chronicles-12:4:1.why: Parallel pattern of invader reaching Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-12:4:2.summary: An oracle commands attack on her battlements without complete destruction, loosely like a limited judgment on Judah.

2-chronicles-12:4:3.summary: Isaiah pictures an invader filling Judea’s breadth, a general picture of invasion without Sousakim or the cities.

2-chronicles-12:4:4.summary: Sennacherib comes against Judea’s “fortified cities” and takes them, closely echoing Sousakim seizing Judah’s fortified cities.
2-chronicles-12:4:4.why: Same invasion pattern in nearly the same words.

2-chronicles-12:4:5.summary: Assyria threatens to do to Jerusalem as to Samaria, only a general threat against Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-12:4:5.why: Jerusalem threatened by a foreign power.

2-chronicles-12:5:1.summary: The Lord’s word comes to “Samaia, the man of God,” the same prophet who confronts Rehoboam here.
2-chronicles-12:5:1.why: Introduces the same prophet’s earlier ministry.

2-chronicles-12:5:2.summary: Shemaiah the man of God in Kings is the same prophet called Samaia in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-12:5:3.summary: The preceding verses state Rehoboam abandoned the Lord’s commandments and Sousakim came because they sinned, the cause Samaia announces.
2-chronicles-12:5:3.why: Gives the sin behind the prophecy.

2-chronicles-12:5:4.summary: David warns Solomon, “if you forsake Him, He will forsake you,” the very principle Samaia applies to Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-12:5:5.summary: Jeremiah’s “burden” wordplay and dashing down share no specific link with Samaia’s forsaking oracle.

2-chronicles-12:5:6.summary: Serving foreign gods leads to serving foreigners, a general retribution theme related to forsaking the Lord.

2-chronicles-12:5:7.summary: The Lord will not abandon the righteous “into his hands,” contrasting with Judah forsaken into Sousakim’s hand.
2-chronicles-12:5:7.why: Contrast of abandonment into enemy hands.

2-chronicles-12:5:8.summary: David chooses to fall into the Lord’s hand rather than human hands; only the hand image overlaps.
2-chronicles-12:5:8.why: Loose image of falling into hands.

2-chronicles-12:5:9.summary: The Lord tells Israel, “you have forsaken Me… I will save you no more,” matching Samaia’s forsaking-then-forsaken oracle.

2-chronicles-12:5:10.summary: The covenant curses for disobedience provide general background for judgment; the shown text has no specific echo.

2-chronicles-12:5:11.summary: Jeremiah says “abandoning Me” brings bitter discipline, a general parallel to forsaking leading to judgment.
2-chronicles-12:5:11.why: Same theme of consequences of abandoning God.

2-chronicles-12:5:12.summary: Jeremiah says their own ways brought calamity, a general theme of self-caused judgment.

2-chronicles-12:6:0.summary: Pharaoh confesses, “The Lord is righteous,” the same confession Judah’s rulers make under judgment.

2-chronicles-12:6:1.summary: Daniel confesses “the Lord our God is righteous” in bringing calamities, matching the rulers’ admission under Sousakim’s attack.

2-chronicles-12:6:2.summary: Adoni-bezek admits God repaid him justly, a general acknowledgment of deserved punishment.

2-chronicles-12:6:3.summary: Manasseh humbles himself when afflicted; the source says the rulers “felt shame,” a related but differently worded response.
2-chronicles-12:6:3.why: Chronicler pattern of repentance under pressure.

2-chronicles-12:6:5.summary: Hosea foresees people seeking God in affliction, a general parallel to Judah’s response under attack.

2-chronicles-12:6:6.summary: Job describes a person blaming himself and admitting lenient treatment, loosely like the rulers’ confession.

2-chronicles-12:6:7.summary: Hezekiah and Jerusalem humble themselves and wrath does not come, a similar pattern though the source uses “felt shame.”

2-chronicles-12:6:8.summary: The Greek-based text says “refuse to reverence Me,” not humbling oneself, so it does not carry the assumed link.
2-chronicles-12:6:8.why: Label relies on Hebrew wording absent here.

2-chronicles-12:6:9.summary: The shown text lists Manasseh’s prayer and sins in the seers’ records, with no shame or confession of God’s righteousness.

2-chronicles-12:6:10.summary: Lamentations confesses “The Lord is righteous, for I embittered His mouth,” the same confession amid judgment.

2-chronicles-12:6:11.summary: Amon did not humble himself as Manasseh did, a loose contrast with the rulers who felt shame.

2-chronicles-12:6:12.summary: When struck, Israel sought God, a general pattern of turning back under judgment.

2-chronicles-12:6:13.summary: “The righteous Lord” cuts sinners’ necks; the shared epithet appears in a different context.
2-chronicles-12:6:13.why: Shared affirmation of the Lord’s righteousness.

2-chronicles-12:6:14.summary: The Greek text says they have not held to God’s ordinances, without the humbling or shame the label assumes.
2-chronicles-12:6:14.why: Assumed link absent in this wording.

2-chronicles-12:6:15.summary: Jeremiah’s call not to exalt oneself relates only generally to the rulers’ shame.

2-chronicles-12:6:16.summary: Paul’s teaching on God’s righteousness versus self-righteousness shares only the word “righteousness.”

2-chronicles-12:6:17.summary: Jeremiah tells “the king and those exercising power” to humble themselves, loosely like Rehoboam and rulers abasing themselves.
2-chronicles-12:6:17.why: King and rulers called to humility.

2-chronicles-12:6:18.summary: James’s call to humble oneself before the Lord is a general teaching paralleling the rulers’ shame.

2-chronicles-12:6:19.summary: The humbled tax collector is justified, a general principle loosely illustrated by Judah’s rulers.

2-chronicles-12:6:20.summary: Solomon asks God to hear prayer when an enemy afflicts the people, general background for Judah’s response.
2-chronicles-12:6:20.why: Temple prayer for times of enemy attack.

2-chronicles-12:6:21.summary: “God… gives grace to the humble” states the principle behind the Lord sparing the ashamed rulers.
2-chronicles-12:6:21.why: Principle of grace to the humble.

2-chronicles-12:6:22.summary: Leviticus foresees the people’s heart will “feel shame” and accept their sins under judgment, the same response the rulers show.
2-chronicles-12:6:22.why: Covenant pattern of shame and confession.

2-chronicles-12:7:0.summary: Here God’s anger “will not be quenched,” a contrast to wrath withheld from Jerusalem after the rulers’ shame.

2-chronicles-12:7:1.summary: Because Ahab was stricken before the Lord, harm is postponed, the same divine relenting after a king’s abasement.
2-chronicles-12:7:1.why: Parallel case of judgment delayed after repentance.

2-chronicles-12:7:2.summary: God’s wrathful anger is brought upon an uncomprehending people, contrasting with wrath withheld here.
2-chronicles-12:7:2.why: Contrast of wrath fully poured out.

2-chronicles-12:7:3.summary: Revelation’s cup of God’s wrath for beast-worshipers shares only the word wrath with this promise of mercy.

2-chronicles-12:7:4.summary: Israel confesses “We have sinned” and God grows weary over their distress, a similar repentance-and-relenting pattern.

2-chronicles-12:7:5.summary: God’s wrath “poured upon this place” that will not be extinguished contrasts with wrath that will not “drip” on Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-12:7:6.summary: The Lord relents, “This certainly will not happen,” before announcing judgment, a loose parallel to limited mercy.

2-chronicles-12:7:7.summary: When their heart will “feel shame,” God remembers His covenant, mirroring the Lord sparing Judah once they felt shame.

2-chronicles-12:7:8.summary: Jeremiah calls Israel only to recognize its injustice, a general call to confession.

2-chronicles-12:7:9.summary: Josiah fears the Lord’s great anger for the fathers’ disobedience, a general parallel of wrath against Judah.

2-chronicles-12:7:10.summary: A plea to pour out wrath on nations shares only the image of poured wrath.

2-chronicles-12:7:11.summary: The prodigal’s confession and the father’s compassion illustrate generally the mercy shown to repentant Judah.
2-chronicles-12:7:11.why: Illustration of mercy to the repentant.

2-chronicles-12:7:12.summary: Bowls of wrath poured out in Revelation contrast loosely with wrath not dripping on Jerusalem; truncated range judged on shown text.

2-chronicles-12:7:13.summary: The Lord pitied Israel and “was unwilling to destroy them,” matching “I will not destroy them.”

2-chronicles-12:7:14.summary: Jehoahaz entreats the Lord and receives deliverance from Syria, a general pattern of partial relief after appeal.

2-chronicles-12:7:15.summary: The psalm says God will “not destroy” and will turn back His wrath, matching God’s decision not to destroy Judah.

2-chronicles-12:8:0.summary: Not serving the Lord leads to serving enemies, exactly the lesson that Judah will learn the difference between the Lord’s service and earthly kingdoms.

2-chronicles-12:8:1.summary: The Greek-based text asks the Lord to “acquire us” and lacks the Hebrew mention of other lords ruling over them.
2-chronicles-12:8:1.why: Assumed link absent in this wording.

2-chronicles-12:8:2.summary: Nations were left to test and teach Israel, loosely like Judah learning through foreign rule.

2-chronicles-12:8:3.summary: Israel is handed over among the nations, a general picture of subjection to foreign powers.

2-chronicles-12:8:4.summary: Jeremiah asks for instruction with judgment, not fury, akin to limited corrective judgment.

2-chronicles-12:8:5.summary: Returned exiles lament “we are slaves today,” the servitude Judah is warned it will taste.
2-chronicles-12:8:5.why: Servitude as the fruit of sin.

2-chronicles-12:9:0.summary: Kings records Solomon making shields of hammered gold, the very gold shields Sousakim takes.

2-chronicles-12:9:2.summary: Ahaz takes gold from the treasuries of “the Lord’s house and the king’s house,” the same twin treasuries Sousakim strips.
2-chronicles-12:9:2.why: Recurring loss of temple and palace treasure.

2-chronicles-12:9:4.summary: Asa takes silver and gold from the king’s house treasuries; the shown text omits the Lord’s house, so overlap is partial.

2-chronicles-12:9:5.summary: Hezekiah gives silver from the Lord’s house and the king’s treasuries to Assyria, another stripping of both treasuries.
2-chronicles-12:9:5.why: Recurring loss of temple and palace treasure.

2-chronicles-12:9:6.summary: The oppressor seizes Zion’s desired things and nations enter her sanctuary, a general picture of temple plunder.

2-chronicles-12:10:0.summary: Sixty mighty men guard Solomon’s couch, a loose parallel to guards protecting the king.

2-chronicles-12:10:1.summary: Cherethites and Pelethites were David’s guard units, but the shown text does not describe them guarding the king’s gate.

2-chronicles-12:10:2.summary: The Greek-based text says David appointed him “to receive his instructions,” not over a guard, so no link to the runners.

2-chronicles-12:10:3.summary: This text says David appointed him over his ancestral house, without any guard or runners.

2-chronicles-12:10:4.summary: Gold growing dim pictures decline, loosely like gold shields replaced with bronze.

2-chronicles-12:12:0.summary: Jehoshaphat is told “good things have been found in you,” the same phrase as “good things in Judah.”
2-chronicles-12:12:0.why: Same Chronicler idiom for mitigating good.

2-chronicles-12:12:1.summary: Manasseh humbles himself and God restores him, the same Chronicler pattern of repentance averting full destruction.
2-chronicles-12:12:1.why: Parallel of repentance leading to restoration.

2-chronicles-12:12:4.summary: Jeroboam’s son has “a good word concerning the Lord” found in him, echoing good being found, in a different context.
2-chronicles-12:12:4.why: Similar idea of good mitigating judgment.

2-chronicles-12:12:5.summary: Lamentations says God “wast not propitiated” after sin, contrasting with wrath turned away here.

2-chronicles-12:12:6.summary: Abraham asks God to spare a city for the righteous in it, loosely like Judah spared for good things found.
2-chronicles-12:12:6.why: Sparing for the sake of the good.

2-chronicles-12:12:7.summary: A tenth remains after judgment, a general remnant idea paralleling judgment short of utter destruction.

2-chronicles-12:12:8.summary: God gives life to the brokenhearted, a general principle behind sparing the ashamed king.

2-chronicles-12:12:9.summary: The Greek-based wording, “He did not answer from His heart,” does not clearly carry the idea of God not willingly afflicting.
2-chronicles-12:12:9.why: Assumed link unclear in this wording.

2-chronicles-12:12:10.summary: Peter’s call to humble oneself under God’s hand matches only generally Rehoboam’s shame bringing relief.

2-chronicles-12:13:1.summary: Deuteronomy’s place the Lord “shall choose… to set His name there” is fulfilled in Jerusalem, chosen to name His name.

2-chronicles-12:13:2.summary: “I chose Jerusalem for My name to be there” states the same choice of Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-12:13:3.summary: Solomon was led astray by foreign women; Rehoboam’s Ammanite mother was one such wife, though the text does not say so.

2-chronicles-12:13:4.summary: The psalm praises God’s city, Zion, generally related to Jerusalem as the chosen city.

2-chronicles-12:13:5.summary: “Every place where I name My name” echoes Jerusalem as the city where the Lord chose “to name His name.”

2-chronicles-12:13:6.summary: In this wording the new city’s name is unspecified, so the link to God’s name in Jerusalem is not carried.
2-chronicles-12:13:6.why: Hebrew name absent in this wording.

2-chronicles-12:13:7.summary: Abijah describes Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, as young and faint-hearted at the start of his reign.
2-chronicles-12:13:7.why: Another view of the same king.

2-chronicles-12:13:8.summary: The law excluding “Ammanites” from God’s assembly bears loosely on Rehoboam’s Ammanite mother.
2-chronicles-12:13:8.why: Raises tension over the Ammanite mother.

2-chronicles-12:13:9.summary: God “chose Judah’s tribe, Mount Zion,” and built His sanctuary there, the same election of Jerusalem from Israel’s tribes.

2-chronicles-12:13:10.summary: The law that an Ammonite shall not enter the Lord’s assembly relates loosely to the king’s Ammanite mother.
2-chronicles-12:13:10.why: Raises tension over the Ammanite mother.

2-chronicles-12:13:11.summary: The place the Lord will choose “for His name to be called upon there” is Jerusalem, as this verse states.

2-chronicles-12:13:12.summary: Solomon took Ammonite and other foreign wives, explaining how Rehoboam’s mother was an Ammanite.

2-chronicles-12:14:0.summary: Jehoshaphat “directed your heart to seek the Lord,” the exact opposite of Rehoboam, who did not.
2-chronicles-12:14:0.why: Same idiom for a contrasting king.

2-chronicles-12:14:1.summary: People hear but do not obey because their heart follows defilements, a general picture of a misdirected heart.

2-chronicles-12:14:2.summary: Isaiah’s call to “Seek God” relates only generally to Rehoboam’s failure to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-12:14:3.summary: God’s statement that He did not say “Seek a futile thing” shares only the verb seek.

2-chronicles-12:14:4.summary: Paul’s call to stand firm and be strong has no specific link to Rehoboam’s undirected heart.

2-chronicles-12:14:5.summary: Paul’s encouragement to be steadfast in the Lord’s work has no specific tie to this verse.

2-chronicles-12:14:6.summary: “Seek the Lord… seek His face continually” states generally what Rehoboam failed to do.

2-chronicles-12:14:7.summary: “Every heart directed to seek the Lord” uses the same phrase that Rehoboam failed to fulfill.
2-chronicles-12:14:7.why: Same Chronicler idiom of a directed heart.

2-chronicles-12:14:8.summary: Israel’s heart “was not upright with Him,” a general parallel to a heart not set on God.

2-chronicles-12:14:10.summary: “A generation that did not direct its heart” uses the same phrase as Rehoboam not directing his heart.

2-chronicles-12:14:11.summary: David prays God to “direct their hearts toward Thee,” the very thing lacking in Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-12:14:12.summary: “My heart is ready” expresses a prepared heart, the opposite of Rehoboam, but with different wording.

2-chronicles-12:14:13.summary: Jesus’ “seek, and you will find” about prayer shares only the verb seek.

2-chronicles-12:14:14.summary: God longs for a heart to fear Him and keep His commandments, generally related to Rehoboam’s heart failure.
2-chronicles-12:14:14.why: God’s desire for a faithful heart.

2-chronicles-12:14:15.summary: Samuel urges Israel to “prepare your hearts toward the Lord,” the heart-direction Rehoboam neglected.
2-chronicles-12:14:15.why: Same call to set the heart on God.

2-chronicles-12:15:0.summary: Solomon’s deeds “first and last” are written in prophets’ and seers’ records, the same source formula used for Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-12:15:1.summary: Samaia the prophet, whose records are cited, is the prophet who confronted Rehoboam over Sousakim.

2-chronicles-12:15:2.summary: Shemaiah the man of God in Kings is the Samaia whose records preserve Rehoboam’s deeds.

2-chronicles-12:15:3.summary: Addo the prophet’s book also records Abijah’s deeds, the same Addo cited for Rehoboam.

2-chronicles-12:16:1.summary: Abijah becomes king over Judah, continuing the succession announced at Rehoboam’s death.
2-chronicles-12:16:1.why: Next step in the same succession.

2-chronicles-12:16:2.summary: Matthew’s genealogy lists “Rehoboam begot Abijah,” the same succession.
2-chronicles-12:16:2.why: Places Rehoboam and Abijah in Christ’s line.

2-chronicles-12:16:3.summary: Rehoboam’s wife Maacah bore Abijah, the son who succeeds him.

2-chronicles-12:16:4.summary: The royal genealogy lists Rehoboam and “Abia his son,” the same father-son succession.

2-chronicles-12:1:4.summary: 1 Kings 12:17 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-12:1:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-12:1:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-12:6:4.summary: Daniel 5:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-12:6:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-12:6:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-12:12:3.summary: Lamentations 3:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-12:12:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-12:12:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-13:1:0.summary: Rehoboam dies and “Abijah his son became king,” the transition this verse dates.

2-chronicles-13:2:0.summary: Maacah is named as Abijah’s mother in both, though her father is given differently (Absalom versus Ouriel).
2-chronicles-13:2:0.why: Same queen mother; notes differing father.

2-chronicles-13:2:1.summary: Kings notes “There was war between Abiou and Jeroboam,” the same statement made here of Abijah.

2-chronicles-13:2:2.summary: The Saints text names “Gabaon,” not Gibeah, so this Gibeah narrative does not carry the assumed place link.
2-chronicles-13:2:2.why: Place link rests on Hebrew Gibeah.

2-chronicles-13:2:3.summary: This Gibeah episode does not match the source’s “Gabaon,” and nothing else connects.
2-chronicles-13:2:3.why: Place link rests on Hebrew Gibeah.

2-chronicles-13:2:4.summary: Benjamin’s city list (Jebus, Gabaothjarim) does not name Gabaon, and nothing else links to Abijah’s mother.

2-chronicles-13:2:6.summary: Saul’s home Gibeah is not the source’s “Gabaon,” so the place link fails in this wording.
2-chronicles-13:2:6.why: Place link rests on Hebrew Gibeah.

2-chronicles-13:3:0.summary: David’s census gives huge troop totals for Israel and Judah, loosely like the two armies’ counts here.

2-chronicles-13:3:1.summary: Asa’s army of hundreds of thousands, “powerful warriors,” resembles Abijah’s muster but is a different event.

2-chronicles-13:3:2.summary: Uzziah’s army counts mighty warriors by the thousands, a general parallel of Judah’s military strength.

2-chronicles-13:3:3.summary: Israel and the foreigners draw up on opposing mountains, a loose image of two armies arrayed.

2-chronicles-13:3:4.summary: Jehoshaphat’s commanders lead hundreds of thousands of mighty men, a similar but separate muster.

2-chronicles-13:3:5.summary: Rehoboam mustered Judah and Benjamin against Israel, an earlier phase of the same Judah–Israel conflict.
2-chronicles-13:3:5.why: Earlier stage of the same war.

2-chronicles-13:4:0.summary: The city list “Bethabara, Sara, and Besana” does not contain Somoron in this wording.
2-chronicles-13:4:0.why: Place link absent in this wording.

2-chronicles-13:4:1.summary: Jotham stands on Mount Gerizim and cries “Listen to me,” like Abijah addressing Israel from a mountain.
2-chronicles-13:4:1.why: Same mountaintop address to a rival.

2-chronicles-13:4:2.summary: Azariah’s “Hear me, Asa and all Judah” shares the formula of a public summons, in a different setting.

2-chronicles-13:4:3.summary: The Zemarite clan in the table of nations has no clear link to Mount Somoron in the shown text.
2-chronicles-13:4:3.why: No shared place in this wording.

2-chronicles-13:5:1.summary: Leviticus speaks of “the salt of the covenant of the Lord,” explaining Abijah’s “covenant of salt.”

2-chronicles-13:5:2.summary: God promises David’s house, kingdom and throne “for ever,” the covenant Abijah invokes.

2-chronicles-13:5:3.summary: Jesus’ sayings on salt share only the salt image, not the covenant sense.

2-chronicles-13:5:4.summary: Solomon notes he sits on David’s throne as promised, a general fulfillment of the Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-13:5:5.summary: Jesus is given “the throne of His father David” to reign forever, fulfilling the everlasting Davidic kingship.
2-chronicles-13:5:5.why: Shows the covenant’s fulfillment in Christ.

2-chronicles-13:5:6.summary: The psalm recounts God choosing and anointing David, the covenant Abijah invokes; truncated range judged on shown text.
2-chronicles-13:5:6.why: Poetic statement of the Davidic covenant.

2-chronicles-13:5:7.summary: Priests throw salt on offerings, sharing only the salt element without the covenant idea.

2-chronicles-13:5:8.summary: David says the Lord chose him “to be king over Israel for ever,” matching kingship given to David for ever.

2-chronicles-13:5:10.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s throne is preserved under God’s authority over the earth, a general theme of God granting kingship; truncated.

2-chronicles-13:5:14.summary: God gives the earth to whom He wills, generally related to God assigning kingship to David.

2-chronicles-13:5:15.summary: Those who hated wisdom share nothing specific with Abijah’s appeal to the Davidic covenant.

2-chronicles-13:5:16.summary: Jephthah argues from what the Lord gave Israel, a loosely similar argument from divine grant in a dispute.

2-chronicles-13:5:17.summary: Samuel anoints David, the origin of the kingship mentioned, but with no covenant wording.

2-chronicles-13:5:18.summary: Nehemiah’s rebuke about usury has no link to the Davidic covenant.

2-chronicles-13:5:19.summary: God chooses a son of Jesse to reign, the background of David’s kingship, without covenant terms.

2-chronicles-13:5:20.summary: Peter’s critique of willful forgetting about creation shares only a rhetorical “do you not know” tone.
2-chronicles-13:5:20.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-13:5:22.summary: Sirach speaks of “a covenant for David” in which the royal inheritance passes from son to son.

2-chronicles-13:6:1.summary: Israel makes Jeroboam king and none follow David’s house but Judah, the revolt Abijah describes.

2-chronicles-13:6:2.summary: “Israel rejected allegiance to David’s house” records the same rebellion against Solomon’s line.

2-chronicles-13:6:3.summary: Jeroboam fears the people will return to “their lord, Rehoboam,” loosely reflecting the rebellion against a lord.
2-chronicles-13:6:3.why: Jeroboam’s fear of the rightful king.

2-chronicles-13:7:0.summary: Abimelech hires “empty” men who follow him, the same picture of worthless men gathering to a usurper.
2-chronicles-13:7:0.why: Parallel of usurper with worthless followers.

2-chronicles-13:7:1.summary: Rehoboam is forty-one at accession, a same-person link that sits in tension with calling him “younger.”

2-chronicles-13:7:2.summary: In this wording the proverb contrasts work with leisure; it lacks any worthless men gathering to a leader.
2-chronicles-13:7:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-13:7:3.summary: Paul’s call to mature thinking has no specific link to Rehoboam’s youth or Jeroboam’s men.

2-chronicles-13:7:4.summary: “Lawless men have gone forth” to lead people astray, echoing the “lawless sons” who gathered to Jeroboam.

2-chronicles-13:7:6.summary: “Sons of lawbreakers” bear false witness against Naboth, sharing the idiom but not the event.

2-chronicles-13:7:7.summary: Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, is told not to fight and turns back from Jeroboam, matching that he “did not withstand him.”

2-chronicles-13:7:8.summary: Wicked men from the marketplace are gathered into a mob, loosely like worthless men gathering to Jeroboam.

2-chronicles-13:7:9.summary: Job describes sons of foolish, dishonored people, a loose parallel to “pestilent men.”

2-chronicles-13:7:10.summary: “Woe to you, city, whose king is young” touches generally on a young, weak ruler.

2-chronicles-13:7:11.summary: The psalmist avoids a council of emptiness and transgressors, a general contrast with such men gathering.

2-chronicles-13:7:12.summary: Men of little means gather around Jephthah, a similar picture of followers gathering to a leader.

2-chronicles-13:7:13.summary: Hebrews’ rebuke of spiritual immaturity has no specific link to Rehoboam’s youth.

2-chronicles-13:7:14.summary: God sets young men as rulers in judgment, generally related to a young, faint-hearted king.

2-chronicles-13:7:15.summary: Insubordinate empty talkers in Crete share only a general notion of unruly people.

2-chronicles-13:7:16.summary: A proverb about pursuing empty things versus working land has no link to Jeroboam’s followers.

2-chronicles-13:7:17.summary: Two “sons of lawbreakers” testify against Naboth, sharing the idiom only.

2-chronicles-13:7:18.summary: Distressed men gather to David, a similar gathering of followers but of a different character.

2-chronicles-13:8:1.summary: Jeroboam appointed priests for “the calves Jeroboam had made,” the same golden calves Abijah denounces.

2-chronicles-13:8:2.summary: Asa faces a “great multitude” trusting God, a similar battle situation against a larger force.

2-chronicles-13:8:4.summary: A plot against Judea’s Davidic king will not stand, a general parallel to opposing the Lord’s kingdom.

2-chronicles-13:8:5.summary: “A king is not saved through a great force” bears generally on Jeroboam’s confidence in numbers.
