2-chronicles-13:8:6.summary: The parable’s enemies refuse the king’s reign, a loose parallel to Israel rejecting David’s line.

2-chronicles-13:8:7.summary: Jehoshaphat faces “this great multitude,” sharing only the phrase for a large enemy force.

2-chronicles-13:8:8.summary: The queen calls Solomon’s throne one set as king “for the Lord,” supporting Abijah’s claim that David’s line is the Lord’s kingdom.
2-chronicles-13:8:8.why: Davidic throne as the Lord’s own.

2-chronicles-13:8:9.summary: Rulers gather “against the Lord and against His anointed,” the same rebellion against God’s chosen king Abijah describes.

2-chronicles-13:8:10.summary: Jehoshaphat affirms that “no one can resist Thee,” generally related to opposing the Lord’s kingdom.

2-chronicles-13:8:11.summary: Hosea condemns Samaria’s “calf” as no god, the same calf worship Abijah cites against Israel.

2-chronicles-13:8:12.summary: Citizens reject the nobleman’s reign, a loose parallel to Israel rejecting David’s line.

2-chronicles-13:8:13.summary: Isaiah’s promise of rule “upon the throne of David and his kingdom” forever relates generally to the Davidic kingdom.

2-chronicles-13:9:1.summary: Nations exchanging gods that “are not gods” parallels loosely the “god who does not exist.”

2-chronicles-13:9:2.summary: Aaron’s sons have their hands consecrated seven days, background to the irregular hand-filling ritual here.

2-chronicles-13:9:3.summary: Aaron’s ordination uses a calf and two rams, loosely contrasting with Jeroboam’s calf and seven rams.

2-chronicles-13:9:4.summary: Paul speaks of being enslaved to beings “that by nature are not gods,” a general false-gods theme.

2-chronicles-13:9:5.summary: Jeroboam appointed priests “from some of the people” and whoever wished became a priest, exactly Abijah’s charge.

2-chronicles-13:9:6.summary: The nations’ idols “are not gods but the work of human hands,” a general false-gods theme.

2-chronicles-13:9:7.summary: Of Samaria’s calf Hosea says “it is no god,” matching the calf-priesthood serving a god who does not exist.

2-chronicles-13:9:8.summary: Israel sacrificed to demons and “not unto God,” a general theme of worshiping non-gods.

2-chronicles-13:9:9.summary: Judah swore “by those who are not gods,” a general false-gods theme.

2-chronicles-13:9:11.summary: David asks who will “fill his hands” for the Lord, sharing the idiom in a different sense.

2-chronicles-13:9:12.summary: Lawful ordination requires “one calf… and two rams,” contrasting with Jeroboam’s calf and seven rams for any volunteer.

2-chronicles-13:9:13.summary: Moses says the Levites have “filled your hands” to the Lord, sharing the consecration idiom.

2-chronicles-13:9:14.summary: Priests are anointed and their hands consecrated to succeed their fathers, background to legitimate priesthood.

2-chronicles-13:9:15.summary: Paul teaches that “things made by hands are not gods,” a general false-gods theme.

2-chronicles-13:10:0.summary: The consecration of Aaron and his sons establishes the priesthood Abijah claims for Judah; truncated, judged on shown text.

2-chronicles-13:10:1.summary: No one “who is not a descendant of Aaron” may approach with incense, supporting Abijah’s boast of Aaronic priests.
2-chronicles-13:10:1.why: Law restricting priesthood to Aaron’s line.

2-chronicles-13:10:2.summary: The refined remnant says “The Lord is my God,” loosely like Judah’s claim not to have abandoned the Lord.

2-chronicles-13:10:3.summary: Israel is called a royal priesthood, only generally related to Judah’s lawful priests.

2-chronicles-13:10:4.summary: Aaron and his sons serve with the Levites assisting them, the same priest-and-Levite order Abijah describes.
2-chronicles-13:10:4.why: Law of Aaronic priests and Levites.

2-chronicles-13:10:5.summary: Faithful Israelites who sought the Lord came to Jerusalem to sacrifice, the background of Judah’s lawful worship.
2-chronicles-13:10:5.why: Shows how Judah kept true priests.

2-chronicles-13:11:0.summary: Solomon plans incense, continual presentation, and whole burnt offerings “morning and evening,” the same rites Abijah lists.

2-chronicles-13:11:2.summary: The law prescribes a daily continual offering on the altar, the burnt-offering duty Judah keeps.

2-chronicles-13:11:3.summary: Aaron and his sons keep the lamp burning “from evening to morning,” matching lamps kindled in the evening.

2-chronicles-13:11:4.summary: The bread of the Presence on the table and the pure gold lampstand are the same furnishings Abijah names; truncated range.
2-chronicles-13:11:4.why: Legal basis for bread and lampstand.

2-chronicles-13:11:5.summary: Zechariah burns incense in the sanctuary, a general example of the ongoing incense duty.

2-chronicles-13:11:6.summary: Grain offerings with frankincense brought to Aaron’s sons relate only generally to temple service.

2-chronicles-13:11:7.summary: Ezekiel mentions “keeping of duties in My holy places,” similar to keeping the Lord’s charges.

2-chronicles-13:11:8.summary: Zadok’s priests “keep the duties” and did not stray when Israel strayed, like Judah keeping charges while Israel abandoned God.

2-chronicles-13:11:10.summary: An angel offers incense before God’s throne, a general connection to incense worship.

2-chronicles-13:11:11.summary: Abraham “kept My charges,” sharing the phrase of keeping God’s charges.

2-chronicles-13:11:12.summary: Levitical priests “kept the duties” when Israel strayed, matching Judah keeping charges while Israel abandoned God.

2-chronicles-13:11:13.summary: Aaron offers incense to stop a plague, a general instance of priestly incense duty.

2-chronicles-13:11:14.summary: Korah’s company takes fire pans in a challenge to Aaron’s priesthood, loosely contrasting with lawful priests.

2-chronicles-13:11:15.summary: Israel “shall keep the charge of God” in the wilderness, sharing only the charge-keeping phrase.

2-chronicles-13:12:0.summary: Gamaliel warns that opponents might be “found fighting against God,” the same warning Abijah gives Israel.

2-chronicles-13:12:1.summary: “If God is for us, who is against us?” states generally the confidence of “the Lord is with us.”

2-chronicles-13:12:3.summary: Fighters prevail “because the Lord is with them,” a general parallel to the Lord with Judah in battle.

2-chronicles-13:12:4.summary: Trust in the Lord’s name over chariots and horses relates generally to Judah’s reliance on God.

2-chronicles-13:12:5.summary: Christ as pioneer of salvation through suffering has no specific link to the Lord commanding Judah’s army.
2-chronicles-13:12:5.why: No real connection in this wording.

2-chronicles-13:12:6.summary: Moses warns that going against the Lord’s word “will not go well for you,” paralleling “it will not prosper for you.”

2-chronicles-13:12:7.summary: A priest goes to war with “the signalling trumpets,” matching priests with signal trumpets in Judah’s army.
2-chronicles-13:12:7.why: Law and precedent for priestly trumpets.

2-chronicles-13:12:8.summary: “You will not prosper in it” shares the not-prospering phrase in a different context.

2-chronicles-13:12:9.summary: “Will it prosper?” asks rhetorically about a doomed vine, sharing only the not-prospering idea.

2-chronicles-13:12:10.summary: Enemy counsel will fail “because the Lord God is with us,” the same confidence Abijah expresses.
2-chronicles-13:12:10.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-13:12:11.summary: The clay questioning the potter pictures futile resistance to God, a general theme.

2-chronicles-13:12:12.summary: God asks Job if he has an arm against the Lord, a general picture of futile opposition.

2-chronicles-13:12:13.summary: Priests sounding trumpets lead Israel to a God-given victory at Jericho, like Judah’s priests with signal trumpets; truncated.
2-chronicles-13:12:13.why: Precedent for priestly trumpets in war.

2-chronicles-13:12:14.summary: Balaam says “the Lord his God is with him,” sharing the presence formula in a different setting.

2-chronicles-13:12:15.summary: The Lord’s chief captain appears to Joshua, loosely related to the Lord being “in command” of Judah.

2-chronicles-13:12:16.summary: Babylon is taken because it “resisted the Lord,” a general theme of opposing God.

2-chronicles-13:12:17.summary: God will not grant success against His people, a general parallel to Israel’s fight not prospering.

2-chronicles-13:12:18.summary: Azarias declares “You shall not prosper” to those who forsook the Lord, the same Chronicler warning.

2-chronicles-13:12:19.summary: Job asks who grew hard against God and endured, a general theme of futile resistance.

2-chronicles-13:12:20.summary: The wicked man runs against the Lord with his shield, a general image of fighting God.

2-chronicles-13:12:21.summary: Saul persecuting Jesus is effectively fighting the Lord, only a general parallel.

2-chronicles-13:12:22.summary: The Lord goes with Israel to fight its enemies, a general statement of God’s presence in battle.

2-chronicles-13:12:23.summary: The ark in Israel’s camp terrifies the foreigners, a loose parallel to God’s presence with the army.

2-chronicles-13:12:24.summary: The covenant curse that God “shall not prosper your ways” shares only the not-prospering idea.

2-chronicles-13:13:0.summary: Joshua orders men to “lie in ambush behind the city,” the same rear-ambush tactic Jeroboam uses.

2-chronicles-13:13:1.summary: Joshua’s ambush takes position near Ai, a general parallel to an ambush maneuver.

2-chronicles-13:13:2.summary: No counsel avails the impious, generally relevant to Jeroboam’s clever ambush failing.

2-chronicles-13:13:3.summary: The Lord sets ambushing foes against each other as Judah praises, a different Chronicler battle.

2-chronicles-13:13:4.summary: Jeremiah’s rebuke of foolish leaders “wise at doing evil” has no specific link to the ambush.

2-chronicles-13:14:0.summary: Asa “cried to the Lord his God” facing a great multitude, the same Chronicler pattern of crying out in battle.
2-chronicles-13:14:0.why: Same appeal to God in battle.

2-chronicles-13:14:1.summary: Israel sees the Egyptians “behind them” and cries to the Lord, like Judah trapped front and behind.

2-chronicles-13:14:2.summary: Israel’s ambush defeats Benjamin at Gibeah, a general parallel of ambush warfare; truncated.

2-chronicles-13:14:3.summary: Freedom from fear of night terror and arrows has no specific link to Judah’s battle cry.

2-chronicles-13:14:4.summary: Joab sees “the battle faced him from the front and from behind,” the same predicament Judah faces; truncated.

2-chronicles-13:14:5.summary: Ai’s men look behind and are trapped, a loose parallel to a battle from both sides.

2-chronicles-13:14:6.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you” states generally the principle Judah acts on.

2-chronicles-13:14:7.summary: Surrounded Jehoshaphat “cried out” and the Lord saved him, the same Chronicler pattern of rescue after a cry.

2-chronicles-13:14:8.summary: Judas’s men sound the trumpet going to battle, a general parallel to battle trumpets.

2-chronicles-13:15:0.summary: “The Lord struck the Ethiopians before Judah” uses the same formula as the Lord striking Israel before Judah.

2-chronicles-13:15:1.summary: Nations shout to God with exultation, sharing only the image of a shout.

2-chronicles-13:15:2.summary: God ascends with a shout and trumpet sound, sharing the shout-and-trumpet image only.

2-chronicles-13:15:3.summary: Naaman’s victories credited to the Lord have no specific link to Judah’s battle cry.

2-chronicles-13:15:4.summary: Gideon’s men sound trumpets and cry out, and the enemy camp is routed, like Judah’s cry and God’s stroke; truncated.
2-chronicles-13:15:4.why: Precedent of shout, trumpet and rout.

2-chronicles-13:15:5.summary: The Lord hands enemies to Israel, who pursue them, a general divine-victory parallel.

2-chronicles-13:15:6.summary: The Lord routs Sisera’s army “before Barak,” the same pattern of the Lord striking the enemy before Israel’s leader.

2-chronicles-13:15:7.summary: A remark about land suited for livestock shares only the idea of land handed over.

2-chronicles-13:15:8.summary: An angel kills the Assyrian army, a general instance of God striking the enemy.

2-chronicles-13:15:9.summary: Singers lead Jehoshaphat’s army with praise, a loose parallel to worship-led victory.

2-chronicles-13:15:10.summary: Priests sound the trumpets and Joshua says “Cry out,” the same trumpets-and-shout before God’s victory.

2-chronicles-13:15:11.summary: The psalmist called on the Lord in affliction and was answered, a general rescue theme.

2-chronicles-13:15:12.summary: Priests sound trumpets, the people raise “a great, mighty shout,” and God gives victory, as with Judah’s shout.

2-chronicles-13:16:0.summary: The Lord “handed them into your hands” because Asa trusted Him, the same formula and trust theme.

2-chronicles-13:16:1.summary: “The Lord our God delivered them all into our hands” repeats a common conquest formula for a different battle.

2-chronicles-13:16:2.summary: God handed the Amorites over to Israel at Gibeon, a common formula in a different battle.

2-chronicles-13:16:3.summary: The Lord gave the Canaanites into Judah’s hand, the same formula for another of Judah’s battles.

2-chronicles-13:16:4.summary: The Lord handed all their enemies into their hands, a general conquest formula.

2-chronicles-13:16:5.summary: God “delivered your enemies into your power,” a general victory formula from Melchizedek’s blessing.

2-chronicles-13:16:6.summary: The Lord delivered Og “into our hands,” a general victory formula.

2-chronicles-13:16:7.summary: Saul wrongly thinks God has sold David “into my hands,” sharing only the hands formula.

2-chronicles-13:16:8.summary: The Lord gave Sihon “into Israel’s hand,” a general victory formula.

2-chronicles-13:17:0.summary: Paul’s question about provoking the Lord has no specific link to Israel’s battlefield losses.

2-chronicles-13:17:1.summary: Abijah’s warning that fighting the Lord “will not prosper” is fulfilled in Israel’s great defeat.

2-chronicles-13:17:2.summary: Mountains shaking before God has no specific link to the slaughter of Israel’s army.

2-chronicles-13:17:3.summary: God’s fire consumes an army so few remain, a general image of divine destruction of a host.

2-chronicles-13:17:4.summary: An angel kills 185,000 Assyrians, a general parallel of massive God-given casualties.

2-chronicles-13:17:6.summary: Israel’s king later kills 120,000 in Judah “because they had abandoned the Lord,” reversing this battle for the same reason.

2-chronicles-13:18:3.summary: Hezekiah “hoped in the Lord,” sharing the phrase but not the battle setting.

2-chronicles-13:18:0.summary: The eastern tribes “prevailed” because they cried to God and “hoped in Him,” the same reason Judah prevailed.

2-chronicles-13:18:1.summary: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him in affliction, a general trust theme.

2-chronicles-13:18:2.summary: Asa prays “we trust in Thee” before defeating a multitude, the same Chronicler theme of victory through reliance on God.

2-chronicles-13:18:4.summary: God saved His servants “who hoped in Him,” sharing the hope phrase in a non-battle setting.

2-chronicles-13:18:6.summary: “In Thee our fathers hoped… they cried out and were saved,” matching Judah hoping in their fathers’ God and crying out.

2-chronicles-13:18:7.summary: Happy is the one “whose hope is in the Lord,” a general statement of trust.

2-chronicles-13:18:8.summary: Jehoshaphat urges Judah to “Trust in the Lord your God” before battle, the same Chronicler theme of victory through trust.

2-chronicles-13:18:9.summary: Believers who hoped in Christ share only the general idea of hoping in God.

2-chronicles-13:19:0.summary: Asa purges “the cities he had seized in Ephraim’s hill country,” referring to cities like those Abijah captured.
2-chronicles-13:19:0.why: Later fate of the captured cities.

2-chronicles-13:19:1.summary: Mount Ephron on Judah’s border shares only the name with the town Abijah seized.

2-chronicles-13:19:2.summary: Joshua takes all the kings’ cities, a general parallel of capturing cities after victory.

2-chronicles-13:19:3.summary: Joshua orders pursuit of the enemy, a general parallel to Abijah pursuing Jeroboam.

2-chronicles-13:19:4.summary: Joshua takes a city “and its villages,” sharing the phrasing but not the place.

2-chronicles-13:19:5.summary: A city called Ephraim near the wilderness may be the same town as Ephron, but the shown text does not establish it.
2-chronicles-13:19:5.why: Possible later mention of the town.

2-chronicles-13:19:6.summary: Israelites abandon their cities after defeat and foreigners take them, a loose parallel to cities seized.

2-chronicles-13:20:1.summary: “The Lord struck Nabal, and he died” uses the same phrasing as the Lord striking Jeroboam so that he died.

2-chronicles-13:20:2.summary: God taking Ezekiel’s wife has no specific link to Jeroboam’s death.

2-chronicles-13:20:3.summary: Enemies pursued until they fail and cannot stand, a general picture of an enemy left powerless.

2-chronicles-13:20:4.summary: An angel of the Lord “struck him” and he died, the same divine striking of a proud ruler.
2-chronicles-13:20:4.why: Same divine judgment on a ruler.

2-chronicles-13:20:5.summary: David says “the Lord will strike him… and he will die,” the same idiom of God striking a king.

2-chronicles-13:20:6.summary: Asa begins to reign in Jeroboam’s twenty-fourth year, showing Jeroboam outlived Abijah.

2-chronicles-13:21:0.summary: David, established as king, takes more wives and has sons and daughters, the same sign of a strengthened king.

2-chronicles-13:21:1.summary: Abimelech killing his seventy brothers has no specific link to Abijah’s many children.

2-chronicles-13:21:3.summary: Gideon had many wives and seventy sons, a general parallel of a leader’s large family.

2-chronicles-13:21:4.summary: Jair had thirty-two sons, a general parallel of a leader’s many sons.

2-chronicles-13:22:0.summary: Solomon’s remaining deeds are written in prophets’ records, the same source formula used for Abijah.

2-chronicles-13:22:1.summary: Addo the seer’s records also preserve Rehoboam’s acts, the same Addo cited for Abijah.

2-chronicles-13:22:2.summary: “The remaining matters are written” in the kings’ writing repeats the same closing source formula.

2-chronicles-13:23:1.summary: The genealogy lists “Abia his son, Asa his son,” the same succession from Abijah to Asa.

2-chronicles-13:23:2.summary: Rehoboam is buried in the City of David and Abiou reigns, the same burial formula for Abijah’s family.

2-chronicles-13:23:3.summary: Solomon’s burial in David’s city and his son’s succession repeat the formula for a different king.

2-chronicles-13:23:4.summary: David is buried in the City of David, the same burial formula for a different king.

2-chronicles-13:23:5.summary: Matthew’s genealogy has “Abijah begot Asaph,” the same Abijah-to-Asa succession.
2-chronicles-13:23:5.why: Places Abijah and Asa in Christ’s line.

2-chronicles-13:5:12.summary: Jeremiah 33:21–22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-13:5:12.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-13:5:12.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-13:5:13.summary: Jeremiah 33:26 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-13:5:13.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-13:5:13.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-13:5:21.summary: Daniel 5:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-13:5:21.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-13:5:21.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-13:8:3.summary: 1 Kings 14:9 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-13:8:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-13:8:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-13:20:0.summary: 1 Kings 14:20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-13:20:0.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-13:20:0.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-14:1:1.summary: Hezekiah “did what was good and right before the Lord his God,” the identical verdict given to Asa.

2-chronicles-14:1:2.summary: Kings says Asa’s heart was whole with the Lord all his days, the parallel verdict on Asa.

2-chronicles-14:1:3.summary: Serving God in righteousness before Him shares only a general idea of right conduct before God.

2-chronicles-14:2:2.summary: Josiah “shattered the pillars, destroyed the groves,” the same reform actions as Asa.

2-chronicles-14:2:6.summary: Hezekiah “removed the high places, shattered all the pillars, and destroyed the groves,” matching Asa’s reforms.

2-chronicles-14:2:9.summary: Josiah pulls down altars and high places and cuts down the sacred groves, the same reform actions.

2-chronicles-14:2:0.summary: Moses commands to pull down altars, break pillars and cut down sacred groves, the law Asa carries out.

2-chronicles-14:2:1.summary: “Tear down their altars, break their pillars, cut down their sacred groves” is the command Asa obeys.

2-chronicles-14:2:3.summary: Kings records Asa’s reforms, including cutting down his mother’s grove, but says he did not remove the high places.

2-chronicles-14:2:4.summary: Later Chronicles says the high places did not depart, though Asa’s heart was complete, in tension with this verse.
2-chronicles-14:2:4.why: Highlights tension on Asa’s high places.

2-chronicles-14:2:5.summary: Gideon pulls down Baal’s altar and cuts down the grove, the same reforming acts against idolatry; truncated.
2-chronicles-14:2:5.why: Earlier precedent for altar and grove removal.

2-chronicles-14:2:7.summary: Josiah burns the grove from the Lord’s house, a related but more specific act of reform.

2-chronicles-14:2:8.summary: Solomon built high places for foreign gods, a background contrast to Asa removing them.

2-chronicles-14:2:10.summary: Under Rehoboam Judah built “high places, standing stones, and groves,” the very things Asa later removed.

2-chronicles-14:2:11.summary: God threatens to lay waste their pillars and wooden images, a general parallel of destroying idolatrous objects.

2-chronicles-14:2:12.summary: The command to burn graven images relates generally to removing idols.

2-chronicles-14:3:0.summary: A king’s resolve to walk blamelessly and remove the lawless relates generally to Asa’s royal reform; truncated.

2-chronicles-14:3:1.summary: Joshua’s call to choose to serve the Lord relates generally to Asa urging Judah to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:3:2.summary: The people swear to keep all the commandments of the law, a general parallel; truncated.

2-chronicles-14:3:3.summary: Nehemiah purifying the treasury chambers has no specific link to Asa’s command to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:3:4.summary: Manasseh “told Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel,” the same royal command Asa gives.

2-chronicles-14:3:5.summary: God gave Judah one heart to carry out the king’s ordinance, a general parallel of royal reform.

2-chronicles-14:3:6.summary: “Seek Me and you will live” relates generally to the command to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:3:7.summary: Hezekiah’s sin offerings share only a king’s command, not seeking the Lord or keeping the law.

2-chronicles-14:3:8.summary: Isaiah’s call to “Seek God” relates generally to Asa’s call to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:3:9.summary: Hezekiah prays for those who “seek the Lord, the God of their fathers,” the same phrase as Asa’s command.

2-chronicles-14:3:10.summary: Seeking God with the whole heart and keeping His commandments matches only generally Asa’s charge.

2-chronicles-14:3:11.summary: Josiah makes all present serve the Lord, “the God of their fathers,” the same reforming king’s charge to Judah.

2-chronicles-14:3:12.summary: Hezekiah ordering a burnt offering shares only a royal command, not the call to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:3:13.summary: Hezekiah telling Levites to hymn the Lord shares only a royal command.

2-chronicles-14:3:14.summary: Abraham will command his household to keep the Lord’s ways, a general parallel to a leader commanding obedience.

2-chronicles-14:3:15.summary: Faithful Israelites “seek the Lord… their fathers’ God,” the same phrase Asa uses in charging Judah.

2-chronicles-14:3:16.summary: Eli failed to admonish his sons, loosely contrasting with Asa commanding Judah.

2-chronicles-14:3:17.summary: Ezra summons Judah to deal with transgression of the law, a general reform parallel; truncated.

2-chronicles-14:3:18.summary: Nehemiah enforces Sabbath law in Jerusalem, a general parallel of a leader enforcing commandments; truncated.

2-chronicles-14:4:0.summary: Josiah pulls down the altars and high places and destroys idols, the same removal of altars and idols.

2-chronicles-14:4:1.summary: Josiah pulls down altars and cuts the idols throughout the land, matching Asa removing altars and idols from all Judah’s cities.

2-chronicles-14:5:0.summary: Same reign of Asa: the Lord “gave them rest all around” after seeking Him, echoing the rest given in 14:5.
2-chronicles-14:5:0.why: Shows rest as the Chronicler’s recurring reward for Asa’s seeking.

2-chronicles-14:5:1.summary: God promises Solomon “rest” and “peace and quietness” in his days; similar divine gift of rest to a king, but a different reign.
2-chronicles-14:5:1.why: Places Asa’s peace within the ideal of Solomon’s rest.

2-chronicles-14:5:2.summary: Formula “the land was quiet for forty years” resembles the land being at peace, but in the Judges era.
2-chronicles-14:5:2.why: Shows a stock formula for God-given peace.

2-chronicles-14:5:3.summary: Solomon says “the Lord my God has given me rest on every side”, closely matching “the Lord had given him rest.”
2-chronicles-14:5:3.why: Links Asa’s peace to the Solomonic pattern of rest.

2-chronicles-14:5:4.summary: God “bringing wars to an end” loosely parallels “there was no war with him”, but only as a general theme.

2-chronicles-14:5:5.summary: “The land was quiet for fifty years” is a similar peace formula from the Judges period, not the same event.

2-chronicles-14:5:6.summary: Rehoboam “built walled cities in Judea”, the same royal fortification programme Asa continues with “walled cities in Judah’s land.”
2-chronicles-14:5:6.why: Shows continuity of Judah’s defensive building.

2-chronicles-14:5:7.summary: “He will provide quiet” loosely matches God giving rest, with no specific link to Asa.
2-chronicles-14:5:7.why: General statement of God as giver of quiet.

2-chronicles-14:5:8.summary: “The land was quiet for eighty years” repeats the peace formula in a different era.

2-chronicles-14:5:9.summary: Solomon builds fortified cities; a general parallel to Asa’s walled cities, not the same event.
2-chronicles-14:5:9.why: Shows royal city-building as a sign of stability.

2-chronicles-14:5:10.summary: “The Lord had given Israel rest from all their enemies all around” closely echoes “the Lord had given him rest.”
2-chronicles-14:5:10.why: Connects Asa’s rest to the promised rest of the conquest.

2-chronicles-14:6:0.summary: The Lord’s eyes on the righteous loosely relates to God responding to those who seek Him; no shared wording.
2-chronicles-14:6:0.why: General teaching on God’s favour toward the faithful.

2-chronicles-14:6:1.summary: Immediately adjacent verse on Asa’s “walled cities” and the rest “the Lord had given him.”
2-chronicles-14:6:1.why: Supplies the narrative context of the same building programme.

2-chronicles-14:6:2.summary: “Walk while you have the Light” shares only the word “while” with “while we hold the land.”
2-chronicles-14:6:2.why: No real link beyond incidental wording.

2-chronicles-14:6:3.summary: “Seek Me earnestly, and you will find Me” parallels Asa’s claim that as they sought the Lord, “He sought us.”
2-chronicles-14:6:3.why: Highlights the reciprocal seeking of God and His people.

2-chronicles-14:6:4.summary: “If you seek Him, He shall be found by you” matches the seeking-and-response principle Asa cites.
2-chronicles-14:6:4.why: States the principle Asa’s reign illustrates.

2-chronicles-14:6:5.summary: Asa “told Judah to seek the Lord” just before saying “we sought the Lord our God.”
2-chronicles-14:6:5.why: Shows the command fulfilled in the immediate context.

2-chronicles-14:6:6.summary: Hezekiah builds “wall and towers”, similar to Asa’s walls and towers, but a different king and occasion.

2-chronicles-14:6:7.summary: “As long as it is called Today” shares only a loose temporal idea with “while we hold the land.”
2-chronicles-14:6:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-14:6:8.summary: “Work... while it is day” shares only the word “while” with Asa’s building speech.

2-chronicles-14:6:9.summary: Solomon’s cities “with walls, gates, and bars” use the same fortification formula as Asa’s “walls, towers, gates, and bars.”
2-chronicles-14:6:9.why: Shared building formula for royal fortresses.

2-chronicles-14:6:10.summary: The Church “had peace and was being built up”, loosely echoing peace and building in Judah.
2-chronicles-14:6:10.why: Loose typological echo of peace and building.

2-chronicles-14:6:11.summary: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened” shares the seeking theme but no specific link to Asa.
2-chronicles-14:6:11.why: General call to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:6:12.summary: “The Lord had given Israel rest from all their enemies all around” matches “gave us rest all around.”
2-chronicles-14:6:12.why: Links Asa’s rest to the conquest’s rest.

2-chronicles-14:6:13.summary: Jesus promises “I will give you rest”; shares only the general idea of rest given by the Lord.

2-chronicles-14:6:14.summary: Simon rebuilt strongholds with “high towers and great walls, gates, and bars”, closely matching Asa’s “walls, towers, gates, and bars.”
2-chronicles-14:6:14.why: Later echo of the same fortification formula.

2-chronicles-14:7:0.summary: Abijah’s army of “powerful warriors” numbered in hundreds of thousands parallels Asa’s muster of powerful warriors.

2-chronicles-14:7:1.summary: Rehoboam musters Judah and Benjamin warriors by number, as Asa’s army is counted from Judah and Benjamin.
2-chronicles-14:7:1.why: Parallel muster of Judah and Benjamin.

2-chronicles-14:7:3.summary: Amaziah finds “three hundred thousand” men “bearing spear and large shield”, matching Asa’s 300,000 with “large shields and spears.”

2-chronicles-14:8:1.summary: The Saints text of this town list does not name Marisa; the shown names have no link to Zare’s invasion.
2-chronicles-14:8:1.why: Greek reading lacks the place link.

2-chronicles-14:8:2.summary: Marisa appears among Rehoboam’s fortified cities, the same city Zare reached.
2-chronicles-14:8:2.why: Identifies Marisa as a fortified Judean city.

2-chronicles-14:8:3.summary: Sousakim’s invasion with chariots and “Ethiopians” parallels Zare the Ethiopian’s huge force and chariots.
2-chronicles-14:8:3.why: Earlier southern invasion with Ethiopian troops.

2-chronicles-14:8:4.summary: The Saints text names Lachish and Odollam but not Marisa, so the place link assumed is absent.
2-chronicles-14:8:4.why: Greek reading lacks the place link.

2-chronicles-14:8:5.summary: Lists Libyans and others falling by the sword; no Ethiopians or Zare shown, only a generic foreign host.

2-chronicles-14:8:6.summary: Nations told they will be defeated because “the Lord God is with us”; a general theme of God defeating strong foes.
2-chronicles-14:8:6.why: Theological frame for God defeating invaders.

2-chronicles-14:8:7.summary: Tharaka king of the Ethiopians “has come out to fight”, like Zare the Ethiopian coming out against Judah.
2-chronicles-14:8:7.why: Another Ethiopian army marching against Judah.

2-chronicles-14:8:8.summary: Kings gathered for eschatological war share only the idea of a large army.

2-chronicles-14:9:0.summary: The Saints source has a ravine “north of Marisa”, not Zephath, so the Sepheth link does not hold.
2-chronicles-14:9:0.why: Greek wording drops the place name.

2-chronicles-14:9:1.summary: Town list with Hormah has no connection to the shown battle north of Marisa.
2-chronicles-14:9:1.why: No link in the Saints text.

2-chronicles-14:10:0.summary: “They will certainly not prevail against you” echoes Asa’s “let no human being prevail against Thee”, in a different setting.
2-chronicles-14:10:0.why: Shared idea of God being unconquerable.

2-chronicles-14:10:1.summary: “Power is made complete in weakness” loosely parallels God saving “with few.”
2-chronicles-14:10:1.why: NT expression of strength through weakness.

2-chronicles-14:10:2.summary: “To Thee they cried out and were saved; in Thee they hoped” matches Asa crying out and trusting in the Lord.
2-chronicles-14:10:2.why: Psalm pattern of crying, trusting, and deliverance.

2-chronicles-14:10:3.summary: Others rely on chariots, “but we... in the name of the Lord our God”, like Asa coming “in Thy name.”
2-chronicles-14:10:3.why: Trust in God’s name over military might.

2-chronicles-14:10:4.summary: “If God is for us, who is against us?” echoes the confidence of Asa’s prayer in general terms.
2-chronicles-14:10:4.why: NT statement of the same confidence.

2-chronicles-14:10:5.summary: Judah, outnumbered, “cried to the Lord” in battle, as Asa “cried to the Lord his God.”

2-chronicles-14:10:6.summary: Calling on the Lord’s name for salvation loosely parallels Asa’s prayer in God’s name.
2-chronicles-14:10:6.why: General principle of calling on God.

2-chronicles-14:10:7.summary: Judah “prevailed, because they hoped in the Lord”, matching Asa’s “we trust in Thee” and plea about prevailing.

2-chronicles-14:10:8.summary: Strength in “the name of the Lord” relates loosely to Asa coming in God’s name.
2-chronicles-14:10:8.why: General wisdom on God’s name as refuge.

2-chronicles-14:10:9.summary: “In Thee they hoped, Lord” shares the trust theme without the military setting.

2-chronicles-14:10:11.summary: “When I was afflicted, I cried, and He heard me” shares only the general cry-and-answer theme.

2-chronicles-14:10:12.summary: God gives strength to the weak, loosely paralleling Asa’s plea “Strengthen us, Lord.”

2-chronicles-14:10:13.summary: God “strengthened you” and adversaries perish; a general promise echoing Asa’s plea for strength against foes.
2-chronicles-14:10:13.why: Prophetic promise of help against enemies.

2-chronicles-14:10:14.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you” fits Asa’s prayer only in general terms.
2-chronicles-14:10:14.why: General invitation to call on God.

2-chronicles-14:10:15.summary: “Hope in Him, and He will act” matches trust in general, not the battle setting.

2-chronicles-14:10:16.summary: “They cried to God in the battle, and He listened... because they hoped in Him” closely parallels Asa’s cry and trust.
2-chronicles-14:10:16.why: Close Chronicler parallel of battle prayer answered.

2-chronicles-14:10:17.summary: “He will call upon Me, and I will hear him” is a general promise of answered prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:18.summary: “With him are arms of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, to save” mirrors Asa’s trust against a vast army.

2-chronicles-14:10:19.summary: “Do not let a human being grow strong” closely echoes Asa’s “let no human being prevail against Thee.”

2-chronicles-14:10:20.summary: “I called upon the Lord and cried out to my God” shares only the general cry for help.

2-chronicles-14:10:21.summary: Christ’s gift of peace and untroubled heart has no specific link to Asa’s battle prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:22.summary: Israel “cried out to the Lord” before an approaching Egyptian army; a general parallel to Asa’s cry.
2-chronicles-14:10:22.why: Similar cry before an overwhelming enemy.

2-chronicles-14:10:23.summary: “This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him” shares only the cry-and-deliverance theme.

2-chronicles-14:10:24.summary: Few pursuing many (“five... a hundred”) illustrates Asa’s confession that God can save “with many or with few.”
2-chronicles-14:10:24.why: Covenant promise of the few defeating the many.

2-chronicles-14:10:25.summary: “A man is not mighty by strength” loosely matches Asa’s reliance on God rather than numbers.

2-chronicles-14:10:26.summary: God saves Israel “by the three hundred men”, a classic case of saving with few.
2-chronicles-14:10:26.why: Concrete example of God saving with few.

2-chronicles-14:10:27.summary: “One pursue a thousand” because the Lord delivered them, matching God’s power to save with few.
2-chronicles-14:10:27.why: Few defeating many by God’s hand.

2-chronicles-14:10:28.summary: “Do not let your heart be troubled” has no specific link to Asa’s prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:29.summary: God’s protection of His people as “the pupil of his eye” is too general to connect to this prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:30.summary: The Lord sees His people “weakened” and acts for them; a general theme behind Asa’s plea.

2-chronicles-14:10:32.summary: Joshua’s battle prayer appeals to God’s “great name”, loosely like Asa’s appeal in God’s name.
2-chronicles-14:10:32.why: Another leader’s prayer in military crisis.

2-chronicles-14:10:33.summary: David comes against the enemy “in the name of the Lord”, as Asa says “in Thy name we have come.”
2-chronicles-14:10:33.why: Same confidence in God’s name against a stronger foe.

2-chronicles-14:10:34.summary: Saul’s conversion vision has no connection to Asa’s battle prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:35.summary: Hezekiah “prayed... and cried out to heaven” facing an invading army, as Asa cried out.

2-chronicles-14:10:36.summary: David’s confidence against the uncircumcised defier is a loose parallel to trusting God against a stronger enemy.

2-chronicles-14:10:37.summary: Jehoshaphat prays against “this great multitude” with eyes on God, matching Asa’s prayer against “this great multitude.”

2-chronicles-14:10:38.summary: God shattering strength and fortresses has no specific link to Asa’s prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:39.summary: Shown text: small Israel faces Syria filling the land and God gives a great force into its hand; loosely parallel.
2-chronicles-14:10:39.why: Example of God giving victory to the outnumbered.

2-chronicles-14:10:40.summary: Exulting “in our God’s name” loosely relates to coming against the foe in God’s name.

2-chronicles-14:10:41.summary: Healing through faith in Jesus’ name shares only the word “name” with Asa’s prayer.

2-chronicles-14:10:42.summary: Jehoshaphat “cried out” when surrounded and “the Lord saved him”, a Chronicler parallel to Asa’s cry.

2-chronicles-14:10:43.summary: “Lord our God... we name Thy name” shares the address and name language loosely.

2-chronicles-14:10:44.summary: God acts lest enemies boast “our hand is exalted”, loosely like Asa’s plea that no human prevail.
2-chronicles-14:10:44.why: God guarding His honour against boasting enemies.

2-chronicles-14:10:45.summary: Abijah warns Israel “you will fight against the Lord”, matching Asa’s idea that opposing Judah is opposing God.
2-chronicles-14:10:45.why: Chronicler’s view of war against God’s people.

2-chronicles-14:10:46.summary: A plea for rescue “for the glory of Thy name” shares the appeal to God’s name generally.

2-chronicles-14:10:47.summary: “Shall not prevail against it” shares only the verb “prevail.”

2-chronicles-14:10:48.summary: Judas says there is no difference “between saving by many or by few”, closely echoing Asa’s “to save with many or with few.”
2-chronicles-14:10:48.why: Near-quotation of Asa’s confession in Maccabees.

2-chronicles-14:11:0.summary: “The Lord struck Jeroboam and Israel before Abijah and Judah” matches “The Lord struck the Ethiopians before Judah.”

2-chronicles-14:11:1.summary: Paul’s athletic metaphor has nothing to do with the Ethiopians’ defeat.

2-chronicles-14:11:2.summary: Thanks to God “who gives us the victory” relates only generally to God routing the Ethiopians.

2-chronicles-14:11:3.summary: God “who struck great kings” shares the idea of God striking enemies, without specific link.

2-chronicles-14:11:4.summary: “Through God we will do a mighty deed” loosely matches victory by God’s power.

2-chronicles-14:11:5.summary: Covenant promise that enemies will be “crushed before your face” and “flee” is fulfilled when the Ethiopians flee before Judah.

2-chronicles-14:11:6.summary: The Lord routs the enemy before Israel and they pursue them, as with the Ethiopians struck and pursued.

2-chronicles-14:11:7.summary: Egyptians “flee” because “the Lord is fighting for them”; general parallel of God routing an army.

2-chronicles-14:11:8.summary: “I will smite” expresses God’s power to strike generally.

2-chronicles-14:11:9.summary: The Lord routs invaders who came against Judah under Jehoshaphat, paralleling the Ethiopians’ rout.
2-chronicles-14:11:9.why: Chronicler parallel of divine victory for Judah.

2-chronicles-14:12:0.summary: The Saints source reads “Gedor”, not Gerar, so the Gerar border reference does not connect.
2-chronicles-14:12:0.why: Greek reading lacks the place link.

2-chronicles-14:12:1.summary: Abraham at Gerar; the Saints source names “Gedor”, so the place link fails.
2-chronicles-14:12:1.why: Greek reading lacks the place link.

2-chronicles-14:12:2.summary: Isaac at Gerar; the Saints source names “Gedor”, not Gerar.
2-chronicles-14:12:2.why: Greek reading lacks the place link.

2-chronicles-14:12:3.summary: Next verse continues the same pursuit, cutting down villages “around Gedor” and plundering spoil.
2-chronicles-14:12:3.why: Direct continuation of the same event.

2-chronicles-14:12:4.summary: “A great force, like a force of God” shares the phrase of a divine “force” with “the Lord and His force.”

2-chronicles-14:12:5.summary: A lament that God does not “go out... with our forces” contrasts with God’s force shattering the Ethiopians.
2-chronicles-14:12:5.why: Contrast of God’s presence or absence in battle.

2-chronicles-14:12:6.summary: Job’s plea not to be destroyed has no link to the Ethiopians’ defeat.

2-chronicles-14:12:7.summary: The “chief captain of the host of the Lord” relates loosely to “the Lord and His force.”

2-chronicles-14:12:8.summary: God’s might in Job is too general to link to this pursuit.

2-chronicles-14:12:9.summary: David “fights the Lord’s war” loosely parallels the battle as the Lord’s.

2-chronicles-14:12:10.summary: Noah’s sons’ genealogy is linked only through the Ethiopians’ ancestry, which the texts do not show.
2-chronicles-14:12:10.why: No link in the shown texts.

2-chronicles-14:12:11.summary: Destruction “from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of His strength” loosely echoes being shattered “before the Lord and His force.”
2-chronicles-14:12:11.why: Similar language of destruction before God.

2-chronicles-14:13:0.summary: “Terror from the Lord fell upon all the kingdoms” matches “terror from the Lord had come upon them.”
2-chronicles-14:13:0.why: Same Chronicler phrase in Jehoshaphat’s reign.

2-chronicles-14:13:1.summary: “The fear of God fell upon the cities around them” closely parallels terror from the Lord on surrounding cities.
2-chronicles-14:13:1.why: Patriarchal precedent for divine terror on cities.

2-chronicles-14:13:3.summary: Spoil taken even by the lame shares only the plunder theme.

2-chronicles-14:13:4.summary: “There was terror from the Lord” in the Philistine camp matches the same phrase here.

2-chronicles-14:13:5.summary: Kings’ minds melted on hearing of God’s acts; a general parallel to divine terror on enemies.
2-chronicles-14:13:5.why: Fear of God among the nations.

2-chronicles-14:13:6.summary: No clear shared element with the plunder of Gedor’s cities.

2-chronicles-14:13:7.summary: God puts “the dread of you” on the nations, loosely like terror from the Lord on the cities.

2-chronicles-14:13:8.summary: The wicked man’s fear in Job has no link to this event.

2-chronicles-14:13:9.summary: Rahab says “fear of you has fallen upon us”, a general parallel to God-sent fear on enemies.

2-chronicles-14:13:10.summary: “We more than conquer” is a spiritual statement without specific link.

2-chronicles-14:13:11.summary: Dividing “spoils” shares only the plunder theme.

2-chronicles-14:13:12.summary: The Lord makes Syria’s camp panic and flee, leaving goods to be plundered, like God-sent terror followed by plunder.
2-chronicles-14:13:12.why: Pattern of divine panic yielding spoil.

2-chronicles-14:13:13.summary: Jehoshaphat’s people “plunder their spoils”, so many it took three days, like the “abundant spoil” here.
2-chronicles-14:13:13.why: Chronicler parallel of abundant spoil after victory.

2-chronicles-14:13:14.summary: Inhabitants “cowering” before Israel loosely parallels terror on enemies.

2-chronicles-14:13:15.summary: People plunder Syria’s abandoned camp; shares only the plunder theme.

2-chronicles-14:13:16.summary: Kings “troubled and shaken” with trembling resembles divine terror generally.

2-chronicles-14:13:17.summary: Samson’s killing at Ashkelon for robes has no link to Judah’s plunder of Gedor.

2-chronicles-14:14:0.summary: Simeonites strike the houses of the Minaioi and take pastures; a loosely similar raid on pastoral peoples.
2-chronicles-14:14:0.why: Similar southern raid on herding peoples.

2-chronicles-14:14:1.summary: David takes “flocks and herds” as spoil, loosely like sheep and camels taken here.

2-chronicles-14:14:2.summary: Shown text counts sheep and cattle taken as plunder from Midian; a general parallel of livestock spoil.

2-chronicles-14:14:3.summary: Israel “plundered their livestock” from Midian; general parallel.

2-chronicles-14:14:4.summary: Captured spoil of “camels” and “sheep” in a God-given victory closely parallels taking “many sheep and camels.”
2-chronicles-14:14:4.why: Specific shared spoil after divine victory.

2-chronicles-14:10:31.summary: Isaiah 2:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-14:10:31.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-14:10:31.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-15:1:0.summary: “The Spirit of God clothed Azarias” before he prophesies, matching the Spirit coming upon Azarias son of Oded.
2-chronicles-15:1:0.why: Same prophetic-inspiration formula with a namesake prophet.

2-chronicles-15:1:2.summary: “God's Spirit came within” Balaam before his oracle, loosely like the Spirit coming upon Azarias.

2-chronicles-15:1:3.summary: Prophets spoke as “borne along by the Holy Spirit”, a general principle behind Azarias’ inspiration.

2-chronicles-15:1:4.summary: “The Spirit of the Lord came upon him” is the identical formula used for Azarias.

2-chronicles-15:1:5.summary: “The Spirit of the Lord spoke in me” relates generally to Spirit-inspired speech.

2-chronicles-15:2:0.summary: “Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you” restates Azarias’ “The Lord is with you while you are with Him.”
2-chronicles-15:2:0.why: NT restatement of reciprocal relationship with God.

2-chronicles-15:2:1.summary: “Because you have forsaken the Lord, He will forsake you” closely echoes “if you forsake Him, He will forsake you.”
2-chronicles-15:2:1.why: Same warning formula from another prophet Azarias.

2-chronicles-15:2:2.summary: Same speech: “He will be found by them” echoes “He shall be found by you.”

2-chronicles-15:2:4.summary: “Seek Me earnestly, and you will find Me” parallels “If you seek Him, He shall be found by you.”
2-chronicles-15:2:4.why: Prophetic parallel of the seek-and-find promise.

2-chronicles-15:2:5.summary: God takes no pleasure in one who “draws back”, loosely like the warning about forsaking Him.

2-chronicles-15:2:6.summary: “Seek God, and when you find Him” matches the promise that seekers will find the Lord.

2-chronicles-15:2:7.summary: “Seek, and you will find” restates the promise “If you seek Him, He shall be found by you.”

2-chronicles-15:2:8.summary: Judah “sought Him... He was found by them”, the fulfilment of Azarias’ promise.

2-chronicles-15:2:9.summary: Warning not to “turn away from the One” who speaks relates loosely to forsaking God.

2-chronicles-15:2:10.summary: Jehoshaphat’s “Hear me, Judah and Jerusalem’s inhabitants” uses the same address formula as “Hear me, Asa and all Judah.”

2-chronicles-15:2:11.summary: “The Lord is with us” shares the theme of God’s presence with Judah.

2-chronicles-15:2:12.summary: “Let the one who has ears hear” is a generic call to listen, not linked to Azarias’ message.

2-chronicles-15:2:13.summary: “God has not rejected His people” loosely contrasts with the warning that God will forsake those who forsake Him.

2-chronicles-15:2:14.summary: “Listen, all Judah... and King Jehoshaphat!” matches the prophetic address “Hear me, Asa and all Judah.”
2-chronicles-15:2:14.why: Parallel prophetic address to king and people.

2-chronicles-15:2:15.summary: “The Lord your God is with you” shares the presence theme generally.

2-chronicles-15:2:16.summary: “With us is the Lord our God” shares the theme of God being with Judah.

2-chronicles-15:2:17.summary: God will “reject the remnant” illustrates being forsaken by God, without shared wording.

2-chronicles-15:2:18.summary: Abijah’s “Listen, Jeroboam and all Israel!” shares only the address formula.

2-chronicles-15:2:19.summary: “The Lord will be with you” shares the presence theme generally.

2-chronicles-15:2:20.summary: Revelation’s “Let the one who hath an ear hear” is a generic hearing formula only.

2-chronicles-15:2:21.summary: “Hear now, O house of David” is a similar prophetic summons to Judah’s royal house.

2-chronicles-15:2:22.summary: Revelation’s hearing formula shares only the call to hear.

2-chronicles-15:2:23.summary: Revelation’s hearing formula shares only the call to hear.

2-chronicles-15:2:24.summary: Revelation’s hearing formula shares only the call to hear.

2-chronicles-15:2:25.summary: Rehoboam “abandoned the Lord’s commandments” and was invaded, illustrating “if you forsake Him, He will forsake you.”
2-chronicles-15:2:25.why: Recent example of the warning in action.

2-chronicles-15:2:26.summary: Revelation’s hearing formula shares only the call to hear.

2-chronicles-15:2:27.summary: Revelation’s hearing formula shares only the call to hear.

2-chronicles-15:2:28.summary: Revelation’s hearing formula shares only the call to hear.

2-chronicles-15:2:29.summary: Jotham’s “Listen to me, men of Shechem” shares only a generic call to listen.

2-chronicles-15:2:30.summary: Manasseh “sought the face of the Lord” in affliction; a general example of seeking God.
2-chronicles-15:2:30.why: Later example of seeking the Lord.

2-chronicles-15:2:31.summary: “Hear these things, all nations” is a generic summons with no link to the message.

2-chronicles-15:3:0.summary: Priest and Levites teach the law to weeping people; the reverse of being “without a priest giving guidance.”

2-chronicles-15:3:2.summary: Priests are to “instruct the sons of Israel”, the role absent in Israel’s lawless days.

2-chronicles-15:3:4.summary: Israel “will remain many days without king... without priesthood” closely parallels “for many days Israel is without... a priest.”
2-chronicles-15:3:4.why: Close prophetic parallel of Israel’s deprivation.

2-chronicles-15:3:5.summary: Corrupt priests teaching for wages loosely relates to the lack of true priestly guidance.

2-chronicles-15:3:6.summary: Priests “will teach My people”; general description of the priestly role missing in the source.

2-chronicles-15:3:7.summary: People “will seek law from his mouth”, matching the source’s pairing of a priest giving guidance and law.

2-chronicles-15:3:8.summary: Chief priests consulted about the Christ’s birthplace has no specific link to Israel’s lawless period.

2-chronicles-15:3:9.summary: Jeroboam’s golden heifers and non-Levitical priests explain why Israel was “without a true God, without a priest.”
2-chronicles-15:3:9.why: Shows the cause of Israel’s apostasy.

2-chronicles-15:3:10.summary: Levites “declare... Thy law unto Israel”, the priestly role absent in the source.

2-chronicles-15:3:11.summary: “Without law” is shared, but Paul’s point on judgment differs from Israel’s historical lawlessness.

2-chronicles-15:3:12.summary: Paul becoming “as without law” to win Gentiles shares only the phrase.

2-chronicles-15:3:13.summary: Sin “apart from law” in Paul’s argument shares only incidental wording.

2-chronicles-15:3:14.summary: “The true God” echoes the source’s “a true God” in a different theological context.
2-chronicles-15:3:14.why: Shared title of the true God.

2-chronicles-15:3:15.summary: Turning from idols to “the living and true God” echoes Israel’s lack of “a true God.”
2-chronicles-15:3:15.why: Contrast of idols and the true God.

2-chronicles-15:3:16.summary: An overseer “able to teach” has no specific link to Israel without a teaching priest.

2-chronicles-15:3:17.summary: “The only true God” shares the title “true God” only.

2-chronicles-15:4:0.summary: “Seek God, and when you find Him” matches returning to the Lord who “will be found by them.”

2-chronicles-15:4:2.summary: “He was found by them” is the fulfilment in Asa’s day of this promise.

2-chronicles-15:4:3.summary: “I was found by those not inquiring of Me” shares “found by” but stresses unsought grace.
2-chronicles-15:4:3.why: Contrasting angle on God being found.

2-chronicles-15:4:4.summary: “Let us go and return to the Lord our God” echoes “They will return to the Lord, Israel’s God.”
2-chronicles-15:4:4.why: Prophetic call to the same return.

2-chronicles-15:4:5.summary: God heard their petition when afflicted; a general pattern of God responding.

2-chronicles-15:4:6.summary: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God” matches the return to “the Lord, Israel’s God.”

2-chronicles-15:4:7.summary: Paul’s “I was found among those who did not seek Me” shares “found” only, with a different emphasis.

2-chronicles-15:4:8.summary: Israel cried to the Lord and He raised a saviour; a general Judges pattern of turning and rescue.

2-chronicles-15:4:9.summary: Israel confesses forsaking God and turns back; a general example of returning to the Lord (shown text truncated).

2-chronicles-15:5:0.summary: Travellers took “twisted roads” in troubled days, loosely like no peace for those going out or coming in.
2-chronicles-15:5:0.why: Insecurity of travel in lawless times.

2-chronicles-15:5:1.summary: “The Lord will guard your coming in and your going out” contrasts with no peace for those going out or coming in.
2-chronicles-15:5:1.why: Contrast of God’s protection with unrest.

2-chronicles-15:5:2.summary: Wars and reports of wars describe general turmoil similar to the lack of peace.

2-chronicles-15:5:3.summary: People hide in caves under threat; general picture of insecurity.

2-chronicles-15:5:4.summary: “Distress among nations” shares only the general theme of turmoil.

2-chronicles-15:6:0.summary: Days of distress and wrath upon the land share the general theme of God-sent turmoil.

2-chronicles-15:6:1.summary: Judah’s great slaughter of Israel is an example of conflict between peoples, not the same description.

2-chronicles-15:6:2.summary: The Lord hands Israel to plunderers in anger; general theme of God-sent affliction.

2-chronicles-15:6:3.summary: “Nation will rise against nation” closely echoes “Nation will fight against nation.”
2-chronicles-15:6:3.why: Jesus echoes this description of turmoil.

2-chronicles-15:6:4.summary: “Nation will rise against nation” closely echoes the source’s phrase.
2-chronicles-15:6:4.why: Jesus echoes this description of turmoil.

2-chronicles-15:6:5.summary: Calamity in a city “that the Lord has not done” loosely matches God terrifying them with affliction.

2-chronicles-15:6:6.summary: God sends a nation against a lawless nation; general theme of divinely directed war.

2-chronicles-15:6:7.summary: “Nation will rise against nation” closely echoes the source’s phrase.
2-chronicles-15:6:7.why: Jesus echoes this description of turmoil.

2-chronicles-15:6:8.summary: The Lord brings Assyria against Manasseh; general theme of God sending affliction.

2-chronicles-15:6:9.summary: Rehoboam fought Jeroboam continually; loosely illustrates ongoing conflict.
2-chronicles-15:6:9.why: Example of the era’s constant war.

2-chronicles-15:6:10.summary: God brings the Chaldeans against Judah; general theme of God-sent affliction.
2-chronicles-15:6:10.why: Later example of judgment by war.

2-chronicles-15:6:11.summary: God hands Israel into nations’ hands; general theme of affliction for apostasy.

2-chronicles-15:7:0.summary: “Be steadfast... your labor is not empty in the Lord” parallels “be strong... there is a reward for your work.”

2-chronicles-15:7:1.summary: “Be strong and courageous” shares the exhortation “be strong” only.

2-chronicles-15:7:2.summary: “Do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward” parallels not growing feeble because there is a reward.

2-chronicles-15:7:3.summary: “Be strong and courageous. Do not be fainthearted” shares the general exhortation.

2-chronicles-15:7:4.summary: “Be strong... and act... until you finish all the work” matches “be strong... there is a reward for your work.”
2-chronicles-15:7:4.why: Exhortation to persevere in God’s work.

2-chronicles-15:7:5.summary: “Your reward shall be exceedingly great” shares the reward idea, in Abram’s vision.

2-chronicles-15:7:6.summary: Not losing “what we have worked for, but receive a full reward” echoes the reward for work.
2-chronicles-15:7:6.why: NT echo of reward for perseverance.

2-chronicles-15:7:7.summary: “There is indeed fruit for the righteous” shares the general idea of reward.

2-chronicles-15:7:8.summary: God will not “forget your work”, matching the assurance “there is a reward for your work.”
2-chronicles-15:7:8.why: NT assurance that faithful work is remembered.

2-chronicles-15:7:9.summary: Receiving “the reward of the inheritance” from the Lord shares the reward theme generally.

2-chronicles-15:7:10.summary: Wages “according to his own labor” relates generally to reward for work.

2-chronicles-15:7:11.summary: “May the Lord repay your work, and may your reward be full” closely echoes “there is a reward for your work.”
2-chronicles-15:7:11.why: Close verbal echo of reward for work.

2-chronicles-15:7:12.summary: Work that remains will “receive wages”; general reward-for-work idea.

2-chronicles-15:7:13.summary: “Be strengthened in the Lord” shares the exhortation to be strong.

2-chronicles-15:7:14.summary: Paul contrasts wages with grace; shares only incidental work and wage language.

2-chronicles-15:7:15.summary: Promises of a prophet’s or disciple’s “reward” share only the reward idea.

2-chronicles-15:7:16.summary: “Your Father... will repay you” shares only the general idea of divine reward.

2-chronicles-15:7:17.summary: “Your Father... will repay you” shares only the general idea of divine reward.

2-chronicles-15:7:18.summary: “Act courageously, and let your heart be strong” shares the call to be strong.

2-chronicles-15:7:19.summary: “What reward do you have?” about loving friends shares only the word “reward.”

2-chronicles-15:7:20.summary: “Your reward will be great” for loving enemies shares only the reward idea.

2-chronicles-15:7:21.summary: “Your Father... will repay you” shares only the general idea of divine reward.

2-chronicles-15:7:22.summary: “Be courageous; be strong” shares the exhortation only.

2-chronicles-15:7:23.summary: “Take courage and be strong” shares the exhortation only.

2-chronicles-15:7:24.summary: Paul’s discussion of his “wages” in preaching shares only incidental wording.

2-chronicles-15:7:25.summary: Losing reward for showy righteousness shares only the word “reward.”

2-chronicles-15:7:26.summary: “Great is your reward in the heavens” for persecuted disciples shares the reward idea generally.

2-chronicles-15:7:27.summary: “Be strong, limp hands... our God repays” combines strengthening feeble hands with God’s repayment, as in the source.
2-chronicles-15:7:27.why: Close image of strengthened hands and reward.

2-chronicles-15:7:28.summary: “In keeping them there is great recompense” shares the reward idea generally.

2-chronicles-15:8:0.summary: Abijah “seized cities” from Jeroboam, explaining the “cities he had seized in Ephraim’s hill country.”

2-chronicles-15:8:1.summary: Solomon’s altar “opposite the sanctuary” is the altar Asa renewed “before the Lord’s sanctuary.”

2-chronicles-15:8:2.summary: Solomon’s bronze altar is the temple altar Asa “renewed.”

2-chronicles-15:8:3.summary: Solomon’s high places for “the abomination of the Sidonians” illustrate the kind of abominations Asa expelled.

2-chronicles-15:8:4.summary: “Lawless acts of idolatry” relates generally to the abominations removed.

2-chronicles-15:8:5.summary: Josiah defiles shrines of “the Ammonites’ abomination”, a later reform parallel to Asa expelling abominations.

2-chronicles-15:8:6.summary: Babylon’s cup of “abominations” shares only the word, not the historical reform.

2-chronicles-15:8:7.summary: Wood cut for an idol has no specific link to Asa’s reform as shown.

2-chronicles-15:8:8.summary: Land profaned by “abominations” relates generally to Asa purging abominations from the land.

2-chronicles-15:8:9.summary: Ahaz displaces the bronze altar, contrasting with Asa renewing the Lord’s altar.
2-chronicles-15:8:9.why: Contrast between faithful and unfaithful kings.

2-chronicles-15:8:10.summary: Hezekiah’s priests purify “the altar of burnt offering”, paralleling Asa’s renewal of the altar.

2-chronicles-15:8:11.summary: Pagan practices in tombs and caves have no specific link to Asa’s reform.

2-chronicles-15:8:12.summary: Command to avoid “abominable practices” underlies Asa’s removal of abominations.

2-chronicles-15:8:13.summary: Hezekiah removed high places and altars, a general parallel of reform.

2-chronicles-15:8:14.summary: A graven image is “an abomination unto the Lord”, defining what Asa removed.

2-chronicles-15:8:15.summary: Paul “took courage” on meeting believers shares only a loose idea of being strengthened.

2-chronicles-15:8:16.summary: Solomon’s high places for foreign idols illustrate the abominations later purged.

2-chronicles-15:8:17.summary: “Be strong and act” shares the strengthening theme only.

2-chronicles-15:8:18.summary: “Vain abominations and all the idols” relates generally to the abominations removed.

2-chronicles-15:9:1.summary: The Church’s peace across Judea and Samaria shares only regional names, not the gathering under Asa.

2-chronicles-15:9:2.summary: Nations join Jews “for we have heard that God is with you”, like Israelites joining Asa seeing “the Lord his God was with him.”
2-chronicles-15:9:2.why: Same motive for joining God’s people.

2-chronicles-15:9:3.summary: Hezekiah invites “Ephraim and Manasse” to Jerusalem, paralleling northerners from Ephraim and Manasse gathering to Asa.

2-chronicles-15:9:4.summary: “His master knew that the Lord was with him” echoes the phrase, but about Joseph.

2-chronicles-15:9:5.summary: Israel rejected David’s house, contrasting with northerners now joining Asa.

2-chronicles-15:9:6.summary: Includes “the resident foreigners who came from Israel’s land”, matching resident foreigners from Ephraim, Manasse, and Symeon.

2-chronicles-15:9:7.summary: “But God was with him” about Joseph shares only the presence phrase.

2-chronicles-15:9:8.summary: All Israel saw God’s discernment in Solomon; loosely like seeing God with Asa.
2-chronicles-15:9:8.why: People recognising God with a king.

2-chronicles-15:9:9.summary: “Saul saw that the Lord was with David, and all Israel loved him” parallels Israelites joining Asa on seeing the Lord with him.
2-chronicles-15:9:9.why: Recognition of God’s presence drawing loyalty.

2-chronicles-15:9:10.summary: “Some from Manasseh came over to David”, paralleling northerners from Manasse defecting to Judah’s king.
2-chronicles-15:9:10.why: Precedent of northern tribesmen joining Judah’s king.

2-chronicles-15:10:0.summary: Esther’s scribes summoned in “the first month” shares only a date formula, not the third month or the assembly.

2-chronicles-15:11:1.summary: A levy “unto the Lord” from war spoil of cattle and sheep parallels Asa sacrificing from the spoil.
2-chronicles-15:11:1.why: Legal precedent for dedicating spoil to God.

2-chronicles-15:11:2.summary: Saul brought spoil animals “to be sacrificed to the Lord” against God’s command, contrasting Asa’s approved sacrifice from spoil.
2-chronicles-15:11:2.why: Contrast between obedient and disobedient use of spoil.

2-chronicles-15:11:3.summary: Solomon’s “thousandfold whole burnt offering” shares only the theme of lavish royal sacrifice.
2-chronicles-15:11:3.why: Royal sacrifice on a grand scale.

2-chronicles-15:11:4.summary: Gifts consecrated “from the wars and from the spoils” for God’s house parallel offering from spoil.
2-chronicles-15:11:4.why: Dedication of war spoil to God.

2-chronicles-15:11:5.summary: Solomon’s sacrifice of thousands of calves and flock animals shares the pattern of large numbered sacrifices.

2-chronicles-15:11:6.summary: Soldiers bring spoil as “the gift unto the Lord”, paralleling sacrifice from the spoil.

2-chronicles-15:11:7.summary: People took spoil animals “to sacrifice before the Lord”, a disobedient contrast to Asa’s sacrifice from spoil.
2-chronicles-15:11:7.why: Contrast in the use of spoil for sacrifice.

2-chronicles-15:12:0.summary: “The God of our fathers” shares only the title “their fathers’ God.”

2-chronicles-15:12:1.summary: Jehoiada made a covenant that the people “should be the Lord’s people”, a parallel covenant renewal.

2-chronicles-15:12:2.summary: Serving God “with all your heart and with all your soul” matches seeking Him “with all the heart and all the soul.”

2-chronicles-15:12:3.summary: Hezekiah resolves “to establish a covenant of the Lord”, paralleling Asa’s covenant.

2-chronicles-15:12:4.summary: The covenant made in Moab shares only the general covenant theme.

2-chronicles-15:12:5.summary: Returning “with all their heart and all their soul” uses the same formula.

2-chronicles-15:12:6.summary: Josiah’s covenant “with the whole heart and the whole soul” to the God of their fathers closely parallels Asa’s.

2-chronicles-15:12:7.summary: People seek Zion and an “everlasting covenant”; general theme of seeking and covenant.

2-chronicles-15:12:8.summary: “That you may enter into the covenant of the Lord” matches Asa’s people passing into a covenant.

2-chronicles-15:12:9.summary: The people “entered into a curse and an oath” to keep God’s law, paralleling a sworn covenant.

2-chronicles-15:12:11.summary: Giving “themselves first to the Lord” relates loosely to wholehearted commitment.

2-chronicles-15:12:12.summary: Azarias’ promise “They will return to the Lord... and He will be found” is what the covenant to seek the Lord enacts.
2-chronicles-15:12:12.why: Links covenant to the prophetic promise.

2-chronicles-15:12:13.summary: “Seek Me... with your whole heart” matches seeking the Lord “with all the heart.”

2-chronicles-15:12:14.summary: Josiah makes a covenant “with the whole heart and whole soul”, closely paralleling Asa’s covenant.

2-chronicles-15:12:15.summary: Leaders establish and seal “a pledge”, a communal covenant commitment like Asa’s.

2-chronicles-15:13:0.summary: He who sacrifices to other gods “shall surely be destroyed”, the law behind the death sanction here.
2-chronicles-15:13:0.why: Legal basis for the death penalty.

2-chronicles-15:13:1.summary: “A man, or woman” whose mind turns from the Lord parallels “man or woman” who does not seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-15:13:2.summary: Elijah executes Baal’s prophets; general parallel of zeal punishing apostasy.

2-chronicles-15:13:3.summary: Death for those who lead others to “serve other gods”, even close family, underlies this covenant sanction.
2-chronicles-15:13:3.why: Legal basis for the death sanction.

2-chronicles-15:13:4.summary: “The small together with the great” shares only the merism “younger to older.”

2-chronicles-15:13:5.summary: Paul testifying “to small and great” shares only the merism.

2-chronicles-15:13:7.summary: The dead “great and small” judged shares only the merism.
2-chronicles-15:13:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-15:13:8.summary: The Passover plague on all firstborn has no specific link to the covenant sanction.

2-chronicles-15:13:9.summary: All classes hiding from judgment shares only a general all-inclusive list.

2-chronicles-15:13:10.summary: “Small and great are there” in Sheol shares only the merism.

2-chronicles-15:13:11.summary: God’s impartiality toward powerful men is not linked to this covenant sanction.

2-chronicles-15:13:12.summary: “From small to great” struck with blindness shares only the merism.

2-chronicles-15:14:0.summary: The people “entered into a curse and an oath” to keep God’s law, parallel to swearing by the Lord.

2-chronicles-15:14:1.summary: The assembly answers “Amen” to an oath-like curse; loosely like the public oath.

2-chronicles-15:14:2.summary: “Sound the trumpet” and raise a shout share the trumpet imagery only.

2-chronicles-15:15:0.summary: “We sought the Lord... He gave us rest all around” matches “sought Him... the Lord gave them rest all around.”
2-chronicles-15:15:0.why: Same reign’s repeated pattern of seeking and rest.
2-chronicles-15:15:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-15:15:1.summary: The covenant to seek the Lord “with all the heart and all the soul” is the oath they rejoiced over.

2-chronicles-15:15:2.summary: Hoping “in Thy name” relates only generally to Judah’s devotion.

2-chronicles-15:15:3.summary: Paul’s boast of sincerity has no specific link to Judah’s oath and rest.

2-chronicles-15:15:4.summary: God’s testimonies as “my heart’s rejoicing” shares only the joy theme.

2-chronicles-15:15:5.summary: “Rejoice in the Lord” shares only the general theme of joy.

2-chronicles-15:15:6.summary: “He will be found by them” is fulfilled in “He was found by them.”
2-chronicles-15:15:6.why: Promise and fulfilment in the same chapter.

2-chronicles-15:15:7.summary: Azarias’ picture of nation fighting nation contrasts with the rest “all around” now given.
2-chronicles-15:15:7.why: Shows the reversal from turmoil to rest.

2-chronicles-15:15:8.summary: “I have sworn” to keep God’s judgments shares the oath idea.

2-chronicles-15:15:9.summary: Rejoicing in good things God has given shares only the joy theme.

2-chronicles-15:15:11.summary: “He will provide quiet” loosely parallels the Lord giving rest.

2-chronicles-15:15:12.summary: God did not say “Seek a futile thing”, loosely affirming that seeking Him is rewarded.
2-chronicles-15:15:12.why: Seeking God is not in vain.

2-chronicles-15:15:13.summary: “The Lord had given Israel rest from all their enemies all around” matches “gave them rest all around.”

2-chronicles-15:15:14.summary: Paul’s “desire to depart” shares only the word “desire.”

2-chronicles-15:15:15.summary: A holy day around the law; loosely like a covenant assembly, but people weep rather than rejoice.

2-chronicles-15:15:16.summary: Hezekiah and the people “rejoiced” at God’s provision; general parallel of joy in reform.

2-chronicles-15:15:17.summary: Wisdom’s paths of peace share only a general peace idea.

2-chronicles-15:15:18.summary: Hezekiah’s intent to make a covenant shares the covenant theme generally.

2-chronicles-15:15:19.summary: Shown text: Jehoiada’s covenant, idol removal, and worship “with rejoicing”, paralleling covenant, reform, and joy here (range truncated).

2-chronicles-15:16:1.summary: Kings’ parallel names Asa’s mother “Ana daughter of Absalom”, the queen mother removed here (Greek name differs from Maacah).
2-chronicles-15:16:1.why: Identifies the queen mother in the parallel account.

2-chronicles-15:16:2.summary: Command to “cut down their sacred groves, and burn” images is fulfilled by Asa cutting down and burning the idol.

2-chronicles-15:16:3.summary: “Maacah daughter of Absalom” names the same queen mother removed by Asa.

2-chronicles-15:16:4.summary: Josiah “burned the grove”, a later reform parallel to Asa burning the idol.

2-chronicles-15:16:5.summary: Josiah “burned it in the Kidron torrent”, matching Asa burning the idol “in the Kedron torrent.”
2-chronicles-15:16:5.why: Same place and act in a later reform.

2-chronicles-15:16:6.summary: Josiah pulled down sacred groves and cut idols to pieces, paralleling Asa’s destruction of the idol.

2-chronicles-15:16:7.summary: Moses burned the calf and cast its dust “into the torrent”, a precedent for burning an idol at a torrent.

2-chronicles-15:16:8.summary: Jesus’ family thinking Him out of His mind has no link to Asa deposing his mother.

2-chronicles-15:16:9.summary: Doing God’s will over family ties loosely parallels Asa putting God above his mother.

2-chronicles-15:16:10.summary: Knowing no one “according to the flesh” has no specific link to the source.

2-chronicles-15:16:11.summary: God will “destroy your wooden images”; general theme of destroying idols.

2-chronicles-15:16:12.summary: Levi disregarded “his father and his mother” to keep God’s covenant, as Asa deposed his mother for God.

2-chronicles-15:16:13.summary: Levites kill kin after the calf; loosely parallel zeal against idolatry even within family.

2-chronicles-15:16:14.summary: “You shall burn the graven images of their gods with fire” is the command Asa fulfilled by burning the idol.

2-chronicles-15:16:15.summary: “Cut down their sacred groves, and burn the graven images” matches Asa cutting down and burning the idol.

2-chronicles-15:16:16.summary: Parents act against their false-prophet son; loosely parallel to acting against kin for God.

2-chronicles-15:16:17.summary: Do not spare even “your mother” or kin who entice to other gods, matching Asa’s removal of his mother.

2-chronicles-15:16:18.summary: Moses burned the calf and ground it fine; general precedent for destroying an idol.

2-chronicles-15:16:19.summary: Asa earlier “cut down the sacred groves” and removed idols, the same king’s reform.

2-chronicles-15:16:20.summary: Josiah threw altars’ dust “into the Kidron torrent”, the same place Asa burned the idol.
2-chronicles-15:16:20.why: Kidron as site of idol disposal.

2-chronicles-15:17:4.summary: “The high places were not removed” is the same qualifying formula used of Asa.

2-chronicles-15:17:0.summary: Jehoshaphat “walked in all the way of Asa his father”, affirming Asa’s upright heart.

2-chronicles-15:17:1.summary: Solomon’s “heart was not whole with the Lord”, contrasting with Asa’s heart that “was complete.”
2-chronicles-15:17:1.why: Contrast of a whole versus divided heart.

2-chronicles-15:17:2.summary: Asa “removed... the high places” in 14:2, in tension with high places not departing in Israel.
2-chronicles-15:17:2.why: Clarifies the scope of Asa’s reform.

2-chronicles-15:17:3.summary: “He did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed” repeats the same formula.

2-chronicles-15:17:5.summary: Offerings only in “the place which the Lord... shall choose” explains why high places were a fault.
2-chronicles-15:17:5.why: Legal basis for criticising high places.

2-chronicles-15:17:6.summary: Later rebuke of Asa concerning a heart “whole toward Him”, qualifying the claim his heart was complete.

2-chronicles-15:17:7.summary: People and Solomon “burning incense at the high places” despite loving the Lord, the same mixed pattern.
2-chronicles-15:17:7.why: Precedent of devotion alongside high places.

2-chronicles-15:18:1.summary: Solomon brought in “the things his father David had consecrated... the silver, gold, and utensils”, closely matching Asa’s act.
2-chronicles-15:18:1.why: Close parallel of dedicating holy things.

2-chronicles-15:18:2.summary: Levites oversaw “the treasuries of the consecrated things” of the Lord’s house, where such holy things were stored.
2-chronicles-15:18:2.why: Explains where holy things were kept.

2-chronicles-15:19:0.summary: “In the thirty-eighth year of Asa’s reign” Baasha attacks, ending the peace dated here.

2-chronicles-15:19:1.summary: Baasha became king “in the third year of Asa”, relevant to dating the war with Baasha.

2-chronicles-15:19:2.summary: Regnal formula for Nadab has no specific link to Asa’s years without war.

2-chronicles-15:3:3.summary: Jeremiah 10:10 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-15:3:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-15:3:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-16:1:0.summary: Many from Israel joined Asa, explaining Baasha’s move to block “exit or entrance” for Asa.

2-chronicles-16:1:1.summary: “No peace for anyone going out or coming in” echoes Baasha’s aim to allow “no exit or entrance.”

2-chronicles-16:1:2.summary: Earlier defection of priests and seekers to Jerusalem (shown text truncated) is background to northern migration.

2-chronicles-16:1:4.summary: Jeroboam feared people going to Jerusalem would turn to Judah’s king, the same fear behind fortifying Rama.

2-chronicles-16:2:0.summary: Ahaz took silver and gold “in the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house” and sent them to a foreign king.
2-chronicles-16:2:0.why: Parallel use of temple treasure to buy foreign help.

2-chronicles-16:2:1.summary: Joash sent gold from “the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house” to Syria’s king.
2-chronicles-16:2:1.why: Parallel payment to Syria from temple treasure.

2-chronicles-16:2:2.summary: Hezekiah gave silver from the Lord’s house and the king’s treasuries to a foreign king.
2-chronicles-16:2:2.why: Parallel royal tribute from temple treasure.

2-chronicles-16:2:3.summary: Ahaz took from the Lord’s house and king’s house for Assour’s king, “but it brought him no help.”
2-chronicles-16:2:3.why: Parallel, with comment on its futility.

2-chronicles-16:3:0.summary: Honouring an oath to one’s neighbour relates loosely to making covenants; the source shows no broken oath.
