2-chronicles-16:3:1.summary: A vice list (“irreconcilable”) has no specific link to Asa’s treaty request.

2-chronicles-16:3:2.summary: Jehoshaphat’s alliance with Ahab is another questionable royal alliance.

2-chronicles-16:3:3.summary: Condemnation for “transgressing a covenant”; the shown source asks for a new covenant, not breaking one.

2-chronicles-16:3:4.summary: Abimelech’s rebuke of Abraham has no link to Asa’s treaty.

2-chronicles-16:3:5.summary: “Make no covenant with those dwelling in this land” relates loosely to Asa covenanting with a foreign king.

2-chronicles-16:3:6.summary: Saul’s breach of the Gibeonite oath has no specific link shown.

2-chronicles-16:3:7.summary: A vice list (“faithless”) is too general to connect.

2-chronicles-16:3:8.summary: Moses’ rebuke of Aaron has no link to Asa’s treaty.

2-chronicles-16:3:9.summary: “What agreement is there between God’s temple and idols?” loosely questions alliances with the ungodly.

2-chronicles-16:3:10.summary: A prophet rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping a sinner, paralleling the rebuke Asa receives for relying on Syria.
2-chronicles-16:3:10.why: Chronicler’s pattern of rebuking foreign alliances.

2-chronicles-16:3:11.summary: Israel keeping its oath to the Gibeonites has no specific link to Asa’s request.

2-chronicles-16:3:12.summary: Woe to those seeking foreign help, “not trusting Israel’s Holy One”, fits Asa’s paid alliance with Syria.
2-chronicles-16:3:12.why: Prophetic critique of relying on foreign powers.

2-chronicles-16:4:0.summary: Abram pursued captors “as far as Dan”, the same city struck here, but unrelated events.

2-chronicles-16:4:1.summary: Pharaoh’s fortified cities share no element with the shown source; the Saints text lacks store-city wording.
2-chronicles-16:4:1.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

2-chronicles-16:4:2.summary: “From Dan to Beersheba” names Dan only as a boundary.

2-chronicles-16:4:3.summary: Jehoshaphat’s building of fortified cities has no link to the Syrian raid on Israel’s cities.

2-chronicles-16:4:4.summary: Solomon’s building programme shares no element with the Syrian raid shown.

2-chronicles-16:4:6.summary: The founding of the city Dan, one of the cities struck by Syria’s commanders.

2-chronicles-16:4:7.summary: Solomon’s fortified cities have no link to the shown raid on northern cities.

2-chronicles-16:4:8.summary: The love of money teaching has no link to Ben-Hadad’s campaign as shown.

2-chronicles-16:4:9.summary: Balaam’s love of wages has no link to the shown source.

2-chronicles-16:6:0.summary: Mizpah, where Samuel judged, is the same site as “Maspha” built by Asa; place only.

2-chronicles-16:6:2.summary: Benjamin’s town list includes “Gaba” and “Ramah”, the places Asa dismantled and fortified.
2-chronicles-16:6:2.why: Locates Gaba and Rama in Benjamin.

2-chronicles-16:6:3.summary: “From Gabe to Remmon” and “Rama” name the same Benjamite places as Gabae and Rama.
2-chronicles-16:6:3.why: Prophetic use of the same places.

2-chronicles-16:6:4.summary: Invaders plundering the king’s house has no link to Asa’s building with Rama’s stones.

2-chronicles-16:6:5.summary: “Gabee” among Benjamin’s Levitical cities is the same Gabae Asa built.
2-chronicles-16:6:5.why: Identifies Gabae as a Benjamite city.

2-chronicles-16:6:6.summary: Samuel’s assembly at Mizpah shares only the place later fortified as Maspha.

2-chronicles-16:6:7.summary: Rama, “Saul’s city”, on the invasion route north of Jerusalem is the same Rama Baasha fortified.

2-chronicles-16:6:8.summary: This Mizpah is in Judah’s lowland list, not the Benjamite Maspha Asa built.
2-chronicles-16:6:8.why: Different place of the same name.

2-chronicles-16:6:9.summary: Samuel’s circuit through Mizpah shares only the place name.

2-chronicles-16:7:0.summary: Jehu “son of Anani the prophet” rebukes Jehoshaphat for his alliance, just as Anani rebuked Asa for relying on Syria.
2-chronicles-16:7:0.why: Father and son prophets both confront kings over foreign alliances.

2-chronicles-16:7:1.summary: Names Jehu son of Hanani, apparently the same prophetic family as Anani, but says nothing about Asa or trust.

2-chronicles-16:7:2.summary: “Do not trust in rulers” and hope in the Lord matches Anani's charge that Asa trusted Syria's king rather than the Lord.

2-chronicles-16:7:3.summary: Woe on those trusting Egypt's horses and chariots and “not trusting Israel’s Holy One” parallels Asa trusting Syria instead of the Lord.
2-chronicles-16:7:3.why: Prophetic condemnation of foreign alliances over trust in God.

2-chronicles-16:7:4.summary: Hezekiah declares “with him are arms of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God,” the trust Asa failed to show.
2-chronicles-16:7:4.why: A later king models the right response to a foreign threat.

2-chronicles-16:7:5.summary: Speaks generally of having hoped in Christ; only a broad trust theme connects it to Asa's rebuke.

2-chronicles-16:7:6.summary: Mentions “Jehu son of Anani” as a royal chronicler, linking only through the prophet's family name.

2-chronicles-16:7:7.summary: Tribes prevailed and enemies “were given into their hands” because “they hoped in Him,” the reverse of Asa's case.
2-chronicles-16:7:7.why: Shows the Chronicler's pattern: trust brings victory.

2-chronicles-16:7:8.summary: Judah prevailed “because they hoped in the Lord,” the Chronicler's victory-through-trust pattern Asa abandoned.
2-chronicles-16:7:8.why: Earlier Judean victory explained by trust in God.

2-chronicles-16:7:9.summary: Hezekiah “hoped in the Lord,” a general contrast with Asa's misplaced trust, without a shared situation.
2-chronicles-16:7:9.why: Model of royal trust in God.

2-chronicles-16:7:10.summary: “Cursed is the person who places his hope in a human… whose heart departs from the Lord” fits Asa trusting Syria's king.
2-chronicles-16:7:10.why: Prophetic curse on trusting human strength.

2-chronicles-16:7:11.summary: A man hiding from rushing water and appearing in Zion has no link to Asa's alliance with Syria.

2-chronicles-16:8:0.summary: Lists “Libyans… and Ethiopians” with vast chariots and horses, the same kind of great southern force Anani recalls.
2-chronicles-16:8:0.why: Shows the great Ethiopian-Libyan armies Judah faced.

2-chronicles-16:8:1.summary: The immediately preceding words of Anani: Asa did not trust the Lord against Syria, contrasted here with his earlier trust.

2-chronicles-16:8:3.summary: “The Lord handed them over into their hands” echoes “He handed them into your hands” about a Judean victory.

2-chronicles-16:8:4.summary: The Lord as refuge who has not abandoned those who hope in Him; a general trust theme.

2-chronicles-16:8:5.summary: Judah prevailed “because they hoped in the Lord,” the same reason Anani gives for Asa's victory over the Ethiopians.
2-chronicles-16:8:5.why: Chronicler's pattern of trust bringing victory.

2-chronicles-16:8:6.summary: The Lord saves the righteous “because they have hoped in Him,” a general statement of the principle Anani applies.
2-chronicles-16:8:6.why: Psalmic form of trust bringing deliverance.

2-chronicles-16:9:0.summary: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” echoes the Lord's eyes looking over the earth for whole hearts.
2-chronicles-16:9:0.why: NT restatement of God's watchful care.

2-chronicles-16:9:1.summary: “The eyes of the Lord are in every place,” observing good and evil, closely matches eyes looking “throughout all the earth.”
2-chronicles-16:9:1.why: Same image of God's all-seeing eyes.

2-chronicles-16:9:2.summary: God's eyes are on all their ways, but in judgment rather than to show strength.
2-chronicles-16:9:2.why: Shares only the image of God's watching eyes.

2-chronicles-16:9:3.summary: A man's ways are before God's eyes; general divine oversight theme.

2-chronicles-16:9:4.summary: “The Lord’s eyes are upon the righteous” parallels the Lord's eyes seeking hearts whole toward Him.
2-chronicles-16:9:4.why: Same image of God's favorable watching.

2-chronicles-16:9:5.summary: God observes human works; general omniscience without the “eyes” image or support for the faithful.
2-chronicles-16:9:5.why: General theme of God seeing all.

2-chronicles-16:9:6.summary: All things are laid open “to His eyes”; shares the eyes image but in a judgment context.
2-chronicles-16:9:6.why: NT echo of God's all-seeing eyes.

2-chronicles-16:9:7.summary: “The Lord’s eyes, looking over all the earth” is a close verbal echo of Hanani's phrase.
2-chronicles-16:9:7.why: Same distinctive phrase in prophetic vision.

2-chronicles-16:9:8.summary: God's eyes are upon human ways to repay each accordingly; shares the eyes image with a judgment emphasis.
2-chronicles-16:9:8.why: Related image of God's watching eyes.

2-chronicles-16:9:9.summary: Solomon asks that God's eyes be open toward the temple; shares only the image of the Lord's eyes.
2-chronicles-16:9:9.why: Different use of the eyes image.

2-chronicles-16:9:10.summary: God looks upon lowly things in heaven and earth; only a broad image of divine watching.

2-chronicles-16:9:11.summary: Exhortation to guard innocence and uprightness loosely relates to a heart “whole toward Him.”

2-chronicles-16:9:12.summary: Samuel rebukes Saul with consequences for his kingdom; the Greek lacks the “foolish” wording, leaving only the prophet-rebukes-king pattern.
2-chronicles-16:9:12.why: Pattern of prophet announcing judgment on a king.
2-chronicles-16:9:12.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-16:9:13.summary: “Foolish Galatians” shares only the idea of folly; the source says Asa “acted ignorantly.”

2-chronicles-16:9:14.summary: The rich fool parable shares only the idea of folly, not Asa's situation.

2-chronicles-16:9:15.summary: Hezekiah walked “with a full heart,” loosely echoing a heart “whole toward Him.”
2-chronicles-16:9:15.why: Example of the wholehearted king God supports.

2-chronicles-16:9:16.summary: David admits “I have become exceedingly foolish,” loosely paralleling Asa having “acted ignorantly,” though David repents.

2-chronicles-16:9:17.summary: Nathan's rebuke ends with “the sword will never depart from your house,” paralleling Hanani's “from now on there will be war with you.”
2-chronicles-16:9:17.why: Prophet announces lasting violence as a king's penalty.

2-chronicles-16:9:19.summary: Job's remarks on rebuking kings and honoring rulers do not connect to Hanani's message.

2-chronicles-16:9:20.summary: Earlier “Asa’s heart was complete,” now contrasted with his failure to keep a heart “whole toward Him.”
2-chronicles-16:9:20.why: Shows Asa's decline from earlier faithfulness.

2-chronicles-16:9:21.summary: “Foolish one!” about resurrection shares only a word for folly.

2-chronicles-16:9:22.summary: Foolish people with eyes that do not see shares only incidental words like “eyes” and folly.

2-chronicles-16:9:23.summary: Jesus' warning about calling a brother “Fool” has no link to Asa's rebuke.

2-chronicles-16:9:24.summary: “His eyes are upon those who fear Him” matches the Lord's eyes seeking hearts whole toward Him.
2-chronicles-16:9:24.why: Wisdom echo of God's watchful favor.

2-chronicles-16:9:25.summary: “The Lord’s eyes… surveying every human way” closely matches eyes looking throughout all the earth.
2-chronicles-16:9:25.why: Vivid wisdom expansion of the same image.

2-chronicles-16:10:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar devouring Jerusalem has no link to Asa imprisoning the prophet.

2-chronicles-16:10:2.summary: Uzziah “became angry” and “raged against the priests” who confronted him, as Asa raged at the prophet.
2-chronicles-16:10:2.why: Chronicler's pattern of kings raging at rebuke.

2-chronicles-16:10:3.summary: David accepts Nathan's rebuke, saying “I have sinned,” contrasting with Asa's anger at Hanani.
2-chronicles-16:10:3.why: Shows the right response to a prophet.

2-chronicles-16:10:4.summary: Humbling prisoners of the earth shares only the idea of prisoners.

2-chronicles-16:10:5.summary: Herod “shut John up in prison” after John rebuked him, as Asa imprisoned the prophet who rebuked him.
2-chronicles-16:10:5.why: Ruler jails the prophet who confronts him.

2-chronicles-16:10:6.summary: Oppressing the powerless loosely relates to Asa maltreating the people, without specific shared detail.

2-chronicles-16:10:7.summary: David confesses “I have acted very foolishly” before Gad's prophetic word, unlike Asa's angry reaction.
2-chronicles-16:10:7.why: Contrasting royal response to a prophet.

2-chronicles-16:10:8.summary: Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned; shares only imprisonment of God's messengers.

2-chronicles-16:10:9.summary: “One who reproves an impious person will bring blame on himself” describes Hanani's fate after rebuking Asa.
2-chronicles-16:10:9.why: Wisdom principle illustrated by Asa's reaction.

2-chronicles-16:10:10.summary: Herod imprisoned John because John kept rebuking him, as Asa jailed Hanani for his rebuke.
2-chronicles-16:10:10.why: Ruler jails the prophet who confronts him.

2-chronicles-16:10:11.summary: David taking Bathsheba has no link to Asa's anger and imprisonment of the prophet.

2-chronicles-16:10:12.summary: The psalmist welcomes a righteous man's correction, unlike Asa's angry rejection of the prophet.

2-chronicles-16:10:13.summary: David's harsh treatment of Ammonite captives does not match Asa maltreating his own people.

2-chronicles-16:10:14.summary: Amaziah threatens the prophet, “Take care that you are not flogged,” another Judean king hostile to a rebuking prophet.
2-chronicles-16:10:14.why: Chronicler's pattern of kings silencing prophets.

2-chronicles-16:10:15.summary: Jeremiah is struck and put “into the trap” in the Lord's house for prophesying, as Hanani was imprisoned.
2-chronicles-16:10:15.why: Prophet confined for an unwelcome word.

2-chronicles-16:10:16.summary: Oppressors forcing Zion to bend down has no link to Asa's treatment of the prophet.

2-chronicles-16:10:17.summary: An overseer is charged to put prophesying persons “into confinement”; a related idea of confining prophets.
2-chronicles-16:10:17.why: Shows prophets being confined by authorities.

2-chronicles-16:11:0.summary: Same regnal formula: Jehoshaphat's acts, “first and last,” are written in a book of the kings.

2-chronicles-16:11:2.summary: Uzziah's acts, “first and last,” were written down, the same closing formula.

2-chronicles-16:11:3.summary: Jotham's acts are written “in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” identical source title.

2-chronicles-16:11:4.summary: Amaziah's acts, “first and last,” in “the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” nearly identical wording.

2-chronicles-16:11:5.summary: Josiah's deeds, “first and last,” in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah, the same formula.

2-chronicles-16:11:6.summary: Hezekiah's deeds are written in “the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” the same source title.

2-chronicles-16:11:7.summary: Shaphan reporting the found law book is unrelated to the regnal source citation.

2-chronicles-16:11:8.summary: Rehoboam's deeds, “first and last,” are cited as written in prophetic records, the same closing formula.

2-chronicles-16:11:9.summary: Solomon's deeds, “first and last,” are cited as written in prophetic records, the same formula.

2-chronicles-16:12:0.summary: Cursed is one who hopes in a human “and whose heart departs from the Lord,” fitting Asa seeking physicians not the Lord.

2-chronicles-16:12:1.summary: Ahaz, “when he was afflicted,” departed further from the Lord, as Asa in illness did not seek the Lord.
2-chronicles-16:12:1.why: Another king turning from God in affliction.

2-chronicles-16:12:2.summary: A woman suffered under “many physicians” without benefit; shares only reliance on physicians.
2-chronicles-16:12:2.why: Illustrates futility of human remedy alone.

2-chronicles-16:12:3.summary: Hanani's earlier words about hearts whole toward God provide context for Asa's later failure to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-16:12:4.summary: Saul “did not seek the Lord,” the same charge made against Asa in his illness.
2-chronicles-16:12:4.why: Same Chronicler verdict on a failing king.

2-chronicles-16:12:5.summary: “Those who are ill” need a physician; shares only illness and physician vocabulary.
2-chronicles-16:12:5.why: Jesus as the true physician, by loose association.

2-chronicles-16:12:6.summary: Those who are ill need a physician; only shared illness and physician vocabulary.

2-chronicles-16:12:7.summary: Job calls his friends “unjust physicians”; shares only the word physician.

2-chronicles-16:12:8.summary: Being judged by one's own measure has no specific link to Asa's illness.

2-chronicles-16:12:9.summary: Christ reproving those He loves is not linked by the text to Asa's illness.
2-chronicles-16:12:9.why: No real link in the shown texts.

2-chronicles-16:12:10.summary: Luke “the beloved physician” shares only the word physician.

2-chronicles-16:12:11.summary: “Is there no physician there?” shares physician imagery about failed healing.

2-chronicles-16:12:12.summary: Teaching on judging and measures has no link to Asa's illness.

2-chronicles-16:12:13.summary: Joseph's “embalmers” prepare Jacob; in this wording there are no physicians, so the link disappears.
2-chronicles-16:12:13.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-16:12:14.summary: Sirach honors the physician as created by the Lord; related to seeking physicians, though the shown text omits seeking God.
2-chronicles-16:12:14.why: Balances Asa's case on using physicians.

2-chronicles-16:12:15.summary: “May the one who sins before his Maker fall into a physician’s hands” loosely ties sin with resorting to physicians.
2-chronicles-16:12:15.why: Wisdom saying linking sin and physicians.

2-chronicles-16:14:0.summary: Jehoram's people “made no funeral procession” like that for his fathers, contrasting with Asa's great procession.
2-chronicles-16:14:0.why: Chronicler contrasts honored and dishonored royal burials.

2-chronicles-16:14:1.summary: Embalmers prepare Israel for burial; shares only the theme of preparing a body.

2-chronicles-16:14:2.summary: Zedekiah will be lamented as his fathers were; in this wording no burial burning or spices, only royal mourning.

2-chronicles-16:14:3.summary: Women bought “spices” to anoint Jesus' body; shares only burial spices.

2-chronicles-16:14:4.summary: Anointing oil made by “a perfumer’s skill” echoes the perfumers' ointments, but for sanctuary use, not burial.

2-chronicles-16:14:5.summary: Jesus is bound with spices and laid in a tomb; shares burial spices and tomb imagery.

2-chronicles-16:14:6.summary: Josiah is buried with his fathers and mourned by all Judah; general royal burial honors.

2-chronicles-16:14:7.summary: Shebna “quarried yourself a memorial” in rock, echoing a tomb dug for oneself, but as rebuke.

2-chronicles-16:14:8.summary: Flies spoiling fragrant oil is a proverb, unrelated to Asa's burial.

2-chronicles-16:9:18.summary: 1 Kings 15:32 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-16:9:18.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-16:9:18.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-17:1:1.summary: Hezekiah “grew strong” by building defenses; shares only the phrase of royal strengthening.

2-chronicles-17:1:2.summary: Matthew's genealogy: “Asaph begot Jehoshaphat,” the same father-son succession.

2-chronicles-17:1:3.summary: “Be strengthened in the Lord” shares only the idea of strength.

2-chronicles-17:1:4.summary: Uzziah “grew exceedingly strong”; same idea of a king strengthened, different context.

2-chronicles-17:1:5.summary: A ruler clothed in devastation has no link to Jehoshaphat's accession.

2-chronicles-17:1:6.summary: Rehoboam's kingdom was established but he then abandoned the Lord; loose contrast with Jehoshaphat's strengthening.
2-chronicles-17:1:6.why: Shows a danger of royal strength.

2-chronicles-17:1:7.summary: “Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah,” the Kings account of the same accession.
2-chronicles-17:1:7.why: Parallel record with synchronism to Ahab.

2-chronicles-17:1:8.summary: David's mighty men “grew strong with him”; shares only the strengthening wording.

2-chronicles-17:1:9.summary: Jonathan strengthening David's hands shares only the word strength.

2-chronicles-17:2:1.summary: Rehoboam fortified cities and “placed leaders in them,” the same defensive policy Jehoshaphat follows.
2-chronicles-17:2:1.why: Shows the Judean pattern of garrisoned cities.

2-chronicles-17:2:2.summary: Rehoboam built walled cities in Judea; general background for Judah's fortified cities.

2-chronicles-17:3:0.summary: “I am with you” is a general promise of God's presence, not tied to Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:3:1.summary: Josiah “walked in every way of his father David,” the same formula of a king walking in his father's ways.

2-chronicles-17:3:2.summary: A closing blessing “The Lord be with your spirit” is only incidentally similar.

2-chronicles-17:3:3.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us”; general divine-presence refrain.

2-chronicles-17:3:4.summary: Christ's promise “I am with you all the days” shares only the divine-presence theme.

2-chronicles-17:3:5.summary: “The Lord is with you” to Gideon; general divine-presence formula.

2-chronicles-17:3:6.summary: “The Lord was with Joseph” uses the same formula as “The Lord was with Jehoshaphat.”
2-chronicles-17:3:6.why: Same narrative formula of divine favor.

2-chronicles-17:3:7.summary: “The Lord was with Joseph” and prospered him, the same formula and outcome as for Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:3:8.summary: “The Lord your God is with you” to Joshua; general divine-presence promise.

2-chronicles-17:3:9.summary: David grew greater “and the Lord Almighty was with him,” the same formula of God's presence with a king.

2-chronicles-17:3:10.summary: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you”; general promise of presence.

2-chronicles-17:3:11.summary: “Is not the Lord with you?” to Solomon's leaders; general royal divine presence.

2-chronicles-17:3:12.summary: Emmanuel, “God with us,” shares only the theme of God's presence.

2-chronicles-17:3:13.summary: “The Lord God is with us” frustrating enemies; general presence theme.

2-chronicles-17:3:14.summary: David's just reign does not connect to Jehoshaphat walking in his father's ways in this wording.
2-chronicles-17:3:14.why: No real link in the shown texts.

2-chronicles-17:3:15.summary: Christ present among two or three gathered shares only a loose presence idea.

2-chronicles-17:3:16.summary: David's vow to find a place for the Lord has no link to Jehoshaphat's faithfulness.

2-chronicles-17:3:17.summary: Israel's denial of following Baal; the source mentions only “idols,” leaving no specific link.
2-chronicles-17:3:17.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-17:3:18.summary: “I will be with you” to Moses; general divine-presence promise.

2-chronicles-17:3:19.summary: “The Lord is with you while you are with Him. If you seek Him…” explains why the Lord was with Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:3:20.summary: Asa's reform, when “the Lord his God was with him,” shows the father's earlier ways Jehoshaphat followed.
2-chronicles-17:3:20.why: Defines the earlier ways being imitated.

2-chronicles-17:3:21.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us”; general divine-presence refrain.

2-chronicles-17:3:22.summary: Hezekiah did right “in accordance with everything his father David had done,” the same formula of following a father's ways.

2-chronicles-17:3:23.summary: God promising to teach Moses what to say has no link to Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:3:24.summary: Solomon served idols and “did not walk after the Lord as David his father did,” opposite to Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:3:25.summary: Ahaz did not do right “as his father David had done,” a contrasting use of the formula.

2-chronicles-17:3:26.summary: Asa's prayer of trust illustrates his father's earlier ways, but without a specific verbal link.

2-chronicles-17:3:27.summary: Abijam “walked in his father’s sins,” a contrasting use of the father's-ways formula.

2-chronicles-17:3:28.summary: Israel turned after the Baalim; loose contrast with Jehoshaphat not seeking idols.

2-chronicles-17:3:29.summary: “The Lord was with the judge”; similar presence formula in a different setting.

2-chronicles-17:3:30.summary: Israel “served the Baalim”; general contrast with not seeking idols.

2-chronicles-17:3:31.summary: Asa did good, removed altars and idols, and told Judah to seek the Lord: the father's earlier ways Jehoshaphat walked in.
2-chronicles-17:3:31.why: Defines the earlier ways being imitated.

2-chronicles-17:3:32.summary: Amaziah did right as his father Joash had done; a related father's-ways formula.

2-chronicles-17:4:0.summary: Jeroboam's golden heifers are the defining “works” of Israel that Jehoshaphat did not follow.

2-chronicles-17:4:1.summary: Zechariah and Elizabeth were “walking blamelessly in all the Lord’s commandments,” echoing walking in the commandments.
2-chronicles-17:4:1.why: NT example of the same obedience.

2-chronicles-17:4:2.summary: Urging believers to “walk worthily of God”; general walking theme.

2-chronicles-17:4:3.summary: Instruction on how to “walk and please God”; general walking theme.

2-chronicles-17:4:4.summary: Judah warned not to share Israel's worship at Gilgal and On; loose Israel-versus-Judah contrast.

2-chronicles-17:4:5.summary: Judah later “walked in the ordinances Israel had made,” the opposite of Jehoshaphat's refusal of Israel's works.

2-chronicles-17:4:6.summary: A king “walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab,” the path Jehoshaphat avoided.

2-chronicles-17:4:7.summary: Jeroboam's worship “became a sin”; part of Israel's works, though brief.

2-chronicles-17:4:8.summary: Ahab's Baal altar and grove exemplify the contemporary “Israel’s works” Jehoshaphat did not follow.

2-chronicles-17:4:9.summary: Jeroboam's self-devised feast and altar are background to Israel's works.

2-chronicles-17:4:10.summary: Faithless Judah followed Israel's adultery; a later reversal of Jehoshaphat's stance.
2-chronicles-17:4:10.why: Prophetic picture of Judah copying Israel.

2-chronicles-17:4:11.summary: Jeroboam's priests for high places were Israel's sin; general background.

2-chronicles-17:5:1.summary: Seeking God's kingdom first and having things added loosely parallels seeking God and receiving wealth.
2-chronicles-17:5:1.why: Loose principle of blessing on seeking God.

2-chronicles-17:5:2.summary: “Unless the Lord builds a house” loosely relates to the Lord establishing the kingdom.

2-chronicles-17:5:3.summary: The magi offering gifts to the Child shares only the word gifts.

2-chronicles-17:5:4.summary: The Lord blessed Job with great wealth; general theme of God-given abundance.

2-chronicles-17:5:5.summary: Many brought “presents to Hezekiah king of Judah” and he was exalted, paralleling gifts to Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-17:5:5.why: Same pattern of honor for faithful kings.

2-chronicles-17:5:6.summary: Pestilent men “brought him no gifts,” rejecting Saul, the opposite of all Judah giving gifts to Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-17:5:6.why: Gifts as sign of accepting a king.

2-chronicles-17:5:7.summary: God establishing believers after suffering shares only the word establish.

2-chronicles-17:5:8.summary: Kings bring God gifts at Jerusalem; shares gift-bringing in a different direction.

2-chronicles-17:5:9.summary: If Solomon walks as David did, “I will establish your royal throne,” the principle realized for Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-17:5:9.why: Promise of a kingdom established through obedience.

2-chronicles-17:5:10.summary: Solomon made gold and silver like stones; general royal wealth.

2-chronicles-17:5:11.summary: Kings offer gifts to the ideal king; shares tribute imagery.

2-chronicles-17:5:12.summary: “They brought gifts and served Solomon”; similar tribute to a king, but from other kingdoms.

2-chronicles-17:5:13.summary: Multiplied silver and gold can make the heart “lifted up” in pride, contrasting with 17:6's heart lifted up in the Lord's way.

2-chronicles-17:5:14.summary: “Each brought his gifts” to Solomon year after year; similar tribute.

2-chronicles-17:5:15.summary: Davidic sons keeping the covenant will remain on the throne; loose link to the kingdom being established.

2-chronicles-17:5:16.summary: David asks God to confirm his house for ever; loose link to the Lord establishing the kingdom.

2-chronicles-17:5:17.summary: All around Him “will bring gifts” to the Lord; gift-bringing to God, not the king.

2-chronicles-17:5:18.summary: Isaac grew very great with flocks and wealth; general blessing with wealth.

2-chronicles-17:5:19.summary: Abram was very rich in silver and gold; general wealth theme.

2-chronicles-17:5:20.summary: Solomon made gold and silver like stones; general royal wealth.

2-chronicles-17:5:21.summary: “Hezekiah had exceedingly great wealth and glory,” the same phrase used of Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-17:5:21.why: Same Chronicler formula for blessed kings.

2-chronicles-17:5:22.summary: Solomon made gold and silver common as stones; general royal wealth.

2-chronicles-17:6:0.summary: “The Lord’s ways are straight; the righteous will walk in them” shares the phrase Lord's ways.
2-chronicles-17:6:0.why: General theme of the Lord's ways.

2-chronicles-17:6:1.summary: Later in Jehoshaphat's reign “the high places still existed,” in tension with his removing them here.
2-chronicles-17:6:1.why: Shows the limits of his reform.

2-chronicles-17:6:2.summary: Under Asa “the high places did not depart,” so Jehoshaphat “further removed” them.

2-chronicles-17:6:3.summary: Blessed are those “who walk in the Lord’s law”; general walking in God's way.
2-chronicles-17:6:3.why: General theme of the Lord's way.

2-chronicles-17:6:4.summary: “Sing in the Lord’s ways” shares the phrase only.
2-chronicles-17:6:4.why: Phrase echo of the Lord's ways.

2-chronicles-17:6:6.summary: Josiah cleansed Judah “of the high places, sacred groves,” the same reform Jehoshaphat carried out.

2-chronicles-17:6:7.summary: “I kept the Lord’s ways” shares the phrase Lord's ways.
2-chronicles-17:6:7.why: Devotional echo of the Lord's way.

2-chronicles-17:6:8.summary: Kings says Jehoshaphat “walked in all the way of Asa his father,” doing right in the Lord's eyes.
2-chronicles-17:6:8.why: Parallel evaluation of the same king.

2-chronicles-17:6:9.summary: Asa “removed… the high places… and cut down the sacred groves,” the reform Jehoshaphat “further” continued.

2-chronicles-17:6:10.summary: Failing to serve the Lord “with gladness and a good heart”; loose contrast with a heart lifted up in God's way.

2-chronicles-17:6:11.summary: Looking up cheerfully toward heaven loosely parallels a heart lifted up in the Lord's way.

2-chronicles-17:6:12.summary: Under Hezekiah Israel “cut down the sacred groves, and demolished the high places,” the same reform.

2-chronicles-17:6:13.summary: Paul's rebuke of a sorcerer for making crooked “the Lord’s straight ways” shares only a phrase.

2-chronicles-17:7:0.summary: Josiah directs the Levites to minister to God's people; in this wording there is no teaching, so only Levites' service links.

2-chronicles-17:7:1.summary: Ecclesiastes “taught the people knowledge”; general teaching theme.

2-chronicles-17:7:2.summary: Israel was “without a priest giving guidance, and without law,” the lack Jehoshaphat's teachers remedy.
2-chronicles-17:7:2.why: Shows the need the teaching mission met.

2-chronicles-17:7:3.summary: Levites help the people understand God's law as Esdras teaches, like Jehoshaphat's teaching mission.
2-chronicles-17:7:3.why: Parallel public instruction in the law.

2-chronicles-17:7:4.summary: Leaders, priests and Levites study the law with Esdras; general law-study theme.

2-chronicles-17:7:5.summary: “I will teach the lawless Thy ways”; general teaching of God's ways.

2-chronicles-17:7:6.summary: Ecclesiastes being king in Jerusalem has no link to Jehoshaphat's teachers.

2-chronicles-17:7:7.summary: Jesus proclaims in other cities and synagogues of Judea; loose itinerant-teaching parallel.

2-chronicles-17:7:8.summary: Luke's prologue on what Jesus began to teach shares only the word teach.

2-chronicles-17:7:9.summary: The people read from “a book of the law”; related to the book used in 17:9.

2-chronicles-17:7:10.summary: Hezekiah encourages Levites of good understanding; loose Levite-instruction theme.

2-chronicles-17:7:11.summary: “I will teach you the fear of the Lord”; general teaching theme.

2-chronicles-17:7:12.summary: Jesus went throughout Galilee teaching; loose itinerant-teaching parallel.

2-chronicles-17:7:13.summary: Kings as foster fathers to Zion has no link to Jehoshaphat's teachers.

2-chronicles-17:7:14.summary: Jesus teaching in parables shares only the word teach.

2-chronicles-17:7:15.summary: Levi “shall declare Thine ordinances… and Thy law unto Israel,” the teaching role exercised here.
2-chronicles-17:7:15.why: Grounds the teaching mission in Levi's calling.

2-chronicles-17:7:16.summary: Moses showed Israel ordinances and judgments; general law-teaching theme.

2-chronicles-17:8:0.summary: Jehoshaphat again appoints “priests, Levites” for the Lord's judgment, extending his use of priests and Levites.

2-chronicles-17:8:1.summary: Esdras, priest and scribe in the law of Moses; only a loose priest-teacher link.
2-chronicles-17:8:1.why: Priests as teachers of the law.

2-chronicles-17:8:2.summary: “A priest’s lips will guard knowledge, and people will seek law from his mouth” fits priests sent to teach.

2-chronicles-17:9:0.summary: Believing Moses' writings about Christ is not linked to Jehoshaphat's teaching tour.

2-chronicles-17:9:1.summary: Israel was entrusted with “the oracles of God”; loose link to the book of the law.

2-chronicles-17:9:2.summary: Searching the Scriptures; loose link to teaching from the law book.

2-chronicles-17:9:3.summary: “He gave law for help”; general value of the law.

2-chronicles-17:9:4.summary: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth” echoes the “book of the Lord’s law” taught in Judah.
2-chronicles-17:9:4.why: Shows the law book's central role.

2-chronicles-17:9:5.summary: Paul explains from “the law of Moses”; loose teaching-from-the-law parallel.

2-chronicles-17:9:6.summary: “You shall teach them to your sons”; general command to teach the law.

2-chronicles-17:9:7.summary: Jesus' dispute over tradition versus God's commandment does not connect to teaching the law book in Judah's cities.

2-chronicles-17:9:8.summary: Levites “were helping the people understand the law,” the same public law instruction as in Jehoshaphat's reform.
2-chronicles-17:9:8.why: Parallel Levitical teaching of the law.

2-chronicles-17:9:9.summary: Moses is proclaimed “in every city” and read regularly, like the law taught through Judah's cities.

2-chronicles-17:9:10.summary: Going “through the cities of Israel” loosely parallels the tour of Judah's cities.

2-chronicles-17:9:11.summary: Jesus reads from a scroll in the synagogue; loose link to teaching from a book.

2-chronicles-17:9:12.summary: Josiah tells the Levites to minister to God's people; in this wording there is no teaching, so only Levites' service links.

2-chronicles-17:9:13.summary: Speaking as God's words and serving with God's strength has no specific link.

2-chronicles-17:9:14.summary: Jesus moved on “to teach and proclaim in their cities”; loose itinerant-teaching parallel.

2-chronicles-17:9:15.summary: Philip proclaimed “in all the towns” as he passed through; loose itinerant parallel.

2-chronicles-17:9:16.summary: The commission to teach the nations to keep Christ's commands loosely parallels teaching the law.

2-chronicles-17:9:18.summary: The law is read in the synagogue before exhortation; loose public-reading theme.

2-chronicles-17:10:0.summary: “Terror from the Lord had come upon them” in Asa's war uses the same phrase as here.
2-chronicles-17:10:0.why: Same Chronicler formula of divine terror.

2-chronicles-17:10:1.summary: Asa was told “there will be war with you,” contrasting with peace under Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:10:2.summary: God promises no one will desire Israel's land; loose theme of protection from neighbors.

2-chronicles-17:10:3.summary: This Greek proverb about righteous deeds over sacrifices lacks the enemies-at-peace idea the label assumes.
2-chronicles-17:10:3.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-17:10:4.summary: “May fear and trembling fall upon them,” on surrounding nations, matches terror falling on the kingdoms around Judah.
2-chronicles-17:10:4.why: Same image of God-sent fear on nations.

2-chronicles-17:10:5.summary: “The fear of God fell upon the cities around them, and they did not pursue” closely parallels the source.
2-chronicles-17:10:5.why: Same pattern: divine fear prevents attack.

2-chronicles-17:10:6.summary: Rahab says “fear of you has fallen upon us” because of the Lord's deeds, like terror on Judah's neighbors.

2-chronicles-17:11:0.summary: “The Minaeans gave gifts to Uzziah,” foreign tribute to another strong Judean king.

2-chronicles-17:11:1.summary: “All Arabia’s kings” brought gold and silver to Solomon, as Arabs and foreigners brought silver to Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-17:11:1.why: Arab tribute to a Judean king.

2-chronicles-17:11:2.summary: Moab became David's servants, “bringing gifts,” foreign tribute like that paid to Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-17:11:3.summary: Mesha rendered lambs and “rams” as tribute to Israel's king, paralleling the Arabs' rams of the flock.

2-chronicles-17:12:0.summary: Hezekiah built cities and storehouses; general royal building and prosperity.

2-chronicles-17:12:1.summary: “Jehoshaphat still had abundant wealth and glory,” continuing the description of his greatness.

2-chronicles-17:12:2.summary: Jotham “built cities in Judah’s hill country… and also dwellings and towers,” the same building pattern.

2-chronicles-17:12:3.summary: Hezekiah “grew strong” and built walls; general royal fortification.

2-chronicles-17:12:4.summary: Solomon built “fortified cities”; general royal building parallel.

2-chronicles-17:12:5.summary: Asa built “walled cities in Judah’s land” during peace given by the Lord, the pattern Jehoshaphat continues.

2-chronicles-17:12:6.summary: Uzziah built cities and towers and “grew strong”; general royal growth.

2-chronicles-17:12:7.summary: The Lord made Solomon “exceedingly great”; general royal greatness.

2-chronicles-17:13:0.summary: Uzziah's building works and recorded mighty forces parallel Jehoshaphat's works and warriors.
2-chronicles-17:13:0.why: Same Chronicler pattern of works and armies.

2-chronicles-17:13:1.summary: David's stewards over storehouses and estates; loose link to royal works.

2-chronicles-17:14:0.summary: Abraham's countless seed has no specific link to Jehoshaphat's army muster.

2-chronicles-17:14:1.summary: The promise of a great nation is unrelated to this military roll.

2-chronicles-17:14:2.summary: Numbering “by their ancestral houses” is the same census formula used for Jehoshaphat's army.

2-chronicles-17:14:3.summary: Rehoboam musters 180,000 warriors of Judah and Benjamin; general Judean army size.

2-chronicles-17:14:4.summary: Uzziah's force of 307,500 “with mighty strength”; general Chronicler army count.

2-chronicles-17:14:5.summary: Seed like sand of the earth is unrelated to the army list.

2-chronicles-17:14:7.summary: Registration “by their descent and ancestral houses” is the same census formula.

2-chronicles-17:16:0.summary: “You mighty ones of the people, bless the Lord” loosely echoes devoted mighty men.

2-chronicles-17:16:1.summary: The people “offered eagerly to the Lord,” echoing Amasia being “eager for the Lord.”

2-chronicles-17:16:2.summary: “The people chose willingly”; loose volunteer theme.

2-chronicles-17:16:3.summary: This Greek psalm verse lacks the “willing” wording the label assumes; no link remains.
2-chronicles-17:16:3.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.
2-chronicles-17:16:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-17:16:4.summary: “If the readiness is present”; loose eagerness theme in giving.

2-chronicles-17:16:5.summary: They “gave themselves first to the Lord”; loose self-offering theme.

2-chronicles-17:16:6.summary: “To offer willingly unto Thee”; loose willing-offering theme.

2-chronicles-17:16:7.summary: “I eagerly offered… Thy people… offer eagerly to Thee” echoes being “eager for the Lord.”

2-chronicles-17:17:0.summary: Saul and Jonathan, Benjaminites, with shield and bow; loose link to Benjamin's archers and shield bearers.

2-chronicles-17:19:1.summary: Rehoboam stocked shields in every city; general garrisoned-city background.

2-chronicles-17:19:2.summary: Rehoboam's sons in “the fortified cities”; general garrisoned-city background.

2-chronicles-17:19:3.summary: Jehoshaphat built “fortified cities” in Judea, the same cities where troops were stationed.

2-chronicles-18:1:0.summary: “He had abundant wealth and glory,” the identical phrase about Jehoshaphat earlier.

2-chronicles-18:1:2.summary: Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for befriending “one hated by the Lord,” judging this alliance with Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:1:3.summary: Jehoshaphat's son walked as Ahab's house did, “for Ahab’s daughter was his wife”: the marriage alliance's fruit.

2-chronicles-18:1:4.summary: Seeking God's kingdom first has no specific link to the marriage alliance.

2-chronicles-18:1:5.summary: Describes Ahab's Baal worship, showing the character of the house Jehoshaphat allied with.
2-chronicles-18:1:5.why: Shows what Ahab's house stood for.

2-chronicles-18:1:6.summary: “Do not become unequally yoked” loosely applies to allying with Ahab's house.

2-chronicles-18:1:7.summary: God gives Solomon “wealth, possessions, and glory”; general royal prosperity.

2-chronicles-18:1:8.summary: Jehoshaphat “continued to grow greater”; background to his wealth.

2-chronicles-18:1:9.summary: Ahaziah's mother Athaliah, of Omri's line, led him to walk “in the way of Ahab’s house,” the alliance's fruit.

2-chronicles-18:1:10.summary: Athaliah destroys the royal offspring; linked only by inference to the marriage alliance, which the shown texts do not connect.

2-chronicles-18:1:11.summary: Jehoshaphat is nearly killed in Ahab's war but the Lord saves him; the same alliance's danger.

2-chronicles-18:1:12.summary: Ahaziah, son of Athaliah, “walked in the way of the house of Ahab,” consequence of the alliance.

2-chronicles-18:1:13.summary: Ahab was sold to do evil, led by Jezebel; general characterization of Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:2:0.summary: Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping “a sinner,” referring to this visit and campaign with Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:2:1.summary: Adonijah “sacrificed sheep, calves” to win support; similar feast-as-persuasion.

2-chronicles-18:2:2.summary: Remmoth-gilead is again the setting of conflict, the same Ramoth in Galaaditis.

2-chronicles-18:2:4.summary: “Slaughtering calves and sacrificing sheep” in heedless feasting; shares only feast wording.
2-chronicles-18:2:4.why: Loose image of feasting before disaster.

2-chronicles-18:2:5.summary: Eating and drinking before the flood shares no specific link with Ahab's feast.

2-chronicles-18:2:6.summary: “After some days” the wadi dried; only an incidental time phrase.

2-chronicles-18:2:7.summary: Nehemiah's absence “after some days” shares only an incidental time phrase.

2-chronicles-18:2:8.summary: Names “Ramoth in Gilead” as a city of refuge for Gad, the same city Ahab wants.

2-chronicles-18:2:9.summary: “Aremoth in Gilead” from Gad, the same Ramoth-gilead.

2-chronicles-18:2:10.summary: “Remath-gilead” as Solomon's district center, the same city.

2-chronicles-18:3:1.summary: Jehoshaphat answers an Israelite king with “As I am, so are you; my people are as your people,” nearly identical words.
2-chronicles-18:3:1.why: Same alliance formula in another war.

2-chronicles-18:3:2.summary: “Do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness”; loose warning against such alliances.
2-chronicles-18:3:2.why: NT principle against partnership in evil.

2-chronicles-18:3:3.summary: Hating those who hate the Lord loosely contrasts with Jehoshaphat joining Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:3:4.summary: Whoever greets the false teacher “shares in his evil works”; loose warning about partnerships.

2-chronicles-18:4:0.summary: “Ask the Lord about us” when a foreign king threatens, as Jehoshaphat urges seeking the Lord before war.
2-chronicles-18:4:0.why: Royal inquiry of the Lord before conflict.

2-chronicles-18:4:1.summary: David asks the Lord, “Shall I go up against the foreigners?” before battle, the practice Jehoshaphat requests.

2-chronicles-18:4:2.summary: David inquires of the Lord and receives battle instructions, the practice Jehoshaphat requests.

2-chronicles-18:4:3.summary: David inquires again before attacking at Keilah and is promised victory.

2-chronicles-18:4:4.summary: David asks, “Shall I go up?” about where to settle; inquiry but not about war.

2-chronicles-18:4:5.summary: David asks the Lord through the ephod whether Saul will come against Keilah, seeking guidance before conflict.

2-chronicles-18:4:6.summary: David asks, “Shall I go and strike these foreigners?” before battle.

2-chronicles-18:4:7.summary: The king of Judah “sent you to seek the Lord,” the same practice of seeking the Lord through a prophet.
2-chronicles-18:4:7.why: Another Judean king seeking the Lord.

2-chronicles-18:4:9.summary: God refuses to be questioned by Israel's elders; loose contrast on inquiring of God.

2-chronicles-18:4:10.summary: Seeking to dwell in the Lord's house is a different kind of seeking.

2-chronicles-18:5:8.summary: The king asks Michaias the same question, “shall I go to Ramoth-galaad for war, or shall I refrain?”
2-chronicles-18:5:8.why: Same question put to the true prophet.

2-chronicles-18:5:0.summary: Elisha tells Israel's king, “Go to your father’s prophets,” the court prophets like these four hundred.

2-chronicles-18:5:1.summary: Zedekiah consults Jeremiah about war's outcome; loose king-consults-prophet parallel.

2-chronicles-18:5:2.summary: People “heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires,” like Ahab's agreeable prophets.

2-chronicles-18:5:3.summary: False prophets say “No evils will come upon you,” like the four hundred promising victory.

2-chronicles-18:5:4.summary: Prophets who say “The Lord says” though “the Lord has not sent them” describes the four hundred.

2-chronicles-18:5:5.summary: A spirit becomes “a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets,” explaining these four hundred's message.

2-chronicles-18:5:6.summary: The false prophet who deceived is judged; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:5:7.summary: People ask Jeremiah to learn “the way we should go”; general seeking prophetic guidance.

2-chronicles-18:5:9.summary: “A spirit established falsehood”; loose echo of false prophetic spirit.

2-chronicles-18:5:10.summary: Prophets say “Calamities will certainly not come upon us,” the same false assurance of success.

2-chronicles-18:5:11.summary: Ahab's court had “four hundred prophets of the groves,” matching the four hundred prophets gathered here.

2-chronicles-18:5:12.summary: In this shorter wording only wives and fields given to others appear; the false-peace prophets are absent.
2-chronicles-18:5:12.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-18:5:13.summary: Jerusalem's prophets “walking in lies”; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:5:14.summary: People asked Jeremiah to pray but did not intend to obey; loose insincere inquiry theme.

2-chronicles-18:5:15.summary: Hananiah, “the false prophet,” promises success against a foreign king, opposing the true prophet, like the four hundred.

2-chronicles-18:5:16.summary: False prophets “strengthened the lawless person’s hands”; loose false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:6:0.summary: Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there no prophet of the Lord here, through whom we may inquire,” nearly identical words.

2-chronicles-18:7:0.summary: “Are not his words good with him” loosely relates to the demand for good prophecies.

2-chronicles-18:7:1.summary: “They hated one who reproved at the gates,” as Ahab hates Michaias for unfavorable words.
2-chronicles-18:7:1.why: Hatred of those who speak truth.

2-chronicles-18:7:2.summary: Blessed when people hate you; general persecution theme.

2-chronicles-18:7:3.summary: Ahab calls Elijah “my enemy” for announcing evil, the same hostility he shows Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:7:4.summary: People tell prophets, “Do not speak to us… announce another deception,” rejecting unwelcome words as Ahab does.

2-chronicles-18:7:5.summary: Ahab calls Elijah “the one perverting Israel,” the same hostility to true prophets.

2-chronicles-18:7:6.summary: Plotting against Jeremiah; general hostility to a prophet.

2-chronicles-18:7:7.summary: Herodias held a grudge against John for his rebuke; loose hostility to a prophet.

2-chronicles-18:7:8.summary: The world hates Jesus “because I testify… that its works are evil,” as Ahab hates Michaias's evil prophecies.

2-chronicles-18:7:9.summary: “Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you” describes Ahab's hatred of Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:7:10.summary: Those who hate the righteous incur guilt; general theme.
2-chronicles-18:7:10.why: General theme of hating the righteous.

2-chronicles-18:7:11.summary: Paul did not hold back God's whole purpose; loose faithful-messenger theme.

2-chronicles-18:7:12.summary: “Have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?” matches Ahab hating Michaias for true words.

2-chronicles-18:7:13.summary: Bloodguilty men “will hate a holy person”; general theme.

2-chronicles-18:7:14.summary: A wise word in a receptive ear contrasts with Ahab's refusal of Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:7:15.summary: A prophet pronounces doom on the king of Israel, who leaves “dispirited,” an example of evil prophecy against Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:7:16.summary: Israel “killed Thy prophets”; general hostility to prophets in Ahab's era.

2-chronicles-18:7:17.summary: They “hated both Me and My Father”; general hatred theme.

2-chronicles-18:7:18.summary: Jezebel striking the Lord's prophets; context of persecution in Ahab's court.

2-chronicles-18:7:19.summary: Herod beheads John in prison; general fate of an unwelcome prophet.

2-chronicles-18:7:20.summary: An enemy harboring anger against the psalmist shares no specific link.

2-chronicles-18:7:21.summary: Michaias vows “whatever God says to me, that I will speak,” why he never prophesies good for Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:7:22.summary: Jehu's reply to Joram about Jezebel's sins has no specific link to Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:7:23.summary: The prophet as watchman must warn the lawless; loose duty to speak hard words.

2-chronicles-18:7:24.summary: Plea for rescue from those hating me shares only the word hate.

2-chronicles-18:7:25.summary: The world hates Christ's followers; general hatred theme.

2-chronicles-18:7:26.summary: Officials say Jeremiah “delivers oracles of evil to this people, not peace,” the same complaint Ahab makes.
2-chronicles-18:7:26.why: Same charge against a true prophet.

2-chronicles-18:8:0.summary: A Babylonian chief eunuch shares only the word eunuch.

2-chronicles-18:8:1.summary: Kings giving produce to eunuchs shares only the word eunuch.

2-chronicles-18:8:2.summary: Royal children made eunuchs in Babylon shares only the word eunuch.

2-chronicles-18:8:3.summary: David's assembly of officials has no eunuch in this wording and no link to summoning Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:8:4.summary: Daniel and the chief eunuch share only the word eunuch.

2-chronicles-18:8:6.summary: The king orders Michaias taken and imprisoned, the outcome of summoning this prophet.

2-chronicles-18:9:0.summary: Kings rising from thrones in Hades shares only the word thrones.

2-chronicles-18:9:1.summary: Prophets “prophesy unjust things to you” though not sent; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:9:3.summary: Apostles on twelve thrones shares only the word thrones.

2-chronicles-18:9:4.summary: Soft clothing in kings' houses; loose image of royal robes.

2-chronicles-18:9:5.summary: Boaz sits at the city gate; loose image of the gate as public place.

2-chronicles-18:9:6.summary: Solomon's glorious clothing compared to lilies has no specific link.

2-chronicles-18:9:7.summary: Thrones set and the Ancient of Days seated; loose throne-scene image, echoed later in Michaias's vision.

2-chronicles-18:9:8.summary: Ahab later has Jehoshaphat wear his clothing in battle, contrasting with their royal robes here.
2-chronicles-18:9:8.why: Royal robes play into the outcome.

2-chronicles-18:9:9.summary: Rulers step down from thrones and strip off clothing; loose throne-and-robe image.

2-chronicles-18:10:0.summary: Horns that scatter Judah and Israel; shares the horn as symbol of military power.

2-chronicles-18:10:1.summary: Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses; loose false-opponent-of-truth theme.

2-chronicles-18:10:2.summary: Hananiah's “Thus said the Lord” promise of victory over a foreign king parallels Sedekias's false oracle.

2-chronicles-18:10:3.summary: “I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied” fits Sedekias claiming “Thus says the Lord.”

2-chronicles-18:10:4.summary: Hananiah's symbolic act with collars and “Thus said the Lord” parallels Sedekias's iron horns; even “iron” appears.

2-chronicles-18:10:5.summary: Prophets “saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ when the Lord has not spoken” describes Sedekias.
2-chronicles-18:10:5.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-18:10:6.summary: False things prophesied in God's name; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:10:7.summary: False prophets promise peace; general false-assurance theme.

2-chronicles-18:10:8.summary: God is against prophets of their own tongue; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:10:9.summary: “A false vision… vain divinations”; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:10:10.summary: Names a false prophet Zedekiah alongside Ahab, but different people from this Sedekias and king.

2-chronicles-18:10:11.summary: Jeremiah makes bonds and collars as a sign; shares the prophetic symbolic object.

2-chronicles-18:11:1.summary: The four hundred said, “Go up, and God will give it into the king’s hands,” the same message.

2-chronicles-18:11:2.summary: False prophets bring destruction; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:11:3.summary: “The prophets have spoken with one mouth favorably about the king,” summarizing this unanimous message.

2-chronicles-18:11:4.summary: Spirits from the false prophet's mouth “go out to the kings… to gather them for the war,” like the lying spirit luring Ahab to battle.
2-chronicles-18:11:4.why: Deceiving spirits draw kings to war.

2-chronicles-18:11:5.summary: Those who “flatter people for the sake of advantage”; loose flattery theme.

2-chronicles-18:11:6.summary: The king of Israel is struck and dies at Ramoth, refuting the promise “you will prosper.”

2-chronicles-18:11:7.summary: The false prophet who deceived is judged; general false-prophet theme.

2-chronicles-18:11:8.summary: Prophets “who lead My people astray… proclaim peace,” like the four hundred promising prosperity.

2-chronicles-18:12:0.summary: This Greek verse about not weeping lacks the silencing-of-prophets idea the label assumes.
2-chronicles-18:12:0.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-18:12:1.summary: “With their falsehoods” they gladdened kings, as prophets spoke favorably to please the king.

2-chronicles-18:12:2.summary: “A spirit established falsehood”; loose false-prophecy image.

2-chronicles-18:12:3.summary: Spiritual discernment and Christ's mind have no specific link to the messenger's request.

2-chronicles-18:12:4.summary: The wicked saying God has forgotten has no link to the messenger's request.

2-chronicles-18:12:5.summary: Kings assembling to war; this wording lacks the “one mouth” idea the label assumes.
2-chronicles-18:12:5.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-18:12:6.summary: Amos is told not to prophesy at the king's sanctuary; loose pressure on a prophet to suit the king.
2-chronicles-18:12:6.why: Pressure on prophets from royal power.

2-chronicles-18:12:7.summary: “Speak to us and announce another deception” matches the messenger urging Michaias to speak favorably.

2-chronicles-18:12:8.summary: Questioning whether God knows has no link to the messenger's request.

2-chronicles-18:13:0.summary: Balaam is told to speak only “the word that I tell you,” matching Michaias’s vow to speak only what God says.
2-chronicles-18:13:0.why: Shows the classic prophetic rule of speaking only God’s word.

2-chronicles-18:13:1.summary: Balaam refuses to transgress “the word of the Lord” and waits to learn what the Lord will say, like Michaias’s oath.
2-chronicles-18:13:1.why: Parallel prophet resisting royal pressure to speak to order.

2-chronicles-18:13:2.summary: Balaam’s “Whatever God says, I must say” closely echoes Michaias’s “whatever God says to me, that I will speak.”
2-chronicles-18:13:2.why: Near-identical prophetic formula under a king’s pressure.

2-chronicles-18:13:3.summary: Paul speaks as entrusted by God, “pleasing not people but God,” a general parallel to Michaias’s refusal to flatter.
2-chronicles-18:13:3.why: Extends the principle of God-pleasing speech to apostles.

2-chronicles-18:13:4.summary: Paul did not hold back declaring “the whole purpose of God,” loosely like Michaias’s commitment to speak what God says.
2-chronicles-18:13:4.why: General faithfulness in proclaiming God’s message.

2-chronicles-18:13:6.summary: Balaam tells Balak he “must do the word that God speaks,” echoing Michaias’s vow before a king.
2-chronicles-18:13:6.why: Repeated prophetic formula of obedience to God’s word.

2-chronicles-18:13:7.summary: The Greek-based Micah text about weeping and Jacob’s house provoking the Spirit does not carry a prophet vowing to speak God’s word.
2-chronicles-18:13:7.why: No clear shared element in the Saints wording.

2-chronicles-18:13:8.summary: Ezekiel is commanded, “You will speak My words to them,” whether or not they listen, like Michaias’s vow.
2-chronicles-18:13:8.why: Prophetic duty to speak God’s words regardless of reception.

2-chronicles-18:13:9.summary: Jeremiah promises “Whatever word the Lord answers, I will tell you,” closely matching Michaias’s vow.
2-chronicles-18:13:9.why: Parallel prophetic pledge to report God’s answer fully.

2-chronicles-18:13:10.summary: Paul speaks God’s word “out of sincerity” before God, a general parallel to Michaias’s honest speech.
2-chronicles-18:13:10.why: General integrity in speaking God’s word.

2-chronicles-18:13:11.summary: The one to whom God’s word comes should “tell My word in truth,” a general parallel to Michaias’s commitment.
2-chronicles-18:13:11.why: Contrasts true prophetic speech with false dreams.

2-chronicles-18:13:12.summary: Paul passing on the Supper tradition received from the Lord has no specific link to Michaias’s oath.

2-chronicles-18:13:13.summary: Paul refuses to please human beings, loosely like Michaias resisting pressure to please the king.
2-chronicles-18:13:13.why: General theme of God over human approval.

2-chronicles-18:13:14.summary: Balaam must “speak what God puts in my mouth,” echoing Michaias’s vow to speak whatever God says.
2-chronicles-18:13:14.why: Repeated prophetic formula before a hostile king.

2-chronicles-18:14:0.summary: Casting bread on the water has no connection to Michaias’s ironic “Go up and prosper.”

2-chronicles-18:14:1.summary: Ironic “Rejoice and be glad” addressed to Idumea before judgment loosely parallels Michaias’s sarcastic “Go up and prosper.”

2-chronicles-18:14:2.summary: Jesus’ “Sleep on now and rest” in Gethsemane has no specific link to Michaias’s answer about Ramoth-galaad.
2-chronicles-18:14:2.why: Only a possible ironic tone; no shared content.

2-chronicles-18:14:3.summary: Amos’s ironic summons to sin at Bethel and Gilgal parallels the sarcastic tone of Michaias’s “Go up and prosper.”

2-chronicles-18:14:5.summary: Elijah’s mocking advice to Baal’s prophets parallels Michaias’s ironic reply, but the setting differs.
2-chronicles-18:14:5.why: Another prophet using sarcasm against false prophecy.

2-chronicles-18:15:1.summary: “I adjure Thee by God” shares the oath-demand formula with the king putting Michaias under oath.

2-chronicles-18:15:2.summary: Exorcists “solemnly charge” by Jesus’ name, a loose parallel to the king’s oath in the Lord’s name.
2-chronicles-18:15:2.why: Only the adjuration formula is shared.

2-chronicles-18:15:3.summary: Saul’s rash curse on eating bread does not involve putting a prophet under oath to speak truth.

2-chronicles-18:15:4.summary: The high priest’s “I adjure Thee by the living God to tell us” closely parallels the king putting Michaias under oath to speak truth.
2-chronicles-18:15:4.why: Authority demands a sworn truthful answer.

2-chronicles-18:16:0.summary: Crowds “as sheep having no shepherd” echoes Michaias’s vision of Israel scattered like shepherdless sheep.

2-chronicles-18:16:5.summary: “Like sheep without a shepherd” directly echoes Michaias’s image of Israel without a leader.
2-chronicles-18:16:5.why: Gospel reuse of the prophetic image.

2-chronicles-18:16:1.summary: Sheep “scattered on every mountain” because there were “no shepherds” closely matches Michaias’s vision.
2-chronicles-18:16:1.why: Develops the scattered-sheep image into judgment on leaders.

2-chronicles-18:16:2.summary: Sheep become plunder “for lack of shepherds,” echoing Israel scattered without a shepherd.
2-chronicles-18:16:2.why: Links leaderless people to failed shepherds.

2-chronicles-18:16:3.summary: Moses asks that the congregation “not be like sheep without a shepherd,” the source of Michaias’s image.
2-chronicles-18:16:3.why: Original use of the shepherdless-sheep phrase.

2-chronicles-18:16:6.summary: David’s message after Saul’s death about being anointed king shares no specific element with the scattered-sheep vision.
2-chronicles-18:16:6.why: Only a general idea of a dead king.

2-chronicles-18:16:7.summary: Jehu’s challenge to set up a master’s son as king has no shepherd or scattering imagery.

2-chronicles-18:16:8.summary: The king of Israel is shot and dies at sunset, fulfilling Michaias’s vision that Israel has no leader.

2-chronicles-18:16:9.summary: Shepherds who “scatter” God’s sheep are judged, developing the image of scattered, shepherdless Israel.

2-chronicles-18:16:10.summary: False diviners leave the people “like sheep” mistreated, linking false prophecy with leaderless sheep as in Michaias’s scene.
2-chronicles-18:16:10.why: Connects lying prophets with scattered flock.

2-chronicles-18:16:11.summary: Ahab’s death and the herald’s “Each man to his own city” fulfill “let each return to his house in peace.”

2-chronicles-18:16:12.summary: Striking the shepherds and scattering the sheep shares the image, though the Saints wording here targets the shepherds.

2-chronicles-18:16:13.summary: Jesus’ reply about the Son of Man on the clouds has no link to the scattered-sheep vision.

2-chronicles-18:16:14.summary: David is called to “shepherd My people Israel,” a general king-as-shepherd link to Israel without a leader.

2-chronicles-18:17:1.summary: The stiff-necked man who rejects reproof and suddenly meets ruin loosely fits Ahab’s rejection of Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:17:2.summary: Earlier the king said Michaias “does not prophesy good concerning me,” which he now repeats.
2-chronicles-18:17:2.why: Same-chapter callback to the king’s complaint.

2-chronicles-18:17:3.summary: Leaders accuse Jeremiah of lying when his message is unwelcome, like the king dismissing Michaias.
2-chronicles-18:17:3.why: Rejection of an unwelcome true prophet.

2-chronicles-18:18:0.summary: A vision of thrones and the Ancient of Days “seated” parallels Michaias seeing the Lord seated on His throne.

2-chronicles-18:18:1.summary: “I saw the Lord seated on a throne” with attendants standing matches Michaias’s throne vision.
2-chronicles-18:18:1.why: Closest parallel throne-room vision with prophetic commission.

2-chronicles-18:18:2.summary: God’s angels and powers who do His will relate generally to the “host of heaven” standing beside the throne.

2-chronicles-18:18:3.summary: Jacob calls a place “the camp of God,” only loosely related to the heavenly host around the throne.
2-chronicles-18:18:3.why: Only the idea of God’s host.

2-chronicles-18:18:5.summary: Shares only the formula “Hear the Lord’s word.”

2-chronicles-18:18:6.summary: Stephen sees God’s glory and Jesus at God’s right hand, a loose parallel to a vision of the Lord with the host at His right.
2-chronicles-18:18:6.why: Another heavenly vision in a hostile setting.

2-chronicles-18:18:7.summary: “Now hear the Lord’s word” addressed to someone silencing a prophet echoes the formula and setting loosely.
2-chronicles-18:18:7.why: Prophet answering opposition with God’s word.

2-chronicles-18:18:8.summary: Heavenly agents sent by the Lord to patrol the earth loosely parallel the host standing ready before the Lord.

2-chronicles-18:18:9.summary: Isaiah’s “Hear the word of the Lord” to a king shares the formula, introducing judgment.
2-chronicles-18:18:9.why: Common formula before announcing doom to a king.

2-chronicles-18:18:10.summary: “Hear the Lord’s word, Zedekiah king of Judah” shares the formula addressed to a king.
2-chronicles-18:18:10.why: Prophetic word addressed to a king.

2-chronicles-18:18:11.summary: Shares only the formula “hear the Lord’s word” addressed to rulers.

2-chronicles-18:18:12.summary: Shares only the formula “Hear the Lord’s word” addressed to rulers.

2-chronicles-18:18:13.summary: “Hear the Lord’s word, kings of Judah” shares the formula and introduces evils on the place.

2-chronicles-18:19:0.summary: Both strength and rout “come from the Lord,” generally matching the Lord determining Ahab’s fall.

2-chronicles-18:19:1.summary: The Greek-based Saints wording of Isaiah 54:16 does not carry God creating a destroyer as the label assumes.
2-chronicles-18:19:1.why: No clear shared element in the shown text.

2-chronicles-18:19:2.summary: “I, the Lord, have led that prophet astray” parallels the Lord seeking one to deceive Ahab through prophets.

2-chronicles-18:19:4.summary: God sends “a working of delusion, so that they believe the falsehood,” parallel to the deception sent on Ahab.
2-chronicles-18:19:4.why: Divine judgment through delusion on those rejecting truth.

2-chronicles-18:19:5.summary: “Impiety falls” is a general proverb loosely matching Ahab going up to “fall.”
2-chronicles-18:19:5.why: General principle of the wicked falling.

2-chronicles-18:19:6.summary: The Saints wording of Job 12:16 speaks of God’s might and knowledge, without the deceiver-and-deceived idea the label assumes.

2-chronicles-18:19:7.summary: A king warned against provoking war “so that you fall” loosely parallels Ahab enticed to go up and fall.
2-chronicles-18:19:7.why: Another king rushing into a fatal war.

2-chronicles-18:19:8.summary: God “tempts no one” stands in tension with the Lord seeking one to deceive Ahab.
2-chronicles-18:19:8.why: Raises the question of divine deception.

2-chronicles-18:19:9.summary: God sends a message that hardens hearers, loosely parallel to judicial deception of Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:20:0.summary: Angels and the devil “stand before the Lord,” like the spirit coming out to stand before the Lord in a heavenly council.

2-chronicles-18:20:1.summary: The serpent deceiving Eve shares the deception theme but not the heavenly-council setting.

2-chronicles-18:20:2.summary: Satan and his ministers disguising themselves share the theme of deceptive spirits loosely.

2-chronicles-18:20:3.summary: The devil comes “to stand before the Lord” among the angels, paralleling the spirit standing before the Lord.

2-chronicles-18:21:0.summary: The devil as a liar with “no truth in him” loosely parallels the “lying spirit.”

2-chronicles-18:21:2.summary: The devil “deceiving the whole inhabited world” shares the deceiving-spirit theme loosely.

2-chronicles-18:21:3.summary: “God sent an evil spirit” between Abimelech and Shechem parallels God permitting a lying spirit against Ahab.
2-chronicles-18:21:3.why: God using a harmful spirit as judgment.

2-chronicles-18:21:4.summary: Satan goes out “to deceive the nations” and gather them for war, loosely like the spirit luring Ahab to battle.

2-chronicles-18:21:5.summary: The same heavenly council where the Lord asks “Who will deceive Ahab,” directly preceding this verse.

2-chronicles-18:21:6.summary: Loving a curse that returns on oneself has no specific link to the lying spirit.

2-chronicles-18:21:7.summary: The Lord grants the devil limited permission over Job, like the Lord authorizing the spirit: “Go out and do so.”
2-chronicles-18:21:7.why: Heavenly permission given to a hostile spirit.

2-chronicles-18:21:8.summary: The Lord gives the devil leave, and “the devil went out from the Lord,” like the spirit sent out.

2-chronicles-18:21:9.summary: The serpent’s lie to Eve shares the theme of a deceiving spirit’s false word.

2-chronicles-18:21:10.summary: Michaias concludes the Lord has put “a lying spirit in the mouth of all these prophets,” directly applying this verse.

2-chronicles-18:21:11.summary: Distinguishing “the spirit of truth and the spirit of error” relates generally to the lying spirit in prophets.

2-chronicles-18:21:12.summary: The beast “deceiveth those dwelling upon the earth” shares only the deception theme.

2-chronicles-18:22:0.summary: “I, the Lord, have led that prophet astray” parallels the Lord putting a lying spirit in the prophets.

2-chronicles-18:22:1.summary: “The Lord mixed for them a spirit of wandering” closely parallels the Lord putting a lying spirit in prophets.
2-chronicles-18:22:1.why: God sending a misleading spirit as judgment.

2-chronicles-18:22:2.summary: The Saints wording of Job 12:16 lacks the deceiver-and-deceived phrase the label relies on.
2-chronicles-18:22:2.why: Greek-based text does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-18:22:3.summary: “Deceiving spirits” and “liars” share the theme of lying spirits behind false teaching.

2-chronicles-18:22:4.summary: The king’s complaint that Michaias prophesies “only evil” is answered by “the Lord has spoken evil against you.”

2-chronicles-18:22:5.summary: “False apostles, deceitful workers” share the theme of deceptive messengers.

2-chronicles-18:22:6.summary: False prophets arising to “lead astray” share the theme of deceptive prophecy.

2-chronicles-18:22:7.summary: Evils happening to the lawless generally parallel the Lord speaking evil against Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:22:8.summary: The Lord “planning calamities” loosely parallels the Lord speaking evil against Ahab.

2-chronicles-18:22:9.summary: The king complained that Michaias’s prophecies are “for evil,” and here Michaias declares the Lord has spoken evil against him.

2-chronicles-18:22:10.summary: God hardening Pharaoh’s heart loosely parallels God sending a lying spirit to lead Ahab to ruin.

2-chronicles-18:22:11.summary: The woe on Judas the betrayer shares no specific element with the lying spirit in Ahab’s prophets.

2-chronicles-18:22:12.summary: “I am shaping evils against you” parallels the Lord speaking evil against Ahab in a general way.

2-chronicles-18:22:13.summary: Joash’s fable of the achouch and cedar has no link to the lying spirit.

2-chronicles-18:22:14.summary: God sends “a working of delusion” to those refusing truth, paralleling the lying spirit sent to Ahab’s prophets.

2-chronicles-18:22:15.summary: Jesus’ woe on His betrayer has no specific link to the lying spirit.

2-chronicles-18:22:16.summary: The Lord answers idolaters coming to a prophet “in the things in which his mind is entangled,” akin to judicial deception through prophets.
2-chronicles-18:22:16.why: God answering the insincere with deception.

2-chronicles-18:23:6.summary: Sedekias son of Chanana, who strikes Michaias, is the false prophet who made the iron horns.
2-chronicles-18:23:6.why: Identifies the striker and his false prophecy.

2-chronicles-18:23:0.summary: Jesus is struck and taunted “Prophesy!”, paralleling a prophet struck and mocked about the Spirit’s word.

2-chronicles-18:23:1.summary: Jeremiah is struck by a religious official and put in the trap, like Michaias struck by a prophet.
2-chronicles-18:23:1.why: Parallel abuse of a true prophet.

2-chronicles-18:23:2.summary: The servant gives his “cheeks to slaps,” loosely paralleling Michaias struck on the jaw.
2-chronicles-18:23:2.why: Suffering servant image of patient abuse.

2-chronicles-18:23:3.summary: Jesus is slapped and taunted “Prophesy to us,” paralleling Sedekias striking Michaias and mocking his prophetic Spirit.

2-chronicles-18:23:5.summary: A priest is rebuked for joining in reviling Jeremiah, a loose parallel to official hostility to Michaias.
2-chronicles-18:23:5.why: Religious opposition to a true prophet.

2-chronicles-18:23:7.summary: “They will strike Israel’s tribes on the cheek” shares the striking-on-the-cheek image.
2-chronicles-18:23:7.why: Striking on the cheek as humiliation.

2-chronicles-18:23:8.summary: Giving the cheek to the one striking him shares the image of being struck on the face.

2-chronicles-18:23:9.summary: The Pharisees’ question about blindness has no specific link to Sedekias striking Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:23:10.summary: An officer slaps Jesus for His answer to the high priest, paralleling Michaias struck for his word.
2-chronicles-18:23:10.why: Blow given to a truthful speaker.

2-chronicles-18:23:11.summary: Ananias orders Paul struck on the mouth, paralleling a prophet struck for speaking.
2-chronicles-18:23:11.why: Speaker of truth struck by authority.

2-chronicles-18:24:0.summary: God’s judgment on the false prophets Ahab and Zedekiah loosely parallels Michaias’s warning to the false prophet Sedekias.

2-chronicles-18:24:1.summary: “When they know, they will be ashamed” loosely matches Sedekias seeing the truth on that day.

2-chronicles-18:24:2.summary: Jeremiah announces the false prophet’s death, which follows, paralleling Michaias’s prediction against Sedekias.
2-chronicles-18:24:2.why: True prophet’s word against a false prophet fulfilled.

2-chronicles-18:24:3.summary: “Enter your inner rooms … hide” shares the hiding-in-a-chamber image but in a protective sense.
2-chronicles-18:24:3.why: Shared image of hiding in rooms.

2-chronicles-18:24:4.summary: The son of Ader flees “into the inner chamber,” the same chamber-to-chamber hiding idiom.
2-chronicles-18:24:4.why: Same idiom of hiding in an inner room after defeat.

2-chronicles-18:24:5.summary: God’s punishment on the false prophet Shemaiah loosely parallels judgment on Sedekias.

2-chronicles-18:25:0.summary: The king earlier summoned Michaias by a eunuch; now he orders him taken away, in the same narrative.

2-chronicles-18:25:1.summary: Maasias “the city ruler” under Josiah shares only an office title with Emer the city’s ruler.

2-chronicles-18:25:2.summary: Felix dismisses Paul and leaves him bound, loosely like the king sending Michaias to custody.

2-chronicles-18:25:3.summary: Jeremiah is put in the pit of Malchiah “the king’s son,” loosely paralleling Michaias handed to Joash the king’s son.
2-chronicles-18:25:3.why: Prophet confined under a king’s son.

2-chronicles-18:25:4.summary: Jeremiah is imprisoned for an unwelcome word and contrasts the lying prophets, closely paralleling Michaias’s treatment (shown text truncated).
2-chronicles-18:25:4.why: True prophet jailed while false prophets are believed.

2-chronicles-18:26:0.summary: Asa angrily puts a prophet in prison, paralleling the king imprisoning Michaias for his word.

2-chronicles-18:26:1.summary: Apostles placed in prison share the general theme of messengers imprisoned.

2-chronicles-18:26:2.summary: People rejoice over the two prophets who tormented them, a loose parallel to hostility toward Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:26:3.summary: Paul’s imprisonments share only the general theme of a servant of God jailed.

2-chronicles-18:26:4.summary: Accusations against Jesus before Pilate have no specific link to Michaias’s imprisonment.

2-chronicles-18:26:5.summary: The Saints wording about the wicked lording it over enemies does not specifically relate to the king’s order.

2-chronicles-18:26:6.summary: Herod, rebuked by John, shuts him up in prison, paralleling a king jailing the prophet who rebuked him.

2-chronicles-18:26:7.summary: The fool “trusting himself” loosely fits the king confidently expecting to “return in peace.”

2-chronicles-18:26:8.summary: Destruction coming when people say “Peace” loosely parallels the king’s confident “until I return in peace.”

2-chronicles-18:26:9.summary: The Pharisees’ Beelzebul charge has no specific link to the order to imprison Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:26:11.summary: “Bread of tears” resembles “bread of affliction” in form only.

2-chronicles-18:26:12.summary: David’s complaint about Nabal repaying evil for good has no link to Michaias’s imprisonment.

2-chronicles-18:26:13.summary: Eating ashes like bread and mixing drink with weeping resembles the “bread of affliction” idiom loosely.

2-chronicles-18:26:14.summary: The crowd demands Paul be removed for his words, a loose parallel to hostility toward Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:26:15.summary: The king who demanded “nothing but truth” now jails Michaias for speaking it.

2-chronicles-18:26:16.summary: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and puts him in the trap, paralleling Michaias’s abuse and confinement.

2-chronicles-18:26:17.summary: “Thus they persecuted the prophets before you” generally covers prophets like Michaias.

2-chronicles-18:26:18.summary: “Bread of affliction and scant water” closely matches “bread of affliction and water of affliction.”

2-chronicles-18:26:19.summary: One who says “May it be well with me” despite warning loosely fits the king expecting to return in peace.

2-chronicles-18:27:0.summary: Jesus’ warning about scribes before all the people has no link to Michaias’s challenge.

2-chronicles-18:27:1.summary: “Let the one who has ears hear” shares only a general call to hear.

2-chronicles-18:27:2.summary: “Hear words, you peoples!” closely echoes Michaias’s “Hear, all you peoples!”
2-chronicles-18:27:2.why: Identical prophetic summons, also from a Micah.

2-chronicles-18:27:3.summary: Sinners who say evils will not come upon them parallel the king’s confidence of returning in peace.

2-chronicles-18:27:4.summary: “Hear and understand” shares only a general summons to listen.

2-chronicles-18:27:5.summary: Paul pronounces an immediate sign of judgment on a false prophet, loosely like Michaias staking his word on the outcome.

2-chronicles-18:27:6.summary: “Listen to Me, all of you” shares only a general summons.
