2-chronicles-18:27:7.summary: Moses stakes his authority on the outcome: if they die normally, “the Lord has not sent me,” like Michaias’s test.

2-chronicles-18:29:0.summary: Saul disguises himself with “other garments” before his fatal battle, as the king of Israel does.

2-chronicles-18:29:1.summary: A prophet disguises himself before the king of Israel, a loose disguise parallel.

2-chronicles-18:29:2.summary: Warning against an enemy’s entreaty has no specific link to the king’s disguise.

2-chronicles-18:29:3.summary: No one can hide from the Lord, implicitly undercutting the king’s attempt to cover himself.

2-chronicles-18:29:4.summary: Josiah enters battle ignoring God’s word and is shot by archers, closely paralleling the disguised king’s fate.
2-chronicles-18:29:4.why: Parallel fatal battle of a king.

2-chronicles-18:29:5.summary: Jeroboam sends his wife to inquire of a prophet (disguise not visible in the truncated text), a loose parallel.

2-chronicles-18:29:6.summary: The adulterer conceals his face thinking no one sees, loosely like the king covering himself.

2-chronicles-18:29:7.summary: Empty, deceitful speech among neighbors has no specific link to the king’s disguise.

2-chronicles-18:30:0.summary: Judging “the small and the great alike” shares only a phrase, used in an unrelated sense.

2-chronicles-18:30:1.summary: The prophet tells Ahab his life will be for the Syrian king he released, explaining Syria’s targeting of the king of Israel.
2-chronicles-18:30:1.why: Background to Ahab’s death at Syria’s hand.

2-chronicles-18:30:2.summary: Ahab spares the son of Ader and makes a covenant, background to the later Syrian enmity.

2-chronicles-18:30:3.summary: Death “from younger to older” for not seeking the Lord shares only a phrase pattern.

2-chronicles-18:30:4.summary: Striking men “from small to great” with blindness shares only the phrase.

2-chronicles-18:31:0.summary: Surrounded Judah “cried to the Lord” and was delivered, paralleling Jehoshaphat crying out when encircled.
2-chronicles-18:31:0.why: Cry for help in battle answered by God.

2-chronicles-18:31:1.summary: Pushed to fall, “the Lord took hold of me,” a general parallel to the Lord saving Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-18:31:2.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us” states general protection.

2-chronicles-18:31:3.summary: God turning a king’s heart loosely parallels God turning the commanders away.

2-chronicles-18:31:4.summary: God as “a helper in the afflictions” states general help.

2-chronicles-18:31:5.summary: “Had the Lord not helped me” expresses rescue from death in general terms.

2-chronicles-18:31:6.summary: Prayer for favor before a king only loosely parallels Jehoshaphat’s cry.

2-chronicles-18:31:7.summary: The Lord hears “the voice of my petition,” generally matching the Lord answering Jehoshaphat’s cry.

2-chronicles-18:31:8.summary: God “delivered us from so great a death,” a general deliverance parallel.

2-chronicles-18:31:9.summary: An angel of the Lord encamps around and rescues, generally like God turning attackers away.

2-chronicles-18:31:10.summary: The Saints wording of Proverbs 16:7 about righteousness and sacrifice lacks the enemies-at-peace idea the label assumes.
2-chronicles-18:31:10.why: Greek-based text does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-18:31:11.summary: God putting something “in the king’s heart” loosely parallels God turning the commanders.

2-chronicles-18:31:12.summary: Israel, trapped by Pharaoh’s army, “cried out to the Lord,” paralleling Jehoshaphat’s cry when encircled.
2-chronicles-18:31:12.why: Cry to God when surrounded by enemies.

2-chronicles-18:31:13.summary: The Lord strengthening Uzziah against foreigners is a general divine-help parallel.
2-chronicles-18:31:13.why: God helps Judah’s king in war.

2-chronicles-18:31:14.summary: Asa “cried to the Lord” before a great army and was saved, paralleling Jehoshaphat’s cry.
2-chronicles-18:31:14.why: Chronicler’s pattern of crying out and deliverance.

2-chronicles-18:31:15.summary: The Lord stirring Cyrus’s spirit loosely parallels God turning the commanders away.

2-chronicles-18:33:0.summary: Men going with Absalom “in their simplicity” likely relates to the Hebrew “at random,” which the Saints “with accurate aim” does not carry.
2-chronicles-18:33:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-18:33:1.summary: Archers shoot Josiah, who asks to be brought out of battle, closely paralleling the wounded king’s words.
2-chronicles-18:33:1.why: Parallel death of a king in battle.

2-chronicles-18:34:0.summary: “Evils will pursue those who sin” is a general proverb fitting Ahab’s death.

2-chronicles-18:34:1.summary: Michaias’s vision of Israel without a leader is fulfilled in the king’s death.

2-chronicles-18:34:2.summary: The proverb about a murderer’s guarantor has no specific link to the king’s death.

2-chronicles-18:34:3.summary: “Evils overtake you” for sin is a general retribution principle.

2-chronicles-18:34:4.summary: Michaias said the king would not return in peace; his death confirms the prophecy.

2-chronicles-19:2:0.summary: Hating “those who hate Thee” contrasts with Jehoshaphat befriending “one hated by the Lord.”
2-chronicles-19:2:0.why: Loyalty to God against His enemies.

2-chronicles-19:2:1.summary: Greeting a false teacher “shares in his evil works,” loosely like helping a sinner.

2-chronicles-19:2:2.summary: Friendship with the world as hostility to God parallels befriending one hated by the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:2:4.summary: Not sharing in works of darkness generally parallels warning against helping a sinner.

2-chronicles-19:2:5.summary: “Wrath came upon Judah” shares the formula of the Lord’s wrath coming for sin.

2-chronicles-19:2:6.summary: Anani the prophet, father of Jehu, rebukes Asa for relying on Syria’s king, a parallel alliance rebuke.
2-chronicles-19:2:6.why: Father and son prophets rebuking alliances.

2-chronicles-19:2:7.summary: Jehu son of Hanani is the same prophet, earlier speaking the Lord’s word to Baasha.

2-chronicles-19:2:8.summary: “Wrath came upon him and upon Judah” shares the wrath formula.

2-chronicles-19:2:9.summary: Jehoshaphat’s acts are recorded in the accounts of “Jehu son of Anani,” the same prophet.

2-chronicles-19:2:10.summary: The note that prophets were once called “the seer” has no specific link to Jehu’s rebuke.

2-chronicles-19:2:11.summary: The fleshly mind as “hostility toward God” loosely relates to one hated by the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:2:12.summary: Being troubled in God’s wrath for lawless deeds is a general parallel to wrath coming on Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-19:2:13.summary: “Those hating Him” as God’s enemies loosely parallels “one hated by the Lord.”

2-chronicles-19:2:14.summary: God’s wrath against ungodliness is a general parallel to wrath from the Lord on Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-19:2:15.summary: “Them that hate Me” shares the idea of those who hate God, in a different context.

2-chronicles-19:2:16.summary: The word against Baasha came through “Jehu the prophet,” the same prophet who rebukes Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-19:2:17.summary: Moses’ blessing on Levi against those who hate him shares only the word “hate.”

2-chronicles-19:2:18.summary: Ahab says he hates the Lord’s prophet Michaias, showing why Ahab is “one hated by the Lord” whom Jehoshaphat helped.

2-chronicles-19:2:19.summary: Approving those who practice evil loosely parallels helping a sinner.

2-chronicles-19:2:20.summary: God repays “them that hate Him,” a general parallel to the Lord’s stance toward Ahab.

2-chronicles-19:2:21.summary: “Haters of God” in a vice list shares only the hating-God idea.

2-chronicles-19:2:22.summary: God repays “them that hate Me,” generally relating to wrath for siding with God’s haters.

2-chronicles-19:2:23.summary: Hating Jesus and the Father shares only the word “hate,” not the alliance issue.

2-chronicles-19:2:24.summary: “Those who hate Me” in the commandments shares the concept of hating God.

2-chronicles-19:2:25.summary: The king’s hand finding those who hate him has no specific link to Jehu’s rebuke.

2-chronicles-19:2:26.summary: Being judged by the Lord as discipline loosely fits the wrath tempered by good things in Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-19:2:27.summary: The righteous holds the wicked in contempt but honors the God-fearing, the opposite of befriending one hated by the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:2:28.summary: The world’s hatred of Jesus’ disciples does not address helping a sinner.

2-chronicles-19:2:29.summary: Jehu son of Hanani speaks against Baasha’s house, the same prophet active earlier.

2-chronicles-19:2:30.summary: Jehoshaphat went up with the king of Israel to Ramoth-galaad, the help Jehu rebukes.

2-chronicles-19:2:31.summary: Ahab “sold to do evil before the Lord” explains why he is called a sinner hated by the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:2:32.summary: Warning not to join with the ungodly loosely parallels Jehoshaphat’s alliance with Ahab (shown text truncated).

2-chronicles-19:2:33.summary: Proclaiming God’s righteousness has no link to Jehu’s rebuke.

2-chronicles-19:3:0.summary: Wrath turned from Rehoboam because “there were also good things in Judah,” echoing “good things have been found in you.”
2-chronicles-19:3:0.why: Chronicler’s mitigation of wrath by good found.

2-chronicles-19:3:1.summary: Jeroboam’s son is mourned because “a good word concerning the Lord was found in him,” echoing good found in Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-19:3:1.why: Same idiom of good found amid judgment.

2-chronicles-19:3:2.summary: Esdras “set it in his heart to seek the law,” echoing Jehoshaphat directing his heart to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:3:3.summary: “Every heart directed to seek the Lord” closely matches Jehoshaphat “directed your heart to seek the Lord.”

2-chronicles-19:3:4.summary: Rehoboam did evil because he “did not direct his heart to seek the Lord,” the opposite of Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-19:3:4.why: Contrasting use of the same phrase.

2-chronicles-19:3:6.summary: Paul’s struggle with indwelling sin has no specific link to good found in Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-19:3:7.summary: “My heart is ready, God” loosely parallels a heart directed toward the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:4:0.summary: John will “turn” the disobedient to the Lord, paralleling Jehoshaphat turning the people back to God.

2-chronicles-19:4:1.summary: Samuel calls Israel to return to the Lord and remove the groves, paralleling Jehoshaphat’s reform and turning people back.

2-chronicles-19:4:2.summary: Hezekiah plans a covenant to turn away wrath, a general reform parallel.

2-chronicles-19:4:3.summary: Asa expels abominations from Judah and Ephraim’s hill country and gathers people, closely paralleling Jehoshaphat’s reform (truncated).
2-chronicles-19:4:3.why: Earlier Judahite reform in same regions.

2-chronicles-19:4:4.summary: Restoring fathers’ hearts loosely parallels turning people back to the God of their fathers.

2-chronicles-19:4:5.summary: Abraham at the Well of the Oath (Beersheba) shares only the place name’s location.

2-chronicles-19:4:6.summary: Samuel traveling a circuit to judge Israel loosely parallels Jehoshaphat going out among the people.

2-chronicles-19:4:7.summary: Mentions “the mountain of Ephraim,” the northern boundary of Jehoshaphat’s circuit.

2-chronicles-19:4:8.summary: Mentions Ephraim’s hill country only geographically.

2-chronicles-19:4:9.summary: “From Dan to Beersheba” is a similar boundary formula to “from Beersabee to the mountain of Ephraim.”

2-chronicles-19:5:1.summary: Authorities appointed by God for justice loosely relates to Jehoshaphat appointing judges (truncated).

2-chronicles-19:5:2.summary: Governors sent by the king to punish evildoers loosely parallel judges appointed by the king.

2-chronicles-19:5:3.summary: Jehoshaphat also appoints judges in Jerusalem, continuing the same judicial reform.

2-chronicles-19:6:1.summary: Officials above officials watching over judgment loosely relate to judges accountable to the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:6:2.summary: Commands to do no injustice in judgment and not admire the mighty match the charge to the judges.

2-chronicles-19:6:3.summary: Jesus’ warning against greed shares only a “see to it” form.

2-chronicles-19:6:4.summary: Warning about being led astray by false messiahs shares only a “see” imperative.

2-chronicles-19:6:5.summary: “Take great care to do the commandments” loosely parallels “Consider what you are doing.”

2-chronicles-19:6:6.summary: “See … Be strong and act” shares a charge formula, not the judicial subject.

2-chronicles-19:6:7.summary: “Take care what you are about to do” closely echoes “Consider what you are doing,” in a different setting.

2-chronicles-19:6:8.summary: God judges among judges and rebukes unjust judging, matching “you judge for the Lord.”

2-chronicles-19:6:9.summary: The centurion’s “What are you about to do?” shares only a casual phrase.

2-chronicles-19:7:0.summary: God “a faithful God, and there is no unrighteousness,” matches “with the Lord our God there is no injustice.”
2-chronicles-19:7:0.why: God’s justice as standard for judges.

2-chronicles-19:7:1.summary: The Judge of all the earth doing justice generally parallels God without injustice.

2-chronicles-19:7:2.summary: “There is no partiality with God” matches no “admiration of a person’s status” with the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:7:4.summary: “Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!” echoes “with the Lord … there is no injustice.”

2-chronicles-19:7:5.summary: “You shall receive no gifts,” for gifts corrupt, matches the ban on “taking of gifts.”

2-chronicles-19:7:6.summary: “There is no partiality” shares the impartiality theme in a different setting.

2-chronicles-19:7:7.summary: God does not “admire their persons,” matching no “admiration of a person’s status.”
2-chronicles-19:7:7.why: Same Greek-based idiom of respecting persons.

2-chronicles-19:7:9.summary: “God shows no partiality” directly parallels no admiration of persons with the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:7:10.summary: Rulers “loving gifts” and failing in judgment are the opposite of the charge, and God promises to restore judges.

2-chronicles-19:7:11.summary: Nehemiah refrains from exploitation “because of the fear of God,” a general parallel.

2-chronicles-19:7:12.summary: Jesus “dost not look at people’s outward status,” paralleling impartiality.

2-chronicles-19:7:13.summary: “God does not favor a person’s outward standing” parallels divine impartiality.

2-chronicles-19:7:14.summary: Moses appoints leaders to judge the people, the model for Jehoshaphat’s judges.

2-chronicles-19:7:15.summary: Corrupt ruler and judge acting for gain contrast with the charge against taking gifts.

2-chronicles-19:7:16.summary: Rejecting the idea that God is unrighteous parallels “there is no injustice” with God.

2-chronicles-19:7:17.summary: “No partiality with Him” shares impartiality in a household setting.

2-chronicles-19:7:18.summary: The righteous man “shaking his hands free of gifts” and hating injustice matches the charge against bribes.

2-chronicles-19:7:19.summary: Judges chosen as “men who fear God” matches “let the fear of the Lord be upon you.”

2-chronicles-19:7:20.summary: The Father “who judges impartially” calls for conduct “in fear,” matching fear of the Lord and impartiality.

2-chronicles-19:7:21.summary: Joseph acts justly because “I fear God,” a general parallel.

2-chronicles-19:7:22.summary: “The Lord is judge, and with Him there is no prestige of persons” closely matches the verse.

2-chronicles-19:8:0.summary: Jehoshaphat earlier sent Levites and priests to teach the law, paralleling his appointing them to judge.
2-chronicles-19:8:0.why: Jehoshaphat’s earlier use of priests and Levites.

2-chronicles-19:8:1.summary: Judges deciding disputes is a general judicial parallel.

2-chronicles-19:8:3.summary: Levites serve as “scribes and judges,” matching Levites appointed to judge.

2-chronicles-19:8:4.summary: Moses’ system of God-fearing judges is the model for Jehoshaphat’s appointments (truncated).

2-chronicles-19:8:5.summary: Levitical priests decide “every dispute,” matching priests and Levites appointed for the Lord’s judgment.

2-chronicles-19:8:6.summary: Levites assigned to “give judgments” parallel Levites appointed as judges.

2-chronicles-19:9:0.summary: “Let the fear of the Lord be upon you” immediately precedes and matches “in the fear of the Lord.”

2-chronicles-19:9:1.summary: Strengthening the fear of God in a person loosely parallels acting in the fear of the Lord.

2-chronicles-19:9:2.summary: Moses’ charge to judges to judge justly because “judgment belongs unto God” parallels Jehoshaphat’s charge.

2-chronicles-19:9:3.summary: The ruler filled with “the fear of God,” judging righteously and girded with truth, matches fear and truth.
2-chronicles-19:9:3.why: Ideal judge in fear and truth.

2-chronicles-19:9:4.summary: Rulers ruling “with judgment” under a righteous king generally parallels the charge.

2-chronicles-19:10:1.summary: Wrath coming on all Israel for one man’s sin parallels the warning so “wrath does not come upon you and your brethren.”

2-chronicles-19:10:2.summary: Paul admonishing each one loosely parallels giving clear instruction.

2-chronicles-19:10:3.summary: “Admonish the disorderly” loosely parallels instructing brethren so they do not sin.

2-chronicles-19:10:4.summary: “Wrath has gone out from before the Lord” on the people shares the wrath-on-community idea.

2-chronicles-19:10:5.summary: The watchman must warn the lawless or bear responsibility, paralleling judges warning so wrath does not come on them.

2-chronicles-19:10:6.summary: The watchman who fails to warn bears blood guilt, paralleling judges’ duty to instruct.

2-chronicles-19:10:7.summary: “Wrath from the Lord has come upon you” recalls the wrath the judges are to avert.

2-chronicles-19:11:0.summary: The Jerusalem court of priests, Levites, and rulers is the body Amarias and Zabdias lead.

2-chronicles-19:11:1.summary: God showing Himself holy with the holy loosely parallels “the Lord will be with the good.”

2-chronicles-19:11:2.summary: Practicing what is just and “the God of peace will be with you” loosely parallels “the Lord will be with the good.”

2-chronicles-19:11:3.summary: “Be strengthened” shares only the exhortation to be strong.

2-chronicles-19:11:4.summary: The Lord directing a person’s steps is a general parallel to the Lord with the good.

2-chronicles-19:11:5.summary: God gives wisdom to “the person who is good before Him,” loosely matching the Lord with the good.

2-chronicles-19:11:6.summary: Joseph of Arimathea as “a good and righteous man” shares only the word “good.”

2-chronicles-19:11:7.summary: God dwelling with those who keep His word loosely parallels the Lord being with the good.

2-chronicles-19:11:8.summary: “Be strong … the Lord your God is with you” matches “Be strong and act, and the Lord will be with the good.”

2-chronicles-19:11:9.summary: “The Lord will be with you” in David’s charge to Solomon matches the commissioning formula.

2-chronicles-19:11:10.summary: A priest Amariah appears in the high-priestly line, possibly the same Amarias the priest.

2-chronicles-19:11:11.summary: A good man managing his words “with judgment” loosely relates to the judicial charge.

2-chronicles-19:11:12.summary: “Be strong and courageous” to Joshua matches the charge “Be strong and act.”

2-chronicles-19:11:13.summary: Walking good paths loosely relates to the Lord being with the good.

2-chronicles-19:11:14.summary: The judges’ earlier charge, “you judge for the Lord,” frames the leadership and exhortation here.

2-chronicles-19:11:15.summary: “Be courageous; be strong” shares the exhortation to be strong.

2-chronicles-19:11:16.summary: People “seek law” from a priest’s mouth, matching Amarias the priest leading “in every matter of the Lord.”
2-chronicles-19:11:16.why: Priest’s role in instruction and judgment.

2-chronicles-19:11:18.summary: God repays good work with life and evil with wrath, loosely relating to the Lord being with the good (truncated).

2-chronicles-19:11:19.summary: “Arise and act, and the Lord be with you” closely matches “Be strong and act, and the Lord will be with the good.”

2-chronicles-19:11:20.summary: “The Lord is with you while you are with Him” parallels the Lord being with the good.

2-chronicles-19:11:21.summary: Oversight “for all the Lord’s ministry and the king’s work” parallels the division into “matter of the Lord” and “matter of the king.”

2-chronicles-19:11:22.summary: “Arise and build” shares the charge-to-act formula.

2-chronicles-19:11:23.summary: Barnabas as “a good man” shares only the word “good.”

2-chronicles-20:1:0.summary: Isaiah taunts hostile nations that they will be defeated; the source only reports a coalition coming to war.
2-chronicles-20:1:0.why: General theme of nations failing against God’s people.

2-chronicles-20:1:1.summary: The psalm lists a coalition including “Moab” and “Ammon” and Idumeans plotting against God’s people, like the alliance attacking Jehoshaphat.
2-chronicles-20:1:1.why: Psalm voicing the kind of coalition threat described here.

2-chronicles-20:1:2.summary: Isaiah condemns Moab’s insolence; the source only names Moab among the invaders.
2-chronicles-20:1:2.why: Background on Moab’s arrogance toward Judah.

2-chronicles-20:1:3.summary: Both open an invasion narrative with “After these/this” and a foreign army coming against Judah after a king’s faithfulness.
2-chronicles-20:1:3.why: Similar narrative pattern of attack following reform.
2-chronicles-20:1:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-20:1:4.summary: The preceding verse closes Jehoshaphat’s reforms; the source’s “After this” follows it, but no shared content.

2-chronicles-20:1:5.summary: Revelation’s reproof of the church has no link to the Moabite-Ammonite invasion.

2-chronicles-20:1:6.summary: Both mention the Minaeans (“Minaioi”), the same people group found among Judah’s neighbors.
2-chronicles-20:1:6.why: Identifies the Minaeans elsewhere in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-20:1:7.summary: Only the same king’s reign links Jehoshaphat appointing judges with the later invasion.

2-chronicles-20:1:8.summary: Both describe allied kings coming up to wage war against Judah/Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-20:1:8.why: Comparable coalition threat in another reign.

2-chronicles-20:1:9.summary: Jehu warns that “wrath from the Lord” has come on Jehoshaphat; the invasion might be read as that wrath, but the text doesn’t say so.
2-chronicles-20:1:9.why: Possible interpretive background for the attack.

2-chronicles-20:1:10.summary: A prayer for gentle correction has no specific link to the invasion report.

2-chronicles-20:2:0.summary: Hazezon-tamar in Genesis matches “Asasanthamar,” which the source identifies as Engaddi.
2-chronicles-20:2:0.why: Identifies the ancient name of the place.

2-chronicles-20:2:1.summary: David stayed at En-gedi, the same place the source calls “Engaddi.”

2-chronicles-20:2:2.summary: This Judean wilderness town list may include En-gedi as “Ankades,” but the Greek form does not plainly show Engaddi.
2-chronicles-20:2:2.why: Possible listing of the same town.

2-chronicles-20:2:3.summary: The Song names the vineyards of En-gedi, the same place as the source’s “Engaddi.”

2-chronicles-20:2:4.summary: Mentions the Salt Sea; the source only says the army came “from beyond the sea.”
2-chronicles-20:2:4.why: Geographic background on the Dead Sea.

2-chronicles-20:2:5.summary: Mentions the Salt Sea as a boundary; the source’s “sea” is only implicitly the same.

2-chronicles-20:2:6.summary: Genesis names the Salt Sea where kings gathered; the source’s “sea” is only implicitly the same.
2-chronicles-20:2:6.why: Geographic background; another coalition of kings nearby.

2-chronicles-20:3:0.summary: Daniel likewise “set my face toward the Lord God” with fasts in a time of national crisis.
2-chronicles-20:3:0.why: Same posture of seeking God with fasting.

2-chronicles-20:3:1.summary: The prophet praises Jehoshaphat because he “directed your heart to seek the Lord,” as he does again here.
2-chronicles-20:3:1.why: Shows seeking the Lord as Jehoshaphat’s habit.

2-chronicles-20:3:2.summary: The king of Nineveh and the people “proclaimed a fast” to seek God’s mercy under threat.
2-chronicles-20:3:2.why: Parallel nationwide fast led from the throne.

2-chronicles-20:3:3.summary: Joel commands “Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service” and to cry to the Lord, as Jehoshaphat does.
2-chronicles-20:3:3.why: Prophetic model for a national fast.

2-chronicles-20:3:4.summary: All the people of Jerusalem and Judah assembled for a fast before the Lord.
2-chronicles-20:3:4.why: Another proclaimed fast for all Judah.

2-chronicles-20:3:5.summary: Joel calls to “Consecrate a fast” and turn to the Lord in a national emergency.
2-chronicles-20:3:5.why: Prophetic pattern of fasting and returning to God.

2-chronicles-20:3:6.summary: Esther calls a communal fast before facing deadly danger; similar response, different setting.
2-chronicles-20:3:6.why: Another leader-called fast in a crisis.

2-chronicles-20:3:7.summary: Israel gathered at Mizpah and fasted before the Lord; the shown text lacks the threat context.
2-chronicles-20:3:7.why: Earlier communal fast before the Lord.

2-chronicles-20:3:8.summary: Ezra “proclaimed a fast” to seek God for protection from enemies, and was heard.
2-chronicles-20:3:8.why: Close parallel of fasting to seek protection.

2-chronicles-20:3:9.summary: Jacob’s wrestling has no specific link to Jehoshaphat’s fear and fast in the shown text.

2-chronicles-20:3:10.summary: All Israel wept and “fasted that day” before the Lord; the shown text lacks the war context.
2-chronicles-20:3:10.why: Another communal fast before the Lord.

2-chronicles-20:3:11.summary: Hezekiah, in distress from an invading king, seeks the Lord and hears “Do not fear.”

2-chronicles-20:3:12.summary: Jesus’ teaching on whom to fear has no specific link beyond the word “fear.”

2-chronicles-20:3:13.summary: The psalmist fears yet hopes in God, as Jehoshaphat’s fear leads him to seek the Lord.

2-chronicles-20:3:14.summary: Mentions those who “gave their heart to seek the Lord”; shared phrase, different context.
2-chronicles-20:3:14.why: Chronicler’s recurring theme of seeking the Lord.

2-chronicles-20:3:15.summary: Jacob was “greatly afraid” of an approaching force and prayed to God for deliverance.
2-chronicles-20:3:15.why: Same pattern of fear leading to prayer.

2-chronicles-20:3:16.summary: The sailors’ fear of the Lord is reverence, not a link to Jehoshaphat’s fear of invasion.

2-chronicles-20:4:0.summary: God invites calling on Him “in the day of affliction”; general theme of seeking God in trouble.
2-chronicles-20:4:0.why: General encouragement to seek God in distress.

2-chronicles-20:4:1.summary: A plea for God’s help against enemies, since “human salvation is vain”; general theme only.

2-chronicles-20:4:2.summary: Only “Judea’s cities” overlaps; the psalm is about rebuilding, not gathering to seek God.

2-chronicles-20:4:3.summary: The poor man cried and the Lord heard him; general theme of seeking God.
2-chronicles-20:4:3.why: General assurance for those who seek God.

2-chronicles-20:4:4.summary: Only the phrase “cities of Judah” overlaps; appointing judges is unrelated to the assembly.

2-chronicles-20:5:1.summary: Hezekiah prays to the Lord God of Israel for rescue from an invading king, as Jehoshaphat does.

2-chronicles-20:5:2.summary: Josiah stood before the Lord in a public assembly; similar setting, different purpose.
2-chronicles-20:5:2.why: Another king leading the people before God.

2-chronicles-20:6:0.summary: David’s prayer also says God rules all things and that “In Thy hand are strength.”
2-chronicles-20:6:0.why: Close verbal echo in another royal prayer.

2-chronicles-20:6:1.summary: Deuteronomy confesses the Lord “is God in heaven above,” as Jehoshaphat’s prayer does.
2-chronicles-20:6:1.why: Echoes a core confession of God’s rule.

2-chronicles-20:6:2.summary: God’s authority over all in heaven and earth; similar theme of sovereignty, different wording.
2-chronicles-20:6:2.why: Theme of God ruling over kingdoms.

2-chronicles-20:6:3.summary: “God reigned over the nations,” echoing God ruling “over all the kingdoms of the nations.”

2-chronicles-20:6:4.summary: Rahab confesses “God in heaven above,” the same confession Jehoshaphat makes.

2-chronicles-20:6:5.summary: Heaven as God’s throne relates loosely to the source’s “God in heaven.”
2-chronicles-20:6:5.why: General picture of God’s heavenly rule.

2-chronicles-20:6:6.summary: The Lord dwelling “in the heights” relates loosely to God in heaven.

2-chronicles-20:6:7.summary: Peter asks who “could hinder God,” loosely like “no one can resist Thee.”

2-chronicles-20:6:8.summary: The petition for deliverance from evil has no specific link to the source’s confession.

2-chronicles-20:6:9.summary: Solomon’s temple prayer opens “Lord, the God of Israel… in heaven above,” like Jehoshaphat’s.
2-chronicles-20:6:9.why: Parallel opening of a temple prayer.

2-chronicles-20:6:10.summary: “Our God is in heaven above… He has done everything He wished,” matching God’s irresistible rule.
2-chronicles-20:6:10.why: Close echo of God’s heavenly sovereignty.

2-chronicles-20:6:11.summary: The Greek Daniel verse is about Nebuchadnezzar being led away, not God’s rule over kingdoms.
2-chronicles-20:6:11.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

2-chronicles-20:6:12.summary: Prayer addressed to God “in the heavens”; only a general overlap.

2-chronicles-20:6:13.summary: God gives the earth and kingdoms to whom He wills by “My great strength.”
2-chronicles-20:6:13.why: Theme of God’s rule over nations.

2-chronicles-20:6:14.summary: The shown verse only introduces “two things” heard; the power statement is not shown.

2-chronicles-20:6:15.summary: Uses the title “the God of your fathers”; a common formula.
2-chronicles-20:6:15.why: Background for the title used in prayer.

2-chronicles-20:6:16.summary: David addresses “Lord, God of… our fathers”; a shared formula in prayer.
2-chronicles-20:6:16.why: Similar address to God in prayer.

2-chronicles-20:6:17.summary: The Lord as “great King over all the earth” relates loosely to ruling all kingdoms.

2-chronicles-20:6:18.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom is given to another; theme of God over kingdoms (truncated range).

2-chronicles-20:6:19.summary: God names Himself “the God of your father”; shares only the ancestral title.

2-chronicles-20:6:20.summary: “Great strength is always at Thy disposal, and who will oppose the might of Thine arm?” echoes “no one can resist Thee.”
2-chronicles-20:6:20.why: Close echo of God’s irresistible might.

2-chronicles-20:7:0.summary: James calls Abraham “friend of God”; the Saints source says “Thy beloved,” so the shared title is weaker.

2-chronicles-20:7:1.summary: “Offspring of Abraham whom I loved” matches the source’s “descendants of Abraham, Thy beloved.”
2-chronicles-20:7:1.why: Same description of Abraham as beloved.

2-chronicles-20:7:2.summary: God promised Abram, “To your seed I will give this land,” the promise the prayer recalls.

2-chronicles-20:7:3.summary: “Thy hand destroyed nations, and Thou didst plant our fathers,” matching God destroying the land’s inhabitants.

2-chronicles-20:7:4.summary: Nehemiah recalls God’s covenant to give Abraham’s offspring the land of the Chananites.
2-chronicles-20:7:4.why: Parallel prayer recalling the land promise.

2-chronicles-20:7:5.summary: Recalls God leading Abraham through the land; the land gift itself isn’t shown.
2-chronicles-20:7:5.why: Background on Abraham in the land.

2-chronicles-20:7:6.summary: God gives the land “to your seed for ever,” as the prayer recalls.

2-chronicles-20:7:7.summary: God takes Israel as His people; general covenant theme only.

2-chronicles-20:7:8.summary: God promises to drive out the Amorites and others, the inhabitants the prayer says He destroyed.

2-chronicles-20:7:9.summary: God drove nations out before His people and gave Israel to Himself “for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:7:9.why: Parallel royal prayer recalling the conquest.

2-chronicles-20:7:10.summary: Asa’s prayer against a great multitude; fits Jehoshaphat’s prayer generally, not this verse’s land theme.

2-chronicles-20:7:11.summary: Covenant with Abraham’s seed as “everlasting”; the land is not mentioned here.

2-chronicles-20:7:12.summary: The Exodus deliverance formula does not mention the land, its inhabitants, or Abraham.

2-chronicles-20:7:13.summary: Lazarus called “our friend”; the Saints source says “beloved,” and the link is only through a title.

2-chronicles-20:7:14.summary: Israel as God’s treasured people; general election theme only.

2-chronicles-20:7:15.summary: God “gave you a land for which you did not labour,” as the prayer recalls God giving the land.
2-chronicles-20:7:15.why: Recalls the land as God’s gift.

2-chronicles-20:7:16.summary: Jesus calling disciples “friends” links only via “friend,” which the Saints source does not use.

2-chronicles-20:8:0.summary: Solomon builds “a house for the name of the Lord,” the sanctuary the prayer recalls.
2-chronicles-20:8:0.why: The temple building recalled in the prayer.

2-chronicles-20:9:1.summary: Solomon prayed that defeated Israel might “pray and plead in this house,” the promise Jehoshaphat invokes.

2-chronicles-20:9:2.summary: Solomon asks God to hear prayer toward the house where His name is invoked.
2-chronicles-20:9:2.why: Promise underlying “Thy name is upon this house.”

2-chronicles-20:9:3.summary: God comes to bless where He names His name; general link to the house bearing His name.
2-chronicles-20:9:3.why: Background on God’s name and presence.

2-chronicles-20:9:4.summary: Gathering in Jesus’ name has no specific link to the temple appeal.

2-chronicles-20:9:5.summary: Solomon lists “famine… death… whatever calamity,” the same disasters Jehoshaphat recalls.
2-chronicles-20:9:5.why: Source of the list of calamities.

2-chronicles-20:9:6.summary: Shares the phrase “My name is upon,” but about an angel, not the temple.

2-chronicles-20:9:7.summary: Sirach lists “death… sword, calamities, famine,” closely echoing the source’s list.

2-chronicles-20:10:3.summary: Jephthah recounts that Israel did not take Moab or Ammon’s land when coming up from Egypt.
2-chronicles-20:10:3.why: Same history of sparing Moab and Ammon.

2-chronicles-20:10:4.summary: The same invasion by Moab and Ammon against Jehoshaphat.

2-chronicles-20:10:5.summary: Edom (Mount Seir) refused Israel passage when coming from Egypt, and Israel turned away.

2-chronicles-20:10:6.summary: The same Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir are routed later in the chapter.

2-chronicles-20:11:0.summary: Moab, Ammon and others plot to destroy Israel “from being a nation” (truncated range).
2-chronicles-20:11:0.why: Psalm voicing the same coalition threat.

2-chronicles-20:11:1.summary: The Saints source lacks the idea of repaying evil for good that this proverb shares with other English versions.

2-chronicles-20:11:2.summary: Repaying evil for good is not in the Saints source text.

2-chronicles-20:11:3.summary: Jephthah tells Ammon that Israel will inherit what the Lord allotted, like the source’s “our inheritance.”
2-chronicles-20:11:3.why: Same claim of a God-given inheritance against Ammon.

2-chronicles-20:11:4.summary: Repaying evils for good is not in the Saints source text.

2-chronicles-20:11:5.summary: Repaying evils is not in the Saints source text.

2-chronicles-20:11:6.summary: Joseph’s charge of repaying evil for good has no link to the Saints source.

2-chronicles-20:12:0.summary: “I lifted my eyes… My help is from the Lord,” like “our eyes are upon Thee.”
2-chronicles-20:12:0.why: Same image of looking to God for help.

2-chronicles-20:12:1.summary: “My eyes are continually toward the Lord,” matching “our eyes are upon Thee.”

2-chronicles-20:12:2.summary: “My eyes are toward Thee, Lord,” matching the source’s closing confession.

2-chronicles-20:12:3.summary: “So our eyes turn to the Lord our God,” closely echoing “our eyes are upon Thee.”

2-chronicles-20:12:4.summary: The Lord judges for His people when He sees them weakened; loosely like the plea for judgment in weakness.
2-chronicles-20:12:4.why: God’s compassion for His powerless people.

2-chronicles-20:12:5.summary: Paul was “burdened far beyond our strength” and relied on God, like Judah’s lack of strength.
2-chronicles-20:12:5.why: Reliance on God when strength fails.

2-chronicles-20:12:6.summary: “Let nations be judged before Thee,” a plea like “wilt Thou not judge among them?”
2-chronicles-20:12:6.why: Same plea for God to judge hostile nations.

2-chronicles-20:12:7.summary: A plea for God to judge against an unholy nation; individual rather than national.

2-chronicles-20:12:8.summary: Jephthah asks the Lord to judge between Israel and “the sons of Ammon.”
2-chronicles-20:12:8.why: Same appeal to God’s judgment against Ammon.

2-chronicles-20:12:9.summary: The woman’s plea to David has no link to Jehoshaphat’s prayer.

2-chronicles-20:12:10.summary: Jonah’s being thrust from God’s eyes is only an incidental “eyes” overlap.

2-chronicles-20:12:11.summary: Judgment on Eli’s house has no link to the prayer for judgment on invaders.

2-chronicles-20:12:12.summary: Christ “judgeth and wageth war” in righteousness; loosely like God judging the invaders.
2-chronicles-20:12:12.why: General theme of God as judge and warrior.

2-chronicles-20:12:13.summary: “The Lord will judge peoples”; general plea for judgment.
2-chronicles-20:12:13.why: General theme of God judging peoples.

2-chronicles-20:12:14.summary: Joel names the “Valley of Jehoshaphat,” where God judges “all the surrounding nations.”
2-chronicles-20:12:14.why: Later prophecy bearing Jehoshaphat’s name and theme.

2-chronicles-20:12:15.summary: Facing an encircling army, Elisha’s servant asks, “What shall we do?”
2-chronicles-20:12:15.why: Same helplessness before an enemy army.

2-chronicles-20:12:16.summary: The Lord can save “by many or by few”; theme of victory not depending on strength.

2-chronicles-20:12:17.summary: God “will judge between the nations”; general theme only.
2-chronicles-20:12:17.why: General theme of God judging nations.

2-chronicles-20:12:18.summary: The servant setting judgment on earth has no specific link to the plea.

2-chronicles-20:12:19.summary: “Rise, Lord… within the boundaries of my enemies”; general appeal against enemies.
2-chronicles-20:12:19.why: General plea for God to act against foes.

2-chronicles-20:12:20.summary: Facing a superior army, the Maccabees cry to Heaven, “What shall we do with these?”
2-chronicles-20:12:20.why: Same cry of helplessness in war.

2-chronicles-20:13:0.summary: A great assembly of “men, women and young men” gathered before God’s house in prayer.
2-chronicles-20:13:0.why: Same picture of whole families before God.

2-chronicles-20:13:1.summary: All of Nineveh, greatest to least, sought God; general whole-community theme.

2-chronicles-20:13:2.summary: Believers prayed together “with wives and children”; similar family gathering in prayer.

2-chronicles-20:13:3.summary: “You stand all this day before the Lord” describes the whole people assembled.
2-chronicles-20:13:3.why: Same picture of all Israel standing before God.

2-chronicles-20:14:1.summary: “The Spirit of God clothed Azarias,” who then prophesied to the people, as with Oziel.
2-chronicles-20:14:1.why: Same pattern of the Spirit moving a Levite to speak.

2-chronicles-20:14:2.summary: Gabriel came while Daniel was still praying; the answer-during-prayer link is implicit.

2-chronicles-20:14:3.summary: God answers “while they are still speaking”; the source implies a quick answer.

2-chronicles-20:14:4.summary: Cornelius’s prayers remembered has no specific link to the Spirit coming on Oziel.

2-chronicles-20:14:5.summary: God says “Behold, I am present” while they still speak; general theme of answered prayer.

2-chronicles-20:14:6.summary: The Spirit rested on the elders, and they prophesied in the camp.
2-chronicles-20:14:6.why: Same motif of the Spirit coming upon people.

2-chronicles-20:14:7.summary: “God’s Spirit came within” Balaam, who then prophesied about Israel.
2-chronicles-20:14:7.why: Same pattern of the Spirit prompting prophecy.

2-chronicles-20:14:8.summary: Cornelius’s answered prayer has no specific link to Oziel’s inspiration.

2-chronicles-20:15:0.summary: Hezekiah: “Do not be terrified before the king… with us is the Lord… to fight our war.”

2-chronicles-20:15:1.summary: “Fear not, neither be… terrified before their face; for the Lord your God… is with you.”
2-chronicles-20:15:1.why: Same command not to fear the enemy.

2-chronicles-20:15:4.summary: “Fear not, neither be fainthearted,” for the Lord goes with you.

2-chronicles-20:15:5.summary: “Neither cower nor fear them… The Lord… shall Himself fight against them.”
2-chronicles-20:15:5.why: Same assurance that God fights the battle.

2-chronicles-20:15:6.summary: “Do not fear, for I am with you”; those warring against Israel will perish (truncated).

2-chronicles-20:15:7.summary: The Lord goes with Israel “to fight with you against your enemies.”
2-chronicles-20:15:7.why: Same teaching that the battle is God’s.

2-chronicles-20:15:8.summary: Facing “a people more numerous than you, you shall not fear them.”
2-chronicles-20:15:8.why: Same command before a superior army.

2-chronicles-20:15:9.summary: The Lord tells Joshua “Do not fear them,” promising to deliver the enemy.

2-chronicles-20:15:10.summary: “Do not fear, for I redeemed you”; general assurance without the battle setting.

2-chronicles-20:15:11.summary: David’s prayer for vindication has no link to the oracle.

2-chronicles-20:15:12.summary: Nehemiah: “Do not be afraid of them. Remember our God,” before enemies.

2-chronicles-20:15:13.summary: “Victory in battle does not lie in the size of an army; strength comes from heaven.”
2-chronicles-20:15:13.why: Same teaching against fearing a great crowd.

2-chronicles-20:17:1.summary: A prophet tells Asa and all Judah, “The Lord is with you.”

2-chronicles-20:17:2.summary: “Do not fear, for I am with you,” matching the source’s closing assurance.

2-chronicles-20:17:3.summary: “Cease your activity and know that I am God… The Lord of powers is with us.”
2-chronicles-20:17:3.why: Same call to rest while God acts.

2-chronicles-20:17:4.summary: Jesus promises “I am with you”; general presence theme.

2-chronicles-20:17:5.summary: Waiting quietly “for the Lord’s salvation,” loosely like seeing the Lord’s salvation.
2-chronicles-20:17:5.why: Theme of waiting on God’s rescue.

2-chronicles-20:17:6.summary: “With us is the Lord our God, to save and to fight our war.”

2-chronicles-20:17:7.summary: “Do not fear… the Lord is among us,” before enemies in the land.

2-chronicles-20:17:8.summary: “If God is for us, who is against us?”; general confidence theme.

2-chronicles-20:17:9.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us,” matching “the Lord will be with you.”

2-chronicles-20:17:10.summary: Isaiah speaks of being saved by turning to God; the Greek lacks the quiet-waiting wording.
2-chronicles-20:17:10.why: Loose theme of salvation by trust.

2-chronicles-20:17:12.summary: Hostile nations will be defeated “because the Lord God is with us.”

2-chronicles-20:17:13.summary: “The Lord God Almighty will be with you,” conditioned on seeking good.

2-chronicles-20:17:14.summary: A closing blessing “The Lord be with your spirit” has no real link.

2-chronicles-20:17:16.summary: The Egyptians flee because “the Lord is fighting for them.”
2-chronicles-20:17:16.why: Classic case of God fighting for Israel.

2-chronicles-20:17:17.summary: The Greek text about Egypt’s futile help lacks the “sit still” idea assumed by the label.
2-chronicles-20:17:17.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-20:18:0.summary: “The people bowed down and worshipped” after God’s message of deliverance.
2-chronicles-20:18:0.why: Same worship response to God’s word.

2-chronicles-20:18:1.summary: All Israel “fell face down… worshiped” before the Lord.

2-chronicles-20:18:2.summary: Abraham’s servant worshipped the Lord; general response of worship.

2-chronicles-20:18:3.summary: Job fell to the ground in worship; similar posture, different occasion.

2-chronicles-20:18:4.summary: “Let us bow down and fall before Him,” matching the source’s prostration.

2-chronicles-20:19:0.summary: Lists Levitical musicians under Asaph praising with instruments; names like Banaias recur, but not Kaath or Kore.

2-chronicles-20:19:1.summary: Levites appointed singers “to sound on high with a voice of gladness” (truncated range).
2-chronicles-20:19:1.why: Origin of the Levites’ loud praise.

2-chronicles-20:19:2.summary: Instruments for God’s songs; general Levitical music theme.

2-chronicles-20:19:3.summary: Levites appointed to praise the Lord with instruments; general role only.

2-chronicles-20:19:4.summary: Levites “raised their voice” to give thanks and praise the Lord.

2-chronicles-20:19:5.summary: Call to shout to God with thanksgiving; general praise theme.

2-chronicles-20:19:6.summary: A call for all nations to hear has no link to the Levites’ praise.

2-chronicles-20:19:7.summary: Recalling God’s past works has no specific link to the Levites standing to praise.

2-chronicles-20:19:8.summary: Lists Levitical singers appointed for praise; Kaath and Kore are not named in the shown text.

2-chronicles-20:19:9.summary: Singers were heard and joy was heard from far away; general loud praise.
2-chronicles-20:19:9.why: Another scene of loud communal praise.

2-chronicles-20:19:10.summary: “Raise a shout to the God of Jacob”; general praise theme.

2-chronicles-20:19:11.summary: Priests and Levites cried “with a loud voice”; similar wording, different occasion.

2-chronicles-20:20:0.summary: Confidence that God is “for us”; general trust theme.

2-chronicles-20:20:1.summary: Believing leads to seeing God’s glory; general faith theme.

2-chronicles-20:20:2.summary: “Believe in God, and believe also in Me” pairs faith in God with His messenger, like Jehoshaphat’s words.
2-chronicles-20:20:2.why: Same paired call to trust God and His spokesman.

2-chronicles-20:20:3.summary: Hearing Moses and the Prophets; theme of heeding God’s prophets.

2-chronicles-20:20:4.summary: Faith is needed to please God; general faith theme.

2-chronicles-20:20:5.summary: The shown fragment speaks of truth, peace and trust “in Thee”; loose link to trust.

2-chronicles-20:20:6.summary: Receiving God’s messenger means receiving God; loosely like trusting His prophet.

2-chronicles-20:20:7.summary: Believing Moses is tied to believing Jesus; loose prophet-trust theme.

2-chronicles-20:20:8.summary: Israel “trusted God and His attendant Moses,” pairing trust in God and His prophet.
2-chronicles-20:20:8.why: Same pairing of faith in God and prophet.

2-chronicles-20:20:9.summary: “If you do not believe, you will certainly not understand”; the Greek lacks the wordplay of “trusted.”

2-chronicles-20:20:10.summary: Jeremiah names Tekoa, the same town as the source’s wilderness of “Thekoe.”

2-chronicles-20:20:11.summary: Joab sends to Tekoa, the same town as the source’s “Thekoe.”

2-chronicles-20:20:12.summary: Rehoboam built “Thekoe,” the town whose wilderness Judah marched to.

2-chronicles-20:21:0.summary: “Give thanks to the Lord… His mercy is for ever” is the same refrain sung by the army.

2-chronicles-20:21:1.summary: “Give thanks to the Lord… His mercy is for ever” is the same refrain sung by the army.

2-chronicles-20:21:2.summary: At the temple dedication singers praised: “Give thanks to the Lord… His mercy endures for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:21:2.why: Same refrain in another praise scene.

2-chronicles-20:21:4.summary: Calls to praise the Lord in His “holy courts”; loosely like praising “the holy things.”

2-chronicles-20:21:5.summary: Bowing to the Lord in His holy courtyard; loosely like praising “the holy things.”

2-chronicles-20:21:6.summary: Levites praised with the refrain “For it is good, for His mercy… endures for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:21:6.why: Same refrain at the temple’s founding.

2-chronicles-20:21:7.summary: Jeremiah foresees voices saying “Give thanks to the Lord… His mercy is for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:21:7.why: Same refrain in a prophecy of restoration.

2-chronicles-20:21:8.summary: Levites gave thanks before the Lord with “For His mercy endures for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:21:8.why: Same Levitical refrain at the temple.

2-chronicles-20:21:9.summary: Israel praised the Lord: “For it is good, for His mercy endures for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:21:9.why: Same refrain at the temple dedication.

2-chronicles-20:21:10.summary: David “took counsel” with leaders and the assembly, like Jehoshaphat consulting the people.
2-chronicles-20:21:10.why: Similar consultation before a sacred act.

2-chronicles-20:21:11.summary: Worship in the Lord’s “holy court”; loosely like praising “the holy things.”

2-chronicles-20:21:12.summary: The psalm’s refrain “Give thanks to the Lord… for His mercy is for ever” matches the army’s song.
2-chronicles-20:21:12.why: Full litany of the same refrain.

2-chronicles-20:21:13.summary: The “splendor of the Lord” has no clear link to the source’s praise of “the holy things.”

2-chronicles-20:21:14.summary: Hezekiah stationed Levites to sing to the Lord with instruments (truncated range).

2-chronicles-20:21:15.summary: Levites brought for songs and instruments at a celebration; general praise theme.

2-chronicles-20:21:16.summary: Priests and Levites hymned the Lord daily with instruments; general praise theme.

2-chronicles-20:21:17.summary: Singers were chosen “to praise the Lord, for His mercy endures for ever.”
2-chronicles-20:21:17.why: Appointed singers with the same refrain.

2-chronicles-20:21:18.summary: “Deliverance is in much counsel,” loosely like Jehoshaphat consulting the people.

2-chronicles-20:21:19.summary: God’s splendor coming from Zion has no specific link to the singers’ praise.

2-chronicles-20:21:20.summary: After victory the Maccabees sang, “For it is good, for His mercy is for ever.”

2-chronicles-20:22:0.summary: The enemy turned their swords on each other: “Each man’s sword was against his neighbour.”
2-chronicles-20:22:0.why: Same pattern of enemies destroying each other.

2-chronicles-20:22:1.summary: The Lord sends fear so that “a man’s sword will be against his brother.”
2-chronicles-20:22:1.why: Same divine confusion of an enemy army.

2-chronicles-20:22:2.summary: Elisha’s servant sees God’s unseen forces; loosely like God’s hidden intervention.
2-chronicles-20:22:2.why: God fighting unseen for His people.

2-chronicles-20:22:4.summary: God rouses Egyptians to fight one another, “each will fight his brother.”
2-chronicles-20:22:4.why: Same motif of enemies turned against each other.

2-chronicles-20:22:5.summary: An angel of the Lord routs the enemies; general theme of divine rout.
2-chronicles-20:22:5.why: General picture of God routing foes.

2-chronicles-20:22:6.summary: The same Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir named in Jehoshaphat’s prayer.
2-chronicles-20:22:6.why: Links the rout to the prayer.

2-chronicles-20:22:7.summary: Jeroboam’s ambush links only via “ambush” wording that the Saints source does not use.

2-chronicles-20:22:8.summary: The Philistine camp was “in turmoil”; the shown text does not show them fighting each other.
2-chronicles-20:22:8.why: Hint of panic in an enemy camp.

2-chronicles-20:23:1.summary: The enemy army’s swords turned “against his neighbour,” as allies destroy one another here.
2-chronicles-20:23:1.why: Same pattern of enemies destroying each other.

2-chronicles-20:23:2.summary: Ezekiel prophesies the desolation of Mount Seir; same place, different event.
2-chronicles-20:23:2.why: Later judgment on the same people.

2-chronicles-20:23:3.summary: God gave Mount Seir to Esau; identifies Seir’s inhabitants.

2-chronicles-20:23:4.summary: Esau (Edom) lived in the mountain of Seir; identifies Seir’s inhabitants.

2-chronicles-20:23:5.summary: Mentions Horites in the mountains of Seir; same place only.

2-chronicles-20:23:6.summary: God gave Mount Seir to Esau’s sons and forbade Israel to fight them.

2-chronicles-20:24:0.summary: Rising in the morning, they “found all the bodies dead” after God struck the enemy camp.
2-chronicles-20:24:0.why: Same scene of finding the enemy dead.

2-chronicles-20:24:1.summary: Many enemies fell “for the war was from God”; general theme.

2-chronicles-20:24:2.summary: “Israel saw the Egyptians dead” after the Lord rescued them without their fighting.
2-chronicles-20:24:2.why: Same picture of seeing the enemy dead.

2-chronicles-20:24:3.summary: Shares “no remnant or survivor,” but about Israel’s possible destruction.

2-chronicles-20:24:4.summary: God “will fill the field with corpses” among the nations; general judgment image.
2-chronicles-20:24:4.why: General image of God judging nations.

2-chronicles-20:24:5.summary: Dead bodies filling Jerusalem in God’s wrath against Judah does not match this victory.

2-chronicles-20:25:0.summary: David recovered spoils and drove flocks and herds after defeating raiders.

2-chronicles-20:25:1.summary: Israel plunders an enemy camp abandoned after the Lord routed it (truncated range).
2-chronicles-20:25:1.why: Same pattern of plundering a God-routed army.

2-chronicles-20:25:2.summary: Moses’ rebuke about captive women has no link to Judah’s plundering.

2-chronicles-20:25:3.summary: Israel uses the defeated army’s weapons for seven years; loosely like a long-lasting harvest of spoils.

2-chronicles-20:25:4.summary: Wisdom’s value over precious stones has no link to battle spoils.

2-chronicles-20:25:5.summary: Mentions dividing “spoils”; the Greek verse is obscure.

2-chronicles-20:25:6.summary: Israel “plundered the Egyptians” of valuable articles; different circumstances.

2-chronicles-20:25:7.summary: Gideon collects gold from Midian’s “spoils”; general spoils theme.

2-chronicles-20:25:8.summary: The promise to “plunder the Egyptians” of silver, gold and clothing; general theme.

2-chronicles-20:25:9.summary: Conquering through Christ’s love has no specific link to plundering spoils.

2-chronicles-20:26:0.summary: After victory Moses named an altar for the Lord, as Judah named the Valley of Blessing.
2-chronicles-20:26:0.why: Same practice of naming a place after God’s victory.

2-chronicles-20:26:1.summary: Zion’s new names have no specific link to the Valley of Blessing.

2-chronicles-20:26:2.summary: Jacob’s plan to appease Esau has no link to naming the valley.

2-chronicles-20:26:3.summary: “Blessed is the Lord” for redeeming His people; general blessing theme.

2-chronicles-20:26:4.summary: Only the formula “to this day” overlaps.

2-chronicles-20:26:5.summary: Calls to thank the Lord for His wonders; general praise after deliverance.

2-chronicles-20:26:6.summary: “Bless the Lord” and remember His benefits; general blessing theme.

2-chronicles-20:26:7.summary: After victory Samuel named the stone Ebenezer: “Thus far the Lord has helped us.”
2-chronicles-20:26:7.why: Same practice of naming a site after deliverance.

2-chronicles-20:26:8.summary: Israel sings to the Lord after He destroyed the enemy without their fighting (truncated range).

2-chronicles-20:26:9.summary: David sang to the Lord on the day of rescue from enemies; general theme.

2-chronicles-20:26:10.summary: A place gets a commemorative name, but for a different reason.

2-chronicles-20:26:11.summary: Heaven praises God for salvation and judgment; general praise theme (truncated).
2-chronicles-20:26:11.why: Heavenly echo of praise after victory.

2-chronicles-20:26:12.summary: Jacob names a place after meeting God; similar naming, different event.

2-chronicles-20:27:0.summary: At Jerusalem “God had made them exceedingly glad,” like “the Lord had made them rejoice.”

2-chronicles-20:27:1.summary: The ransomed return to Zion with joy; general joyful return theme.

2-chronicles-20:27:2.summary: God did not let enemies rejoice over the psalmist; inverse of Judah rejoicing over enemies.

2-chronicles-20:27:3.summary: Exulting in God’s salvation; general rejoicing theme.

2-chronicles-20:27:4.summary: Hannah rejoices in salvation, her mouth opened “against enemies.”

2-chronicles-20:27:5.summary: David leads Israel into Jerusalem with shouting and trumpet; similar procession.

2-chronicles-20:27:6.summary: The gathered return to Zion with gladness; general joyful return.

2-chronicles-20:27:7.summary: Heaven rejoices over a judged enemy; general theme.

2-chronicles-20:27:8.summary: Jesus as forerunner has no specific link to Jehoshaphat leading Judah home.

2-chronicles-20:27:9.summary: The king goes before the people and the Lord leads them; loosely like Jehoshaphat leading.
2-chronicles-20:27:9.why: Image of a king leading the people.

2-chronicles-20:28:0.summary: Heavenly lyre music and song; general music theme.

2-chronicles-20:28:1.summary: Praise with tambourine and psaltery; general instruments theme.

2-chronicles-20:28:2.summary: Levites praised with instruments; general music theme.

2-chronicles-20:28:3.summary: Praise with trumpet, psaltery and lyre; general instruments theme.

2-chronicles-20:28:4.summary: Singers “in the Lord’s house with cymbals, nablai, and kinyrai,” the same instruments.
2-chronicles-20:28:4.why: Same distinctive instruments in the temple.

2-chronicles-20:28:5.summary: David and Israel celebrate before the Lord with lyres, harps and other instruments on the way to Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-20:28:6.summary: All Israel played before God with lyres, harps and trumpets in procession.
2-chronicles-20:28:6.why: Similar procession with the same instruments.

2-chronicles-20:28:7.summary: “Awake, psaltery and lyre!”; general instruments theme.

2-chronicles-20:28:8.summary: Praise on psaltery and lyre; general instruments theme.

2-chronicles-20:29:1.summary: The Lord made Syria hear a great army and flee; general theme of God-sent panic.

2-chronicles-20:29:2.summary: God sends fear before Israel and confounds all the nations.
2-chronicles-20:29:2.why: Same divine terror on the nations.

2-chronicles-20:29:3.summary: “The fear of God fell upon the cities around them,” so they did not attack.

2-chronicles-20:29:4.summary: “Terror from the Lord had come upon them,” the same phrase in Asa’s victory.
2-chronicles-20:29:4.why: Same Chronicler phrase in an earlier war.

2-chronicles-20:29:5.summary: Nations “heard” what the Lord did to kings and came to submit.
2-chronicles-20:29:5.why: Same effect of God’s deeds on nations.

2-chronicles-20:29:6.summary: “Fear of you has fallen upon us. For we have heard” what the Lord did.
2-chronicles-20:29:6.why: Same fear on hearing of God’s victories.

2-chronicles-20:29:7.summary: The nations heard and trembling seized Edom and Moab after God’s victory.
2-chronicles-20:29:7.why: Same terror on Moab and Edom.

2-chronicles-20:29:8.summary: Kings “heard” of God’s deed for Israel and their minds melted.
2-chronicles-20:29:8.why: Same fear on hearing God’s works.

2-chronicles-20:30:1.summary: Under Asa “the land was at peace… gave us rest all around,” the same wording.
2-chronicles-20:30:1.why: Same peace and rest under Jehoshaphat’s father.

2-chronicles-20:30:2.summary: David was secure from surrounding enemies; the Greek says “possession” rather than rest.
2-chronicles-20:30:2.why: Similar security for a faithful king.

2-chronicles-20:30:3.summary: Jesus’ gift of peace has no specific link to Jehoshaphat’s peaceful reign.

2-chronicles-20:30:4.summary: The Lord had given Israel “rest from all their enemies all around.”

2-chronicles-20:30:5.summary: The Greek proverb on righteous deeds lacks the “enemies at peace” idea the label assumes.
2-chronicles-20:30:5.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-20:30:6.summary: “He will provide quiet”; general theme of God-given rest.
2-chronicles-20:30:6.why: General theme of God granting quiet.

2-chronicles-20:32:0.summary: Asa later trusted Syria rather than the Lord; contrasts with the praise of Asa’s ways (truncated).
2-chronicles-20:32:0.why: Shows Asa’s ways were not all good.

2-chronicles-20:32:1.summary: Asa “did what was good and right before the Lord,” the ways Jehoshaphat followed.

2-chronicles-20:32:2.summary: The wicked man’s deceit has no link to Jehoshaphat’s faithfulness.

2-chronicles-20:32:3.summary: Asa’s trust in God against a great multitude parallels Jehoshaphat’s, not this verse.

2-chronicles-20:32:4.summary: “Asa did what was right before the Lord,” the same verdict.

2-chronicles-20:32:5.summary: Jehoshaphat “walked in his father’s earlier ways,” the same evaluation.
2-chronicles-20:32:5.why: Earlier statement of the same verdict.

2-chronicles-20:32:6.summary: “I kept the Lord’s ways… not… turning from my God”; general faithfulness.

2-chronicles-20:33:0.summary: Earlier Jehoshaphat “removed the high places,” yet here they still existed.

2-chronicles-20:33:1.summary: Jehoshaphat himself “directed your heart to seek the Lord,” but the people had not.

2-chronicles-20:33:2.summary: Rehoboam “did not direct his heart to seek the Lord,” the same failing as the people here.

2-chronicles-20:33:3.summary: Asa removed “the high places,” while here they still existed.

2-chronicles-20:33:4.summary: Samuel urges Israel to “Prepare your hearts toward the Lord” and remove groves.
2-chronicles-20:33:4.why: Same call to direct the heart to God.

2-chronicles-20:33:5.summary: “Every heart directed to seek the Lord, the God of their fathers” is the same phrase.
2-chronicles-20:33:5.why: Same phrase used of later worshipers.

2-chronicles-20:33:6.summary: The Lord had not given Israel a heart to know; loosely like the people’s undirected heart.
2-chronicles-20:33:6.why: Theme of the people’s unready heart.

2-chronicles-20:34:0.summary: The Lord’s word came through Jehu son of Hanani, the same prophet-chronicler.

2-chronicles-20:34:1.summary: Jehu son of Anani the prophet confronted Jehoshaphat himself.

2-chronicles-20:34:2.summary: Jehu son of Hanani spoke against Baasha; the same prophet.

2-chronicles-20:34:3.summary: Asa’s deeds, “first and last, are written” in a book: the same closing formula.

2-chronicles-20:34:4.summary: Abijah’s deeds are written in the book of a prophet, as with Jehu.
2-chronicles-20:34:4.why: Same formula citing a prophetic source.

2-chronicles-20:34:5.summary: Rehoboam’s deeds “first and last” are written in prophets’ records.
2-chronicles-20:34:5.why: Same formula citing a prophetic source.

2-chronicles-20:35:0.summary: Kings reports Jehoshaphat’s ship to Sophir wrecked at Ezion-geber, and his dealings with Israel’s king.
2-chronicles-20:35:0.why: Parallel account, with different detail on the partnership.

2-chronicles-20:35:1.summary: Ahaziah king of Samaria sought Baal Fly, illustrating why he “acted lawlessly” (truncated range).

2-chronicles-20:36:0.summary: Solomon built a ship at Ezion-geber, the port the source calls “Gasion-gaber.”
2-chronicles-20:36:0.why: Earlier use of the same port.

2-chronicles-20:36:1.summary: Solomon’s ships traveled to “Tharsis,” the same destination.

2-chronicles-20:36:2.summary: Solomon had a Tarshish ship with Hiram’s ships; same trade route.

2-chronicles-20:37:0.summary: Walking with fools brings harm; loosely like Jehoshaphat’s alliance with Ahaziah.

2-chronicles-20:37:2.summary: Achan’s sin and defeat have no specific link to the shipwreck prophecy.

2-chronicles-20:37:3.summary: Solomon’s ships reached Tharsis, while Jehoshaphat’s could not.

2-chronicles-20:37:4.summary: Jehoshaphat’s ship “was wrecked at Ezion-geber,” the same event.

2-chronicles-20:37:5.summary: A call to leave foolishness has no specific link to the prophecy.

2-chronicles-20:37:6.summary: The Lord disciplines those He loves; a general reading of the shipwreck.

2-chronicles-20:37:7.summary: A prophet rebukes Asa for relying on a foreign king’s alliance and announces consequences.
2-chronicles-20:37:7.why: Same pattern of a rebuked royal alliance.

2-chronicles-20:37:8.summary: “I reprove and discipline”; a general reading of the shipwreck.

2-chronicles-21:1:1.summary: Solomon “fell asleep” and was buried in David’s city, his son reigning in his place.

2-chronicles-21:1:2.summary: Rehoboam was buried with his fathers in David’s city; his son reigned.

2-chronicles-21:1:3.summary: The same Joram’s reign and burial in David’s city.

2-chronicles-21:1:4.summary: Joram son of Jehoshaphat became king of Judah.

2-chronicles-21:2:0.summary: Gathering Levites has no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:2:1.summary: Only “Israel” as a name for Judah links them; the Saints source says “king of Judah.”

2-chronicles-21:2:2.summary: Collecting temple silver has no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:2:3.summary: Ahaz’s idolatry has no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:2:5.summary: Jehoiada’s burial has no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:2:6.summary: Manasseh’s records have no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:2:7.summary: The Saints source says “king of Judah,” so the “king of Israel” usage link is absent.
2-chronicles-21:2:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-21:2:8.summary: Josiah’s Passover has no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:2:9.summary: Ahaz’s burial has no link to the list of Jehoshaphat’s sons.

2-chronicles-21:3:0.summary: Rehoboam placed his sons in fortified cities with abundant provisions while naming one heir.
2-chronicles-21:3:0.why: Same royal practice of providing for sons.

2-chronicles-21:3:1.summary: Abraham gave gifts to his other sons but kept the inheritance for Isaac.
2-chronicles-21:3:1.why: Same pattern of gifts versus inheritance.

2-chronicles-21:3:2.summary: Rehoboam built walled cities in Judea; only the cities overlap.

2-chronicles-21:3:3.summary: The law gives the firstborn the right of inheritance, as Joram received the kingdom.
2-chronicles-21:3:3.why: Legal basis for the firstborn’s right.

2-chronicles-21:4:0.summary: Abimelech killed his brothers to secure rule, as Joram did.
2-chronicles-21:4:0.why: Same crime of fratricide for power.

2-chronicles-21:4:1.summary: Joram’s own sons are later taken; possible retribution, not stated here.

2-chronicles-21:4:2.summary: Cain killed his brother; general fratricide theme.

2-chronicles-21:4:3.summary: Athaliah destroyed the royal offspring, a similar massacre in the same royal house.
2-chronicles-21:4:3.why: Echo of royal bloodshed in Judah.

2-chronicles-21:4:4.summary: Cain slaughtered his brother because his works were evil; general theme.

2-chronicles-21:4:5.summary: Jehu killed Judah’s rulers and Ahaziah’s brethren; similar killing of royal kin.

2-chronicles-21:4:6.summary: God repaid Abimelech for killing his brothers; possible retribution theme.

2-chronicles-21:6:2.summary: Jeroboam’s golden heifers began the way of Israel’s kings; the source names Ahab’s house.
2-chronicles-21:6:2.why: Origin of “the way of Israel’s kings.”

2-chronicles-21:6:3.summary: Omri and Ahab did evil before the Lord; the house whose way Joram followed (truncated).
2-chronicles-21:6:3.why: Shows the ways of Ahab’s house.

2-chronicles-21:6:4.summary: Athaliah, daughter of Omri’s house, is Joram’s wife and Ahaziah’s mother.

2-chronicles-21:6:5.summary: Foreign marriages turned even Solomon aside; similar theme of a wife’s influence.
2-chronicles-21:6:5.why: Theme of marriage leading kings astray.

2-chronicles-21:7:0.summary: God keeps a son on the throne so David “may have a place before Me always”; the Greek lacks “lamp.”

2-chronicles-21:7:1.summary: “I have prepared a lamp for My anointed” echoes the lamp promised to David.
2-chronicles-21:7:1.why: Same lamp image for David’s line.

2-chronicles-21:7:3.summary: A “horn of salvation” in David’s house; general Davidic promise.
2-chronicles-21:7:3.why: New Testament fulfillment of the promise.

2-chronicles-21:7:4.summary: Light shining on those in darkness is not tied to David’s lamp in the shown text.

2-chronicles-21:7:5.summary: God will not take the whole kingdom “because of David My servant.”
2-chronicles-21:7:5.why: Same reason for sparing David’s house.

2-chronicles-21:7:6.summary: The psalmist laments God overturning David’s covenant, in tension with God’s faithfulness here.

2-chronicles-21:7:8.summary: Joash is rescued from the royal massacre, preserving David’s line.
2-chronicles-21:7:8.why: Shows the promise kept in practice.

2-chronicles-21:7:9.summary: David’s men call him “Israel’s lamp,” the same image as the lamp for David.

2-chronicles-21:7:11.summary: God will punish David’s sons’ sins but never profane His covenant with David.

2-chronicles-21:7:12.summary: The Lord swore to David to set his offspring on his throne.

2-chronicles-21:7:13.summary: David speaks of God’s “everlasting covenant with me.”
2-chronicles-21:7:13.why: David’s own witness to the covenant.

2-chronicles-21:7:14.summary: A plot to replace Judah’s king fails; loose theme of preserving the line.
2-chronicles-21:7:14.why: Another threat to David’s house thwarted.

2-chronicles-21:8:1.summary: Edom has a king allied with Judah here; only background for Edom’s status.
2-chronicles-21:8:1.why: Background on Edom before its revolt.

2-chronicles-21:8:2.summary: Mount Seir (Edom) is routed in Jehoshaphat’s day; Edom isn’t named.

2-chronicles-21:8:3.summary: “Edom has remained apart from Judah to this day” continues the same revolt.

2-chronicles-21:8:4.summary: The Greek says “no king in Syria,” so the link to Edom’s king is lost.

2-chronicles-21:8:5.summary: Isaac foretells Esau will “loosen his yoke from your neck,” fulfilled in Edom’s revolt.

2-chronicles-21:10:0.summary: The Assyrian king fights against “Lomna,” the same town that rebelled.

2-chronicles-21:10:1.summary: Israel provoked God and faces punishment through a nation; general apostasy theme.
2-chronicles-21:10:1.why: General theme of punishment for apostasy.

2-chronicles-21:10:2.summary: Abijah says “we have not abandoned the Lord,” contrasting Joram’s abandonment.

2-chronicles-21:10:3.summary: God tears part of the kingdom away because of apostasy; general theme.
2-chronicles-21:10:3.why: Similar loss of territory for apostasy.

2-chronicles-21:10:4.summary: Territory is torn away “because he abandoned Me,” matching the reason given here.

2-chronicles-21:10:5.summary: “If you forsake Him, He will forsake you,” the principle at work here.
2-chronicles-21:10:5.why: States the principle behind the revolt.

2-chronicles-21:10:6.summary: Libnah is likely the same as “Lomna,” but the names differ in the texts shown.

2-chronicles-21:10:7.summary: God’s people “abandoned Me”; general apostasy theme.

2-chronicles-21:11:0.summary: Both use prostitution language for idolatry, but Leviticus concerns an individual prostituting “after rulers,” not a king leading a nation.

2-chronicles-21:11:1.summary: Leviticus speaks of Israel prostituting themselves after “vain things,” sharing only the general image of idolatry as prostitution.
2-chronicles-21:11:1.why: Law's framing of idolatry as unfaithfulness.

2-chronicles-21:11:2.summary: Solomon, like Jehoram, is a king of David's line who “built a high place” for foreign gods, a precedent for royal idolatry.
2-chronicles-21:11:2.why: Earlier royal precedent for high places.

2-chronicles-21:11:3.summary: The psalm says Israel “prostituted themselves” through their practices, a general echo of the source's charge.

2-chronicles-21:11:5.summary: Habakkuk's woe on making a neighbor drunk has no real link to building high places or idolatry.

2-chronicles-21:11:7.summary: Manasseh likewise “led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray,” nearly the same wording used of Jehoram.
2-chronicles-21:11:7.why: Same royal sin formula for another king.

2-chronicles-21:11:8.summary: The beast forcing worship of its image in Revelation shares nothing specific with Jehoram's high places; the English “compelled” idea is absent here.
2-chronicles-21:11:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-21:11:9.summary: Jehu cites the “prostitutions of Jezebel,” the house Jehoram married into, but this verse does not name Ahab's house.

2-chronicles-21:11:10.summary: Ezekiel's long allegory of Jerusalem prostituting herself to idols shares the image only generally (truncated range).

2-chronicles-21:11:11.summary: The great prostitute leading the earth into immorality is a broad parallel to causing a people to prostitute themselves (truncated range).

2-chronicles-21:11:12.summary: Manasseh “caused Judah to sin through their idols,” a close parallel charge against another Judean king.
2-chronicles-21:11:12.why: Same pattern in a later king.

2-chronicles-21:11:13.summary: Ezekiel describes sacrifices on “every high hill,” a general parallel to high-place worship.

2-chronicles-21:11:14.summary: Jezebel teaching others into immorality and idol food parallels leading people astray only loosely.

2-chronicles-21:11:15.summary: The psalm's “hills” (high places) and carvings that provoked God loosely recall Jehoram's high places.
2-chronicles-21:11:15.why: Shows God's response to high places.

2-chronicles-21:11:16.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's command to bow to the golden image has no specific link; the Saints text says “led astray,” not compelled.
2-chronicles-21:11:16.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-21:11:18.summary: Deuteronomy orders destruction of hilltop worship places, the opposite of Jehoram building high places.

2-chronicles-21:11:19.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's threat of the furnace for refusing to bow is unrelated to Jehoram's high places.

2-chronicles-21:12:0.summary: Jehoshaphat “walked in his father's earlier ways,” exactly the way Elias says Jehoram did not walk.

2-chronicles-21:12:1.summary: Asa “did what was good and right” and removed high places, the king whose ways Jehoram did not follow.

2-chronicles-21:12:2.summary: Same prophet Elijah (Elias), but this verse tells of his being taken up, not his message to Jehoram.
2-chronicles-21:12:2.why: Raises the chronology of Elijah's letter.

2-chronicles-21:12:3.summary: A hand writing on Baltasar's wall shares only the idea of writing to a king; no specific link.

2-chronicles-21:12:4.summary: A written prophetic roll pronounces judgment on a Judean king, loosely like Elias's written message (truncated range).
2-chronicles-21:12:4.why: Another written oracle against a king.

2-chronicles-21:12:5.summary: Asa “did what was right before the Lord,” the conduct Jehoram failed to imitate.

2-chronicles-21:12:6.summary: Jehoshaphat “walked in all the way of Asa his father,” the very ways named in Elias's letter.
2-chronicles-21:12:6.why: Links both kings named by Elias.

2-chronicles-21:12:7.summary: God commands Jeremiah to write oracles on a roll, loosely parallel to a written prophetic message.

2-chronicles-21:12:8.summary: Jehoiakim burning the roll has no specific connection beyond the general idea of written prophecy.

2-chronicles-21:12:9.summary: Same prophet Elijah, but the verse narrates his ascension, not his letter.

2-chronicles-21:12:10.summary: Daniel reads writing announcing judgment on a king, a loose parallel to a written oracle of doom (truncated range).
2-chronicles-21:12:10.why: Another written verdict on a king.

2-chronicles-21:12:11.summary: Ezekiel's scroll of “woe” is a written divine message, but otherwise unrelated.

2-chronicles-21:13:1.summary: Both verses say Jehoram caused Jerusalem's inhabitants “to prostitute themselves”; Elias's letter restates the narrative charge.
2-chronicles-21:13:1.why: Same charge in narrative and prophecy.

2-chronicles-21:13:3.summary: Describes Ahab's Baal worship, the “Ahab's house” whose prostitution Jehoram imitated.

2-chronicles-21:13:4.summary: Joseph's brothers feel guilt over wronging their brother, a loose echo of Jehoram's killing his brothers.
2-chronicles-21:13:4.why: General theme of guilt toward brothers.

2-chronicles-21:13:5.summary: A woe on building with bloodshed shares only the general theme of violence.

2-chronicles-21:13:6.summary: “The prostitutions of Jezebel” names the very prostitution of Ahab's house that Jehoram copied.

2-chronicles-21:13:7.summary: Judah follows Israel and “prostituted herself,” matching the charge that Jehoram walked in Israel's kings' ways.

2-chronicles-21:13:8.summary: The earth uncovering blood of the slain loosely relates to Jehoram's killing his brothers.

2-chronicles-21:13:9.summary: Omri, Ahab's father, did evil, one of the “Israel's kings” Jehoram followed, but only generally.

2-chronicles-21:13:10.summary: Deuteronomy predicts the people will “go a-whoring” after foreign gods, sharing the general image.

2-chronicles-21:13:11.summary: Joab killed two men “better than himself,” closely matching Jehoram's brothers “better than you” (truncated range).
2-chronicles-21:13:11.why: Same verdict on killing better men.

2-chronicles-21:13:12.summary: Cain killed his brother whose works were righteous, paralleling Jehoram killing brothers better than he.

2-chronicles-21:13:13.summary: Exodus warns against prostituting themselves to foreign gods, a general echo.

2-chronicles-21:13:14.summary: Abel's blood crying out after fratricide loosely parallels Jehoram's killing his brothers.

2-chronicles-21:13:15.summary: Abimelech killed his seventy brothers to rule and God repaid him, closely paralleling Jehoram's murder of his brothers.

2-chronicles-21:14:0.summary: Leviticus threatens “blows” for disobedience, a general covenant-curse echo of the “great blow.”

2-chronicles-21:14:1.summary: Micah condemns keeping “the works of Achaab's house,” leading to ruin, as Jehoram followed Ahab's house.

2-chronicles-21:14:2.summary: Ephraim's oppression and following worthless things has no specific link to the strike on Jehoram's family.

2-chronicles-21:14:3.summary: God repaying fathers' sins on children loosely matches the blow on Jehoram's sons.

2-chronicles-21:15:1.summary: Judas' “entrails poured out,” like Jehoram's belly coming out, describes a gruesome death for a wicked man.
2-chronicles-21:15:1.why: Similar death of a wicked man.

2-chronicles-21:15:2.summary: A curse making the belly swell shares only a general bodily-curse image.

2-chronicles-21:15:3.summary: Deuteronomy threatens “diseases grievous and enduring,” matching the “grievous sickness” lasting day to day.

2-chronicles-21:15:4.summary: Becoming a byword among nations has no link to Jehoram's bowel disease.

2-chronicles-21:15:5.summary: Longing for morning or evening in fear has no specific link to the illness.
