2-chronicles-21:15:6.summary: The Egyptian ulcer and incurable afflictions are a general covenant-disease parallel.

2-chronicles-21:15:7.summary: A curse entering the “innards” loosely echoes a disease of the belly.

2-chronicles-21:15:8.summary: Deuteronomy threatens “every infirmity” until destruction, a general covenant-curse echo.

2-chronicles-21:15:9.summary: Herod is struck by the Lord and eaten by worms, like a king struck with a fatal inner disease.
2-chronicles-21:15:9.why: Divine judgment by disease on a ruler.

2-chronicles-21:16:0.summary: The same “foreigners” and “Arabs” brought gifts to Jehoshaphat but are stirred against his son.

2-chronicles-21:16:1.summary: The Arabs' raiding band that killed all the older sons is this same invasion against Joram.
2-chronicles-21:16:1.why: Records the outcome of the invasion.

2-chronicles-21:16:2.summary: “The Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon,” as he stirs up foreigners against Joram for sin.
2-chronicles-21:16:2.why: God raising enemies against a sinful king.

2-chronicles-21:16:3.summary: “The Lord brought against them” Assyria's commanders, a parallel divine act against a sinful king.
2-chronicles-21:16:3.why: God using foreign armies as judgment.

2-chronicles-21:16:4.summary: “The Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon” parallels God stirring foreigners against Joram.
2-chronicles-21:16:4.why: God raising enemies against a sinful king.

2-chronicles-21:16:5.summary: The Lord strengthened Uzziah against “the foreigners” and “the Arabs,” the same peoples stirred against Joram.

2-chronicles-21:16:6.summary: Calamity in a city comes from the Lord, a general statement of divine sovereignty.

2-chronicles-21:16:7.summary: God announces loss of kingdom for disobedience, a general judgment theme.

2-chronicles-21:16:8.summary: “The Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus,” the same idiom of God stirring a foreign ruler.

2-chronicles-21:16:9.summary: David speaks of God “stirring you up against me,” the same idiom of divine incitement.

2-chronicles-21:16:10.summary: God “create[s] calamities,” a general statement of sovereignty over disaster.
2-chronicles-21:16:10.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-21:16:11.summary: God “stirred” the spirits of returnees, sharing the verb but for a good purpose.

2-chronicles-21:16:12.summary: God sends Assyria as the rod of his anger against a lawless nation, like foreigners against Joram.

2-chronicles-21:16:13.summary: The Lord in anger “incited David against them,” a parallel of divine incitement as judgment.
2-chronicles-21:16:13.why: God inciting as judgment on sin.

2-chronicles-21:17:1.summary: Another Judean king defeated and Jerusalem plundered, a loosely similar disaster.

2-chronicles-21:17:2.summary: Names “Ahaziah son of Joram,” the surviving youngest son of this verse.

2-chronicles-21:17:3.summary: Mentions Athaliah's sons and temple plundering, loosely related to the royal family's fate.

2-chronicles-21:17:4.summary: Job's words on fools' sons far from deliverance generally echo the loss of Jehoram's sons.
2-chronicles-21:17:4.why: Wisdom on the fate of the wicked's sons.

2-chronicles-21:18:1.summary: An angel of the Lord “struck” Herod with a fatal disease, as the Lord struck Jehoram in his belly.

2-chronicles-21:18:2.summary: Records Ahaziah's accession, the successor after Joram's death, but nothing about the sickness.

2-chronicles-21:19:0.summary: Asa received “an exceedingly great funeral procession,” whereas Jehoram's people made none.

2-chronicles-21:19:1.summary: Zedekiah is promised mourning as for his fathers, the honor Jehoram is denied.

2-chronicles-21:20:0.summary: Jehoiakim will not be mourned, paralleling Jehoram departing “without praise.”

2-chronicles-21:20:1.summary: Jeconiah dishonored like a useless vessel loosely echoes Jehoram's dishonorable end.

2-chronicles-21:20:2.summary: Joash was likewise buried “in David's city” but not in the tomb of the kings.

2-chronicles-21:20:3.summary: Ahaz was likewise buried in David's city but not brought “into the tombs of Israel's kings.”
2-chronicles-21:20:3.why: Same burial dishonor for a wicked king.

2-chronicles-21:20:4.summary: The righteous are remembered “with praises” while the impious name is extinguished, as Jehoram “departed without praise.”

2-chronicles-21:20:5.summary: The people rejoice at Athaliah's death, loosely like the lack of mourning for Jehoram.

2-chronicles-21:7:10.summary: Jeremiah 33:20–26 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-21:7:10.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-21:7:10.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-21:11:6.summary: 1 Kings 14:9 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-21:11:6.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-21:11:6.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-21:11:17.summary: 1 Kings 14:16 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-21:11:17.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-21:11:17.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-22:1:2.summary: Joash is presented as the king's son to reign, a later step in the same succession crisis.

2-chronicles-22:1:3.summary: “The people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place,” the same succession formula.

2-chronicles-22:1:4.summary: “All the people of the land took Uzziah … and made him king in place of his father,” a parallel formula.

2-chronicles-22:1:5.summary: The people of the land installed Jehoahaz as king in his father's place, the same formula.

2-chronicles-22:1:6.summary: The genealogy lists “Joram his son, Ahaziah his son,” the same father and son.
2-chronicles-22:1:6.why: Places Ahaziah in the royal line.

2-chronicles-22:2:1.summary: Omri and his son Ahab are named, identifying Athaliah's family line.

2-chronicles-22:2:2.summary: Jehoram's wife was “Ahab's daughter,” the same Athaliah who is Ahaziah's mother.

2-chronicles-22:3:0.summary: Rebekah urges Jacob to obey her in deceiving his father, a loose parallel of a mother steering a son wrongly.

2-chronicles-22:3:1.summary: The law forbids heeding a close relative who entices to serve other gods, exactly what Ahaziah's mother did.
2-chronicles-22:3:1.why: Law Ahaziah violated by heeding her.

2-chronicles-22:3:2.summary: Malachi on guarding one's spirit and the wife of one's youth has no link to a mother counseling sin.

2-chronicles-22:3:3.summary: Intermarriage “will turn your son away from Me,” fulfilled when Ahab's daughter's son walked in Ahab's ways.
2-chronicles-22:3:3.why: Shows the danger the law foresaw.

2-chronicles-22:3:4.summary: The giants and the flood generation's wickedness have no specific link to Ahaziah's mother.

2-chronicles-22:3:5.summary: Loving mother more than Christ loosely relates to following a mother's sinful counsel.

2-chronicles-22:3:6.summary: Obeying God rather than men is a general principle against following bad counsel.

2-chronicles-22:3:7.summary: Foreign wives turning Solomon aside loosely parallels a wife's family drawing a king to sin (truncated range).

2-chronicles-22:3:8.summary: “Prompted by her mother,” Herodias' daughter asks for John's head, a vivid case of a mother counseling sin.

2-chronicles-22:3:9.summary: Micah's mother funds an idol, a loose example of a mother promoting idolatry.

2-chronicles-22:4:0.summary: Walking with fools brings harm, a general principle behind evil counselors.

2-chronicles-22:4:1.summary: After Jehoiada's death rulers counsel the king into idolatry, paralleling counselors after Jehoram's death.
2-chronicles-22:4:1.why: Same pattern of bad counsel after a death.

2-chronicles-22:4:2.summary: A son neglecting discipline meditates evil, loosely related to bad counsel.

2-chronicles-22:4:3.summary: Warning a son not to let the ungodly “lead you astray” is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-22:4:4.summary: The impious “steer deceits,” a general statement about wicked counsel.

2-chronicles-22:5:0.summary: Remmath-gilead is contested with the king of Syria, the same place of Joram's battle.

2-chronicles-22:5:1.summary: Ahab drew Jehoshaphat to war at Ramoth in Galaaditis, as Ahab's son now draws Ahaziah there.
2-chronicles-22:5:1.why: Repeated alliance at the same place.

2-chronicles-22:5:2.summary: Introduces Hazael, the Syrian against whom Joram and Ahaziah fought.

2-chronicles-22:5:4.summary: “All the works of Achaab's house… you walked in their counsels,” matching Ahaziah following their counsels.

2-chronicles-22:5:5.summary: Jehoshaphat is rebuked for helping a sinner hated by the Lord, the same Ahab alliance Ahaziah repeats.

2-chronicles-22:5:6.summary: The earlier battle at the same site when Jehoshaphat was nearly killed, a loose parallel.

2-chronicles-22:5:8.summary: Blessed is one who does not walk “in the counsel of the ungodly,” the opposite of Ahaziah.

2-chronicles-22:6:0.summary: Kings records Joram returning to Jezreel to heal wounds from fighting Hazael, the same event.

2-chronicles-22:6:1.summary: Identifies “Ahaziah son of Joram king of Judah,” the same king visiting Joram.

2-chronicles-22:6:3.summary: Notes Ahaziah as the sole surviving son, background only.

2-chronicles-22:6:4.summary: Ahaziah's brothers came down to Jezreel and were slain by Jehu, part of the same visit episode.

2-chronicles-22:6:5.summary: The next verse continues the visit, explaining Ahaziah's fatal going to Joram.

2-chronicles-22:7:0.summary: A “reversal from God” governs events, as Ahaziah's downfall “came from God.”

2-chronicles-22:7:2.summary: “The turn of events came from the Lord,” paralleling Ahaziah's downfall coming from God.

2-chronicles-22:7:3.summary: God orders Jehu son of Nimshi anointed king, the Lord's anointed Jehu named here.

2-chronicles-22:7:4.summary: The impious grow weak in the Lord's ways, a general principle.
2-chronicles-22:7:4.why: General wisdom on the wicked's fall.

2-chronicles-22:7:5.summary: Trampling the lawless on the day of the Lord has no specific link to Ahaziah's downfall.

2-chronicles-22:7:6.summary: God's counsel stands, a general sovereignty theme.

2-chronicles-22:7:7.summary: Samson's marriage “was from the Lord,” a parallel of God working through a visit to bring judgment.

2-chronicles-22:7:8.summary: The day of vengeance when the foot slips is a general judgment theme.

2-chronicles-22:7:9.summary: The Lord arranges for Ahab to “fall at Remmath-gilead,” as he arranges the downfall of Ahab's house.
2-chronicles-22:7:9.why: God arranging the fall of Ahab's house.

2-chronicles-22:7:11.summary: The sinner caught in his own works, a general retribution theme.

2-chronicles-22:9:0.summary: Jehu's vengeance on Ahab's house and the killing of Ahaziah's kin immediately precede his capture.

2-chronicles-22:9:1.summary: The killing of older sons in 22:1 explains why no one could hold power, but only indirectly.

2-chronicles-22:9:2.summary: The rebuke of the disobedient man of God has no link to Ahaziah's death or burial.

2-chronicles-22:9:3.summary: Joram “killed all his brethren,” helping explain why no one in the house could hold power.

2-chronicles-22:9:4.summary: Jehoshaphat “sought the Lord,” the reason given for Ahaziah's honorable burial.

2-chronicles-22:9:5.summary: “No son remained… except Ahaziah,” so with his death no one could hold power.

2-chronicles-22:9:7.summary: A good word found in Jeroboam's son earns mourning, loosely like Ahaziah's burial for his grandfather's sake.

2-chronicles-22:9:8.summary: Jehu orders Jezebel buried “for she is a king's daughter,” paralleling burial due to royal lineage.

2-chronicles-22:10:1.summary: Introduces Athaliah as Ahaziah's mother and counselor in sinning.

2-chronicles-22:11:0.summary: The Lord nullifies rulers' counsels, a general theme behind Athaliah's foiled plan.

2-chronicles-22:11:1.summary: No counsel avails with the impious, a general sovereignty theme.

2-chronicles-22:11:2.summary: God's promise to set David's throne upright forever is what Joash's rescue preserves.

2-chronicles-22:11:3.summary: Ezekiel's priests' chambers have no link to hiding Joash in a chamber.

2-chronicles-22:11:5.summary: God not destroying everyone for the blessing in the cluster loosely matches the surviving heir.

2-chronicles-22:11:6.summary: “For David's sake the Lord gave him a remnant,” as one heir of David survives.

2-chronicles-22:11:7.summary: Jehoiada, husband of Jehoshabeath, emerges to restore Joash.

2-chronicles-22:11:8.summary: God's purpose determining events is a general providence theme.

2-chronicles-22:11:9.summary: The psalm about human thought keeping a feast has no specific link to Joash's rescue.

2-chronicles-22:11:10.summary: The Lord was “unwilling to destroy David's house” and promised a lamp always, fulfilled in Joash's rescue.

2-chronicles-22:12:0.summary: Asking why the impious prosper loosely fits Athaliah's six-year rule.

2-chronicles-22:12:1.summary: God “hid me in a tent… in the hiding place of His tent,” as Joash was hidden in God's house.

2-chronicles-22:12:2.summary: The ungodly walking around loosely fits Athaliah ruling.

2-chronicles-22:12:3.summary: Being scourged daily has no specific link to Joash hidden in God's house.

2-chronicles-22:12:4.summary: The wicked suddenly cast down loosely anticipates Athaliah's end.

2-chronicles-22:12:5.summary: Habakkuk's confidence in God's appointed judge has no specific link to Joash's hiding.

2-chronicles-22:5:7.summary: Daniel 5:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-22:5:7.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-22:5:7.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-23:1:1.summary: The pledge sealed by rulers assumes a covenant, but the Saints text here says only that Jehoiada took commanders “into a house.”
2-chronicles-23:1:1.why: Covenant wording absent in Greek-based text.

2-chronicles-23:1:2.summary: Asa's covenant to seek the Lord assumes a covenant link that the Saints wording “into a house” does not carry.
2-chronicles-23:1:2.why: Covenant wording absent in Greek-based text.

2-chronicles-23:2:0.summary: Priests and Levites gathering to Jerusalem from all territories loosely parallels Levites gathered from Judah's cities (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:2:1.summary: Jesus' saying about sheep among wolves has no link to gathering Levites and rulers.

2-chronicles-23:2:2.summary: Paul's call to walk wisely has no specific link to Jehoiada's gathering.

2-chronicles-23:2:3.summary: David addresses the “rulers of the Levites' ancestral houses,” sharing the leadership term only.

2-chronicles-23:2:4.summary: Lists “the ancestral rulers of the priests and Levites,” a shared term but different occasion.

2-chronicles-23:2:5.summary: A kind lender managing words with judgment has no link to gathering Levites.

2-chronicles-23:2:6.summary: The list of Jehoshaphat's sons shares at most the name Azarias; no real link to this gathering.

2-chronicles-23:3:0.summary: The Lord's promise to David's house and “a lamp always” is what Jehoiada invokes for the king's son.

2-chronicles-23:3:2.summary: God's word that David would “never lack a man… upon the throne” is the promise cited here.

2-chronicles-23:3:3.summary: “As I covenanted with David… A man leading in Israel will not be removed,” the word Jehoiada cites.

2-chronicles-23:3:4.summary: Kings records Jehoiada making a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people in the same coup.

2-chronicles-23:3:5.summary: God's word that “a man shall not be cut off for you from Israel's throne,” as spoken concerning David's house.

2-chronicles-23:3:6.summary: “As I told your father David… a man ruling in Israel shall not be removed,” the promise invoked.

2-chronicles-23:3:7.summary: God will establish David's seed and throne forever, the promise behind letting the king's son reign.
2-chronicles-23:3:7.why: Psalm form of the Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-23:3:8.summary: A census of priests and ancestral rulers in Jerusalem has no specific link to the covenant with the king (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:3:9.summary: “His seed will remain for ever, and his throne” matches the Davidic promise Jehoiada cites.
2-chronicles-23:3:9.why: Psalm form of the Davidic promise.

2-chronicles-23:3:10.summary: Israel's elders made a covenant with King David before the Lord, as Judah's assembly covenants with the king.

2-chronicles-23:3:12.summary: Jehoiada's covenant between himself, the people, and the king belongs to this same event.

2-chronicles-23:3:13.summary: David made a covenant with the elders “before the Lord” and was anointed king, a precedent.

2-chronicles-23:4:0.summary: Zechariah serving in his division's order loosely matches priestly shifts entering on the Sabbath.

2-chronicles-23:4:1.summary: David's division of priests by ancestral houses gives background for the shifts used here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:4:2.summary: David's organization of Levites, including gatekeepers, is general background for guarding the gates.

2-chronicles-23:4:3.summary: Gatekeepers assigned by lot to each gate loosely relate to stationing guards at entrances.

2-chronicles-23:4:4.summary: Levites came in “for seven days, from time to time,” the weekly rotation behind Sabbath shifts.

2-chronicles-23:5:0.summary: Ezekiel's ruler at the gate and people bowing at the vestibules loosely relates to temple gates.

2-chronicles-23:5:1.summary: The lame man at the Beautiful Gate has no link to stationing guards at the Middle Gate.

2-chronicles-23:5:3.summary: Ezekiel's shut gate for the Lord and ruler has no specific link to this arrangement.

2-chronicles-23:6:0.summary: Levites are stationed to minister in the Lord's house and its holy things, the role reserved for them here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:6:1.summary: Kings' parallel assigns thirds at the gates and “keep watch over the Lord's house for the king.”

2-chronicles-23:7:0.summary: “The outsider who touches shall die” parallels “anyone entering the house will die.”

2-chronicles-23:7:1.summary: Priests guard the sanctuary and “the outsider who touches shall die,” the same holy-boundary rule.

2-chronicles-23:7:2.summary: Bounds set at Sinai with death for trespassers is a general holy-boundary parallel.

2-chronicles-23:7:3.summary: Taking a murderer from the altar has no specific link to the Levites guarding the king.

2-chronicles-23:8:1.summary: David's priestly divisions are the “divisions” Jehoiada did not dismiss (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:9:0.summary: Goliath's sword was kept at the sanctuary and given to David, as David's weapons were kept in God's house.

2-chronicles-23:9:1.summary: The Saints text speaks of “gold armlets” David brought to Jerusalem, not shields, so the weapons link is loose.

2-chronicles-23:10:0.summary: Solomon stood before the altar facing the assembly, only a general temple-layout parallel.

2-chronicles-23:10:2.summary: Placing the altar by the tent doors has no specific link to stationing armed guards.

2-chronicles-23:11:0.summary: The people shout “May the king live!” at Saul's presentation, the same acclamation.

2-chronicles-23:11:1.summary: “The testimonies” placed in the ark share the word used of what was placed on Joash.

2-chronicles-23:11:3.summary: The psalm's profaned “consecrated thing” of David's line loosely relates; the crown is not named in the Saints text.

2-chronicles-23:11:5.summary: The “crown of life” for those who endure trial has no real link to Joash's royal crown.

2-chronicles-23:11:6.summary: Priest and prophet anoint Solomon and cry “Long live King Solomon!” as Jehoiada does for Joash.

2-chronicles-23:11:7.summary: “The royal crown” taken from Saul's head is the same regalia placed on Joash.

2-chronicles-23:11:8.summary: The “tablets of the testimony” share the word testimony only.

2-chronicles-23:11:9.summary: The Saints text says “law for help,” with no testimony wording; no specific link to the coronation.
2-chronicles-23:11:9.why: Wording does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-23:11:10.summary: Kings are told to receive instruction and serve the Lord, loosely like giving the king the testimonies.

2-chronicles-23:11:11.summary: Zadok anoints Solomon and the people say “Long live King Solomon!” matching Joash's anointing.

2-chronicles-23:11:12.summary: Believers made a kingdom and priests has no specific link to Joash's coronation.

2-chronicles-23:11:13.summary: Samuel anoints Saul as ruler with oil, a parallel royal anointing.

2-chronicles-23:11:14.summary: God anointed David with holy oil, a general parallel to anointing his descendant.

2-chronicles-23:11:15.summary: Jesus crowned with glory through death has no real link to Joash's crowning.

2-chronicles-23:11:16.summary: God's “holy sign” blossoming on David's heir loosely evokes the crown; the Saints text does not say crown.

2-chronicles-23:11:17.summary: The crowds hail the Son of David, a loose echo of acclaiming David's heir.

2-chronicles-23:11:18.summary: God placed “upon his head a crown,” as the royal crown was placed on Joash.

2-chronicles-23:11:19.summary: Kings as foster fathers and ruling women as nurses only loosely fit the rescued child-king.

2-chronicles-23:11:20.summary: Elders with golden crowns in heaven have no real link to Joash's crowning.

2-chronicles-23:11:21.summary: Christ's many diadems share only the idea of a crown.

2-chronicles-23:11:22.summary: The elders “anointed David king,” the same act of anointing a king.

2-chronicles-23:11:23.summary: Recounts how Joash, the “king's son” brought out here, was hidden and saved.

2-chronicles-23:11:24.summary: Hushai's “Long live the king!” is the same acclamation.

2-chronicles-23:11:25.summary: God choosing the poor as heirs of the kingdom has no link to Joash's coronation.

2-chronicles-23:11:26.summary: The Saints text of Isaiah on sealing up the law has no specific link to giving the king the testimonies.

2-chronicles-23:11:27.summary: Rulers gathering against God's anointed loosely echoes the anointed king opposed by Athaliah.

2-chronicles-23:11:28.summary: Elders throwing crowns before the throne has no real link to Joash's coronation.

2-chronicles-23:11:29.summary: God “raised a testimony in Jacob,” sharing the word testimony.

2-chronicles-23:12:1.summary: The violent death of Jezebel, Athaliah's mother, loosely foreshadows Athaliah's fall (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:13:0.summary: “When the righteous are praised, peoples will rejoice,” as the people rejoice at the rightful king.

2-chronicles-23:13:1.summary: Priests sounding trumpets before the ark loosely parallels trumpets around the king.

2-chronicles-23:13:2.summary: Cowering in fear where there was no fear has no specific link to Athaliah's cry.

2-chronicles-23:13:3.summary: Ahab accuses Elijah of perverting Israel, loosely like Athaliah's accusation of attack.

2-chronicles-23:13:4.summary: A city prospering through the righteous is only a general parallel to the people's rejoicing.

2-chronicles-23:13:5.summary: David's appointed singers with instruments are background for the singers here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:13:6.summary: Jehu's supporters sound a trumpet and proclaim a new king, a parallel coronation acclaim.

2-chronicles-23:13:7.summary: David appoints singers with instruments of gladness, background for singers praising here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:13:8.summary: Judging others while doing the same loosely fits the usurper crying “attacking.”

2-chronicles-23:13:9.summary: All the people rejoice with great joy at Solomon's anointing, as at Joash's crowning.

2-chronicles-23:13:10.summary: People trapped suddenly at an evil time loosely fits Athaliah's sudden downfall.

2-chronicles-23:13:11.summary: Gladness in Israel at David's accession is a general parallel to the rejoicing.

2-chronicles-23:13:12.summary: Josiah stood “by the pillar” before the Lord; the Saints text here says “at his station,” so the pillar link is not carried.
2-chronicles-23:13:12.why: Royal standing place in the temple.

2-chronicles-23:13:13.summary: Joram of Ahab's house cries “Deceit” at Jehu's coup, paralleling Athaliah's cry “You are attacking!”
2-chronicles-23:13:13.why: Ahab's house crying out at a coup.

2-chronicles-23:13:14.summary: The king stood “beside the pillar”; the Saints text here says “at his station,” so the link is loose.
2-chronicles-23:13:14.why: Royal standing place in the temple.

2-chronicles-23:13:15.summary: Gideon's men sound horn trumpets and cry out in a surprise attack, sharing only trumpets and a sudden overthrow (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:13:16.summary: Gideon's men taking horn trumpets has no specific link to the coronation scene.

2-chronicles-23:13:17.summary: The silver trumpets summon the congregation and rulers, general background for trumpets around the king (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:13:18.summary: David's linen robe shares only the word robe with Athaliah tearing hers.

2-chronicles-23:14:0.summary: From the same coup in Kings, but this verse concerns guarding the king, not Athaliah's removal.

2-chronicles-23:14:1.summary: A murderer is taken from God's altar to die, loosely like removing Athaliah from the house before execution.
2-chronicles-23:14:1.why: Holy place not a refuge for the guilty.

2-chronicles-23:14:3.summary: Jehu's officers strike Baal's worshippers with the sword and throw them out, a parallel purge of Ahab's house's religion.

2-chronicles-23:14:4.summary: God commands the house to be defiled with the slain, the opposite of Jehoiada's care not to kill in it.

2-chronicles-23:15:0.summary: The Horse Gate near the king's house is likely the “Gate of the Horsemen” where Athaliah died.
2-chronicles-23:15:0.why: Locates the site of her death.

2-chronicles-23:15:1.summary: Athaliah destroyed the royal offspring, the crime for which she now dies.
2-chronicles-23:15:1.why: Shows the justice of her death.

2-chronicles-23:15:2.summary: Names “the eastern Horse Gate” in Jerusalem, likely the same gate as the Gate of the Horsemen.
2-chronicles-23:15:2.why: Locates the site of her death.

2-chronicles-23:15:3.summary: The Lord abhors a man of bloodshed and deceit, a general principle fitting Athaliah.

2-chronicles-23:15:4.summary: Men of bloodshed will not live out half their days, a general retribution theme.

2-chronicles-23:15:5.summary: Those who shed saints' blood are given blood to drink, a general just-recompense theme.

2-chronicles-23:15:6.summary: Adoni-bezek says “As I have done, so God has repaid me,” a general retribution parallel.

2-chronicles-23:15:7.summary: Judgment without mercy for the merciless loosely fits Athaliah's end.

2-chronicles-23:15:8.summary: “With the measure you use, it will be measured to you,” a general retribution principle.

2-chronicles-23:16:0.summary: Leaders seal a written pledge, a general covenant-renewal parallel.

2-chronicles-23:16:1.summary: Hezekiah resolves “to establish a covenant of the Lord,” a parallel royal covenant renewal.

2-chronicles-23:16:3.summary: Josiah established a covenant and made the inhabitants of Jerusalem enter it, a parallel renewal.

2-chronicles-23:16:4.summary: The people bind themselves by oath to walk in God's law, a general covenant-renewal parallel (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:16:5.summary: Ezra's covenant to put away foreign wives shares only covenant-making.

2-chronicles-23:16:6.summary: Asa's people “passed into a covenant to seek the Lord,” a close parallel renewal.

2-chronicles-23:16:7.summary: The people swear by the Lord with trumpets, part of Asa's covenant, a loose parallel.

2-chronicles-23:16:8.summary: People declaring “I belong to God” loosely echoes becoming “the Lord's people.”

2-chronicles-23:16:9.summary: The covenant in Moab is general background for covenant renewal (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:16:10.summary: Nehemiah has priests swear to uphold a word, a general oath parallel.

2-chronicles-23:16:11.summary: The Lord chose Israel “to be unto Him a people,” matching the goal “that they should be the Lord's people.”

2-chronicles-23:16:12.summary: The Horeb covenant made with the living generation is a general covenant parallel.

2-chronicles-23:16:13.summary: Joshua made a covenant with the people to serve the Lord and remove foreign gods, a close parallel.

2-chronicles-23:17:0.summary: Elijah has Baal's prophets seized and slaughtered, as Matthan priest of Baal is killed.

2-chronicles-23:17:1.summary: God will destroy idols' names and false prophets, a general anti-idolatry theme.

2-chronicles-23:17:2.summary: Josiah “pulled down… the altars of the Baals” and pulverized idols, matching this destruction.

2-chronicles-23:17:3.summary: Handmade idols hidden away is a general idol-removal theme.

2-chronicles-23:17:4.summary: Hezekiah removed high places and shattered pillars, a parallel royal purge of idolatry.

2-chronicles-23:17:6.summary: “You shall pull down their altars… burn the graven images,” the command this act fulfills.

2-chronicles-23:17:7.summary: Josiah “pulled down the… altars, cut the idols into fine pieces,” closely matching this verse.

2-chronicles-23:17:8.summary: The law requires death for one who leads people to other gods, as Baal's priest is killed (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:17:9.summary: Jehu's men “tore down Baal's house” and pulled down its pillars, the northern parallel to this purge.

2-chronicles-23:18:0.summary: Numbers prescribes the burnt offerings “written in Moses' law” that Jehoiada restored (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:18:1.summary: Priests and Levites carry the ark at the dedication, a general temple-service parallel.

2-chronicles-23:18:2.summary: Hezekiah stations Levites with instruments “according to the command of King David,” paralleling “David's direction.”

2-chronicles-23:18:3.summary: David's organization of Levites over the Lord's house is the arrangement Jehoiada reestablished (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:18:4.summary: David appointed the singers with instruments, the “songs according to David's direction” (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:19:0.summary: Gatekeepers appointed by David and Samuel guard the gates of the Lord's house, as here.

2-chronicles-23:19:1.summary: The “divisions of the gates” are David's arrangement of gatekeepers stationed here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-23:20:1.summary: Jotham built the “upper gate” of the Lord's house; the Saints text here says “Inner Gate,” so the link is uncertain.

2-chronicles-23:20:2.summary: Kings' account of the same coup, with captains of hundreds obeying Jehoiada.

2-chronicles-23:21:1.summary: The righteous rejoice at vengeance on the ungodly, a general parallel to rejoicing at Athaliah's death.

2-chronicles-23:21:2.summary: Heaven rejoices over Babylon's judgment, a general parallel.
2-chronicles-23:21:2.why: Joy at the fall of the wicked.

2-chronicles-23:21:3.summary: A city prospering through the righteous loosely relates to the quiet city; the shown text lacks the wicked's fall.

2-chronicles-23:21:4.summary: Praise at the great prostitute's judgment is a distant parallel to joy at Athaliah's death.

2-chronicles-23:1:3.summary: 1 Samuel 18:3 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-23:1:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-23:1:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-24:1:0.summary: The genealogy lists “Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,” placing Joash in the line.
2-chronicles-24:1:0.why: Places Joash in the royal line.

2-chronicles-24:2:0.summary: Uzziah sought the Lord “in the days of Zacharias,” a parallel of piety tied to a mentor's lifetime.

2-chronicles-24:2:1.summary: Amaziah “did what was right before the Lord, but not with a full heart,” a qualified approval like Joash's.

2-chronicles-24:2:2.summary: After Jehoiada's death Joash listened to rulers and turned to idols, fulfilling the limit implied here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-24:2:3.summary: Their heart was not upright or faithful, a general theme of shallow devotion.

2-chronicles-24:2:4.summary: Honoring God with lips while the heart is far is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-24:2:5.summary: Believing then quickly forgetting is a general theme of short-lived faith.

2-chronicles-24:2:7.summary: Those without root last only for a time, a general parallel to Joash's temporary faithfulness.

2-chronicles-24:3:0.summary: Abraham arranges a wife for Isaac, a general parallel to Jehoiada taking wives for Joash.

2-chronicles-24:3:1.summary: Lamech “took two wives,” sharing only the phrase.

2-chronicles-24:3:2.summary: Jesus' teaching on marriage from creation relates only generally to taking two wives.

2-chronicles-24:3:3.summary: Records the death of the same Jehoiada who arranged Joash's marriages.

2-chronicles-24:3:4.summary: Hagar takes a wife for Ishmael, a general parallel of a guardian arranging marriage.

2-chronicles-24:5:0.summary: Under Josiah, silver gathered by Levites from all Israel is used “to strengthen the house,” closely parallel.

2-chronicles-24:5:1.summary: The list of Jehoshaphat's sons has no link to collecting silver for the temple.

2-chronicles-24:5:2.summary: Hezekiah opened and repaired the doors of the Lord's house, a parallel royal temple repair.

2-chronicles-24:6:1.summary: Levites appointed over the Tent of Testimony is general background for Moses' prescriptions.

2-chronicles-24:6:2.summary: Aaron's budding staff in the Tent of Testimony shares only the tent's name.

2-chronicles-24:6:3.summary: Recalls the Tent of Testimony made as Moses was directed, general background.

2-chronicles-24:6:4.summary: Levites joining Aaron before the Tent of Testimony is general background.

2-chronicles-24:6:5.summary: Joab questioning David's census has no link to Joash's rebuke about the temple levy.

2-chronicles-24:7:0.summary: Tells of raiders carrying off Joram's sons, background to the royal family, but it does not mention Athaliah's sons damaging God's house.
2-chronicles-24:7:0.why: Gives some family background, not the temple desecration.

2-chronicles-24:7:1.summary: Both use “Baalim” for an unfaithful woman's idolatry, but Hosea's image is Israel as an adulterous wife, not Athaliah.
2-chronicles-24:7:1.why: Matches the prophets' picture of Baal worship as unfaithfulness.

2-chronicles-24:7:2.summary: Ahaz also misused and cut up the articles of the Lord's house, a later case of temple things being desecrated.
2-chronicles-24:7:2.why: Shows another king of Judah abusing temple property.

2-chronicles-24:7:3.summary: In Hosea, God-given silver and gold are made into objects for Baal, which echoes holy things being used for the Baalim.
2-chronicles-24:7:3.why: Shows God's gifts being diverted to Baal.

2-chronicles-24:7:4.summary: A general charge of forsaking God for foreign gods, with no specific link to Athaliah or the temple.
2-chronicles-24:7:4.why: Gives the broad Mosaic warning against apostasy.

2-chronicles-24:7:5.summary: A general proverb about the name of the impious; nothing ties it to Athaliah or the temple.

2-chronicles-24:7:6.summary: Ezekiel accuses Jerusalem of taking God's gold, silver and offerings for idols, a broad parallel to holy things used for Baal.
2-chronicles-24:7:6.why: Gives the prophetic picture of turning sacred gifts to idols.

2-chronicles-24:7:7.summary: Belshazzar profanes the vessels of God's house while praising idols, another misuse of temple things.
2-chronicles-24:7:7.why: A later, foreign example of profaning temple vessels.

2-chronicles-24:7:8.summary: Only the word “lawless” is shared; the eschatological lawless one has no real connection to Athaliah.

2-chronicles-24:7:9.summary: In Kings, Joash's order about the silver of the “holy things” for the Lord's house belongs to the same repair campaign, though not to this verse's charge.
2-chronicles-24:7:9.why: Links to the Kings account of the temple repairs.

2-chronicles-24:7:10.summary: Esther's denunciation of the wicked Haman has nothing to do with Athaliah or the desecration of the temple.

2-chronicles-24:7:11.summary: “The woman Jezebel” who leads people into idolatry loosely matches “the lawless woman” Athaliah, but the text shown names no family tie.
2-chronicles-24:7:11.why: Draws a typological comparison between wicked queens.

2-chronicles-24:7:12.summary: The vessels of God's house are used to honour idols, a general parallel to holy things used for the Baalim.
2-chronicles-24:7:12.why: Another case of temple objects serving idolatry.

2-chronicles-24:8:1.summary: Both scenes involve a box for collecting offerings at the temple, but the link is only by type.
2-chronicles-24:8:1.why: Shows temple offering practice in Jesus' day.

2-chronicles-24:9:0.summary: In the same narrative, Joash asks why the Levites have not collected from Judah and Jerusalem what Moses prescribed, which explains the proclamation.
2-chronicles-24:9:0.why: Gives the immediate setup for the collection.

2-chronicles-24:9:1.summary: The didrachma temple tax is a later form of the Mosaic contribution, but the text shown does not mention Moses.
2-chronicles-24:9:1.why: Shows the temple levy continuing in the New Testament.

2-chronicles-24:10:0.summary: Generous communal giving is the only shared idea; the Corinthian collection is a different context.
2-chronicles-24:10:0.why: A general parallel on generous giving.

2-chronicles-24:10:1.summary: Willing giving is a general theme; Paul's “cheerful giver” teaching is not tied to the temple collection.
2-chronicles-24:10:1.why: Gives a New Testament principle of willing giving.

2-chronicles-24:10:2.summary: The early church's sharing of property differs from contributions to a temple collection box; only a loose idea of giving is shared.

2-chronicles-24:10:3.summary: The rulers and people offer eagerly to the Lord for the temple, closely matching all the rulers and people filling the collection box.
2-chronicles-24:10:3.why: Shows the precedent of whole-hearted giving for God's house.

2-chronicles-24:10:4.summary: Isaiah's confession of sin and God's anger has nothing to do with giving for the temple.

2-chronicles-24:11:0.summary: Both involve regularly gathering contributions, but Paul's weekly setting-aside for the saints is a different collection.
2-chronicles-24:11:0.why: A loose parallel on how a collection is organized.

2-chronicles-24:12:0.summary: Under Josiah, the silver gathered by Levites is handed to workers, craftsmen and builders to repair the Lord's house, the same procedure as here.
2-chronicles-24:12:0.why: Shows a later temple repair following the same pattern.

2-chronicles-24:12:1.summary: Only Solomon's “stonecutters” for the temple building are shared; it is a different project.
2-chronicles-24:12:1.why: Shows the kind of labor temple work needed.

2-chronicles-24:13:0.summary: David prepares for a great temple to be built, a general link to work on the Lord's house.
2-chronicles-24:13:0.why: Recalls the original vision for the temple.

2-chronicles-24:13:1.summary: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction, which runs opposite to the restoration narrative with no specific link.
2-chronicles-24:13:1.why: Shares only the topic of the temple building.

2-chronicles-24:13:2.summary: Nehemiah speaks of “growth” on Jerusalem's walls as breaches are repaired, a loose echo of the work increasing.
2-chronicles-24:13:2.why: A comparable picture of restoration making progress.

2-chronicles-24:13:3.summary: Haggai contrasts the rebuilt house with its former glory; the only shared idea is temple restoration.
2-chronicles-24:13:3.why: A loose parallel on restoring the temple.

2-chronicles-24:14:0.summary: Solomon's gold bowls, dishes and censers are the kind of articles remade here, but this is the original furnishing.
2-chronicles-24:14:0.why: Shows what the temple vessels were.

2-chronicles-24:14:1.summary: A proverb about an incorrigible fool has nothing to do with temple vessels or offerings.

2-chronicles-24:14:2.summary: Numbers commands the “continual” daily whole burnt offering, the regular sacrifice resumed here (judged on the truncated text shown).
2-chronicles-24:14:2.why: Gives the legal basis for the continual burnt offerings.

2-chronicles-24:14:3.summary: Exodus sets out the morning and evening lambs as a “continual” offering, the sacrifice offered continually in Jehoiada's days.
2-chronicles-24:14:3.why: Gives the ordinance behind the restored daily worship.

2-chronicles-24:15:0.summary: David too was “old and full of days” at the end of a faithful life, the same formula used of Jehoiada.

2-chronicles-24:15:1.summary: God promises Abraham burial at a good old age, a general picture of a blessed death in old age.
2-chronicles-24:15:1.why: Places a long life as covenant blessing.

2-chronicles-24:15:2.summary: Jacob also gives his age as a hundred and thirty years, a shared number in an otherwise unrelated scene.

2-chronicles-24:15:3.summary: The psalm's normal span of seventy or eighty years sets off Jehoiada's exceptional hundred and thirty.
2-chronicles-24:15:3.why: Shows how unusual his long life was.

2-chronicles-24:15:4.summary: Abraham dies “an old man and full of days,” the same formula of a blessed death given to Jehoiada.
2-chronicles-24:15:4.why: Links Jehoiada to the patriarchal pattern of a blessed death.

2-chronicles-24:15:5.summary: The promise of “length of days” for the faithful loosely matches Jehoiada's long life.
2-chronicles-24:15:5.why: Reads his age as a sign of God's favor.

2-chronicles-24:15:6.summary: Coming to the grave like ripe grain in season is a general image of a timely death in old age.
2-chronicles-24:15:6.why: A poetic picture of a full life ending.

2-chronicles-24:16:0.summary: God does not forget service done for His name, a general parallel to Jehoiada being honoured for doing good toward God's house.
2-chronicles-24:16:0.why: States the principle that faithful service is remembered.

2-chronicles-24:16:1.summary: Hezekiah “did what was good” before the Lord, a similar verdict on someone who served God's house.
2-chronicles-24:16:1.why: Shows the Chronicler's praise for reformers.

2-chronicles-24:16:2.summary: Nehemiah asks that his kindness done for God's house be remembered, close in idea to Jehoiada's good toward His house.
2-chronicles-24:16:2.why: Shows service to the temple being honoured.

2-chronicles-24:16:4.summary: Mentions David's burial and tomb, which loosely relates to Jehoiada's burial in David's city.
2-chronicles-24:16:4.why: Recalls the royal tombs in David's city.

2-chronicles-24:16:5.summary: The principle that God honours those who honour Him fits a priest given a king's burial, but the link is general.
2-chronicles-24:16:5.why: Offers a reason for his honoured burial.

2-chronicles-24:16:6.summary: David is buried in the City of David, the same burial place where Jehoiada is laid with the kings.

2-chronicles-24:17:0.summary: Moses foresees the people turning aside “after my death,” just as Judah's rulers turn the king once Jehoiada dies.
2-chronicles-24:17:0.why: Shows the pattern of apostasy after a godly leader dies.

2-chronicles-24:17:1.summary: After his father's death, Ahaziah's counselors lead him into evil, a close parallel to Joash heeding Judah's rulers after Jehoiada died.
2-chronicles-24:17:1.why: The same pattern in Judah's recent royal history.

2-chronicles-24:17:2.summary: Daniel's prophecy about defiling the covenant has no specific link to Joash's courtiers.

2-chronicles-24:17:3.summary: Paul expects misleaders to arise after his departure, a general parallel to corruption following Jehoiada's death.
2-chronicles-24:17:3.why: Shows the danger when a faithful leader is gone.

2-chronicles-24:17:4.summary: Peter's wish that his teaching be remembered after his departure is not about apostasy or bad counsel.
2-chronicles-24:17:4.why: Only the phrase about departure loosely overlaps.

2-chronicles-24:17:5.summary: Flattery spreading a net loosely matches the rulers bowing to the king before leading him astray.

2-chronicles-24:17:6.summary: A proverb on false tongues has no specific connection to the rulers' homage to Joash.

2-chronicles-24:17:8.summary: Someone led astray by persuasive speech to his ruin is a general parallel to Joash listening to the rulers.

2-chronicles-24:17:9.summary: Rehoboam abandons the elders' counsel and listens to his courtiers, a close parallel to a king heeding the wrong advisers.
2-chronicles-24:17:9.why: An earlier king of Judah ruined by bad counsel.

2-chronicles-24:17:10.summary: A proverb about giving glory to a fool has no clear tie to the rulers bowing to Joash.

2-chronicles-24:17:11.summary: “When a king listens to an unjust word, all those under him are lawless” fits the king listening to the rulers and the apostasy that follows.
2-chronicles-24:17:11.why: States the principle at work in the account.

2-chronicles-24:18:0.summary: Achar's sin brought “wrath came upon” the whole congregation, a shared formula about wrath for unfaithfulness.
2-chronicles-24:18:0.why: Shows wrath falling on the community for sin.

2-chronicles-24:18:1.summary: God's wrath on the disobedient is a general principle; there is no specific link to Judah's idols.
2-chronicles-24:18:1.why: Gives the New Testament statement of the principle.

2-chronicles-24:18:2.summary: “Wrath from the Lord has come upon you” is a similar formula, but it is aimed at Jehoshaphat's alliance, not idolatry.
2-chronicles-24:18:2.why: Part of the Chronicler's pattern of sin bringing wrath.

2-chronicles-24:18:3.summary: Joash's earlier zeal to repair the Lord's house contrasts with the later abandonment of the Lord.
2-chronicles-24:18:3.why: Shows how far the king fell.

2-chronicles-24:18:4.summary: Judah's rulers face God's outpoured judgment, a general parallel to the rulers' apostasy bringing wrath.
2-chronicles-24:18:4.why: A prophetic charge against Judah's leaders.

2-chronicles-24:18:5.summary: “The Lord's furious wrath is upon Israel” for sin is a similar formula in a different episode.
2-chronicles-24:18:5.why: Shows the recurring theme of wrath.

2-chronicles-24:18:6.summary: Judah's high places, pillars and groves under Rehoboam are a general parallel to serving Astartes and idols.

2-chronicles-24:18:7.summary: “Wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem” repeats the formula of wrath on Judah and Jerusalem for unfaithfulness.
2-chronicles-24:18:7.why: The Chronicler's repeated pattern of retribution.

2-chronicles-24:18:8.summary: God as a lion to Judah's house is a general image of judgment on Judah.
2-chronicles-24:18:8.why: A vivid prophetic picture of the wrath.

2-chronicles-24:18:9.summary: The command to cut down sacred groves and burn idols is the opposite of serving Astartes and idols.

2-chronicles-24:18:10.summary: The Lord's anger blazing against Israel is a general parallel; the cause there, David's census, is different.
2-chronicles-24:18:10.why: Shows only the theme of divine anger.

2-chronicles-24:18:11.summary: God's hand against Judah and Jerusalem for Baal worship and turning away from the Lord broadly matches the apostasy here.
2-chronicles-24:18:11.why: A later prophetic indictment of the same sin.

2-chronicles-24:18:13.summary: Joram leading Judah and Jerusalem into Ahab-like idolatry is a related earlier apostasy, but its focus differs.
2-chronicles-24:18:13.why: Shows the recent background of idolatry in Judah.

2-chronicles-24:18:14.summary: Solomon turned to “Astarte” and idols in his old age, an earlier precedent for serving the Astartes.
2-chronicles-24:18:14.why: Traces Astarte worship back to Solomon.

2-chronicles-24:18:15.summary: The leaders' breaches of faith, prophets sent and mocked, and wrath without healing follow the same sequence as 24:18–19.
2-chronicles-24:18:15.why: The Chronicler's closing summary of this pattern.

2-chronicles-24:18:16.summary: Choosing “new gods” is a general idea of idolatry; there is no specific link.

2-chronicles-24:18:17.summary: “The Lord became fiercely angry with Judah and Jerusalem” for unfaithfulness is the same formula of wrath on Judah and Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-24:18:17.why: Shows the recurring wrath theme in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-24:18:18.summary: Manasseh's pillars, groves and idolatry are a later and worse version of serving idols (truncated text).
2-chronicles-24:18:18.why: Shows how idolatry in Judah grew worse later.

2-chronicles-24:19:0.summary: God sending His servants the prophets though “you did not listen” matches prophets sent who were not heeded.

2-chronicles-24:19:1.summary: The call to let those with ears hear is a general exhortation with no specific tie to Joash's Judah.
2-chronicles-24:19:1.why: Only the idea of hearing is shared.

2-chronicles-24:19:2.summary: An invitation to listen to God's law for the nations is not about prophets sent and rejected.

2-chronicles-24:19:3.summary: God sent His servants the prophets, “but they did not listen” or turn from their evils, closely matching this verse.
2-chronicles-24:19:3.why: The same pattern of prophetic warning rejected.

2-chronicles-24:19:4.summary: Not hearing Moses and the Prophets shows a general refusal to heed God's messengers.

2-chronicles-24:19:5.summary: God kept sending the prophets, “and you did not listen,” calling them to turn, the same pattern as here.

2-chronicles-24:19:6.summary: Prophets “who testified among them to turn them back” closely echoes prophets who testified to turn them back.
2-chronicles-24:19:6.why: A historical review of exactly this behavior.

2-chronicles-24:19:7.summary: God sent all His prophets, “and they did not hear Me,” matching the repeated refusal to listen.
2-chronicles-24:19:7.why: Shows the long history of ignoring prophets.

2-chronicles-24:19:8.summary: A general call to give ear has no specific link to the rejected prophets.

2-chronicles-24:19:9.summary: People who will not hear and turn reflects a refusal to listen, though in a different setting.
2-chronicles-24:19:9.why: Shows the spiritual dullness behind the refusal.

2-chronicles-24:19:10.summary: The Lord “sent through prophets” out of mercy, and they mocked them, the Chronicler's own summary of this pattern.

2-chronicles-24:19:11.summary: Isaiah's invitation to listen and live is not about prophets being rejected.

2-chronicles-24:19:12.summary: The Lord warned through all His prophets to turn, “but they did not listen,” the same sequence as here.
2-chronicles-24:19:12.why: The Kings summary of rejected prophetic warning.

2-chronicles-24:19:13.summary: In the parable, the owner sends one servant after another and each is rejected, picturing God sending prophets to an unheeding people (truncated).

2-chronicles-24:19:14.summary: “If you hear His voice, do not harden” calls for listening, a general parallel.

2-chronicles-24:19:15.summary: Jesus speaks of God sending prophets who were killed, through to Zechariah slain “between the altar and the house,” recalling this episode.
2-chronicles-24:19:15.why: Shows how Jesus used this story of a rejected prophet.

2-chronicles-24:19:16.summary: A rhetorical “who will give ear” has no specific link to Joash's time.
2-chronicles-24:19:16.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-24:20:0.summary: “Why do you transgress the Lord's word? Things will not go well for you” closely echoes Azarias' “Why do you transgress… You shall not prosper.”

2-chronicles-24:20:1.summary: Sins removing good things is a general parallel to transgression ruling out prosperity.
2-chronicles-24:20:1.why: Explains the loss as the result of sin.

2-chronicles-24:20:3.summary: The Spirit of the Lord comes upon a Levite in the assembly to deliver God's word, a close pattern of inspired speech in Chronicles.
2-chronicles-24:20:3.why: Shows the Chronicler's model of inspired speech.

2-chronicles-24:20:4.summary: Jesus' “Zechariah… murdered between the sanctuary and the altar” traditionally points to this priest, but the Saints text names him “Azarias” and this verse has no murder.
2-chronicles-24:20:4.why: Links to Jesus' words, though the Greek name differs.

2-chronicles-24:20:5.summary: “A spirit clothed Amasai” and he spoke, the same idiom of the Spirit clothing a speaker.
2-chronicles-24:20:5.why: The same expression for Spirit-empowered speech.

2-chronicles-24:20:6.summary: “The Spirit of God clothed Gideon” uses exactly the wording used of Azarias.
2-chronicles-24:20:6.why: The same idiom of the Spirit clothing a person.

2-chronicles-24:20:7.summary: Abandoning the Lord is bitter and brings its own discipline, a general parallel to “forsaken… He will forsake you.”

2-chronicles-24:20:8.summary: A prophet asks a king “why” he has despised the Lord's word, a similar rebuke in a different case.
2-chronicles-24:20:8.why: A comparable confrontation between prophet and king.

2-chronicles-24:20:9.summary: Their own ways have brought disaster, a general idea of self-inflicted judgment.
2-chronicles-24:20:9.why: Shows that sin brings its own consequences.

2-chronicles-24:20:10.summary: “If you forsake Him, He will forsake you” matches Azarias' “Because you have forsaken the Lord, He will forsake you.”

2-chronicles-24:20:11.summary: Serving foreign gods brings punishment in kind, a general parallel to forsaking and being forsaken.
2-chronicles-24:20:11.why: Illustrates judgment that fits the sin.

2-chronicles-24:20:12.summary: Forsaking the covenant of the God of their fathers explains disaster, a general parallel.
2-chronicles-24:20:12.why: Gives the Deuteronomic explanation of judgment.

2-chronicles-24:20:13.summary: Refusing the words sent “by His Spirit through the former prophets” loosely relates to Spirit-led warning and rejection.

2-chronicles-24:20:14.summary: Samuel tells Saul his kingdom will not stand for disobedience, a general parallel to “you shall not prosper.”
2-chronicles-24:20:14.why: Another prophet rebuking a disobedient king.

2-chronicles-24:20:15.summary: Jehoiada and his sons, Azarias among them, anointed Joash king, which sets up the irony of Joash later killing that son.
2-chronicles-24:20:15.why: Shows what Joash owed this family.

2-chronicles-24:21:0.summary: Stephen is stoned after testifying, a general parallel to the stoning of a Spirit-filled witness.
2-chronicles-24:21:0.why: A New Testament martyrdom by stoning.

2-chronicles-24:21:1.summary: Israel “killed Thy prophets who testified among them,” which sums up exactly this kind of killing of prophets.
2-chronicles-24:21:1.why: Places Azarias among the slain prophets.

2-chronicles-24:21:2.summary: Jesus names Zechariah “murdered between the sanctuary and the altar” and Jerusalem “stones those sent,” matching a prophet stoned in the temple court, though the Greek name differs.

2-chronicles-24:21:3.summary: In the parable the tenants stone the owner's slaves, a general parallel to the stoning of God's messenger.
2-chronicles-24:21:3.why: A parable figure for this violence.

2-chronicles-24:21:4.summary: A plot against God's prophet is a general parallel; Jeremiah was not stoned.

2-chronicles-24:21:5.summary: Plotters want to wipe out the prophet, a general parallel to Azarias' killing.
2-chronicles-24:21:5.why: Shows hostility toward a faithful prophet.

2-chronicles-24:21:6.summary: Officials demand the prophet's death and the king hands him over, a loose parallel to a prophet killed at a king's command.
2-chronicles-24:21:6.why: A king giving in to violence against a prophet.

2-chronicles-24:22:0.summary: God's vow to “require” shed blood gives the principle behind the dying plea for the Lord to judge.
2-chronicles-24:22:0.why: The basis for blood being avenged.

2-chronicles-24:22:1.summary: The blood of Zechariah, who perished between altar and house, “will be required,” answering the dying “May the Lord see and judge,” though the Saints text names him Azarias.
2-chronicles-24:22:1.why: Jesus' view of how this plea is answered.

2-chronicles-24:22:2.summary: Slain martyrs cry for God to “judge and avenge our blood,” closely matching the dying prophet's appeal.
2-chronicles-24:22:2.why: Martyrs pleading for justice in Revelation.

2-chronicles-24:22:3.summary: Good works repaid by stoning loosely matches Joash repaying Jehoiada's kindness by killing his son.

2-chronicles-24:22:4.summary: God avenges the blood of His slaves, a general answer to a plea for judgment.
2-chronicles-24:22:4.why: Shows God avenging His servants in the end.

2-chronicles-24:22:5.summary: “Thou seest” trouble and acts for the helpless loosely echoes “May the Lord see.”
2-chronicles-24:22:5.why: Expresses trust that God sees injustice.

2-chronicles-24:22:6.summary: The Lord will repay a wrongdoer, a general parallel to leaving judgment to God.
2-chronicles-24:22:6.why: A New Testament case of leaving vengeance to God.

2-chronicles-24:22:7.summary: Jeremiah asks to “see the vengeance from Thee” from the Lord who judges justly, closely matching “May the Lord see and judge.”

2-chronicles-24:22:8.summary: Killing a true prophet brings “innocent blood” guilt, a general parallel.
2-chronicles-24:22:8.why: Shows the guilt of killing a prophet.

2-chronicles-24:22:9.summary: Repaying evil instead of good brings lasting evil on one's house, describing Joash's ingratitude toward Jehoiada.
2-chronicles-24:22:9.why: States the moral principle Joash broke.

2-chronicles-24:22:10.summary: The Lord repays Babylon's recompense, a general idea of divine retribution.

2-chronicles-24:22:11.summary: Ingratitude among the healed loosely matches Joash not remembering Jehoiada's mercy.

2-chronicles-24:22:12.summary: Love answered with slander loosely matches kindness repaid with murder.

2-chronicles-24:22:13.summary: God judging the case of prophets against their persecutor is a general answer to the plea.
2-chronicles-24:22:13.why: Shows the final vindication of prophets.

2-chronicles-24:22:14.summary: Paul's “May it not be counted against them” contrasts with Azarias' dying call for judgment.

2-chronicles-24:23:1.summary: The rulers' apostasy and the wrath on Judah and Jerusalem explain why Syria's army now comes and destroys those rulers.
2-chronicles-24:23:1.why: Gives the cause of this judgment.

2-chronicles-24:23:2.summary: God's promise to repay in the day of vengeance is a general basis for the Syrian invasion as judgment.
2-chronicles-24:23:2.why: Shows the divine retribution behind events.

2-chronicles-24:23:3.summary: A call for kings to serve the Lord with fear has no specific link to the Syrian attack.

2-chronicles-24:23:4.summary: Rulers who “fall like one of the rulers” loosely matches the destruction of Judah's rulers.

2-chronicles-24:23:5.summary: The righteous see vengeance and say God judges on earth, a general answer to the prophet's plea.
2-chronicles-24:23:5.why: Ties the invasion to God judging.

2-chronicles-24:23:6.summary: “At the return of the year” Syria musters against Israel, closely matching Syria's army coming “after the year's completion.”
2-chronicles-24:23:6.why: The same phrase for Syria's seasonal campaigns.

2-chronicles-24:23:7.summary: A prophet warns that “at the return of the year” Syria's king will come up, the same seasonal Syrian attack.
2-chronicles-24:23:7.why: Shows the yearly pattern of Syrian invasion.

2-chronicles-24:24:0.summary: The covenant promise that a few will rout many is reversed here, as a few Syrians defeat Judah's great army.
2-chronicles-24:24:0.why: Shows the covenant blessing turned around.

2-chronicles-24:24:1.summary: Jehu's killing of Ahaziah's relatives is a separate event, not about Syria's victory over Judah.

2-chronicles-24:24:2.summary: The covenant curse “handed into enemies' hands” is fulfilled as God delivers Judah to Syria.

2-chronicles-24:24:3.summary: Being unable to withstand enemies is a general covenant curse.

2-chronicles-24:24:4.summary: “At the voice of five, many will flee” pictures a few routing the many in judgment, as here.
2-chronicles-24:24:4.why: A prophetic picture of the same reversal.

2-chronicles-24:24:5.summary: The covenant curse of defeat before enemies for unfaithfulness is enacted in Judah's rout.
2-chronicles-24:24:5.why: Gives the Deuteronomic basis for the defeat.

2-chronicles-24:24:6.summary: Serving enemies sent by the Lord is a general covenant curse.

2-chronicles-24:24:7.summary: God appointing an enemy for judgment loosely matches Syria executing judgment on Joash.
2-chronicles-24:24:7.why: Shows a foreign army as God's instrument.

2-chronicles-24:24:8.summary: Because Asa trusted, God handed a great force “into your hands,” the opposite of the great army now handed to Syria.

2-chronicles-24:24:9.summary: Azarias warned “Because you have forsaken the Lord, He will forsake you,” which is fulfilled in this defeat.

2-chronicles-24:24:10.summary: Jehoshaphat's helplessness before a “great multitude” contrasts with Judah's great army failing; the link is loose.

2-chronicles-24:24:11.summary: Assyria as the rod of God's anger is a general idea of a foreign army as His instrument.
2-chronicles-24:24:11.why: Illustrates God using nations to judge.

2-chronicles-24:24:12.summary: A few routing many only because the Lord “had delivered them up” explains the small Syrian force's victory.
2-chronicles-24:24:12.why: Gives the theological explanation for the defeat.

2-chronicles-24:24:13.summary: Even wounded Chaldeans would prevail, a loose picture of God giving victory to a weak enemy.
2-chronicles-24:24:13.why: Shows judgment that cannot be resisted.

2-chronicles-24:24:14.summary: An eschatological army from a distant land has no specific tie to the Syrian invasion.

2-chronicles-24:25:0.summary: The stoning of Jehoiada's son and his dying plea explain why Joash's servants killed him “because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada.”
2-chronicles-24:25:0.why: Shows the cause of Joash's assassination.

2-chronicles-24:25:1.summary: Ahaz is buried in David's city but not brought into the tombs of the kings, the same burial verdict as Joash.
2-chronicles-24:25:1.why: The Chronicler's sign of a dishonoured king.

2-chronicles-24:25:2.summary: Those who shed the blood of prophets receive blood in return, a general parallel to Joash killed for a prophet's blood.

2-chronicles-24:25:3.summary: Joram dies of grievous sickness and is buried in David's city “but not in the tombs of the kings,” closely matching Joash's end.
2-chronicles-24:25:3.why: The same pattern of a dishonoured death.

2-chronicles-24:25:4.summary: Jehoiada was buried in David's city “with the kings,” while Joash was refused the kings' tomb.
2-chronicles-24:25:4.why: Shows the priest honoured and the king disgraced.

2-chronicles-24:25:5.summary: The psalm's “Thou seest” trouble has no specific link to Joash's illness, murder or burial.
2-chronicles-24:25:5.why: No meaningful link to this verse.

2-chronicles-24:25:7.summary: A king wounded by the Syrians and recovering loosely matches Joash left with grave illnesses after Syria's attack.
2-chronicles-24:25:7.why: Another royal casualty of Syrian wars.

2-chronicles-24:25:8.summary: The Lord stirring foreign enemies against Joram is not about Joash's death or burial.

2-chronicles-24:25:9.summary: Amaziah is killed by conspirators, the same fate as his father Joash, though this is a separate event.
2-chronicles-24:25:9.why: Shows royal assassinations repeating in Judah.

2-chronicles-24:27:0.summary: The Kings account of the same Joash shows him giving the temple treasures to Hazael of Syria, part of the story summed up in this closing notice.
2-chronicles-24:27:0.why: Supplies the Kings version of Joash's reign.

2-chronicles-24:27:2.summary: The “remaining deeds” of Abijah are written in another record, the same formula closing a reign.

2-chronicles-24:27:3.summary: “The remaining deeds of Solomon… written in the records” is the same closing formula.
2-chronicles-24:27:3.why: Shows how the Chronicler cites his sources.

2-chronicles-24:27:4.summary: The genealogy lists “Amasias his son” in the royal line, the Amaziah who succeeds here.

2-chronicles-24:27:5.summary: Amaziah's accession formula picks up right after he “reigned in his place.”

2-chronicles-24:27:6.summary: The shown text of this verse does not mention Joash's temple repair, which is described in the candidate; the only link is the same king.

2-chronicles-24:27:7.summary: “The rest of Jehoshaphat's acts… are written” is the same closing formula for a reign.

2-chronicles-24:27:8.summary: Asa's deeds “are written in the Book of the Kings,” the same closing formula referring to the kings' records.

2-chronicles-24:17:7.summary: Proverbs 20:19 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-24:17:7.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-24:17:7.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-24:18:12.summary: 1 Kings 14:9 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-24:18:12.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-24:18:12.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-25:2:0.summary: Purifying “you of divided mind” loosely matches serving God “not with a full heart.”
2-chronicles-25:2:0.why: New Testament teaching on a divided heart.

2-chronicles-25:2:1.summary: Amaziah later worshipped the gods of Seir, which shows concretely what “not with a full heart” meant.
2-chronicles-25:2:1.why: Gives the evidence of his half-hearted devotion.

2-chronicles-25:2:2.summary: Honouring God with the lips while the “heart is far” is a general parallel to outward rightness without a full heart.
2-chronicles-25:2:2.why: Shows the problem of outward-only devotion.

2-chronicles-25:2:3.summary: Joash “did what was right before the Lord” only while Jehoiada lived, the same qualified verdict passed on to his son.
2-chronicles-25:2:3.why: Father and son both receive a qualified verdict.

2-chronicles-25:2:4.summary: “Your heart is not upright before God” is a general parallel to an incomplete heart.
2-chronicles-25:2:4.why: A New Testament example of a defective heart.

2-chronicles-25:2:5.summary: God looks at the heart, which gives the general principle behind judging Amaziah's heart.
2-chronicles-25:2:5.why: Explains why God's verdict looks at the heart.

2-chronicles-25:2:6.summary: Uzziah “did what was right before the Lord, according to everything his father Amaziah had done,” the same formula linked to Amaziah.
2-chronicles-25:2:6.why: Shows the son's verdict mirroring the father's.

2-chronicles-25:2:8.summary: A “man of divided mind” is unstable, a general parallel to Amaziah's half-heartedness.

2-chronicles-25:2:9.summary: “They divided their hearts” describes split loyalty, which loosely matches “not with a full heart.”
2-chronicles-25:2:9.why: A prophetic picture of a divided heart.

2-chronicles-25:2:10.summary: A heart “not upright with Him” is a general parallel to an incomplete heart toward God.

2-chronicles-25:3:2.summary: The principle that shed blood is required underlies executing the king's murderers, but the link is general.
2-chronicles-25:3:2.why: Gives the basis for punishing murderers.

2-chronicles-25:3:3.summary: Law requiring death for a guilty killer gives general support for executing the assassins.

2-chronicles-25:3:4.summary: Someone who kills by deceit must be put to death, a general rule fitting the treacherous servants.
2-chronicles-25:3:4.why: Gives the legal precedent for executing them.

2-chronicles-25:4:1.summary: “The son will not receive his father's injustice” states the same principle of personal responsibility quoted here.
2-chronicles-25:4:1.why: Ezekiel's restatement of the law cited.

2-chronicles-25:4:2.summary: “Each will die in his own sin” closely matches the quoted law “each shall die for his own sin.”

2-chronicles-25:4:4.summary: “The soul that sins will die,” with father and son treated alike, gives the same principle of individual guilt.

2-chronicles-25:5:1.summary: Jehoshaphat's muster by ancestral houses under commanders of thousands, starting with three hundred thousand of Judah, closely matches Amaziah's census.
2-chronicles-25:5:1.why: A comparable count of Judah's army.

2-chronicles-25:5:2.summary: Rehoboam assembles young warriors of Judah, a general parallel to mustering an army.

2-chronicles-25:5:3.summary: “Commanders of thousands and of hundreds” is shared wording only, in a different context.

2-chronicles-25:5:4.summary: Asa had three hundred thousand men of Judah “carrying large shields and spears,” closely matching Amaziah's numbers and weapons.
2-chronicles-25:5:4.why: A parallel army count in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-25:5:5.summary: Uzziah's army of three hundred seven thousand five hundred is a similar figure in a later muster.
2-chronicles-25:5:5.why: Compares the sizes of Judah's armies.

2-chronicles-25:5:6.summary: Moses appointing capable men as leaders of thousands and hundreds is the origin of the organization, but in a judicial setting.
2-chronicles-25:5:6.why: Shows where the command structure came from.

2-chronicles-25:5:7.summary: “Commanders of thousands and hundreds” over divisions under David shares the military terms only.
2-chronicles-25:5:7.why: Shows the organization of the army.

2-chronicles-25:5:8.summary: Samuel's warning about kings appointing commanders of thousands and hundreds shares only the terms.

2-chronicles-25:7:0.summary: A prophet rebukes a king of Judah for helping the northern king, as the man of God warns Amaziah against Israel's army.
2-chronicles-25:7:0.why: The Chronicler's pattern against alliances with Israel.

2-chronicles-25:7:1.summary: Jeroboam's golden heifers explain Israel's apostasy, the background to why the Lord is not with Ephraim.
2-chronicles-25:7:1.why: Shows the source of the northern kingdom's sin.

2-chronicles-25:7:2.summary: Hosea's judgment on Ephraim loosely supports the Lord not being with Ephraim.
2-chronicles-25:7:2.why: A prophetic picture of Ephraim under judgment.

2-chronicles-25:7:3.summary: An unnamed “man of God” confronts a king by the Lord's word, a similar kind of prophetic encounter.
2-chronicles-25:7:3.why: Another anonymous man of God warning a king.

2-chronicles-25:7:4.summary: Hosea's oracle about Ephraim's children has no specific link to Israel's army going with Amaziah.
2-chronicles-25:7:4.why: Only the name Ephraim is shared.

2-chronicles-25:7:5.summary: Abijah tells Israel's sons the Lord is with Judah and “it will not prosper for you,” matching the claim that the Lord is not with Israel.
2-chronicles-25:7:5.why: An earlier Chronicler speech on the same point.

2-chronicles-25:7:6.summary: Only the title “man of God” is shared; Paul's charge to Timothy is unrelated.

2-chronicles-25:7:7.summary: Woe on Ephraim's pride shows the northern kingdom under the Lord's wrath, a general support.

2-chronicles-25:7:8.summary: A prophet sent to confront a king is a general parallel.
2-chronicles-25:7:8.why: Shows the role of prophets toward kings.

2-chronicles-25:7:9.summary: “Person of God” equipped by Scripture shares only the title.

2-chronicles-25:8:0.summary: Asa confesses that the Lord can save “with many or with few,” the same truth that strength and rout come from Him.
2-chronicles-25:8:0.why: Shows the trust Amaziah is called to.

2-chronicles-25:8:1.summary: “In Thy hand is mighty strength, and no one can resist Thee” states that strength comes from the Lord.

2-chronicles-25:8:2.summary: God supplying every need in Christ has no link to military strength or rout.

2-chronicles-25:8:3.summary: Receiving many times more for the kingdom's sake relates loosely to the hundred talents (25:9), not to this verse on strength.

2-chronicles-25:8:4.summary: God reduces Gideon's force so that He saves by a few, showing that victory is not from numbers.
2-chronicles-25:8:4.why: A classic example of God-given victory.

2-chronicles-25:8:5.summary: God's gift of wisdom and wealth to Solomon is unrelated to strength in battle.

2-chronicles-25:8:6.summary: Job's statement about God turning away anger has no specific tie to this warning.

2-chronicles-25:8:7.summary: The earth belonging to the Lord is too general to link to military rout.

2-chronicles-25:8:8.summary: Advice to youth about future judgment does not concern relying on hired troops.

2-chronicles-25:8:9.summary: Some rely on chariots and horses, but we rely on the Lord's name, the same contrast as relying on hired men.
2-chronicles-25:8:9.why: A psalm's statement of the same trust.

2-chronicles-25:8:10.summary: “A king is not saved through a great force” directly supports the warning against trusting in numbers.
2-chronicles-25:8:10.why: States the principle of the warning.

2-chronicles-25:8:11.summary: Joel's summons of the nations to judgment does not address strength coming from the Lord (truncated).
2-chronicles-25:8:11.why: Only the language of war is shared.

2-chronicles-25:8:12.summary: “Nor battle to the mighty” loosely matches the idea that numbers do not decide victory.
2-chronicles-25:8:12.why: A wisdom reflection on uncertain outcomes.

2-chronicles-25:8:13.summary: Strong nations defeated because God is with His people is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-25:8:14.summary: “The Lord is not constrained from saving by many or by few” states the same principle as the man of God.
2-chronicles-25:8:14.why: Jonathan's confession of the same truth.

2-chronicles-25:8:15.summary: God “gives you strength” to gain wealth, loosely matching strength coming from the Lord.
2-chronicles-25:8:15.why: Shows God as the source of strength.

2-chronicles-25:8:16.summary: The shown text, “these two things I heard,” does not itself mention strength.
2-chronicles-25:8:16.why: Nothing in the shown text links.

2-chronicles-25:8:17.summary: God owning silver and gold relates more to the talents of 25:9 than to strength and rout.

2-chronicles-25:8:18.summary: Michaias' ironic “go up and prosper” is a different situation, with no link to strength coming from the Lord.

2-chronicles-25:8:19.summary: God both wounds and heals, a general parallel to both strength and rout coming from Him.
2-chronicles-25:8:19.why: Shows God's sovereignty over both outcomes.

2-chronicles-25:8:20.summary: The Lord's blessing making rich is not about military strength.
2-chronicles-25:8:20.why: No meaningful link to this verse.

2-chronicles-25:8:21.summary: The Lord frustrates the counsels of nations and rulers, a general picture of His sovereignty over outcomes.

2-chronicles-25:8:22.summary: Jesus being handed over to sinners has no link to Amaziah's army.

2-chronicles-25:9:0.summary: The Lord's blessing makes rich, loosely supporting the promise that He can give more than the hundred talents.

2-chronicles-25:9:1.summary: God gives strength to gain wealth, a general reassurance about losing the talents.
2-chronicles-25:9:1.why: Shows God as the source of wealth.

2-chronicles-25:10:0.summary: Angry words between the men of Israel and Judah are a general parallel to Ephraim's anger at Judah.
2-chronicles-25:10:0.why: Shows tension between north and south.

2-chronicles-25:10:1.summary: A prophetic word sends troops home to avoid conflict with Israel, a loose parallel to the soldiers being dismissed.
2-chronicles-25:10:1.why: Another army sent home at God's word.

2-chronicles-25:10:2.summary: A general proverb about wrathful men is not specifically tied to the dismissed troops.

2-chronicles-25:11:1.summary: The shown psalm verse about God rejecting His people does not mention Edom or the Valley of Salts.
2-chronicles-25:11:1.why: Nothing in the shown text links.

2-chronicles-25:11:2.summary: David struck eighteen thousand in Idumea, an earlier victory over Edom matching Amaziah's defeat of Seir.

2-chronicles-25:12:0.summary: Mount Seir is named as a hostile neighbour, giving a loose background for the war on Seir's sons.

2-chronicles-25:12:1.summary: David's harsh treatment of captured Ammonites is a general parallel to the cruel execution of Edomite captives.
2-chronicles-25:12:1.why: Shows brutal treatment of captives in war.

2-chronicles-25:12:2.summary: Edom broke away from Judah under Joram, the background to Amaziah's campaign against Edom.

2-chronicles-25:12:3.summary: David's harsh treatment of Ammonite captives is a general parallel to the cliff executions.

2-chronicles-25:13:0.summary: Solomon built Upper and Lower “Baithoron,” the town reached by the raiders.

2-chronicles-25:13:1.summary: Omri's founding of Samaria (Saemeron) identifies the raiders' starting point, but it is only a place link.

2-chronicles-25:13:2.summary: Ahab reigning in Samaria shares only the place name, with no bearing on the raid.

2-chronicles-25:13:3.summary: Upper Beth-horon is named among Solomon's building projects, a place link only.

2-chronicles-25:14:0.summary: Ahaz also turns to the gods of a nation he deals with and sacrifices to them, the same folly as Amaziah with Seir's gods.
2-chronicles-25:14:0.why: A parallel case of a king adopting foreign gods.

2-chronicles-25:14:1.summary: The command against other gods and “You shall not bow down to them” is what Amaziah broke.

2-chronicles-25:14:3.summary: Isaiah mocks worshipping what one has made, a general critique of idolatry.

2-chronicles-25:14:4.summary: Moses commanded burning the graven images of the nations' gods, the opposite of Amaziah setting them up for himself.
2-chronicles-25:14:4.why: Shows how he reversed the law.

2-chronicles-25:14:5.summary: David also took the abandoned gods of defeated enemies, but there is no worship of them, unlike Amaziah.
2-chronicles-25:14:5.why: Compares two kings with captured idols.

2-chronicles-25:15:0.summary: The gods of the nations are demons, a general verdict on worshipping Seir's gods.
2-chronicles-25:15:0.why: Shows what such gods really are.

2-chronicles-25:15:2.summary: Pagan sacrifices go to demons, a general warning about worshipping foreign gods.

2-chronicles-25:15:3.summary: Bel and Dagon “cannot be saved from war” and go into captivity, the same mockery of gods that could not rescue their people.
2-chronicles-25:15:3.why: Shows the helplessness of defeated gods.

2-chronicles-25:15:5.summary: A prophet sent with a rebuking “Why…?” to a king of Judah, as with Azarias' warning to Joash.
