2-chronicles-25:15:5.why: Shows the Chronicler's pattern of prophetic rebuke.

2-chronicles-25:15:6.summary: Idols that cannot see, hear or act are a general parallel to gods that could not rescue.
2-chronicles-25:15:6.why: A classic critique of powerless idols.

2-chronicles-25:15:7.summary: Nathan is sent to rebuke a king, a general parallel to prophets sent to Amaziah (truncated).
2-chronicles-25:15:7.why: Another prophet sent to confront a king.

2-chronicles-25:15:8.summary: A prophet speaks against a king of Judah for a wrong alliance, a general parallel of prophetic rebuke.
2-chronicles-25:15:8.why: The Chronicler's habit of prophets rebuking kings.

2-chronicles-25:15:9.summary: Following futile things instead of the Lord is a general parallel to seeking useless gods.
2-chronicles-25:15:9.why: Shows the folly of turning from God.

2-chronicles-25:15:10.summary: Idol-makers fashion things that “will not help them,” loosely matching gods unable to rescue.

2-chronicles-25:15:11.summary: A prophet announcing “wrath from the Lord” on a king is a similar formula for a different sin.

2-chronicles-25:15:12.summary: The command not to bow to the land's gods but to shatter their images is broken by Amaziah's worship.

2-chronicles-25:15:13.summary: A prophet rebukes a king for misplaced trust, a general parallel to Amaziah's misplaced worship.
2-chronicles-25:15:13.why: Shows a prophet confronting misplaced reliance.

2-chronicles-25:15:14.summary: “An idol is nothing” is a general verdict on the gods Amaziah sought.
2-chronicles-25:15:14.why: Paul's view that idols are nothing.

2-chronicles-25:15:15.summary: An earlier man of God had already warned Amaziah, so this is a repeated prophetic warning to the same king.
2-chronicles-25:15:15.why: Shows God warning Amaziah more than once.

2-chronicles-25:16:0.summary: Leaders questioning by what authority someone speaks loosely matches the king asking who made the prophet a counselor.

2-chronicles-25:16:1.summary: “All My counsel will stand” loosely supports God having purposed Amaziah's destruction.

2-chronicles-25:16:2.summary: People rejoicing over the slain prophets in Revelation does not connect to the silencing of Amaziah's prophet.

2-chronicles-25:16:3.summary: A king orders a prophet who brought an unwelcome message to be detained, a general parallel to the threat against this prophet.

2-chronicles-25:16:4.summary: Vessels of wrath fitted for destruction loosely matches God purposing to destroy the stubborn king.
2-chronicles-25:16:4.why: A theological comment on divine judgment.

2-chronicles-25:16:5.summary: Prophets put into confinement loosely matches threats against God's prophets.

2-chronicles-25:16:6.summary: People who will not endure sound teaching is a general parallel to rejecting the prophet's counsel.

2-chronicles-25:16:7.summary: Asa “became enraged with the prophet” and imprisoned him, a close parallel to Amaziah's threat against the prophet.
2-chronicles-25:16:7.why: An earlier king of Judah persecuting a prophet.

2-chronicles-25:16:8.summary: Another Amaziah, a priest, orders the prophet Amos to stop prophesying, a close parallel to silencing a prophet's unwelcome message.
2-chronicles-25:16:8.why: Shows official efforts to silence prophets.

2-chronicles-25:16:9.summary: God hardening Sihon so he is delivered up loosely matches God purposing to destroy the stubborn king.

2-chronicles-25:16:10.summary: God allowing a king to be deceived toward his downfall is a loose parallel to purposed destruction.
2-chronicles-25:16:10.why: Shows God steering a stubborn king to ruin.

2-chronicles-25:16:11.summary: God's predetermined purpose is a general parallel to “He has purposed against you.”

2-chronicles-25:16:12.summary: God preserving Pharaoh to show His power is a general parallel to God's purpose with a resisting king.
2-chronicles-25:16:12.why: Shows God's purposes through stubborn rulers.

2-chronicles-25:16:13.summary: Rebuking the impious brings dishonour on the rebuker, which describes the threat to the prophet.

2-chronicles-25:16:14.summary: People telling prophets “Do not speak to us” closely matches the king silencing the prophet.

2-chronicles-25:16:15.summary: God working according to His will in election is too general to link to judgment on Amaziah.

2-chronicles-25:16:16.summary: Joash had a prophet stoned, and his son Amaziah now threatens a prophet with violence, a repeated family pattern.
2-chronicles-25:16:16.why: Shows father and son both attacking prophets.

2-chronicles-25:16:17.summary: “They would not listen… for the Lord was firmly resolved to destroy them” closely matches unheeded counsel and God's purpose to destroy.
2-chronicles-25:16:17.why: The same link between refusing and judgment.

2-chronicles-25:17:1.summary: A fool entangling himself in strife loosely matches Amaziah provoking a needless war.

2-chronicles-25:17:2.summary: Abner's challenge to a contest is a loose parallel to Amaziah's “let us appear face to face.”

2-chronicles-25:17:3.summary: Israel's dismissed troops raiding Judah's cities gives the likely provocation for Amaziah's challenge.

2-chronicles-25:18:0.summary: Jotham's fable of the trees and the bramble is the closest biblical parallel to Joash's thorn-and-cedar fable (truncated).
2-chronicles-25:18:0.why: Another plant fable used to mock a ruler.

2-chronicles-25:18:1.summary: A wild beast ravaging God's vine loosely matches animals trampling the achouch.

2-chronicles-25:18:2.summary: The “cedar in Lebanon” appears in Solomon's sayings about trees, a shared image only.
2-chronicles-25:18:2.why: Shows the cedar as a proverbial figure.

2-chronicles-25:19:0.summary: Uzziah's “heart was lifted up to destruction” after growing strong, closely matching Amaziah's heart lifting him up.
2-chronicles-25:19:0.why: The Chronicler's repeated pattern of royal pride.

2-chronicles-25:19:1.summary: Hezekiah's “heart was lifted up” and wrath came on Judah, the same pride with the same consequence.
2-chronicles-25:19:1.why: Shows pride as a recurring royal failing.

2-chronicles-25:19:2.summary: A foreign king warns a king of Judah not to engage in battle, a warning he ignores, as Amaziah does here.
2-chronicles-25:19:2.why: A parallel unheeded warning against war.

2-chronicles-25:19:3.summary: Honour in turning from strife loosely matches the advice to stay home.

2-chronicles-25:19:4.summary: Insolence leading to evil loosely matches Amaziah's pride.
2-chronicles-25:19:4.why: Shows the link between pride and evil.

2-chronicles-25:19:5.summary: “Let no strong man boast in his strength” loosely matches Amaziah's boast over Idumea.

2-chronicles-25:19:6.summary: “You become lifted up in heart” warns of the same pride that lifts Amaziah up after success.
2-chronicles-25:19:6.why: The Mosaic warning against pride after success.

2-chronicles-25:19:7.summary: A fool's lips leading to evils loosely matches Amaziah's rash challenge.

2-chronicles-25:19:8.summary: Meddling in a quarrel like grabbing a dog's tail loosely matches provoking an unnecessary war.

2-chronicles-25:19:9.summary: “God opposes the proud” is a general principle that applies to Amaziah's pride.
2-chronicles-25:19:9.why: A New Testament principle on pride.

2-chronicles-25:19:10.summary: No flesh may boast before God, a general parallel to Amaziah's boasting.

2-chronicles-25:19:11.summary: Habakkuk on the faithfulness of the righteous has no clear link to Amaziah's pride.

2-chronicles-25:19:12.summary: “Insolence leads before ruin… before a fall” fits the warning that pride will make Amaziah “fall.”

2-chronicles-25:19:13.summary: Only Daniel 5:23 is shown, about not honouring God; it does not address a heart lifted up toward war.
2-chronicles-25:19:13.why: The shown text does not carry the link.

2-chronicles-25:19:14.summary: A king weighing whether he can win before going to war loosely matches the advice not to provoke battle.

2-chronicles-25:19:15.summary: “God opposes the proud” is a general principle that applies to Amaziah.
2-chronicles-25:19:15.why: A New Testament principle on pride.

2-chronicles-25:19:16.summary: An insatiable man judges rashly, a loose parallel to Amaziah's rash ambition.

2-chronicles-25:20:0.summary: The king “did not listen… for the turn of events came from the Lord,” the same pattern of not listening as part of God's purpose.
2-chronicles-25:20:0.why: An earlier case of God working through a deaf king.

2-chronicles-25:20:1.summary: “Ahaziah's downfall came from God” through his own choices, matching Amaziah's defeat coming from the Lord.
2-chronicles-25:20:1.why: The Chronicler's pattern of downfall ordained by God.

2-chronicles-25:20:2.summary: God giving those who “did not listen” over to their own ways loosely matches Amaziah's refusal and its result.

2-chronicles-25:20:3.summary: Hearts grown dull so that they do not listen is a general parallel to Amaziah not listening.

2-chronicles-25:20:4.summary: Stumbling by disobeying, “to this they were also appointed,” loosely matches refusal ordained for judgment.

2-chronicles-25:20:5.summary: The prophet said God had purposed to destroy Amaziah for not heeding counsel, which this verse fulfils.
2-chronicles-25:20:5.why: Links the prophecy with its fulfilment.

2-chronicles-25:20:6.summary: God sending delusion on those who reject truth is a loose parallel to Amaziah's God-ordained refusal.

2-chronicles-25:21:0.summary: “Bethsamys” is listed among Judah's allotted cities, confirming that Baithsamys belongs to Judah.

2-chronicles-25:21:1.summary: Beth-shemesh is named in the ark narrative, a place link only.
2-chronicles-25:21:1.why: Gives earlier history of the place.

2-chronicles-25:21:2.summary: The men of Beth-shemesh are struck for looking at the ark, a place link only.
2-chronicles-25:21:2.why: Recalls a judgment at this site.

2-chronicles-25:22:0.summary: “Each man to his own city” after a defeat loosely echoes each man fleeing to his tent.
2-chronicles-25:22:0.why: A similar scattering formula after defeat.

2-chronicles-25:22:1.summary: “Each fled to his dwelling” after Israel's defeat is the same formula of a routed army scattering.

2-chronicles-25:22:2.summary: Judah is delivered into the hands of Israel's king and defeated because they abandoned the Lord, a later repeat of this defeat.
2-chronicles-25:22:2.why: Shows Judah's defeats by Israel recurring.

2-chronicles-25:23:0.summary: Raiders overpower Judah and carry off the king's household, a general parallel to Jerusalem's humiliation.

2-chronicles-25:23:1.summary: The Ephraim Gate is named, a place link only.

2-chronicles-25:23:2.summary: The Corner Gate is named as the boundary of the rebuilt city, a place link only.

2-chronicles-25:23:3.summary: Uzziah built towers at the Corner Gate, apparently repairing the stretch of wall his father lost.
2-chronicles-25:23:3.why: Shows the damage being restored next.

2-chronicles-25:23:4.summary: Ahaziah's accession after raiders killed his brothers is not about Amaziah's capture or the broken wall.

2-chronicles-25:23:5.summary: The Ephraim Gate is named on Nehemiah's dedication route, a place link only.

2-chronicles-25:23:6.summary: Edom's pride that “lifted you up” only to be brought down loosely matches Amaziah's pride and humiliation.

2-chronicles-25:23:7.summary: A king of Judah captured and carried off by a foreign king is a general parallel.

2-chronicles-25:23:8.summary: A king taken away with the vessels of the Lord's house loosely matches Amaziah's capture and the looting.
2-chronicles-25:23:8.why: A later royal capture and temple plundering.

2-chronicles-25:23:9.summary: Manasseh is seized and taken away, a general parallel of a captured king of Judah.
2-chronicles-25:23:9.why: Another king of Judah taken captive.

2-chronicles-25:23:10.summary: Insolence bringing a man low loosely fits proud Amaziah's capture.

2-chronicles-25:23:11.summary: Joram's wounds and Ahaziah's visit have no connection to Amaziah's capture.

2-chronicles-25:23:12.summary: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” is a general principle seen in Amaziah's fall.

2-chronicles-25:23:13.summary: Insolence going before a fall loosely matches the result of Amaziah's pride.
2-chronicles-25:23:13.why: A proverb on pride and ruin.

2-chronicles-25:23:14.summary: Nebuchadnezzar praising God for setting up and removing kings is too general to link to Amaziah's capture.

2-chronicles-25:24:0.summary: Abdedom was assigned to the storehouse, explaining the temple treasures kept “with Abdedom.”

2-chronicles-25:24:2.summary: Sousakim took the treasures of the Lord's house and the king's house, the same double plundering as here.
2-chronicles-25:24:2.why: An earlier looting of both treasuries.

2-chronicles-25:26:0.summary: “The rest of… acts, first and last, are written” is the same closing formula for a reign.

2-chronicles-25:26:1.summary: The Kings closing notice for Joash cites the same war “how he fought Amaziah king of Judah” with the same formula.
2-chronicles-25:26:1.why: The Kings record of the same conflict.

2-chronicles-25:27:1.summary: Amaziah's father Joash was also killed by conspirators, so father and son both die by assassination after turning from the Lord.

2-chronicles-25:27:2.summary: Lachish is named in Joshua's conquest, a place link only.

2-chronicles-25:27:3.summary: “If you forsake Him, He will forsake you” gives the principle behind the attack that followed Amaziah departing from the Lord.
2-chronicles-25:27:3.why: States the principle behind his end.

2-chronicles-25:15:4.summary: Jeremiah 10:7 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-25:15:4.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-25:15:4.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-26:1:0.summary: Uzziah appears in Jesus' genealogy as Joram's descendant and Jotham's father, the same king.
2-chronicles-26:1:0.why: Places Uzziah in the Messianic line.

2-chronicles-26:1:1.summary: The people made Ahaziah king “in his place” after crisis, the same pattern of a popular enthronement.
2-chronicles-26:1:1.why: Shows the people stepping in at succession.

2-chronicles-26:1:2.summary: After a king is assassinated, “the people of the land made his son… king in his place,” closely matching this succession.
2-chronicles-26:1:2.why: The same pattern after an assassination.

2-chronicles-26:1:3.summary: Kings tells of Azariah son of Amaziah becoming king at sixteen, the same king and accession.
2-chronicles-26:1:3.why: The Kings parallel of Uzziah's reign.

2-chronicles-26:1:5.summary: The genealogy lists “Azariah his son” after Amasias, the same king under his other name.

2-chronicles-26:2:1.summary: Ailath is later lost to Syria and Edom, the same town Uzziah built and restored to Judah.

2-chronicles-26:2:0.summary: Amaziah's capture and the breached wall have no direct link to Uzziah building Ailath.

2-chronicles-26:2:3.summary: Solomon went to coastal Ailath in Idumea, the same port Uzziah later restored.
2-chronicles-26:2:3.why: Shows Ailath's earlier role under Solomon.

2-chronicles-26:2:4.summary: Amaziah's burial with his fathers is the “king fell asleep with his fathers” referred to here.
2-chronicles-26:2:4.why: Identifies the king whose death is meant.

2-chronicles-26:3:1.summary: Amos prophesied “in the days of Uzziah king of Judah,” the same king.

2-chronicles-26:3:2.summary: The earthquake “in the days of Oziah king of Judah” refers to the same reign.
2-chronicles-26:3:2.why: Recalls a notable event of his reign.

2-chronicles-26:3:3.summary: Hosea's ministry is dated to the days of Uzziah, the same king.

2-chronicles-26:3:4.summary: Isaiah's vision is dated to the reign of Oziah, the same king.

2-chronicles-26:3:5.summary: Isaiah's call came “in the year that King Oziah died,” marking the end of this reign.
2-chronicles-26:3:5.why: Ties Isaiah's call to Uzziah's death.

2-chronicles-26:4:0.summary: Amaziah also “did what was right before the Lord,” but not fully, the father whose example Uzziah followed.

2-chronicles-26:5:0.summary: Seeking the Lord brings blessing: Uzziah “sought the Lord” and prospered, as Azariah told Asa “If you seek Him, He shall be found by you.”
2-chronicles-26:5:0.why: States the Chronicler’s principle behind Uzziah’s success.

2-chronicles-26:5:2.summary: David promises Solomon the Lord “will grant success” if he keeps the commands, parallel to the Lord making Uzziah prosper.
2-chronicles-26:5:2.why: Shows obedience-linked prosperity as a recurring royal theme.

2-chronicles-26:5:3.summary: Pharaoh’s remark on Joseph having God’s Spirit has no specific link to Zacharias understanding the fear of the Lord.
2-chronicles-26:5:3.why: Only a loose idea of a God-given wise counselor.

2-chronicles-26:5:4.summary: Belshazzar offering Daniel rewards for interpretation is unrelated to Zacharias, who “understood the fear of the Lord.”
2-chronicles-26:5:4.why: Only generic link of a wise advisor.

2-chronicles-26:5:5.summary: Daniel “understood” a vision, loosely echoing Zacharias who “understood,” though the Septuagint source speaks of the fear of the Lord, not visions.
2-chronicles-26:5:5.why: Loose parallel of godly understanding in a counselor.

2-chronicles-26:5:6.summary: Joseph’s dream interpretation shares nothing specific with Zacharias’s understanding of the fear of the Lord.
2-chronicles-26:5:6.why: No real connection beyond a wise figure.

2-chronicles-26:5:7.summary: Daniel receiving a night vision has no specific link to Zacharias in the Greek wording, which mentions fear of the Lord, not visions.
2-chronicles-26:5:7.why: Label assumes visions absent from this reading.

2-chronicles-26:5:8.summary: A prophet tells Amaziah, Uzziah’s father, that strength comes from the Lord, matching the Lord making Uzziah prosper.
2-chronicles-26:5:8.why: Shows the Lord as source of royal strength in the same narrative.

2-chronicles-26:5:9.summary: God gave Daniel understanding, loosely parallel to Zacharias who “understood the fear of the Lord.”
2-chronicles-26:5:9.why: Pictures understanding as God’s gift to a counselor.

2-chronicles-26:5:10.summary: Judah’s fleeting mercy “like a morning cloud” loosely matches Uzziah’s faithfulness lasting only “in his days” of Zacharias.

2-chronicles-26:5:11.summary: Israel served the Lord “all the days of Joshua” and the elders, as Uzziah sought the Lord “in the days of Zacharias.”
2-chronicles-26:5:11.why: Faithfulness tied to a godly leader’s lifetime.

2-chronicles-26:5:12.summary: David tells Solomon the Lord “will grant success,” parallel to the Lord prospering Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:5:12.why: Same Chronicles theme of God-given success.

2-chronicles-26:5:13.summary: Paul warning of men drawing disciples away has no specific link to Uzziah seeking the Lord in Zacharias’s days.
2-chronicles-26:5:13.why: Only a vague idea of later falling away.

2-chronicles-26:5:14.summary: Rocky-soil hearers who last “only for a time” loosely mirror Uzziah’s devotion limited to Zacharias’s days.

2-chronicles-26:5:15.summary: The righteous man for whom “everything he does will be prospered” matches the Lord making Uzziah “prosper” when he sought Him.
2-chronicles-26:5:15.why: Links Uzziah’s prosperity to the blessed man of Psalm 1.

2-chronicles-26:6:0.summary: Isaiah warns the “foreigners” (Philistines) not to rejoice, related to Uzziah fighting the foreigners, though no event is named.
2-chronicles-26:6:0.why: Prophetic view of Philistine oppression and judgment.

2-chronicles-26:6:1.summary: The Lord stirred “the foreigners, the Arabs” against Joram, the same peoples Uzziah later defeats.
2-chronicles-26:6:1.why: Shows reversal: Joram’s enemies become Uzziah’s defeated foes.

2-chronicles-26:6:2.summary: The foreigners brought the ark to Ashdod, the city whose walls Uzziah pulled down (named “Azotus” in the source).
2-chronicles-26:6:2.why: Background on Ashdod/Azotus as a Philistine city.

2-chronicles-26:6:3.summary: David “struck the foreigners and routed them,” as Uzziah “fought the foreigners” and broke their walls.
2-chronicles-26:6:3.why: Uzziah follows David’s pattern of subduing Philistines.

2-chronicles-26:6:4.summary: The Lord’s hand on Ashdod links to Azotus (Ashdod) whose walls Uzziah pulled down.

2-chronicles-26:6:5.summary: David struck the foreigners and took “Geth,” the same Philistine city whose walls Uzziah later pulled down.
2-chronicles-26:6:5.why: Geth repeatedly targeted by Judah’s kings.

2-chronicles-26:7:0.summary: Against Joram the Lord stirred up “the foreigners, the Arabs”; against them He strengthened Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:7:0.why: Reversal of the same enemies in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-26:7:1.summary: Paul “received help from God,” echoing the Lord strengthening Uzziah, but in an unrelated setting.

2-chronicles-26:7:2.summary: God gave the Transjordan tribes victory over the Hagaraeans, an Arab-type people, as He strengthened Uzziah against Arabs.
2-chronicles-26:7:2.why: Parallel of God-given victory over desert peoples.

2-chronicles-26:7:3.summary: “The foreigners” and “the Arabs” brought Jehoshaphat tribute, the same peoples Uzziah subdued and who gave gifts.
2-chronicles-26:7:3.why: Same peoples submitting to a strong Judean king.

2-chronicles-26:7:4.summary: By God the psalmist crosses a wall and escapes raiders, generally matching the Lord strengthening Uzziah in war.
2-chronicles-26:7:4.why: God as source of military success.

2-chronicles-26:7:5.summary: God trains the psalmist’s hands for war and supports him, matching the Lord strengthening Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:7:6.summary: Isaiah addresses the “foreigners” as a people whose striker was broken, loosely tied to Uzziah’s campaign against them.

2-chronicles-26:7:7.summary: The “Minaeans” who came against Jehoshaphat are the same people the Lord helped Uzziah against.

2-chronicles-26:7:8.summary: Asa prays “Strengthen us, Lord,” the help the Lord gave Uzziah against his foes.
2-chronicles-26:7:8.why: Shows the prayer behind divine strengthening.

2-chronicles-26:7:9.summary: Amasai declares “your God has helped you” to David, generally matching God helping Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:7:9.why: God’s help for a king in war.

2-chronicles-26:8:0.summary: Genesis on the origin of the Ammanites has no link to the Minaeans in the Greek source, which does not mention Ammon.
2-chronicles-26:8:0.why: Label assumes Ammonites absent from this reading.

2-chronicles-26:8:1.summary: Foreigners and Arabs brought Jehoshaphat “gifts,” as the Minaeans gave gifts to Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:8:1.why: Tribute from neighbors marks a strong king.

2-chronicles-26:8:2.summary: Moab became David’s servants “bringing gifts,” loosely like the Minaeans giving gifts to Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:8:3.summary: “David made a name for himself,” as Uzziah’s name reached Egypt.

2-chronicles-26:8:4.summary: Nahash the Ammonite besieging Jabesh has no link to the Minaeans named in the Greek source.
2-chronicles-26:8:4.why: Label assumes Ammonites not in this reading.

2-chronicles-26:8:5.summary: God promises to make Abram’s name great, loosely like Uzziah’s name spreading as far as Egypt.
2-chronicles-26:8:5.why: General theme of a great name.

2-chronicles-26:8:6.summary: Instructions about the sons of Ammon do not connect to the Minaeans in the Greek source.

2-chronicles-26:8:7.summary: The “Minaeans” appear alongside Moab and Ammon against Jehoshaphat, the same people who give Uzziah gifts.

2-chronicles-26:8:8.summary: Jesus’ fame “spread throughout Syria” loosely parallels Uzziah’s name reaching Egypt.
2-chronicles-26:8:8.why: Only a shared idea of spreading renown.

2-chronicles-26:8:9.summary: Jephthah’s history of Moab and Ammon’s land has no link to the Minaeans in the source verse (truncated text shown).
2-chronicles-26:8:9.why: Label assumes Ammonites absent from this reading.

2-chronicles-26:8:10.summary: Solomon’s wisdom exceeding all made him famous, loosely like Uzziah’s renown, but the shown text does not mention his name spreading.

2-chronicles-26:9:4.summary: Jeremiah promises a city rebuilt “to the Corner Gate,” the same gate where Uzziah built towers.
2-chronicles-26:9:4.why: Locates the Corner Gate in Jerusalem’s defenses.

2-chronicles-26:9:0.summary: The Valley Gate repaired in Nehemiah likely corresponds to Uzziah’s “Ravine Gate,” though the names differ.

2-chronicles-26:9:2.summary: Joash broke down Jerusalem’s wall to the “Corner Gate” under Amaziah; Uzziah then fortified that gate.
2-chronicles-26:9:2.why: Explains why Uzziah rebuilt defenses there.

2-chronicles-26:9:3.summary: Nehemiah inspects the “Valley Gate,” probably Uzziah’s Ravine Gate, though wording differs.
2-chronicles-26:9:3.why: Later state of the same gate.

2-chronicles-26:9:5.summary: Nehemiah’s night inspection of Jerusalem’s wall and gates is only generally related to Uzziah’s towers.

2-chronicles-26:9:6.summary: Zechariah names the “Gate of Corners” in Jerusalem, matching the Corner Gate where Uzziah built towers.

2-chronicles-26:9:7.summary: Bani repaired “to the corner,” echoing Uzziah’s towers “at the corners,” in later wall repairs.
2-chronicles-26:9:7.why: Later work on the same defensive corners.

2-chronicles-26:9:8.summary: Repairs at “the tower of the ascent adjoining the corner” echo Uzziah’s towers at the corners.

2-chronicles-26:9:9.summary: Repairs at the Sheep Gate share nothing specific with Uzziah’s towers at the Corner or Ravine Gates.

2-chronicles-26:10:0.summary: Isaiah mentions “Mount Chermel” as fertile land, loosely related to Uzziah’s vinedressers in Carmel.
2-chronicles-26:10:0.why: Carmel as a symbol of fruitful land.

2-chronicles-26:10:1.summary: Isaac digs wells for his herds, as Uzziah “hewed many cisterns” for his herds.

2-chronicles-26:10:2.summary: Mesha, a sheep-breeder, rendered huge flocks, loosely like Uzziah’s many herds.

2-chronicles-26:10:3.summary: David’s overseers of farming, vineyards, plain, and cattle parallel Uzziah’s herds, plain, and vinedressers.
2-chronicles-26:10:3.why: Shows royal agricultural estates in Judah.

2-chronicles-26:10:4.summary: Sennacherib boasts of reaching “the woodland of its Carmel,” sharing only the place name with Uzziah’s Carmel.

2-chronicles-26:11:0.summary: Syrian raiders capturing a girl has no specific link to Uzziah’s numbered army.

2-chronicles-26:13:0.summary: Asa’s army of three hundred thousand mighty warriors parallels Uzziah’s fighting force of over three hundred thousand.
2-chronicles-26:13:0.why: Comparable army counts of Judah’s kings.

2-chronicles-26:13:1.summary: Amaziah, Uzziah’s father, mustered “three hundred thousand” warriors, nearly matching Uzziah’s force.
2-chronicles-26:13:1.why: Shows continuity of the royal army.

2-chronicles-26:13:2.summary: Abijah’s force of mighty warriors is another numbered Judean army, generally comparable.
2-chronicles-26:13:2.why: Pattern of army counts in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-26:13:3.summary: Rehoboam’s hundred and eighty thousand warriors is a comparable army count.

2-chronicles-26:13:4.summary: Jehoshaphat’s army lists “mighty sons of strength” by hundreds of thousands, parallel to Uzziah’s mighty force.

2-chronicles-26:14:0.summary: Benjamite slingers throwing stones parallel Uzziah providing “slings for stones.”
2-chronicles-26:14:0.why: Shows the use of slings in Israel’s warfare.

2-chronicles-26:14:1.summary: David’s sling, stone, and the foreigner’s “helmet” echo items in Uzziah’s armory.

2-chronicles-26:15:0.summary: Jesus’ report spreading throughout Syria loosely echoes Uzziah’s machines being “heard of far away.”
2-chronicles-26:15:0.why: Only shared idea of fame spreading.

2-chronicles-26:15:1.summary: Bezalel enabled “to plan and design,” echoing machines “devised by a designer.”

2-chronicles-26:15:2.summary: Huram can “devise every design,” echoing Uzziah’s machines “devised by a designer.”

2-chronicles-26:15:3.summary: Solomon requests a skilled craftsman, generally like Uzziah’s skilled designer, but for temple not war.

2-chronicles-26:16:0.summary: Hezekiah’s “heart was lifted up” and wrath came, just as Uzziah’s heart was lifted up to destruction.
2-chronicles-26:16:0.why: Same pattern of pride after blessing.

2-chronicles-26:16:1.summary: “Insolence leads before ruin” states the principle shown when Uzziah’s heart was lifted up to destruction.

2-chronicles-26:16:2.summary: Habakkuk contrasts one who “draws back” with the faithful, loosely related to Uzziah’s pride.
2-chronicles-26:16:2.why: General contrast of pride and faith.

2-chronicles-26:16:3.summary: Joash warns Amaziah his heart “lifts you up” so he will fall, the same pride that ruined his son Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:16:3.why: Pride of heart repeats in father and son.

2-chronicles-26:16:4.summary: Moses warns lest “you become lifted up in heart” and forget the Lord, as Uzziah did when strong.

2-chronicles-26:16:5.summary: Moses warns against crediting “my strength,” the attitude when Uzziah “grew strong” and his heart was lifted.

2-chronicles-26:16:6.summary: Being “puffed up without cause” loosely parallels Uzziah’s heart being lifted up.

2-chronicles-26:16:7.summary: Jacob grew fat and “forsook God,” the pattern of prosperity leading to pride seen in Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:16:8.summary: Korah’s followers took fire pans and incense, an unauthorized offering like Uzziah’s attempt to burn incense.

2-chronicles-26:16:9.summary: Fire consumed the two hundred fifty “presenting the incense,” judgment on unauthorized incense like Uzziah’s.
2-chronicles-26:16:9.why: Shows the danger of Uzziah’s act.

2-chronicles-26:16:10.summary: Introduces Korah, whose rebellion over priestly privilege parallels Uzziah’s incense offense.

2-chronicles-26:16:11.summary: Ahaz the king went up on the altar to offer, a king acting at the altar like Uzziah, though not incense.

2-chronicles-26:16:12.summary: Joash tells Amaziah “your heart has lifted you up,” the same pride that later overtakes Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:16:13.summary: Moses tells Korah to put incense before the Lord, who will choose the holy one, testing priestly right as with Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:16:14.summary: Jeroboam “went up onto the altar to offer” and was confronted by a man of God, as Uzziah was by priests (truncated text).
2-chronicles-26:16:14.why: King usurping priestly ministry and rebuked.

2-chronicles-26:17:0.summary: An “Azariah” served as priest in Solomon’s temple, the same priestly name as Azarias who confronted Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:17:0.why: Places Azarias in the high-priestly line.

2-chronicles-26:17:1.summary: Sadok, “mighty in strength,” among priestly men, loosely echoes the eighty “mighty” priests.

2-chronicles-26:17:2.summary: Levite gatekeepers called “mighty” share only that word with Azarias’s priests.

2-chronicles-26:18:2.summary: No one takes the honor himself unless called “as Aaron was,” as the priests told Uzziah incense belongs to Aaron’s sons.

2-chronicles-26:18:3.summary: The king told to humble himself as his crown of glory falls loosely echoes “no glory from the Lord.”

2-chronicles-26:18:4.summary: A prophet rebukes King Jehoshaphat to his face, like the priests withstanding Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:18:5.summary: God takes kingdoms from kings, loosely related to God humbling Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:18:6.summary: Disciples brought before kings has no specific link to priests withstanding Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:18:7.summary: Fearing God rather than men has no specific link in the texts to the priests’ rebuke of Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:18:7.why: Only a loose inferred theme of courage.

2-chronicles-26:18:8.summary: Aaron, the lawful priest, takes the fire pan and incense to make atonement, showing incense belongs to Aaron as the priests said.
2-chronicles-26:18:8.why: Lawful priestly incense contrasted with Uzziah’s.

2-chronicles-26:18:9.summary: “I will honour only those who honour Me” loosely parallels “no glory from the Lord” for Uzziah.
2-chronicles-26:18:9.why: God withholds honor from the disobedient.

2-chronicles-26:18:10.summary: John telling Herod “It is not lawful” parallels priests telling Uzziah “it does not belong to you.”

2-chronicles-26:18:11.summary: Paul opposed Cephas “to his face,” loosely like the priests standing against Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:18:12.summary: Seeking “glory that comes from the only God” loosely echoes “no glory from the Lord God.”
2-chronicles-26:18:12.why: Theme of true glory from God.

2-chronicles-26:18:13.summary: Knowing no one according to the flesh has no specific link to the priests’ rebuke of Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:18:14.summary: A prophet rebukes King Asa for not trusting the Lord, a parallel confrontation of a king.

2-chronicles-26:18:15.summary: Fire pans remind that “no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron” may offer incense, the very law the priests cite to Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:18:16.summary: Handing a man over to Satan is unrelated to the priests’ rebuke, though one might link it to Uzziah’s leprosy.

2-chronicles-26:18:17.summary: Warning against favoritism has no specific link to the priests withstanding the king.

2-chronicles-26:19:0.summary: Miriam became “leprous” suddenly for challenging Moses, as Uzziah was struck with leprosy for challenging the priests.

2-chronicles-26:19:1.summary: Amaziah angrily silences a prophet, like his son Uzziah raging against the priests.

2-chronicles-26:19:2.summary: Gehazi went out “afflicted with leprosy” as judgment for sin, as leprosy rose on Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:19:3.summary: Asa “became enraged with the prophet,” as Uzziah “became angry” and raged against the priests.
2-chronicles-26:19:3.why: Kings angry at rebuke from God’s servants.

2-chronicles-26:20:0.summary: Leprosy in houses shares only the word “leprosy” with Uzziah’s judgment.

2-chronicles-26:20:1.summary: Haman hurries home grieving and humiliated, loosely like Uzziah hurrying out in disgrace.

2-chronicles-26:20:2.summary: The Lord smiting with disease is a covenant curse, loosely matching the Lord striking Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:20:3.summary: The Lord smiting “unto the crown of your head” with incurable ulcer loosely recalls leprosy on Uzziah’s forehead.

2-chronicles-26:21:2.summary: Four lepers stay outside the city gate, illustrating the isolation Uzziah lived in.

2-chronicles-26:21:3.summary: Leprous Miriam was “set apart outside the camp,” as leprous Uzziah was “separated from the Lord’s house.”

2-chronicles-26:21:4.summary: The law sends “everyone with leprosy” out of the camp where God dwells, explaining Uzziah’s separation from the Lord’s house.

2-chronicles-26:22:0.summary: Isaiah prophesied during the reign of “Oziah” (Uzziah), the prophet Jessias said to record his acts.
2-chronicles-26:22:0.why: Identifies the prophet who chronicled Uzziah.

2-chronicles-26:22:1.summary: Isaiah’s vision came “in the year that King Oziah died,” tying the prophet to Uzziah’s reign.
2-chronicles-26:22:1.why: Links Isaiah’s call to Uzziah’s death.

2-chronicles-26:22:2.summary: Solomon’s deeds “first and last” were written by prophets, the same formula used for Uzziah’s acts.

2-chronicles-26:22:3.summary: Rehoboam’s deeds “first and last” written by Samaia the prophet uses the same formula as Uzziah’s.

2-chronicles-26:23:0.summary: Joram was buried “not in the tombs of the kings,” like Uzziah buried in the field apart because he was leprous.

2-chronicles-26:23:1.summary: Ahaz “fell asleep with his fathers” and was not buried in kings’ tombs; “his son … reigned in his place.”

2-chronicles-26:23:2.summary: “The year that King Oziah died” refers to Uzziah’s death recorded here.
2-chronicles-26:23:2.why: Dates Isaiah’s call by Uzziah’s death.

2-chronicles-26:23:4.summary: The priests’ rebuke explains the leprosy that caused Uzziah’s separate burial.
2-chronicles-26:23:4.why: Earlier context in the same chapter.

2-chronicles-26:23:5.summary: Manasseh “lay down with his fathers” and was buried apart, with “his son … reigned in his place.”
2-chronicles-26:23:5.why: Same succession formula with unusual burial.

2-chronicles-27:1:0.summary: The genealogy lists “Azariah his son, Joathan his son,” naming Uzziah and Jotham.

2-chronicles-27:1:1.summary: Isaiah prophesied under “Oziah, Joatham, Achaz,” including Jotham.

2-chronicles-27:1:2.summary: Hosea prophesied “in the days of Uzziah, Jotham,” Jotham being the king introduced.

2-chronicles-27:1:3.summary: “Uzziah begot Jotham” places Jotham in Christ’s genealogy.

2-chronicles-27:1:5.summary: Micah prophesied “in the days of Jotham,” the king whose reign begins here.

2-chronicles-27:2:1.summary: “He did what was right before the Lord, according to everything his father … had done” is the same formula for Uzziah.

2-chronicles-27:2:2.summary: The psalmist’s fear of God’s judgments has no link to Jotham’s not entering the sanctuary.

2-chronicles-27:2:4.summary: People not daring to join the apostles has no link to Jotham avoiding the sanctuary.
2-chronicles-27:2:4.why: Only an inferred idea of reverent distance.

2-chronicles-27:3:0.summary: Manasseh built a wall “toward Ophla,” the same Jerusalem area where Jotham built.
2-chronicles-27:3:0.why: Later fortification of the same quarter.

2-chronicles-27:3:1.summary: Nehemiah’s repairs reach “the wall of the Ophla,” the wall Jotham built up.

2-chronicles-27:3:2.summary: Jeremiah mentions a gate of the “upper house” in the Lord’s house, possibly the Upper Gate Jotham built.
2-chronicles-27:3:2.why: Possible later reference to the gate.

2-chronicles-27:3:3.summary: A gate of the Lord’s house in Joash’s coronation, related to the temple gates but not clearly the Upper Gate.

2-chronicles-27:4:0.summary: Rehoboam “built walled cities in Judea,” as Jotham built cities in Judah’s hill country.

2-chronicles-27:4:2.summary: Asa urges building “cities … walls, towers,” as Jotham built cities and towers.

2-chronicles-27:4:3.summary: Caleb asks for the hill country with fortified cities, loosely tied to Jotham building in Judah’s hill country.

2-chronicles-27:4:4.summary: Mary going to “the hill country” of Judah shares only the location phrase.

2-chronicles-27:5:0.summary: The sons of Ammon fought Jehoshaphat, a prior conflict with the same enemy Jotham defeated.

2-chronicles-27:5:1.summary: David’s war with the king of the sons of Ammon is an earlier conflict with the same people (truncated).

2-chronicles-27:5:2.summary: Jeremiah’s oracle against Ammon’s sons concerns the same nation Jotham subdued (truncated text).

2-chronicles-27:5:3.summary: Jephthah fought the sons of Ammon, an earlier victory over the same people (truncated text).

2-chronicles-27:6:1.summary: Jehoshaphat commended for directing his heart to seek the Lord parallels Jotham preparing his ways before the Lord.
2-chronicles-27:6:1.why: Heart set toward God as source of blessing.

2-chronicles-27:7:0.summary: “The rest of Jehoshaphat’s acts … are written in” a book of the kings, the same formula used for Jotham.

2-chronicles-27:7:1.summary: Hezekiah’s deeds are written “in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” the same source as Jotham’s.

2-chronicles-27:7:3.summary: “The rest of Uzziah’s acts … were written,” the same formula as for his son Jotham.

2-chronicles-28:1:0.summary: Isaiah prophesied during the reign of “Achaz,” the Greek form of Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:1:1.summary: “Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son” lists Ahaz in David’s line.

2-chronicles-28:1:2.summary: “Jotham begot Ahaz” places Ahaz in Christ’s genealogy.

2-chronicles-28:1:3.summary: Hosea prophesied in the days of “Ahaz,” among other kings.

2-chronicles-28:1:4.summary: Micah prophesied in the days of “Ahaz.”

2-chronicles-28:1:6.summary: Isaiah confronts “Achaz, son of Joatham” during the Aram-Israel attack (truncated text).

2-chronicles-28:1:7.summary: Jehoshaphat walked in his father’s earlier ways, contrasting Ahaz who did not walk as David had done.
2-chronicles-28:1:7.why: Contrast of faithful and unfaithful kings.

2-chronicles-28:2:0.summary: “You shall not make cast gods,” the command Ahaz broke by making carved images.

2-chronicles-28:2:1.summary: Israel served the Baalim, the general sin of idolatry Ahaz practiced, though source names no Baal.

2-chronicles-28:2:2.summary: God will remove the Baalim’s names, generally related to idolatry; the source names no Baal.

2-chronicles-28:2:3.summary: Ahaziah “walked in the way of Ahab’s house,” paralleling Ahaz walking in the ways of Israel’s kings.

2-chronicles-28:2:4.summary: Israel served Baal and the Astartes, general idolatry like Ahaz’s.

2-chronicles-28:2:5.summary: Joram “walked in the way of Israel’s kings,” nearly the same words as Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:2:6.summary: Ahab’s Baal worship defines “the ways of Israel’s kings” that Ahaz followed.

2-chronicles-28:2:7.summary: Jehu destroying Baal’s pillars contrasts Ahaz making images, but only general idolatry link.

2-chronicles-28:2:8.summary: “Neither shall you make cast gods,” the command Ahaz broke with his images.

2-chronicles-28:2:9.summary: God punishes the days of the Baalim, a general judgment on idolatry like Ahaz’s.

2-chronicles-28:3:0.summary: Manasseh followed “the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the sons of Israel,” identical to Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:3:1.summary: Manasseh “passed his children through fire in Gai-banai-ennom,” the same act and place as Ahaz.
2-chronicles-28:3:1.why: Repeated child sacrifice in same valley.

2-chronicles-28:3:2.summary: The law against giving one’s seed to “a ruler” (Molech) addresses child sacrifice, though the Greek wording obscures it.

2-chronicles-28:3:3.summary: Joshua names “the ravine of Onom,” the valley where Ahaz sacrificed (“Gaibenenom”).

2-chronicles-28:3:4.summary: Josiah defiled Tapheth “in the valley of the son of Ennom” where children passed through fire, as Ahaz had done.

2-chronicles-28:3:5.summary: Ezekiel condemns sacrificing sons and daughters, the sin Ahaz committed.

2-chronicles-28:3:6.summary: Jeremiah condemns Judah’s kings for innocent blood and Baal high places near the valley (truncated text).
2-chronicles-28:3:6.why: Prophetic judgment on the same practices.

2-chronicles-28:3:8.summary: Micah asks “Shall I give my firstborn” for sin, touching child sacrifice as Ahaz practiced.

2-chronicles-28:3:9.summary: Burning incense on roofs to foreign gods relates to Ahaz’s idolatry generally.

2-chronicles-28:3:10.summary: Israel “sacrificed their sons and their daughters” to idols, the abomination Ahaz committed.

2-chronicles-28:3:12.summary: Do not learn “the abominations of those nations,” the very abominations Ahaz followed.

2-chronicles-28:3:13.summary: Topheth “in the ravine of the son of Hinnom” where they burned their children matches Ahaz’s sacrifices there.

2-chronicles-28:3:14.summary: Offering sons and daughters in “the Valley of the Son of Hinnom” matches Ahaz’s sin in that valley.

2-chronicles-28:3:15.summary: Blood of innocent lives on Judah’s hands relates generally to child sacrifice.

2-chronicles-28:4:0.summary: God will destroy high-place idols, generally related to Ahaz burning incense on high places.

2-chronicles-28:5:0.summary: Raasson king of Aram and Phakee king of Israel attacked Jerusalem in Achaz’s days, the same war.
2-chronicles-28:5:0.why: Isaiah’s account of the same invasion.

2-chronicles-28:5:2.summary: God delivered Judah to Syria’s army for abandoning the Lord, as He delivered Ahaz to Syria’s king.
2-chronicles-28:5:2.why: Same pattern of judgment by Syria.

2-chronicles-28:5:3.summary: The first commandment has no specific link to Ahaz’s defeat by Syria and Israel.
2-chronicles-28:5:3.why: Only an inferred cause of idolatry.

2-chronicles-28:5:4.summary: God “handed everything into their hands” of the Chaldeans, a later instance of God delivering Judah to a foreign king, as with Ahaz.
2-chronicles-28:5:4.why: Pattern of judgment through foreign kings.

2-chronicles-28:5:5.summary: The Lord brought Assyria’s commanders against Manasseh, another king handed to a foreign power.
2-chronicles-28:5:5.why: Recurring divine judgment by foreign armies.

2-chronicles-28:5:6.summary: Jehoiakim’s regnal summary has no specific link to Ahaz’s defeat by Syria and Israel.

2-chronicles-28:5:7.summary: The Lord “delivered them into the hand of plunderers” and enemies, as He delivered Ahaz to Syria’s and Israel’s kings.

2-chronicles-28:5:8.summary: Aram and Israel plan to “go up into Judea” and install their own king, the same Syro-Ephraimite war against Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:6:0.summary: “You turned away from Me … I will … destroy you” matches Judah’s slaughter for abandoning the Lord.

2-chronicles-28:6:1.summary: “Abandoning Me is bitter for you” expresses the cause of Judah’s defeat: they “had abandoned the Lord.”

2-chronicles-28:6:2.summary: “Those abandoning the Lord will be brought to an end,” as Judah fell because they “abandoned the Lord.”

2-chronicles-28:6:3.summary: Joshua warns that if you “forsake the Lord” He will consume you, fulfilled in Judah’s slaughter.

2-chronicles-28:6:4.summary: “Phakee son of Romelias became king over Israel,” the same king who killed Judah’s men.

2-chronicles-28:6:5.summary: Ephraim and Manasseh “together … will besiege Judah,” loosely matching Israel’s attack on Judah.
2-chronicles-28:6:5.why: Prophetic view of Israel against Judah.

2-chronicles-28:6:6.summary: Disaster comes “because they forsook the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers,” the same reason given for Judah’s slaughter.

2-chronicles-28:6:7.summary: Isaiah calls “the son of Romelias” a smoking firebrand, the same Phakee who struck Judah.
2-chronicles-28:6:7.why: Prophetic perspective on the same enemy.

2-chronicles-28:6:8.summary: Following other gods kindles the Lord’s wrath to destroy, the general cause of Judah’s defeat.

2-chronicles-28:6:9.summary: Transgressing the covenant by serving other gods brings disaster, generally underlying Judah’s defeat.

2-chronicles-28:6:10.summary: “If you forsake Him, He will forsake you” explains why Judah fell after abandoning the Lord.

2-chronicles-28:6:11.summary: “Phakee son of Romelias, king of Israel” went up against Ahaz, the same war in Kings.

2-chronicles-28:6:13.summary: Transgressing the covenant leads to a curse and few left, a general covenant-judgment theme.

2-chronicles-28:6:14.summary: Abijah’s Judah killed five hundred thousand of Israel, the reverse of Israel slaughtering Judah under Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:6:15.summary: Israel will “forsake Me” and God will forsake them and they will be devoured, fulfilled in Judah’s defeat.

2-chronicles-28:6:16.summary: Isaiah names “Romelias’s son” as head of Samaria, the Phakee who killed Judah’s men.
2-chronicles-28:6:16.why: Prophetic word about the same king.

2-chronicles-28:6:17.summary: The Lord began sending “Phakee son of Romelias against Judah,” the same campaign.
2-chronicles-28:6:17.why: Shows the Lord behind the attack.

2-chronicles-28:6:18.summary: God turns His face from a faithless generation, a general judgment theme.

2-chronicles-28:6:19.summary: Curses come for disobedience, generally underlying Judah’s defeat.

2-chronicles-28:7:0.summary: Joseph riding as Pharaoh’s second has no link to Ezekri killing the king’s deputy, despite “second” rank in the Hebrew label.
2-chronicles-28:7:0.why: Label assumes a “second to the king” wording absent here.
2-chronicles-28:7:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-28:7:1.summary: Mordecai “acted as deputy” to the king, sharing only the office title with Elkana, “the king’s deputy.”
2-chronicles-28:7:1.why: Clarifies the office of royal deputy.

2-chronicles-28:7:2.summary: Joseph’s brothers taking double silver has no link to Ezekri’s killings.
2-chronicles-28:7:2.why: Label relies on Hebrew “second” not in text.
2-chronicles-28:7:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-28:7:3.summary: Taking double silver is unrelated to the killing of Ahaz’s officials.

2-chronicles-28:8:0.summary: The Lord forbade Judah to “fight your brethren,” the kinship Israel violated by capturing their brethren.
2-chronicles-28:8:0.why: Contrast with obeying God about brethren.

2-chronicles-28:8:1.summary: Being given to slaughter before enemies is a covenant curse fulfilled in Judah’s defeat.

2-chronicles-28:8:2.summary: “Sons and daughters … shall go into captivity,” fulfilled as Israel took Judah’s “sons, and daughters” captive.

2-chronicles-28:8:3.summary: Paul addressing “brothers” shares only the word with Israel’s captives.

2-chronicles-28:8:4.summary: Moses rebukes Israelites wronging “brothers,” loosely like Israel enslaving their brethren.

2-chronicles-28:9:0.summary: Ezra says offenses “have grown to heaven,” as Oded says Israel’s anger “has reached the heavens.”
2-chronicles-28:9:0.why: Same image of sin reaching heaven.

2-chronicles-28:9:1.summary: Babylon’s sins “piled up as far as heaven,” the same image as Oded’s rebuke.

2-chronicles-28:9:2.summary: God gave His people to Babylon who “gave them no mercy,” as Israel killed Judah in anger beyond God’s purpose.
2-chronicles-28:9:2.why: Instrument of judgment exceeding its mandate.

2-chronicles-28:9:4.summary: The Lord’s wrath and a prophet sent to Amaziah parallel Oded speaking of wrath, but the audience differs.

2-chronicles-28:9:5.summary: They “persecuted the one Thou didst strike,” as Israel added cruelty to Judah whom God had struck.

2-chronicles-28:9:6.summary: A prophet tells Israel’s king God gives the enemy into his hands, like Oded saying God delivered Judah into Israel’s hands.

2-chronicles-28:9:7.summary: Isaiah questioning Hezekiah about Babylonian envoys is unrelated beyond a prophet meeting people.

2-chronicles-28:9:8.summary: A prophet confronts Israel’s king after victory over Syria, loosely like Oded confronting the victorious army.

2-chronicles-28:9:9.summary: God “delivered him into Israel’s king’s hands,” the same event Oded interprets.

2-chronicles-28:9:10.summary: Abel’s blood cries to God, loosely like the slaughter reaching the heavens.

2-chronicles-28:9:11.summary: Assyria as the rod of God’s anger goes beyond its commission, as Israel killed Judah in excess anger.

2-chronicles-28:9:12.summary: A prophet “went out to meet” a returning king and announced “wrath from the Lord,” as Oded met the returning army.

2-chronicles-28:9:13.summary: Jeremiah’s lonely lament has no specific link to Oded’s rebuke.

2-chronicles-28:9:14.summary: A prophet warning Ahab of Syria’s return shares only a prophet addressing Israel.

2-chronicles-28:9:15.summary: Babel’s tower reaching “unto heaven” shares the heaven-reaching image, but not about sin.

2-chronicles-28:9:16.summary: God judges Idumea and the foreigners for vengeance on Judah, loosely like excess against Judah (truncated text).

2-chronicles-28:9:17.summary: The Lord “sold them into the hands” of Syria’s king in anger, as He delivered Judah to its enemies.
2-chronicles-28:9:17.why: Judges pattern of delivering to enemies.

2-chronicles-28:9:18.summary: Tyre rejoices over Jerusalem’s fall and is judged, loosely like guilt for mistreating God’s stricken people.
2-chronicles-28:9:18.why: Judgment on those exploiting Judah’s fall.

2-chronicles-28:9:19.summary: Edom is condemned for “slaughter … toward your brother Jacob,” as Israel slaughtered its brethren Judah (truncated text).
2-chronicles-28:9:19.why: Guilt for violence against a brother nation.

2-chronicles-28:10:1.summary: Judgment beginning with God’s house loosely parallels Oded reminding Israel of its own sins.

2-chronicles-28:10:2.summary: Feeding an enemy instead of enslaving loosely relates to returning the captives.

2-chronicles-28:10:3.summary: Noticing the beam in your own eye matches Oded’s question whether Israel too has sins against the Lord.

2-chronicles-28:10:4.summary: If judgment begins with God’s city, others will not escape, loosely matching Israel’s own guilt.

2-chronicles-28:11:0.summary: “Judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy,” fitting Oded’s demand that Israel release captives under wrath.

2-chronicles-28:11:1.summary: “Blessed are the merciful” generally matches showing mercy to captives.

2-chronicles-28:11:2.summary: The 300,000 “brethren” taken captive are the captivity Oded demands be returned.

2-chronicles-28:11:3.summary: Releasing a “Hebrew brother” is commanded, as Oded tells Israel to return the captives from their brethren.

2-chronicles-28:11:4.summary: Leaders act “to turn the wrathful anger of our God away,” loosely as releasing captives averts wrath.

2-chronicles-28:11:5.summary: Being judged with the measure one uses loosely fits Israel facing wrath for its harshness.

2-chronicles-28:11:6.summary: “Remember the prisoners” loosely relates to caring for the captives.

2-chronicles-28:11:7.summary: “Release the crushed” and loosen bonds of injustice matches returning the captive brethren.
2-chronicles-28:11:7.why: God desires release of the oppressed.

2-chronicles-28:12:0.summary: David assembling Israel’s rulers shares only the word “rulers” with Ephraim’s leaders.

2-chronicles-28:12:1.summary: Making the house like Shiloh has no link to Ephraim’s rulers withstanding the army.

2-chronicles-28:13:0.summary: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” loosely echoes “adding to our sins.”

2-chronicles-28:13:1.summary: Righteous blood coming upon Jesus’ hearers has no specific link to refusing captives.

2-chronicles-28:13:2.summary: “To add still more to the fury of the Lord’s anger against Israel” closely matches “adding to our sins … wrath is upon Israel.”
2-chronicles-28:13:2.why: Same fear of increasing God’s wrath.

2-chronicles-28:13:3.summary: Israel’s leaders fear one sin bringing “wrath … upon all Israel,” as Ephraim’s rulers fear adding to Israel’s sin.

2-chronicles-28:13:4.summary: Storing up wrath by an unrepentant heart loosely matches adding to Israel’s sins.

2-chronicles-28:15:1.summary: “Jericho, the city of palms” is where the captives were returned.

2-chronicles-28:15:0.summary: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” as Ephraim fed and clothed captured Judeans.

2-chronicles-28:15:2.summary: “The City of Palms” is the same name for Jericho where captives were brought.

2-chronicles-28:15:3.summary: Elisha tells the king to set bread before captives and send them home, as Ephraim fed and returned captives.
2-chronicles-28:15:3.why: Close parallel of mercy to prisoners.

2-chronicles-28:15:4.summary: “Love your enemies; do good” illustrated by feeding and clothing enemy captives.

2-chronicles-28:15:5.summary: Job clothed the naked and fed the needy, generally like care given the captives (truncated text).

2-chronicles-28:15:6.summary: “Naked and you clothed Me … gave Me food” matches covering the naked and feeding the captives (truncated text).
2-chronicles-28:15:6.why: Christ’s judgment on works of mercy.

2-chronicles-28:15:7.summary: Giving clothing and food to the needy matches the captives’ care in general terms.

2-chronicles-28:15:8.summary: “If you see someone naked, clothe him … do not overlook … your own family” fits clothing their brethren.

2-chronicles-28:15:9.summary: Loving a brother in need by deed loosely matches caring for their brethren.

2-chronicles-28:15:10.summary: A demoniac with no garment shares only nakedness with the captives.

2-chronicles-28:15:11.summary: The healed man “clothed” shares only the word with captives being clothed.

2-chronicles-28:15:12.summary: Dorcas made garments for widows, loosely like clothing the needy.

2-chronicles-28:15:13.summary: Assisting the afflicted and good works loosely parallel caring for captives.

2-chronicles-28:15:14.summary: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” matches Ephraim feeding enemy captives.

2-chronicles-28:15:15.summary: The named Ephraimite rulers are “the men called by name” who cared for the captives.

2-chronicles-28:15:16.summary: The strong bearing the weaknesses of the weak loosely matches carrying “every weak person” on animals.

2-chronicles-28:16:0.summary: Isaiah warns God will bring “the king of the Assyrians” on Ahaz’s house, the king Ahaz sought for help.
2-chronicles-28:16:0.why: Shows the irony of Ahaz’s appeal.

2-chronicles-28:16:2.summary: Isaiah urges Achaz not to fear Aram and Israel, the threat that drove him to seek Assyria (truncated text).

2-chronicles-28:17:0.summary: Obadiah condemns Edom’s “slaughter … toward your brother Jacob,” matching the Idumeans striking Judah.

2-chronicles-28:17:2.summary: Discipline “seven times more” for disobedience loosely explains continuing attacks on Judah.

2-chronicles-28:17:3.summary: Obadiah forbids Edom from attacking and capturing fugitives of Judah, the kind of raid described.

2-chronicles-28:18:0.summary: Judah as a reproach to “daughters of foreigners” loosely matches the foreigners seizing Judah’s cities.

2-chronicles-28:18:1.summary: God hands Jerusalem to “daughters of foreigners” who hate her, loosely like the foreigners’ conquest.

2-chronicles-28:18:2.summary: “Socoh” in Judah’s allotment is the Socho the foreigners captured.

2-chronicles-28:18:3.summary: The boundary passes the “City of the Sun,” likely Baithsamys (Beth-shemesh), though the shown name differs.
2-chronicles-28:18:3.why: Locates the region of the losses.

2-chronicles-28:18:4.summary: “Geddor” among Judah’s lowland cities may correspond to Gaderoth, though names differ.
2-chronicles-28:18:4.why: Possible location of a lost town.

2-chronicles-28:18:5.summary: “Aialon” was fortified by Rehoboam; it is the Ailon later taken by the foreigners.
2-chronicles-28:18:5.why: Earlier fortification of the lost city.

2-chronicles-28:18:6.summary: “Beth-shemesh” on the Philistine border is Baithsamys captured by the foreigners.
2-chronicles-28:18:6.why: Earlier history of the same town.

2-chronicles-28:18:7.summary: Samson’s “Timnah” among the foreigners is Thamna captured in Ahaz’s day.

2-chronicles-28:19:0.summary: A list of Jehoshaphat’s sons, “king of Judah,” has no link to the Lord humbling Judah because of Ahaz.
2-chronicles-28:19:0.why: Label relies on a naming quirk only.

2-chronicles-28:19:1.summary: God extinguishes the arrogant, loosely like the Lord humbling Judah.

2-chronicles-28:19:2.summary: Ephraim suffered because it “began to follow worthless things,” loosely like Ahaz departing from the Lord.

2-chronicles-28:19:3.summary: “He humbles and raises high” states generally the Lord’s act of humbling Judah.

2-chronicles-28:19:4.summary: Insolence brings a man low, loosely parallel to Judah humbled for Ahaz’s sin.

2-chronicles-28:19:5.summary: The sojourner rises while Israel descends “lower and lower,” loosely matching Judah humbled before foreigners.

2-chronicles-28:19:6.summary: Laodicea’s nakedness has no link; the Greek source speaks of humbling, not making Judah naked.
2-chronicles-28:19:6.why: Label assumes Hebrew “naked” wording absent here.

2-chronicles-28:19:7.summary: Adam and Eve knowing they were naked has no link to the Greek source, which lacks nakedness.

2-chronicles-28:19:8.summary: Israel handed to nations and “humbled beneath their hands” for lawless deeds matches the Lord humbling Judah.
2-chronicles-28:19:8.why: Psalm pattern of humbling for sin.

2-chronicles-28:19:9.summary: Walking in the counsels of Ahab’s house leads to being handed over, loosely like Ahaz’s apostasy humbling Judah.

2-chronicles-28:19:10.summary: God asking “Who told you that you are naked?” has no link to Judah’s humbling in the Greek text.

2-chronicles-28:19:11.summary: Keeping garments lest one walk naked has no link to the Greek source.

2-chronicles-28:19:12.summary: Aaron “scattered” the people to their enemies’ delight, loosely like a leader causing Judah’s humiliation.

2-chronicles-28:20:0.summary: “Thaglathphellasar king of the Assyrians” is the same Assyrian king who came against Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:20:1.summary: Fleeing on horses has no specific link to Thaglath-phellasar striking Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:20:2.summary: “Thaglathphalnasar king of Assour” deported the Transjordan tribes, the same king who struck Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:20:3.summary: An Assyrian king besieging Samaria is a related Assyrian campaign, not the same king or event.

2-chronicles-28:20:4.summary: Isaiah foretells the Lord shaving Judah with the razor of “the king of the Assyrians,” fulfilled when Assyria struck Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:20:6.summary: Trusting Pharaoh becomes shame, a similar failed foreign alliance to Ahaz’s appeal to Assyria.

2-chronicles-28:20:7.summary: Ephraim “went to the Assyrians” but the king “could not heal you,” as Assyria brought Ahaz no help.

2-chronicles-28:20:8.summary: The Lord rejected Judah’s hope in foreign help, loosely like Ahaz’s failed reliance on Assyria.

2-chronicles-28:21:0.summary: Sousakim “took the treasures in the Lord’s house and the king’s house,” the same treasuries Ahaz emptied.
2-chronicles-28:21:0.why: Temple treasures lost to foreign kings.

2-chronicles-28:21:2.summary: Hezekiah gave silver from “the Lord’s house” and king’s house “to the king of the Assyrians,” as Ahaz did.
2-chronicles-28:21:2.why: Same act repeated by his son.

2-chronicles-28:21:3.summary: A proverb on rash vows has no link to Ahaz stripping treasure for Assyria.

2-chronicles-28:22:0.summary: Scourged, they “would not return,” as Ahaz, when afflicted, departed further from the Lord.

2-chronicles-28:22:1.summary: “Why should you be struck again as you add lawlessness?” fits Ahaz sinning more under affliction.

2-chronicles-28:22:2.summary: Ezekiel’s obscure saying about a rejected tribe has no link to Ahaz’s response.

2-chronicles-28:22:3.summary: “In their affliction they will rise early toward Me” contrasts Ahaz, who when afflicted departed further.
2-chronicles-28:22:3.why: Shows the right response to affliction.

2-chronicles-28:22:4.summary: The man who “did not make God his helper” loosely matches Ahaz seeking help elsewhere.

2-chronicles-28:22:5.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction” contrasts Ahaz turning from the Lord when afflicted.

2-chronicles-28:22:7.summary: People under plagues “did not repent,” like Ahaz departing further when afflicted.

2-chronicles-28:22:8.summary: Esther naming “this wicked Haman” shares no element with Ahaz; the link rests on a Hebrew demonstrative.
2-chronicles-28:22:8.why: Label assumes Hebrew phrasing absent here.

2-chronicles-28:23:1.summary: The invader credits “strength” to his god, loosely like Ahaz thinking Syria’s gods strengthen them.

2-chronicles-28:23:2.summary: “In your destruction, Israel, who will help?” loosely answers Ahaz’s hope that gods would support him.

2-chronicles-28:23:4.summary: Those abandoning the Lord will be ended, loosely like Ahaz’s gods becoming his ruin.

2-chronicles-28:23:5.summary: Judeans reason that burning incense to the queen of heaven made them prosper, like Ahaz sacrificing to gods he thought helped Syria (truncated).

2-chronicles-28:23:6.summary: Idols “will not do evil, and no good is in them,” refuting Ahaz’s belief Syria’s gods were striking him and would support him.

2-chronicles-28:23:7.summary: Jeremiah answers that burning incense to other gods brought desolation, as Syria’s gods became Ahaz’s stumbling block (truncated).

2-chronicles-28:24:0.summary: “They shut the sanctuary’s doors,” Hezekiah’s description of what Ahaz did.
2-chronicles-28:24:0.why: Hezekiah recalls Ahaz’s closing of the temple.

2-chronicles-28:24:1.summary: Manasseh built altars in Jerusalem and the Lord’s house, repeating Ahaz’s altar-making.

2-chronicles-28:24:3.summary: Under Hezekiah they “demolished the altars in Jerusalem,” removing altars such as Ahaz made.

2-chronicles-28:24:4.summary: Altars multiplied like heaps in fields loosely match altars at every corner.

2-chronicles-28:24:6.summary: Athens “full of idols” loosely resembles Jerusalem filled with altars.

2-chronicles-28:24:7.summary: An altar to an unknown god in Athens loosely parallels altars to other gods.

2-chronicles-28:24:8.summary: Gods “as numerous as your cities” and sacrifices by Jerusalem’s streets match altars at every corner.
2-chronicles-28:24:8.why: Prophetic picture of the same practice.

2-chronicles-28:24:9.summary: The Chaldeans broke up the temple’s bronze articles, loosely like Ahaz cutting up the articles, but a different event (truncated).

2-chronicles-28:25:0.summary: Ahaz’s earlier abominations in Gaibenenom are part of the same idolatry that provoked the Lord.

2-chronicles-28:26:1.summary: “The rest of Jehoshaphat’s acts, first and last, are written” uses the same formula.

2-chronicles-28:26:2.summary: Jotham’s acts are in “the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” the same source for Ahaz, with Ahaz succeeding him.

2-chronicles-28:27:0.summary: Joram was “buried in David’s city, but not in the tombs of the kings,” exactly as Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:27:1.summary: Joash was buried “in David’s city, but … not … in the tomb of the kings,” as Ahaz.

2-chronicles-28:27:2.summary: “The name of the impious is extinguished” loosely fits Ahaz’s dishonored burial.

2-chronicles-28:27:3.summary: Uzziah “fell asleep with his fathers” and was buried apart, with his son reigning in his place.

2-chronicles-28:27:4.summary: Manasseh “lay down with his fathers,” buried outside royal tombs, “his son … reigned in his place.”

2-chronicles-28:27:5.summary: “The one who despises Me will be dishonoured” loosely explains Ahaz’s denied burial honor.

2-chronicles-28:27:6.summary: Isaiah’s oracle came “in the year King Achaz died,” dating to Ahaz’s death.
2-chronicles-28:27:6.why: Dates a prophecy by this event.

2-chronicles-29:1:1.summary: “Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son” places Hezekiah in David’s line.

2-chronicles-29:1:2.summary: A “Zacharias” who guided Uzziah shares the name of Hezekiah’s maternal grandfather; identity is uncertain.

2-chronicles-29:1:3.summary: Micah prophesied in the days of “Hezekiah.”

2-chronicles-29:1:4.summary: Hosea prophesied in the days of “Hezekiah.”

2-chronicles-29:1:5.summary: “Ahaz begot Hezekiah; Hezekiah begot Manasseh” places Hezekiah in Christ’s genealogy.

2-chronicles-29:1:6.summary: Isaiah prophesied during the reign of “Hezekiah.”

2-chronicles-29:1:7.summary: “Zechariah son of Barachias,” Isaiah’s witness, may be Hezekiah’s grandfather Zacharias; not certain.

2-chronicles-29:2:0.summary: Josiah did what was upright and walked in “the ways of his father David,” the same commendation as Hezekiah.
2-chronicles-29:2:0.why: Two reforming kings likened to David.

2-chronicles-29:2:1.summary: Ahaz “did not do what was right … as David his father had done,” the opposite of Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-29:2:2.summary: Sirach says Hezekiah “stood strong in the ways of his father David,” the same commendation.

2-chronicles-29:3:1.summary: The fathers “shut the sanctuary’s doors”; Hezekiah opened them.

2-chronicles-29:3:2.summary: “Seek first the kingdom of God” loosely fits Hezekiah’s first-month priority on the temple.

2-chronicles-29:3:3.summary: Doing whatever one’s hand finds with strength loosely fits Hezekiah’s prompt action.

2-chronicles-29:3:4.summary: Josiah early in his reign began to seek the Lord and cleanse Judah, as Hezekiah acted in his first month.

2-chronicles-29:3:5.summary: Paul acting without delay loosely parallels Hezekiah’s immediate action; otherwise unrelated.

2-chronicles-29:3:6.summary: Refusing to set lawlessness before one’s eyes loosely fits Hezekiah’s reforming resolve.

2-chronicles-29:3:7.summary: Ahaz altered the temple’s altar and furnishings, the desecration Hezekiah began to repair (truncated text).

2-chronicles-29:4:0.summary: Hezekiah gathers the people in a square to address them, a similar assembly scene with commanders, not priests.

2-chronicles-29:4:1.summary: Jeremiah sent to the Charsith Gate has no link to priests stationed on the east side.

2-chronicles-29:4:2.summary: The “East Gate” keeper loosely relates to the east side where Hezekiah stationed priests.

2-chronicles-29:5:0.summary: Josiah’s Levites are told to prepare holy things for the Passover; a later reform where Levites are again charged, but no purification of the house.
2-chronicles-29:5:0.why: Shows a later king giving Levites similar reform duties.

2-chronicles-29:5:1.summary: Paul calls believers “God’s temple” that is “holy”; Hezekiah orders the Lord’s house purified—a general holiness-of-temple theme.
2-chronicles-29:5:1.why: Applies temple holiness to the Christian community.

2-chronicles-29:5:2.summary: Josiah begins to “cleanse Judah and Jerusalem” of idolatrous objects, a close parallel to Hezekiah’s cleansing reform (shown text only).
2-chronicles-29:5:2.why: Pairs the two great reforming kings’ purges.

2-chronicles-29:5:3.summary: Ezekiel sees abominations and idols inside the temple—the kind of defilement Hezekiah orders cast out, though from a different era.
2-chronicles-29:5:3.why: Illustrates what temple uncleanness looked like.

2-chronicles-29:5:4.summary: David tells the Levite heads “Purify yourselves” before bringing up the ark, the same command Hezekiah gives the Levites.
2-chronicles-29:5:4.why: Same command to Levites in an earlier temple-related task.

2-chronicles-29:5:5.summary: Same episode: the Levites “purified themselves” more eagerly than the priests, showing their response to Hezekiah’s summons.
2-chronicles-29:5:5.why: Shows the Levites’ zealous obedience to this command.

2-chronicles-29:5:6.summary: Narrates the fulfillment: Levites purify themselves and priests “cast out all the uncleanness” from the Lord’s house.
2-chronicles-29:5:6.why: Records the carrying out of Hezekiah’s order.

2-chronicles-29:5:7.summary: Paul urges believers to “cleanse ourselves from every defilement”; echoes the call to self-purification in a spiritual sense.

2-chronicles-29:5:8.summary: Ezekiel is carried in vision to the temple gate; no purification or Levite command is present.

2-chronicles-29:5:9.summary: The Lord tells Moses to “purify” the people before Sinai; shares the verb of ritual preparation, not the temple setting.
2-chronicles-29:5:9.why: Background for purification before meeting God.

2-chronicles-29:5:10.summary: Christ cleanses the Church to make it holy “without blemish”; a loose typological parallel to cleansing the sanctuary.

2-chronicles-29:5:11.summary: Paul asks what agreement “God’s temple” has with idols; general theme of a temple kept pure.
2-chronicles-29:5:11.why: Links temple purity to the believing community.

2-chronicles-29:5:12.summary: Instruction to be ready three days and abstain from women; no direct link to purifying the temple.

2-chronicles-29:5:13.summary: Jesus “cast out” traders from the temple; a cleansing of God’s house, though of commerce, not ritual uncleanness.

2-chronicles-29:5:14.summary: God promises to cleanse Israel “from all your uncleannesses and all your idols”; shares the uncleanness-removal theme.

2-chronicles-29:6:0.summary: Men stand with “their backs toward the Lord’s temple”, the exact posture Hezekiah says the fathers took.
2-chronicles-29:6:0.why: Vivid picture of turning the back on the temple.

2-chronicles-29:6:1.summary: “They turned their backs toward Me, not their faces”—the same image of apostasy Hezekiah uses.
2-chronicles-29:6:1.why: Prophetic use of the same back-turning image.

2-chronicles-29:6:2.summary: “Our fathers sinned”; shares confession of ancestral sin but no detail of forsaking the temple.

2-chronicles-29:6:3.summary: Nations confess how “our fathers acquired false idols”; general theme of ancestral idolatry.

2-chronicles-29:6:4.summary: Jesus on loving father or mother more than Him; “father” is only an incidental word.

2-chronicles-29:6:5.summary: Confession that “our fathers acted arrogantly” and did not listen; same confessional pattern about fathers’ sin.

2-chronicles-29:6:6.summary: Josiah says wrath burned “because our fathers did not heed the Lord’s words”; closely parallels Hezekiah’s confession of fathers’ sin bringing wrath.
2-chronicles-29:6:6.why: Parallel royal confession linking fathers’ sin and wrath.

2-chronicles-29:6:7.summary: Prayer naming hardship of kings, priests and “fathers”; general corporate confession.

2-chronicles-29:6:8.summary: “They abandoned Me”—the same charge Hezekiah makes that the fathers “abandoned Him.”
2-chronicles-29:6:8.why: Prophetic statement of the same abandonment.

2-chronicles-29:6:9.summary: “Has abandoning Me not brought these things upon you?”—shares abandonment and consequence, briefly.
2-chronicles-29:6:9.why: Links forsaking God with resulting disaster.

2-chronicles-29:6:10.summary: Describes Ahaz’s idolatry—the immediately preceding evil Hezekiah refers to as “our fathers” doing evil.
2-chronicles-29:6:10.why: Identifies the specific sins Hezekiah confesses.

2-chronicles-29:6:11.summary: Ezra confesses “from the days of our fathers” great offense; general ancestral-sin confession.
2-chronicles-29:6:11.why: Post-exilic echo of the same confession.

2-chronicles-29:6:12.summary: Incense burned by “your fathers, your kings” remembered by the Lord; ancestral idolatry theme.
2-chronicles-29:6:12.why: Shows ancestral sins remembered by God.

2-chronicles-29:6:13.summary: Daniel confesses “our fathers’ acts of ignorance” bringing reproach on Jerusalem; general confessional parallel.
2-chronicles-29:6:13.why: Confession of ancestral sin in prayer.

2-chronicles-29:6:14.summary: Jesus rebukes those who fill up their “fathers” measure; the fathers theme is incidental, not confession of forsaking the temple.

2-chronicles-29:6:15.summary: “Our fathers provoked the God of heaven” and the house was dismantled; ancestral sin linked to the temple’s fate.
2-chronicles-29:6:15.why: Shows the later outcome of such sin.

2-chronicles-29:7:1.summary: Commands to burn the lamp continually before the Lord; the ordinance Hezekiah says was neglected when lamps were extinguished.
2-chronicles-29:7:1.why: Gives the law that was broken.

2-chronicles-29:7:2.summary: Hezekiah “opened the doors of the Lord’s house”, reversing the shutting of doors described here.

2-chronicles-29:7:3.summary: Ahaz dismantles temple furnishings because of Assyria; related to the fathers’ neglect, but not shutting doors.

2-chronicles-29:7:4.summary: “Doors will be shut” and the altar not kindled; strong verbal and situational echo of shut doors and ceased offerings.
2-chronicles-29:7:4.why: Prophetic use of the same shut-doors image.

2-chronicles-29:8:0.summary: God will make the land “a ruin, a hissing” — the same judgment term “hissing” used by Hezekiah.
2-chronicles-29:8:0.why: Prophetic statement of the same judgment.

2-chronicles-29:8:1.summary: Jerusalem and Judah made “a desolation… and a hissing”; same objects and same judgment vocabulary.

2-chronicles-29:8:2.summary: Under Joash they abandoned the Lord and “wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem”; same formula of wrath on Judah and Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-29:8:2.why: Earlier instance of the same pattern.

2-chronicles-29:8:3.summary: “A ruin and a hissing” for the city; shares the distinctive hissing judgment.

2-chronicles-29:8:5.summary: Covenant curse: the Lord gives Israel over before enemies and scatters them; general covenant-judgment background.

2-chronicles-29:8:6.summary: Curses for not hearkening to the Lord’s voice; general covenant-curse background to the wrath described.
2-chronicles-29:8:6.why: Shows the covenant basis of the anger.

2-chronicles-29:8:7.summary: Defiling the Lord’s house led to the Lord’s anger rising “until there was no healing”; later climax of the same pattern.
2-chronicles-29:8:7.why: Shows where such wrath finally led.

2-chronicles-29:8:8.summary: Because they “abandoned Me”, the Lord’s anger is kindled on this place; similar wrath-for-abandonment theme.

2-chronicles-29:8:9.summary: God will desolate the land so enemies “marvel at it”; parallels the astonishment of judgment.

2-chronicles-29:8:10.summary: Plagues “great and astonishing”; general covenant-curse theme of astonishing judgment.

2-chronicles-29:8:11.summary: Their land made “an eternal hissing”, all passing astonished; strong echo of the hissing judgment.

2-chronicles-29:9:0.summary: Idumeans struck Judah and “carried away captives” under Ahaz—the captivity Hezekiah refers to.

2-chronicles-29:9:2.summary: “Our fathers sinned… we bore their lawless acts”; general theme of descendants suffering for fathers.

2-chronicles-29:9:3.summary: Covenant curse: falling before enemies; general background to fathers struck by the sword.

2-chronicles-29:10:0.summary: Return to the Lord in “an everlasting covenant”; shares covenant-making but in a different context.

2-chronicles-29:10:1.summary: Jehoiada made a covenant that they should be the Lord’s people; a parallel royal covenant renewal in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-29:10:2.summary: “Let us make a covenant with our God” to address sin; parallel covenant renewal to avert wrath.

2-chronicles-29:10:3.summary: Nehemiah’s people establish and seal a pledge; covenant renewal theme, mostly list of names in shown text.

2-chronicles-29:10:4.summary: The Lord “did not turn from His great burning wrath” despite Josiah’s reform; contrasts Hezekiah’s hope that wrath will turn.

2-chronicles-29:10:5.summary: Josiah “made a covenant before the Lord”; a parallel royal covenant renewal.
2-chronicles-29:10:5.why: Parallel covenant by a reforming king.

2-chronicles-29:10:6.summary: Josiah “established a covenant before the Lord” in the temple; close parallel to Hezekiah’s covenant intent.

2-chronicles-29:10:8.summary: People “concluded a covenant before Me in the house”; a covenant in the temple, but about releasing slaves.

2-chronicles-29:10:9.summary: Macedonians gave themselves to the Lord; no covenant or wrath element.

2-chronicles-29:10:10.summary: “It came upon the heart of David” to build a house; echoes Hezekiah’s “in my heart” expression.

2-chronicles-29:10:11.summary: Men who did not uphold “My covenant which they made before Me”; contrasts covenant-making with breaking.

2-chronicles-29:11:0.summary: The Levites are taken and purified to serve before the Lord; the basis of their being chosen to minister.

2-chronicles-29:11:3.summary: The tribe of Levi set apart to “minister” before the Tent; the origin of their chosen ministry.

2-chronicles-29:11:4.summary: Unauthorized men presenting incense are consumed; contrasts with those chosen to burn incense.
2-chronicles-29:11:4.why: Shows the danger of unauthorized incense.

2-chronicles-29:11:5.summary: Sowing and reaping teaching; no link to Levites’ chosen ministry or slackening.

2-chronicles-29:12:0.summary: “Maath” appears among Levites appointed under Hezekiah—same name and reign.

2-chronicles-29:12:1.summary: Lists Gershon, Kohath, Merari—the three Levite clans whose sons appear here, under Hebrew-style names.

2-chronicles-29:12:2.summary: Sons of Kohath and Merari listed; clan background to the named Levites.

2-chronicles-29:12:3.summary: “Gedson, Kaath, and Merari” and Gedson’s line including “Zemma” and “Joach”, matching Joa son of Zemmath.
2-chronicles-29:12:3.why: Same clan names and possibly same family line.
