2-chronicles-31:14:14.summary: The guilt offering is “most holy,” background to the most holy things; shown text truncated.

2-chronicles-31:14:15.summary: Tithes and firstfruits not eaten in the cities relate generally to centralized gifts.

2-chronicles-31:14:16.summary: Gifts and freewill offerings presented to God relate loosely.

2-chronicles-31:14:17.summary: Giving at the Feast of Weeks as the Lord has blessed relates loosely.

2-chronicles-31:14:18.summary: Gatekeeper divisions ministering in the Lord’s house relate generally to Kore’s role.

2-chronicles-31:15:0.summary: Lists cities assigned to Aaron’s sons; the source concerns Hezekiah’s distribution to priests by divisions, not the priestly cities (truncated range judged on shown text).
2-chronicles-31:15:0.why: Background on where the priests lived.

2-chronicles-31:15:1.summary: Chronicles list of cities and lands given to Aaron’s sons; only loosely related to distributing portions to priests by divisions (truncated).

2-chronicles-31:15:2.summary: Levite gatekeepers appointed “in their faithfulness”; the source has Levites “faithfully distributing,” a verbal echo in a different setting.
2-chronicles-31:15:2.why: Shows faithfulness as a mark of Levitical service.

2-chronicles-31:15:3.summary: Levitical service courses arranged “for the small and for the great,” echoing “to great and small alike” in the source.
2-chronicles-31:15:3.why: Parallels the impartial treatment of all ranks.

2-chronicles-31:15:4.summary: Same administration of Hezekiah’s storehouses, naming officers appointed under Chonenias and Semei alongside the source’s distributors.
2-chronicles-31:15:4.why: Immediate context naming the other officials.

2-chronicles-31:15:5.summary: List of Levites who rose under Hezekiah; only a general overlap of Levite names and roles with the source’s distributors.
2-chronicles-31:15:5.why: Introduces Levites active in Hezekiah’s reforms.

2-chronicles-31:16:0.summary: Daily offerings “day by day” at the Festival of Booths; loosely parallels the source’s “daily account” of temple ministry.

2-chronicles-31:16:1.summary: Rules for a blemished priest eating holy things; no real link to counting males from three years old for daily ministry.

2-chronicles-31:16:2.summary: Levites numbered “from thirty years old and upward”; shares an age-based enrollment formula with the source’s “three years old and upward.”
2-chronicles-31:16:2.why: Compares age thresholds in Levitical registers.

2-chronicles-31:17:2.summary: Returnees unable to declare their “family house” and descent, contrasting the source’s orderly enrollment by ancestral houses.

2-chronicles-31:17:3.summary: Long list of Levite family divisions; generally related to enrollment of Levites “in their divisions” (truncated range).

2-chronicles-31:17:4.summary: Registering Levites “by their ancestral houses, by their divisions” from an age “and upward,” echoing the source’s enrollment formula.

2-chronicles-31:17:5.summary: Merari’s sons as “divisions of the Levites by their ancestral houses”; shares formulaic wording only.
2-chronicles-31:17:5.why: Shows the origin of Levite divisions.

2-chronicles-31:17:6.summary: Hezekiah “arranged the divisions of priests and Levites,” the same reform whose enrollment by divisions the source describes.
2-chronicles-31:17:6.why: Opens the account of the same reorganization.

2-chronicles-31:17:7.summary: Merari’s sons “registered by their divisions and ancestral houses”; formulaic echo of the source’s enrollment.

2-chronicles-31:17:8.summary: Levites registered “by their divisions and ancestral houses” under Moses; shares the enrollment formula.

2-chronicles-31:17:9.summary: Twelve staffs taken by ancestral house to vindicate Aaron; only the phrase “ancestral houses” is shared.

2-chronicles-31:17:10.summary: Gershon’s sons “registered by their divisions and ancestral houses”; formulaic echo only.

2-chronicles-31:17:11.summary: Levites serve “from twenty-five years old and upward,” contrasting with the source’s twenty-year threshold.
2-chronicles-31:17:11.why: Shows how service age shifted over time.

2-chronicles-31:17:12.summary: Levites enter work “from twenty-five years old and upward,” compared with the source’s “twenty years old and upward.”

2-chronicles-31:18:0.summary: God exalted through judgment and glorified as holy; no link to Levites purifying the holy place in faithfulness.

2-chronicles-31:18:1.summary: Paul’s priestly service of the gospel among Gentiles; only a general notion of priestly sanctity is shared.

2-chronicles-31:18:2.summary: Gatekeepers listed in “their enrollment” and appointed “in their faithfulness,” echoing the source’s “enrollment” and “in faithfulness.”

2-chronicles-31:18:3.summary: Immediately preceding verse of the same passage, where priests are “faithfully distributing” to their brethren by divisions.
2-chronicles-31:18:3.why: Continuous context of the same distribution.

2-chronicles-31:19:0.summary: Same passage on Hezekiah’s storehouses: tithes faithfully brought and distributed by named Levites (truncated range).
2-chronicles-31:19:0.why: Supplies the officials and system described.

2-chronicles-31:19:1.summary: Levites given towns and surrounding lands; relates loosely to priests living in “their cities” in the source (truncated).

2-chronicles-31:19:2.summary: Fields of Levitical cities may not be sold; only a background link to priests in their cities.

2-chronicles-31:19:3.summary: “The men called by name” cared for captives; echoes the source’s “men designated by name” in a different event.

2-chronicles-31:19:4.summary: Dwelling places for “Aaron’s sons” in their villages; background to the priests’ cities in the source.

2-chronicles-31:19:5.summary: Benjamite cities with surrounding lands given to priests; general background to the priests’ cities.

2-chronicles-31:20:0.summary: Hezekiah himself prays that he “did what was good” before the Lord, matching the source’s verdict on him.
2-chronicles-31:20:0.why: Hezekiah’s own testimony to his faithfulness.

2-chronicles-31:20:1.summary: Josiah “did what was right in the Lord’s eyes”; the same regnal formula applied to a different king.

2-chronicles-31:20:2.summary: Paul’s striving for a blameless conscience; no specific link to Hezekiah’s reforms.

2-chronicles-31:20:3.summary: Gaius acting faithfully toward brothers; no specific link to the source.

2-chronicles-31:20:4.summary: Paul’s devout and just conduct among believers; no specific link to Hezekiah’s deeds.

2-chronicles-31:20:5.summary: Nathanael called an Israelite without deceit; no real link to the source.

2-chronicles-31:20:6.summary: David “did what was right before the Lord”; the same evaluative formula used for the model king.

2-chronicles-31:21:0.summary: Seeking God’s kingdom first and receiving all things loosely parallels seeking God and prospering.

2-chronicles-31:21:1.summary: Seeking God “with your whole heart” parallels Hezekiah seeking God “with his whole soul.”

2-chronicles-31:21:2.summary: Keeping “this book of the law” brings prosperity—“you shall prosper,” matching Hezekiah’s keeping the law and prospering.
2-chronicles-31:21:2.why: Covenant pattern: obedience leads to success.

2-chronicles-31:21:3.summary: Love God “with all your soul”; loosely echoes Hezekiah seeking God “with his whole soul.”
2-chronicles-31:21:3.why: Grounds wholehearted devotion in the Shema.

2-chronicles-31:21:4.summary: Doing every task “with your strength” loosely parallels Hezekiah’s energetic work.

2-chronicles-31:21:5.summary: Parable of houses on rock and sand; no specific link to Hezekiah’s seeking God and prospering.

2-chronicles-31:21:6.summary: God will “grant success” if Solomon does the “ordinances,” paralleling Hezekiah’s keeping the ordinances and prospering.
2-chronicles-31:21:6.why: Same Chronicler principle of obedience and success.

2-chronicles-31:21:8.summary: Naming of the Valley of Blessing; no link to Hezekiah’s seeking God.

2-chronicles-31:21:9.summary: Uzziah “sought the Lord” and “the Lord made him prosper,” the same pattern said of Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-31:21:10.summary: Keeping the covenant words so as to understand all one does; general obedience-and-success theme.

2-chronicles-31:21:11.summary: Asa: “we sought the Lord our God” and “He... prospered us,” the same seeking-and-prospering pattern.
2-chronicles-31:21:11.why: Parallel reforming king blessed for seeking God.

2-chronicles-31:21:12.summary: Walking before God “with all their heart and all their soul”; loose echo of Hezekiah’s whole-souled seeking.

2-chronicles-31:21:13.summary: The one delighting in “the Lord’s law” is one whose doings will “be prospered,” matching the law-and-prosperity link.
2-chronicles-31:21:13.why: Wisdom portrait of the blessed law-keeper.

2-chronicles-31:21:14.summary: “Give your hearts and your souls to seek the Lord” and build His house, echoing Hezekiah’s whole-souled seeking and temple service.

2-chronicles-32:1:7.summary: Isaiah’s parallel narrative of Sennacherib coming against Judea’s fortified cities in Hezekiah’s reign (truncated range).
2-chronicles-32:1:7.why: Fuller parallel account of the invasion.

2-chronicles-32:1:1.summary: Isaiah foretells days when God brings “the king of the Assyrians” upon Judah; prophetic background to the invasion.

2-chronicles-32:1:2.summary: Woe on the Assyrians as God’s rod, boasting of taking cities; general background to Sennacherib’s campaign (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:1:3.summary: A king breaking through and leading the people out; no clear link to Sennacherib’s invasion.

2-chronicles-32:1:4.summary: The Assyrian king’s deportation of Samaria; earlier Assyrian action preceding the attack on Judah.

2-chronicles-32:1:5.summary: Assyria captures Samaria and deports Israel; background to the threat now facing Judah.

2-chronicles-32:1:6.summary: Isaiah’s image of the king of the Assyrians flooding Judea and walking over its walls; prophetic background.

2-chronicles-32:1:8.summary: An earlier Assyrian king, Phul, came against the land; only a general Assyrian-invasion parallel.

2-chronicles-32:1:9.summary: “After this” enemies came against Jehoshaphat; similar narrative pattern of invasion following faithfulness.

2-chronicles-32:1:10.summary: Assur as Ephraim’s king; no link to Sennacherib’s campaign against Judah.

2-chronicles-32:2:0.summary: Hazael “set his face to go up against Jerusalem,” a close verbal echo of Sennacherib’s face set against Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-32:2:0.why: Same idiom for a foreign king targeting Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-32:2:1.summary: Jesus’ “face was set toward Jerusalem”; shares the idiom but in an entirely different context.

2-chronicles-32:2:2.summary: Jesus “set His face to go to Jerusalem”; idiom shared, context unrelated to a military threat.

2-chronicles-32:3:1.summary: Proverb on counsel among those who deliberate; illustrates Hezekiah consulting his elders.

2-chronicles-32:3:2.summary: War conducted with guidance and help from deliberation; fits Hezekiah’s war counsel generally.

2-chronicles-32:3:3.summary: No one counsels the Lord; unrelated to Hezekiah consulting his officials.

2-chronicles-32:3:4.summary: Hezekiah’s fountain and aqueduct bringing water into the city, the same waterworks behind blocking the springs.
2-chronicles-32:3:4.why: Kings’ record of Hezekiah’s water project.

2-chronicles-32:3:5.summary: Isaiah describes the pool’s water diverted into the city and houses pulled down to fortify the wall—Hezekiah’s defensive preparations.
2-chronicles-32:3:5.why: Prophetic critique of the same preparations.

2-chronicles-32:3:6.summary: Rhapsakes mocks Hezekiah’s “Counsel and strength for war,” deriding the very counsel and strengthening the source describes.

2-chronicles-32:3:7.summary: Hezekiah and his leaders “took counsel” about Passover; shows his consultative style in another matter.

2-chronicles-32:3:8.summary: No one became the Lord’s counselor; unrelated to Hezekiah’s war council.

2-chronicles-32:4:1.summary: Sennacherib’s arrival against Judah, the threat that prompted blocking the springs.

2-chronicles-32:4:2.summary: Elisha sacrificing his oxen and following Elijah; no link to Hezekiah blocking waters.

2-chronicles-32:4:3.summary: Hezekiah’s prayer that Assyrian kings devastated nations; general Assyrian threat, not the water-blocking.

2-chronicles-32:4:4.summary: Sennacherib went up against Judah’s fortified cities in Hezekiah’s reign, the same invasion.

2-chronicles-32:4:5.summary: Altars thrown into the Kedron torrent; possibly the stream through the city, but the source names no river.

2-chronicles-32:4:6.summary: Solomon’s prayer for a discerning heart; no link to the source.

2-chronicles-32:4:7.summary: Two women come before Solomon for judgment; no link to the source.

2-chronicles-32:4:8.summary: A fragment of Assyrian pride; nothing about waters or Hezekiah’s defense.

2-chronicles-32:4:9.summary: Hezekiah’s fountain and aqueduct and bringing water into the city, the waterworks connected with blocking the springs.
2-chronicles-32:4:9.why: Kings’ record of the water project.

2-chronicles-32:4:10.summary: Salamanassar besieges Samaria in Hezekiah’s fourth year; earlier Assyrian context, not this event.

2-chronicles-32:5:0.summary: Joash tore down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem’s wall, possibly the “demolished wall” Hezekiah rebuilt.
2-chronicles-32:5:0.why: Possible origin of the breached wall.

2-chronicles-32:5:1.summary: Mentions the City of David in Solomon’s day; only the place name is shared.

2-chronicles-32:5:2.summary: David built up the city of David from the citadel; background to the fortifications Hezekiah strengthened.
2-chronicles-32:5:2.why: Origin of the City of David defenses.

2-chronicles-32:5:4.summary: A “gate between the walls” in Jerusalem, possibly reflecting the double wall Hezekiah built.
2-chronicles-32:5:4.why: Later trace of Jerusalem’s double wall.

2-chronicles-32:5:5.summary: Solomon built the citadel and closed the enclosure of the City of David; earlier work on the same fortifications.
2-chronicles-32:5:5.why: Earlier phase of the same defenses.

2-chronicles-32:5:6.summary: Asa builds cities with “walls, towers”; a similar royal fortification program.

2-chronicles-32:5:7.summary: Abimelech made king by the house of Maallon at Shechem; the Greek text carries no link to Jerusalem’s fortifications.
2-chronicles-32:5:7.why: Label relies on a Hebrew place name.

2-chronicles-32:5:8.summary: Rehoboam, once secured, abandoned the Lord; contrasts with Hezekiah, whose strength accompanied faithfulness.

2-chronicles-32:5:9.summary: Uzziah “grew exceedingly strong”; shares the Chronicler’s strengthening formula only.

2-chronicles-32:5:11.summary: Jehoiada “grew strong” before a palace coup; only the stock phrase is shared.

2-chronicles-32:5:12.summary: Uzziah prepared weapons and devices on Jerusalem’s “towers,” paralleling Hezekiah’s towers and many weapons.
2-chronicles-32:5:12.why: Earlier king’s comparable defenses of Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-32:5:13.summary: Joash killed at the house of Mallo; a name match only, unrelated to Hezekiah’s building.

2-chronicles-32:5:14.summary: Jehoshaphat “grew strong” and garrisoned fortified cities; a general parallel of military preparation.

2-chronicles-32:6:0.summary: Hezekiah “spoke to every heart” of the Levites, the same idiom and same king as speaking to the commanders’ hearts.

2-chronicles-32:6:1.summary: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem”; shares the comforting idiom in a different context.

2-chronicles-32:6:2.summary: Tents in the city’s open squares and by a gate; only a general setting of gathering in squares.

2-chronicles-32:6:3.summary: The people gathered and sat in the open square; similar assembly setting only.

2-chronicles-32:6:4.summary: Shechem “spoke... according to her heart”; shares the idiom of speaking to the heart only.

2-chronicles-32:6:5.summary: Jehoshaphat’s commanders of thousands; a general parallel to appointing commanders of war (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:6:6.summary: David’s commanders of the army divisions; general parallel to appointing war commanders (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:6:7.summary: The people gathered in the open space before the Water Gate; similar assembly at a gate square.

2-chronicles-32:7:16.summary: “Act courageously and be strong; do not fear or be terrified” closely matches Hezekiah’s charge to his commanders.
2-chronicles-32:7:16.why: Same formula of encouragement in Chronicles.

2-chronicles-32:7:1.summary: “If God is for us, who is against us?” echoes the conviction that more are with us than with the enemy.
2-chronicles-32:7:1.why: New Testament restatement of the confidence.

2-chronicles-32:7:2.summary: Be strengthened in the Lord’s might; a general parallel to “Be strong” in the face of an enemy.
2-chronicles-32:7:2.why: Spiritual application of strength in God.

2-chronicles-32:7:3.summary: “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” parallels “more are with us than with him.”
2-chronicles-32:7:3.why: Same assurance of a greater power on our side.

2-chronicles-32:7:4.summary: “Do not fear or be terrified before this great crowd” before an invading army, closely matching Hezekiah’s words.
2-chronicles-32:7:4.why: Parallel Chronicler crisis with the same encouragement.

2-chronicles-32:7:5.summary: The Assyrian envoy warns not to let Hezekiah make them hope in the Lord, countering this very speech.
2-chronicles-32:7:5.why: Shows the enemy’s reply to Hezekiah’s encouragement.

2-chronicles-32:7:6.summary: “Be strong, be of good courage, and act. Do not fear,” for “the Lord my God is with you,” echoes Hezekiah’s charge.
2-chronicles-32:7:6.why: Same formula in David’s charge to Solomon.

2-chronicles-32:7:7.summary: “Do not fear... Take courage and be strong” to Daniel; shared words in a vision context unrelated to war.

2-chronicles-32:7:8.summary: “Be strong; do not fear!” because God will come and save; a general echo of the encouragement.

2-chronicles-32:7:9.summary: “Let your hands be strong” in temple rebuilding; shares only the exhortation to strength.

2-chronicles-32:7:10.summary: “Be courageous and strong; fear not... neither be terrified,” for the Lord is with you, closely echoed by Hezekiah.
2-chronicles-32:7:10.why: Mosaic source of the encouragement formula.

2-chronicles-32:7:11.summary: “Be courageous and strong,” with the promise “He shall be with you,” matches Hezekiah’s exhortation.

2-chronicles-32:7:12.summary: Isaiah tells Hezekiah’s men “Do not fear” the king of the Assyrians’ words, in the same crisis.
2-chronicles-32:7:12.why: Prophetic encouragement in the same siege.

2-chronicles-32:7:13.summary: “God is with you” said of Judeans by the nations; shares only the God-with-us idea.

2-chronicles-32:7:14.summary: Repeated “be strong and courageous. Do not be fainthearted or afraid” to Joshua, the classic form of Hezekiah’s charge (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:7:15.summary: “Be strengthened in the grace” of Christ; a general spiritual echo of being strong.

2-chronicles-32:7:17.summary: “Be strong and act,” David’s charge to Solomon, echoes “Be strong and act courageously.”

2-chronicles-32:8:0.summary: Cursed is one who rests “the flesh of his arm” on a human, matching the contrast “arms of flesh” versus the Lord.
2-chronicles-32:8:0.why: Same image of human strength versus God.

2-chronicles-32:8:1.summary: “You will not have to wage war... the Lord will be with you,” paralleling the Lord fighting Judah’s war.

2-chronicles-32:8:2.summary: The Lord stood by and strengthened Paul and rescued him; general theme of the Lord’s help.

2-chronicles-32:8:3.summary: “I am with you, and no one will attack you”; general assurance of God’s presence and protection.

2-chronicles-32:8:4.summary: “The battle array belongs to God, not to you,” paralleling the Lord who will “fight our war.”
2-chronicles-32:8:4.why: Same conviction that God fights for Judah.

2-chronicles-32:8:5.summary: “Do not fear, for I am with you”; general promise of God’s presence and strength.

2-chronicles-32:8:6.summary: The One in believers is greater than the one in the world; loosely parallels God versus arms of flesh.

2-chronicles-32:8:7.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us,” echoing “with us is the Lord our God.”
2-chronicles-32:8:7.why: Psalm refrain of the same confidence.

2-chronicles-32:8:8.summary: “The Lord is with us in command” in battle against Israel, echoing “with us is the Lord our God... to fight.”
2-chronicles-32:8:8.why: Chronicler parallel of God fighting for Judah.

2-chronicles-32:8:9.summary: Facing a larger army, “you shall not fear them; for the Lord your God is with you,” matching Hezekiah’s reasoning.
2-chronicles-32:8:9.why: Law of war behind Hezekiah’s speech.

2-chronicles-32:8:10.summary: Asa trusts God against a great multitude, praying “let no human being prevail against Thee,” paralleling flesh versus the Lord.

2-chronicles-32:8:12.summary: “Do you have an arm against the Lord?”; shares the arm image of human versus divine power.

2-chronicles-32:8:13.summary: Enemy counsel will fail “because the Lord God is with us,” echoing Hezekiah’s confidence against Assyria.

2-chronicles-32:8:14.summary: Good news gladdens the heart; loosely matches the people taking courage from Hezekiah’s words.

2-chronicles-32:8:15.summary: Jehoshaphat urges Judah to trust in the Lord before battle; a general parallel of a king’s encouragement.

2-chronicles-32:8:16.summary: The Assyrian says “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you,” directly countering Hezekiah’s assurance of salvation.
2-chronicles-32:8:16.why: Enemy’s rebuttal in the same crisis.

2-chronicles-32:8:17.summary: A closing blessing, “The Lord be with your spirit”; no real link to the source.

2-chronicles-32:8:18.summary: “The Lord... fought alongside Israel,” paralleling the Lord who will “fight our war.”
2-chronicles-32:8:18.why: Precedent of God fighting Israel’s battles.

2-chronicles-32:8:19.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us,” echoing “with us is the Lord our God.”
2-chronicles-32:8:19.why: Psalm refrain of the same confidence.

2-chronicles-32:8:20.summary: Sennacherib’s message denies that Hezekiah’s God can save, directly answering Hezekiah’s claim.
2-chronicles-32:8:20.why: Enemy’s challenge to the same assurance.

2-chronicles-32:8:21.summary: “Fight our war” addressed to Simon by the people; verbal echo in a different context.
2-chronicles-32:8:21.why: Same phrase in a later crisis.

2-chronicles-32:9:1.summary: Joshua besieged Lachish; shares only the place where Sennacherib was encamped.

2-chronicles-32:9:2.summary: The king of Lachish in Joshua’s list; only the place name is shared.

2-chronicles-32:9:3.summary: Rapsakes finds the Assyrian king besieging Lomna, the parallel account of the king’s movements during the campaign.
2-chronicles-32:9:3.why: Isaiah’s parallel of the king’s siege operations.

2-chronicles-32:9:4.summary: The Assyrian king sent Rapsakes “from Lachis to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah,” the same mission.

2-chronicles-32:9:5.summary: Lachish in Judah’s town list; only the place name is shared.

2-chronicles-32:9:6.summary: Micah addresses the inhabitant of Lachish amid chariots; links by place and military threat only.

2-chronicles-32:10:0.summary: “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: ‘What do you trust in?’” parallels the same speech.
2-chronicles-32:10:0.why: Isaiah’s version of the same message.
2-chronicles-32:10:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:11:0.summary: Same speech continues: “do not let Hezekiah deceive you,” your God will not save you.

2-chronicles-32:11:1.summary: Taunt that “there is no salvation for him in his God” resembles the claim that God will not save.
2-chronicles-32:11:1.why: Similar mockery of trust in God.

2-chronicles-32:11:2.summary: Enemies taunt “Where is your God?”; similar mockery of trust in God.
2-chronicles-32:11:2.why: Same pattern of taunting the faithful.

2-chronicles-32:11:4.summary: Rapsakes speaks to the people on the wall who will “eat dung and drink urine,” the hunger and thirst threat.
2-chronicles-32:11:4.why: Isaiah’s parallel of the siege threat.

2-chronicles-32:11:5.summary: Enemies say “God has forsaken him... there is no rescuer”; similar taunt that God will not save.
2-chronicles-32:11:5.why: Similar mockery of trust in God.

2-chronicles-32:11:6.summary: “Do not let your God, in whom you trust,” persuade you Jerusalem will not be handed over, the same Assyrian argument.

2-chronicles-32:11:7.summary: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, saying, ‘Your God will rescue you,’” the same accusation.
2-chronicles-32:11:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:11:8.summary: Rhapsakes threatens the men on the wall with eating dung and drinking urine, the hunger and thirst of the siege.
2-chronicles-32:11:8.why: Kings’ parallel of the siege threat.

2-chronicles-32:11:9.summary: Mockers say “He trusts in God; let Him rescue Him”; similar taunt of trust in divine rescue.
2-chronicles-32:11:9.why: Same taunt pattern at the cross.

2-chronicles-32:11:10.summary: The psalmist trusts the Lord while foes mock his trust; a loose parallel of taunted faith.

2-chronicles-32:11:11.summary: “He hoped in the Lord; let Him rescue him”; similar mockery of trust in God’s deliverance.
2-chronicles-32:11:11.why: Classic taunt against trust in God.

2-chronicles-32:12:0.summary: Hezekiah’s reform demolished “the high places and altars” throughout Judah, the act the Assyrian cites.
2-chronicles-32:12:0.why: Records the reform the enemy distorts.

2-chronicles-32:12:1.summary: Offerings only “in the place which the Lord your God shall choose,” the law behind “Before this altar you shall bow.”

2-chronicles-32:12:2.summary: Solomon’s bronze altar; possibly the altar meant, but no direct link in the text.

2-chronicles-32:12:3.summary: “If you say, ‘We trust the Lord our God’” opens the same argument about Hezekiah removing the altars (verse shown only in part).
2-chronicles-32:12:3.why: Isaiah’s parallel of the same taunt.
2-chronicles-32:12:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:12:4.summary: Offerings brought to the place the Lord chooses, on His altar; background to a single altar.

2-chronicles-32:12:5.summary: Instructions for the incense altar; loosely related to burning incense at the one altar.

2-chronicles-32:12:6.summary: Hezekiah “removed the high places” and ended illicit incense, the reform the Assyrian mentions.
2-chronicles-32:12:6.why: Kings’ record of the same reform.

2-chronicles-32:12:7.summary: Solomon placed the gold altar in the Lord’s house; background on the temple altar.

2-chronicles-32:12:9.summary: Moses placed the gold altar and burned incense on it; background on the legitimate altar.

2-chronicles-32:12:10.summary: Instructions for the bronze altar; general background to the one altar (truncated).
2-chronicles-32:12:10.why: Background on the altar of offering.

2-chronicles-32:13:0.summary: “Have the gods of the nations ever rescued, each his own country, from the hand of the king of the Assyrians?” the same boast.

2-chronicles-32:13:1.summary: An idol is nothing and there is one God; answers the boast about powerless gods.

2-chronicles-32:13:2.summary: Thaglathphellasar took Galilee and Naphtali; an example of Assyrian conquests the boast recalls.

2-chronicles-32:13:3.summary: No God apart from the Lord; idol-makers futile; general theme of powerless gods.

2-chronicles-32:13:5.summary: The Assyrian boasts he seized the world in his hand, “no one who will escape me,” mirroring the source’s boast.
2-chronicles-32:13:5.why: Isaiah’s portrait of the same Assyrian arrogance.

2-chronicles-32:13:6.summary: Gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish; general contrast of idols with the Creator.
2-chronicles-32:13:6.why: Contrasts idols with the true God.

2-chronicles-32:13:7.summary: Nebuchadnezzar praises the God of gods who removes kings; a loosely related reversal of royal pride.

2-chronicles-32:13:8.summary: Nebuchadnezzar boasts of Babylon built by his might; a parallel of royal arrogance.

2-chronicles-32:13:9.summary: The nations’ idols are powerless works of hands, unlike God in heaven; answers the boast generally.

2-chronicles-32:13:10.summary: Assyrian boast: “Did I not take... Damascus and Samaria?... I will also take all the dominions,” like the source’s boast.
2-chronicles-32:13:10.why: Isaiah’s version of the same boast.

2-chronicles-32:13:11.summary: Hezekiah admits Assyrian kings destroyed the nations’ gods, “for they are not gods,” answering this boast.
2-chronicles-32:13:11.why: Hezekiah’s prayer replying to the boast.

2-chronicles-32:13:12.summary: Same narrative: he spoke against Jerusalem’s God as against the nations’ gods, “works of human hands.”
2-chronicles-32:13:12.why: Narrator’s comment on the same boast.

2-chronicles-32:13:13.summary: Hezekiah’s prayer: Assyrian kings cast idols into fire, “for they were not gods,” answering the boast.

2-chronicles-32:13:14.summary: Assyria besieged and captured Samaria; an instance of the conquests behind the boast.

2-chronicles-32:13:16.summary: “Did the gods of the nations my fathers destroyed rescue them?” the same boast in Isaiah.

2-chronicles-32:13:17.summary: Jacob’s portion is the Creator, unlike idols; generally contrasts Israel’s God with the nations’ gods.

2-chronicles-32:13:18.summary: “Things made by hands are not gods”; shares the theme of powerless handmade gods.
2-chronicles-32:13:18.why: New Testament echo of idol critique.

2-chronicles-32:14:0.summary: God will not give His glory to carved images; general contrast with the Assyrian’s equation of gods.

2-chronicles-32:14:1.summary: The enemy’s boast “my hand shall have dominion” and “Who is like Thee among the gods?”; loose parallel of an overthrown boaster.
2-chronicles-32:14:1.why: Exodus precedent of a boasting enemy.

2-chronicles-32:14:2.summary: Pharaoh supposes Israel is trapped in the wilderness; no specific link to the gods-cannot-save boast.
2-chronicles-32:14:2.why: Only a vague parallel of enemy presumption.

2-chronicles-32:14:3.summary: Assyrian boast “as I did to Samaria... so I will also do to Jerusalem,” then God’s judgment on Assyria’s ruler.
2-chronicles-32:14:3.why: Isaiah’s view of the same boast and its end.

2-chronicles-32:15:2.summary: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you... Have the nations’ gods each rescued his own country?” the same speech.

2-chronicles-32:15:0.summary: Nebuchadnezzar asks “What god will rescue you from my hands?” closely echoing Sennacherib’s defiance.
2-chronicles-32:15:0.why: Same imperial taunt against God’s power.

2-chronicles-32:15:1.summary: Pharaoh’s “Who is He... I do not know the Lord”; a loose parallel of a ruler defying God.
2-chronicles-32:15:1.why: Earlier ruler’s defiance of the Lord.

2-chronicles-32:15:3.summary: Paul on pleasing God rather than people; no link to the Assyrian taunt.

2-chronicles-32:15:5.summary: Earlier in the same speech: “Is Hezekiah not deceiving you?” saying the Lord will save.
2-chronicles-32:15:5.why: Same taunt in the immediate context.

2-chronicles-32:15:6.summary: Pilate boasts of authority over Jesus, who replies it is given from above; loose parallel of human boasting of power.
2-chronicles-32:15:6.why: Human power claim answered by God’s sovereignty.

2-chronicles-32:15:7.summary: “Do not let your God, in whom you trust, lift you up,” the same Assyrian argument in Kings.

2-chronicles-32:15:8.summary: A lying spirit deceives Ahab’s prophets; shares only the word “deceive.”

2-chronicles-32:15:9.summary: Handmade things are not gods, said of Paul’s preaching; the source verse does not discuss handmade gods.
2-chronicles-32:15:9.why: Theme belongs to nearby verses, not this one.

2-chronicles-32:16:0.summary: The wicked “set their mouth toward heaven”; general picture of speaking against God.

2-chronicles-32:16:1.summary: Persecution because of Jesus’ name; no specific link to Assyrians speaking against God and Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-32:16:2.summary: The wicked raise hands against the Lord in insolence; general theme of defying God.

2-chronicles-32:17:0.summary: God’s reply to Sennacherib’s raging: a bridle in his lips to “turn you back,” answering the reproach in the letter.
2-chronicles-32:17:0.why: God’s answer to the same blasphemy.

2-chronicles-32:17:1.summary: Hezekiah takes “the document from the messengers,” the very letter Sennacherib wrote.
2-chronicles-32:17:1.why: Shows Hezekiah’s response to the letter.

2-chronicles-32:17:3.summary: The ax boasting against the one who wields it; general picture of Assyria’s arrogance.

2-chronicles-32:17:5.summary: The beast opens its mouth in blasphemies against God; a general parallel of blaspheming rulers.

2-chronicles-32:17:6.summary: “Through messengers you reproached the Lord,” God’s reply to the same reproachful message.

2-chronicles-32:17:7.summary: “Whom have you reproached and blasphemed?... Israel’s Holy One,” God’s answer to the same reproach.

2-chronicles-32:17:8.summary: Sanaballat sends an open letter; shares only a hostile letter motif.

2-chronicles-32:17:9.summary: God answers Sennacherib’s arrogance with hooks and bridle to turn him back.

2-chronicles-32:17:10.summary: Sennacherib “sent messengers to Hezekiah,” introducing the same written message.

2-chronicles-32:18:0.summary: Rapsakes “cried in a loud voice in Judean” to the people, the same event.
2-chronicles-32:18:0.why: Isaiah’s parallel of the shouted speech.

2-chronicles-32:18:2.summary: Goliath defies Israel’s battle line to intimidate them; similar psychological warfare.

2-chronicles-32:18:4.summary: Enemies were “frightening us” to stop the wall work; similar intimidation of Jerusalem’s people.

2-chronicles-32:19:1.summary: People bowed to “the works of their hands”; shares the idol phrase only.

2-chronicles-32:19:2.summary: The ungodly provoke God thinking He will not call to account; general theme of defying God.

2-chronicles-32:19:3.summary: The nations are answered that the Lord founded Zion; loosely counters speaking against Jerusalem’s God.

2-chronicles-32:19:4.summary: The Lord loves Zion’s gates, “city of God”; loosely relates to the God of Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-32:19:5.summary: Israel and Judah doing evil from youth; no link to blaspheming Jerusalem’s God.

2-chronicles-32:19:6.summary: Satire of a carved god made from firewood; general theme of gods as human handiwork (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:19:7.summary: The wicked “spoke injustice against the height” and set their mouth toward heaven; general speech against God.

2-chronicles-32:19:8.summary: Curse on an image, “the work of the hands of a craftsman”; shares the handmade-god idea.

2-chronicles-32:19:9.summary: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands,” the same phrase the source uses.
2-chronicles-32:19:9.why: Psalm articulating the same verdict on idols.

2-chronicles-32:19:10.summary: “The nations’ idols are silver and gold, works of human hands,” matching the source’s phrase.
2-chronicles-32:19:10.why: Psalm articulating the same verdict on idols.

2-chronicles-32:19:11.summary: “Other gods, the works of men’s hands, wood and stone,” closely matching the source’s description.

2-chronicles-32:19:12.summary: The same Assyrian speeches equating Israel’s God with the nations’ gods (truncated range).

2-chronicles-32:19:13.summary: Goliath “defied the battle line of the living God”; similar defiance of Israel’s God.

2-chronicles-32:19:14.summary: Judah “bowed down to the works of their hands”; shares the idol phrase only.

2-chronicles-32:19:15.summary: God known in Judea, His dwelling in Zion; loosely relates to “the God of Jerusalem.”

2-chronicles-32:19:16.summary: The Lord chose Zion as His dwelling; background to “the God of Jerusalem.”

2-chronicles-32:19:17.summary: Idols are “a carpenter’s work”; general theme of handmade gods.

2-chronicles-32:19:18.summary: Heavenly Jerusalem and the living God; no specific link to the Assyrian blasphemy.

2-chronicles-32:19:19.summary: Hezekiah’s prayer: the nations’ idols “were not gods, but works of human hands,” the same verdict.
2-chronicles-32:19:19.why: Hezekiah’s reply to the same blasphemy.

2-chronicles-32:19:20.summary: Plea against bloodthirsty men; the Greek wording carries no clear link to speaking against God.
2-chronicles-32:19:20.why: Label’s link not carried by this text.

2-chronicles-32:19:21.summary: Idols of worked silver are “artisans’ works”; general handmade-gods theme.

2-chronicles-32:19:22.summary: God chose Jerusalem for His name; background to “the God of Jerusalem.”

2-chronicles-32:19:23.summary: The wicked raise hands against the Lord in insolence; general picture of defiance.

2-chronicles-32:19:24.summary: Samaria’s calf: “A craftsman made it, and it is no god”; shares the handmade-god theme.

2-chronicles-32:19:25.summary: God chose Judah and Mount Zion; background to the God of Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-32:20:4.summary: Hezekiah’s full prayer to the Lord about Sennacherib’s reproach, the same prayer (truncated).
2-chronicles-32:20:4.why: Isaiah’s full text of the prayer.

2-chronicles-32:20:0.summary: “He will call upon Me, and I will hear him”; general promise answered in Hezekiah’s prayer.

2-chronicles-32:20:1.summary: Hezekiah sends to “Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos” asking for prayer about Rhapsakes’ words.
2-chronicles-32:20:1.why: Kings’ account of Hezekiah and Isaiah praying.

2-chronicles-32:20:2.summary: Asa cries to the Lord before a great army; a parallel royal prayer in a different crisis.
2-chronicles-32:20:2.why: Pattern of kings crying to God.

2-chronicles-32:20:3.summary: Jehoshaphat prays to the God in heaven against invaders; a parallel royal prayer (truncated).
2-chronicles-32:20:3.why: Pattern of kings praying in crisis.

2-chronicles-32:20:5.summary: Hezekiah enters the Lord’s house and sends to “the prophet Isaiah son of Amos” to plead with God.
2-chronicles-32:20:5.why: Isaiah’s account of the same appeal.

2-chronicles-32:20:7.summary: “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you”; general promise fitting the prayer.

2-chronicles-32:20:8.summary: They called on the Lord and “the Holy One quickly heard them from heaven and redeemed them by Isaiah’s hand.”
2-chronicles-32:20:8.why: Sirach’s retelling of the same prayer.

2-chronicles-32:21:0.summary: An angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian camp; the king returns and is killed by his sons in his god’s house.

2-chronicles-32:21:1.summary: Mighty men “slept their sleep” and found nothing; a psalm traditionally tied to Assyria’s defeat, loosely parallel.
2-chronicles-32:21:1.why: Psalm celebrating sudden defeat of warriors.

2-chronicles-32:21:2.summary: “Thou art fearsome, and who will withstand Thee?” general praise fitting the defeat.

2-chronicles-32:21:3.summary: An angel of the Lord strikes the proud Herod; similar angelic judgment on an arrogant king.
2-chronicles-32:21:3.why: Parallel of angelic judgment on pride.

2-chronicles-32:21:4.summary: God magnifies salvation for His king and David’s seed; general praise for delivering the Davidic king.
2-chronicles-32:21:4.why: God’s saving help for David’s line.

2-chronicles-32:21:5.summary: “Who grew hard against Him and endured?” general theme of God defeating opponents.
2-chronicles-32:21:5.why: No one resists God and survives.

2-chronicles-32:21:6.summary: A fragment of Assyrian self-exaltation; nothing about the angel or the king’s death.

2-chronicles-32:21:7.summary: Isaiah foresees the Lord shattering the lofty in insolence, the high falling “by a sword,” fulfilled in Assyria’s fall.

2-chronicles-32:21:8.summary: Kings and commanders hide from the Lamb’s wrath; no specific link to the Assyrian defeat.

2-chronicles-32:21:9.summary: Daniel saved from lions by God; general divine rescue, without the angelic strike on an army.

2-chronicles-32:21:10.summary: God tells Hezekiah through Isaiah: “I heard what you prayed... about Sennacherib,” prefacing the deliverance.
2-chronicles-32:21:10.why: God’s answer leading to the deliverance.

2-chronicles-32:21:11.summary: The Lord will send dishonor against Assyria’s glory and leave few survivors, prefiguring the camp’s destruction and shame.

2-chronicles-32:21:12.summary: God “takes away rulers’ spirits” and is fearsome among kings; fits the slaughter of commanders generally.

2-chronicles-32:21:13.summary: Angels separating the wicked at the age’s end; no specific link beyond angels executing judgment.

2-chronicles-32:21:14.summary: God will not give His glory to carved images; no specific link to this verse.

2-chronicles-32:21:15.summary: “At the Lord’s voice the Assyrians will be defeated by the blow with which He strikes them,” prophesying this defeat.

2-chronicles-32:21:16.summary: “Wherever insolence enters, dishonor is there too”; fits the king returning with shame of face.

2-chronicles-32:21:17.summary: God will “clothe his enemies with shame” for David’s line; loosely parallels the king’s shame.
2-chronicles-32:21:17.why: Promise of shame for David’s foes.

2-chronicles-32:21:19.summary: Rapsakes scorns Judah’s inability to face one governor, ironically reversed when the Assyrian commanders are wiped out.
2-chronicles-32:21:19.why: Ironic reversal of the Assyrian boast.

2-chronicles-32:21:20.summary: God’s destroying angel over Jerusalem; similar angelic destruction motif, different event.

2-chronicles-32:21:21.summary: God tells Hezekiah via Isaiah that his prayer about Sennacherib is heard, introducing the deliverance.

2-chronicles-32:21:22.summary: Raging nations driven away—“before morning it will be gone”; resembles the overnight destruction, but unnamed.
2-chronicles-32:21:22.why: Prophetic image of sudden enemy collapse.

2-chronicles-32:21:23.summary: “Insolence leads before ruin”; proverb illustrated by Sennacherib’s fall.
2-chronicles-32:21:23.why: Wisdom on pride preceding a fall.

2-chronicles-32:21:24.summary: The Lord rises and nations are consumed; general picture of God defeating proud foes.

2-chronicles-32:21:25.summary: God “sent His angel and saved His servants”; shares the angelic rescue motif in a different setting.

2-chronicles-32:21:26.summary: Nations marching against Jerusalem vanish like a dream; resembles the sudden end of the siege (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:21:27.summary: Feast on the flesh of kings, commanders and mighty ones; general imagery of a destroyed army.
2-chronicles-32:21:27.why: Apocalyptic picture of a defeated host.

2-chronicles-32:21:28.summary: “He struck the Assyrians’ camp, and His angel destroyed them,” Sirach’s retelling of the same event.
2-chronicles-32:21:28.why: Later summary of the same deliverance.

2-chronicles-32:22:0.summary: The Lord will “shield Jerusalem, rescue, preserve and save,” prophesying the salvation described here.

2-chronicles-32:22:1.summary: God rescues His king from enemies and magnifies salvation; general praise for royal deliverance.
2-chronicles-32:22:1.why: Psalm of deliverance for the king.

2-chronicles-32:22:2.summary: The Spirit guiding into truth; the label assumes a “guided them” reading, but the Greek-based text says “gave them rest.”
2-chronicles-32:22:2.why: Link rests on a Hebrew reading.
2-chronicles-32:22:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:22:3.summary: God “gives salvation to kings” and rescues David from the sword; general royal deliverance.

2-chronicles-32:22:4.summary: God will save Judah “not by bow, sword, war,” fitting deliverance by an angel rather than arms.
2-chronicles-32:22:4.why: Salvation of Judah without human weapons.
2-chronicles-32:22:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:22:5.summary: The Lord directs hearts into love; relies on a “guided” reading absent from the Saints text.
2-chronicles-32:22:5.why: Link rests on a Hebrew reading.
2-chronicles-32:22:5.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:22:6.summary: The Lord rescues and saves the righteous from sinners; general deliverance theme.

2-chronicles-32:22:7.summary: God continually with His people like a watered garden; no link to deliverance from Sennacherib.
2-chronicles-32:22:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:22:8.summary: “Do not fear the Assyrians, My people dwelling in Zion,” the wrath will cease—fulfilled in this deliverance.

2-chronicles-32:22:9.summary: God shepherds us forever; relies on a “guided” reading not in the Saints text.
2-chronicles-32:22:9.why: Link rests on a Hebrew reading.
2-chronicles-32:22:9.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:22:10.summary: God guides by counsel and receives in glory; the source has rest, not guidance.
2-chronicles-32:22:10.why: Link rests on a Hebrew reading.

2-chronicles-32:22:11.summary: “The Lord our king; this One will save us”; general confidence in the Lord saving Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-32:22:11.why: Zion’s trust in the Lord as savior.

2-chronicles-32:22:12.summary: God brought the psalmist back from many troubles; general deliverance theme.

2-chronicles-32:23:0.summary: All Judah gave gifts to Jehoshaphat, who had wealth and glory; similar royal blessing.
2-chronicles-32:23:0.why: Parallel honoring of a faithful king.

2-chronicles-32:23:1.summary: God made Solomon exceedingly great; loosely parallels Hezekiah being exalted.
2-chronicles-32:23:1.why: Similar divine exaltation of a king.

2-chronicles-32:23:2.summary: Magi offer gifts to Jesus; only the gift motif is shared.

2-chronicles-32:23:3.summary: Foreigners brought gifts to Solomon year after year; similar tribute to a king.

2-chronicles-32:23:4.summary: Nations bring offerings and silver to God’s house; general theme of gifts to the Lord at Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-32:23:5.summary: Kings will offer gifts to the king; similar tribute motif.

2-chronicles-32:23:6.summary: Each brought gifts to Solomon year after year; similar tribute to a king.

2-chronicles-32:23:7.summary: The queen of Sheba’s gifts to Solomon; general royal-tribute parallel.

2-chronicles-32:23:8.summary: The queen of Saba’s gifts to Solomon; general royal-tribute parallel.

2-chronicles-32:23:9.summary: Toi sends vessels to David, which he dedicates to the Lord; foreign gifts to a king and to God.
2-chronicles-32:23:9.why: Foreign gifts to king and Lord.

2-chronicles-32:23:10.summary: Kingdoms brought gifts and served Solomon; similar tribute motif.

2-chronicles-32:23:11.summary: “Over Jerusalem, kings will bring Thee gifts,” matching gifts brought to the Lord at Jerusalem.
2-chronicles-32:23:11.why: Psalm describing the same kind of homage.

2-chronicles-32:23:12.summary: The Lord made Solomon exceedingly great before all Israel; similar royal exaltation.

2-chronicles-32:23:13.summary: Foreigners brought Jehoshaphat gifts; similar foreign tribute to a faithful king.

2-chronicles-32:23:14.summary: Blessing God for moving a Persian king to glorify the temple; no specific link to gifts after Sennacherib’s fall.

2-chronicles-32:23:15.summary: Foreign king’s silver and gold offered to God in Jerusalem; general foreign gifts to the Lord (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:24:0.summary: Hezekiah “ill to the point of death” prays and is given added years and a sign (truncated range).
2-chronicles-32:24:0.why: Isaiah’s full account of the illness.

2-chronicles-32:24:2.summary: Hezekiah’s fig poultice and his question about “the sign,” part of the same illness narrative.
2-chronicles-32:24:2.why: Details of the healing and sign.

2-chronicles-32:25:0.summary: “Wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem,” the identical Chronicler formula for divine anger.
2-chronicles-32:25:0.why: Same formula for judgment on Judah.

2-chronicles-32:25:1.summary: Uzziah’s “heart was lifted up” after growing strong, the same pride that afflicted Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-32:25:2.summary: The Babylonian envoys episode where God tested Hezekiah’s heart, the occasion of his pride.
2-chronicles-32:25:2.why: Explains the occasion of Hezekiah’s pride.

2-chronicles-32:25:3.summary: God’s anger against Israel and David’s census; a loose parallel of a king’s sin bringing wrath.

2-chronicles-32:25:4.summary: Judgment on Israel for David’s census; general parallel of wrath on the people for a king’s sin (truncated).
2-chronicles-32:25:4.why: Wrath on a nation for its king.

2-chronicles-32:25:5.summary: Amaziah’s “heart has lifted you up,” warning he will fall with Judah, echoing pride bringing wrath on Judah.

2-chronicles-32:25:6.summary: Warning against crediting one’s own might for wealth; general theme of pride after blessing.

2-chronicles-32:25:7.summary: Tyre’s ruler: “Your heart was exalted”; shares the lifted-heart pride motif.

2-chronicles-32:25:8.summary: Only one leper returned to give glory to God; parallels failing to repay God’s benefit.

2-chronicles-32:25:10.summary: “God opposes the proud”; general teaching on pride and humility.

2-chronicles-32:25:11.summary: Hezekiah proudly shows the envoys all his treasuries, the episode behind his lifted-up heart.

2-chronicles-32:25:12.summary: Returning to God to “repay the fruit of our lips”; shares the idea of repaying God.

2-chronicles-32:25:13.summary: Belshazzar did not bless the God who gave him his kingdom; general ingratitude and pride.

2-chronicles-32:25:14.summary: God has no pleasure in one who draws back; no specific link to Hezekiah’s pride.

2-chronicles-32:25:15.summary: “Do you thus repay the Lord?” echoes Hezekiah not repaying according to God’s recompense.

2-chronicles-32:25:16.summary: Wrath from the Lord came upon Jehoshaphat; shares the wrath formula for a king’s failing.
2-chronicles-32:25:16.why: Similar divine displeasure on a king.

2-chronicles-32:25:17.summary: “What shall I repay to the Lord?” the grateful response Hezekiah failed to make.

2-chronicles-32:25:18.summary: Tyre’s ruler “your heart was exalted”; shares the proud-heart motif.

2-chronicles-32:25:20.summary: The devil stirs David to number Israel; no specific link to Hezekiah’s pride.

2-chronicles-32:25:21.summary: Paul given a thorn “so that I might not be exalted”; general theme of guarding against pride after blessing.

2-chronicles-32:25:22.summary: David’s census sin and the resulting judgment; general parallel of a king’s sin bringing wrath (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:25:23.summary: Warning against becoming conceited and falling; general teaching on pride.

2-chronicles-32:25:24.summary: Tyre’s ruler: “your heart was exalted in your strength”; similar pride from prosperity.

2-chronicles-32:25:25.summary: Amaziah’s heart “lifts you up,” so that he and Judah would fall—pride endangering Judah as with Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-32:26:0.summary: Hezekiah and Judah “feared the Lord and entreated the Lord’s face,” and the Lord ceased from the evils—matching his humbling.

2-chronicles-32:26:1.summary: Manasseh humbled himself greatly before God; a parallel of a king’s humbling.

2-chronicles-32:26:2.summary: Josiah humbled himself, so the evils would not come in his days, matching wrath delayed beyond Hezekiah’s days.
2-chronicles-32:26:2.why: Same pattern of humbling and deferred judgment.

2-chronicles-32:26:3.summary: “Humble yourselves before the Lord”; general teaching on humility.

2-chronicles-32:26:4.summary: Judgment pronounced on Ahab for Naboth; no link without the following verses on his humbling.

2-chronicles-32:26:6.summary: Hezekiah accepts the word of judgment, saying “Let there indeed be peace... in my days,” the deferred wrath.
2-chronicles-32:26:6.why: Shows the judgment deferred past his reign.

2-chronicles-32:26:7.summary: Ahab humbled himself, so harm would not come “in his days,” the same deferral pattern.

2-chronicles-32:26:8.summary: Amon “did not humble himself” as Manasseh did; contrasts with Hezekiah’s humbling.

2-chronicles-32:26:9.summary: Manasseh’s prayer and turning back recorded; loosely parallels a king’s repentance.

2-chronicles-32:26:10.summary: When their uncircumcised heart feels shame and they confess, God remembers; general humbling theme.

2-chronicles-32:27:0.summary: Solomon made silver and gold plentiful as stones; a similar picture of royal wealth.

2-chronicles-32:27:1.summary: Officials over David’s treasuries and storehouses; similar royal stores (truncated).

2-chronicles-32:27:2.summary: Jehoshaphat “had abundant wealth and glory,” the same phrase used of Hezekiah.
2-chronicles-32:27:2.why: Same blessing formula for faithful kings.

2-chronicles-32:27:3.summary: The Lord’s blessing makes the righteous rich; general principle behind Hezekiah’s wealth.

2-chronicles-32:27:4.summary: God promises Solomon “wealth, possessions, and glory,” matching Hezekiah’s “wealth and glory.”

2-chronicles-32:28:0.summary: Solomon’s many broodmares and horsemen; only a loose link to Hezekiah’s mangers for animals.

2-chronicles-32:28:1.summary: David taken from the sheepfold to rule; only the word “fold” is shared.

2-chronicles-32:28:2.summary: Uzziah built towers and cisterns for his many herds; similar royal agricultural infrastructure.

2-chronicles-32:29:0.summary: David’s prayer that “wealth and glory” come from God generally parallels the Lord giving Hezekiah “exceedingly many possessions.”
2-chronicles-32:29:0.why: Frames royal wealth as God’s gift.

2-chronicles-32:29:1.summary: Uzziah, like Hezekiah, built in the land and had many herds; both describe a Judean king’s building and livestock wealth.
2-chronicles-32:29:1.why: Shows a recurring Chronicler pattern of blessed kings.

2-chronicles-32:29:3.summary: Job’s restored flocks of sheep and oxen as the Lord’s blessing loosely parallel Hezekiah’s God-given sheep and cattle.

2-chronicles-32:29:4.summary: “The Lord makes poor and makes rich” states generally the principle behind the Lord giving Hezekiah possessions.

2-chronicles-32:29:5.summary: The devil’s question whether Job serves God for nothing has no specific link to Hezekiah’s building and flocks.

2-chronicles-32:29:6.summary: Abram and Lot were rich in livestock with many “possessions,” a general parallel to Hezekiah’s sheep, cattle and possessions.

2-chronicles-32:29:7.summary: “The Lord can give you far more than these” anticipates generally the Lord giving Hezekiah abundant possessions.

2-chronicles-32:29:8.summary: “The Lord’s blessing… makes rich” expresses the principle behind God giving Hezekiah great possessions.

2-chronicles-32:29:9.summary: Overseers of David’s cattle, camels and sheep show royal livestock holdings, loosely like Hezekiah’s great stock.

2-chronicles-32:29:10.summary: Job’s vast sheep, camels and oxen form a general parallel to Hezekiah’s great stock of sheep and cattle.

2-chronicles-32:29:11.summary: God “richly provides us all things” echoes God giving possessions, but the focus on the rich’s duty is broader.

2-chronicles-32:30:0.summary: Gihon appears as the site of Solomon’s anointing; it shares only the place name with Hezekiah’s water works.

2-chronicles-32:30:1.summary: Isaiah describes diverting the old pool’s water into the city and providing water between the walls, matching Hezekiah’s rerouting of waters.
2-chronicles-32:30:1.why: Prophetic critique of the same water works.

2-chronicles-32:30:2.summary: Solomon was anointed at Gihon; only the place name links it to Hezekiah’s Gihon outlet.

2-chronicles-32:30:3.summary: Joshua is promised to “prosper” through keeping the law, loosely echoing that Hezekiah “prospered in all his works.”

2-chronicles-32:30:4.summary: Solomon was led to Gihon for anointing; shares only the place name with the source.

2-chronicles-32:30:6.summary: The righteous man by “outlets of waters” whose deeds are “prospered” loosely echoes Hezekiah’s water outlet and prosperity.

2-chronicles-32:30:7.summary: Hezekiah blocked the waters of the springs, the same water-blocking project described in the source.
2-chronicles-32:30:7.why: Explains the reason for the water works.

2-chronicles-32:30:8.summary: Sirach recalls Hezekiah bringing water into his city by digging through rock, the same project.
2-chronicles-32:30:8.why: Later Wisdom tradition remembers the feat.

2-chronicles-32:31:1.summary: Hearts are tested before the Lord as metal in a furnace, matching God testing Hezekiah “to know what was in his heart.”
2-chronicles-32:31:1.why: Explains divine testing of the heart.

2-chronicles-32:31:2.summary: Christ as the vine and abiding has no specific link to God leaving Hezekiah to test him.

2-chronicles-32:31:3.summary: Hezekiah’s illness and the sign given him is the “wonder” the Babylonian envoys came to learn about.
2-chronicles-32:31:3.why: Supplies the context of the envoys’ visit.

2-chronicles-32:31:4.summary: “God tested Abraham” parallels the Lord leaving Hezekiah “to test him.”
2-chronicles-32:31:4.why: Classic example of God testing a servant.

2-chronicles-32:31:5.summary: God refining and testing his people as silver and gold is a general parallel to testing Hezekiah’s heart.

2-chronicles-32:31:6.summary: God led Israel in the wilderness “to test you,” with Deuteronomy’s related aim of knowing the heart, paralleling Hezekiah’s test.
2-chronicles-32:31:6.why: God tests to reveal the heart.

2-chronicles-32:31:7.summary: Babylon’s king sent envoys to Hezekiah after his recovery and he showed them everything, the same embassy episode.
2-chronicles-32:31:7.why: Full narrative of the Babylonian envoys.

2-chronicles-32:31:8.summary: God permits Job to be tested by touching his possessions; a general parallel to God leaving Hezekiah to test him.
2-chronicles-32:31:8.why: God allows testing of the faithful.

2-chronicles-32:31:9.summary: “Thou didst test me and know me” closely matches God testing Hezekiah “to know what was in his heart.”
2-chronicles-32:31:9.why: God’s testing reveals the inner self.

2-chronicles-32:31:10.summary: James says God tempts no one, a nuance contrasting with the Lord leaving Hezekiah to test him.

2-chronicles-32:31:11.summary: The Lord refining like silver and gold is a general image of testing, loosely parallel to Hezekiah’s test.

2-chronicles-32:31:12.summary: The sun’s shadow turning back ten steps is the sign given to Hezekiah, the “wonder” the envoys inquired about.

2-chronicles-32:31:13.summary: Faith tested like gold by fire is a general parallel to God testing Hezekiah’s heart.

2-chronicles-32:31:14.summary: “The Lord God tests you, to know whether you love” him with all your heart closely matches testing Hezekiah to know his heart.

2-chronicles-32:31:16.summary: God hands Job over for testing, a general parallel to the Lord leaving Hezekiah to be tested.

2-chronicles-32:31:17.summary: A prayer to be upheld and not shamed shares no specific element with God leaving Hezekiah to test him.

2-chronicles-32:31:18.summary: Samson did not know the Lord had departed from him, loosely echoing the Lord leaving Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-32:31:19.summary: The plea not to be cast away from God’s face loosely relates to the Lord leaving Hezekiah.

2-chronicles-32:31:20.summary: “Do not… abandon me” loosely relates to the Lord leaving Hezekiah for a time.

2-chronicles-32:31:21.summary: “Test me, God, and know my heart” closely mirrors God testing Hezekiah to know what was in his heart.

2-chronicles-32:32:0.summary: 2 Kings 18 narrates Hezekiah’s reign, part of the Book of the Kings record the source cites for his deeds.

2-chronicles-32:32:1.summary: Isaiah 36 narrates Hezekiah and Sennacherib, part of Isaiah’s record of Hezekiah the source cites.

2-chronicles-32:32:2.summary: Hezekiah did what was good and prospered, summarizing the deeds and goodness referenced in the source.

2-chronicles-32:33:0.summary: “The memory of righteous people is with praises” parallels Judah giving Hezekiah glory and honor at death.
2-chronicles-32:33:0.why: The righteous are honored in memory.

2-chronicles-32:33:1.summary: “David lay down with his fathers and was buried” uses the same royal death formula as Hezekiah’s.

2-chronicles-32:33:2.summary: Solomon “slept with his fathers… and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place” repeats the succession formula.
2-chronicles-32:33:2.why: Standard royal death and succession formula.

2-chronicles-32:33:3.summary: Manasseh, named as successor, begins his reign in 2 Chronicles 33.
2-chronicles-32:33:3.why: Continues the narrative with Hezekiah’s son.

2-chronicles-32:33:4.summary: All Israel mourned and buried Samuel, a general parallel to Judah honoring Hezekiah at his death.
2-chronicles-32:33:4.why: National honor for a leader’s death.

2-chronicles-32:33:5.summary: Israel mourned Moses thirty days, a general parallel to national honor at Hezekiah’s death.

2-chronicles-32:33:6.summary: The great lamentation for Jacob loosely parallels the honor given Hezekiah at death.

2-chronicles-32:33:7.summary: “I will honour those who honour Me” fits Hezekiah being honored at death, but only as principle.
2-chronicles-32:33:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-32:33:8.summary: Asa’s great funeral procession in David’s city loosely parallels Hezekiah’s honorable burial.

2-chronicles-32:33:9.summary: All Israel wept for Aaron thirty days, a general parallel to national honor at Hezekiah’s death.

2-chronicles-32:33:10.summary: “Lies down with his fathers” shares the death idiom only, without other link to Hezekiah.
2-chronicles-32:33:10.why: Shows the idiom for royal death.
