2-chronicles-34:27:7.summary: Sennacherib's taunt about Hezekiah's altars has no link to Josiah's humility.

2-chronicles-34:27:8.summary: Because they “felt shame,” God would not destroy them and wrath would not fall on Jerusalem.

2-chronicles-34:27:9.summary: Jehoiakim heard the words yet did not tear his garments, contrasting Josiah's response.
2-chronicles-34:27:9.why: Two kings' opposite reactions to God's word.

2-chronicles-34:27:11.summary: God looks to the humble one “who trembles at My words,” as Josiah humbled himself on hearing them.
2-chronicles-34:27:11.why: God's favor toward the humble hearer.

2-chronicles-34:27:12.summary: The Lord heard the needy and attended to their heart; general theme.

2-chronicles-34:27:13.summary: God gives life to the brokenhearted; general humility theme.

2-chronicles-34:27:14.summary: “Humble yourselves before the Lord” and weep; general teaching on humility.

2-chronicles-34:27:15.summary: God listened to Manasseh's prayer; loose parallel of God hearing a repentant king.

2-chronicles-34:27:16.summary: A new heart of flesh; the Greek “heart felt shame” does not carry a tender-heart link.
2-chronicles-34:27:16.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

2-chronicles-34:28:0.summary: A peaceful person has a remnant; loose link to dying in peace.

2-chronicles-34:28:1.summary: Hezekiah welcomes “peace … in my days,” judgment deferred beyond his lifetime like Josiah's.
2-chronicles-34:28:1.why: Parallel of judgment delayed past a king.

2-chronicles-34:28:2.summary: Judgment will not be averted even by Moses and Samuel; general theme of fixed judgment.

2-chronicles-34:28:3.summary: Josiah died and “was buried with his fathers,” fulfilling being added to his fathers.
2-chronicles-34:28:3.why: Fulfillment of the promise to Josiah.

2-chronicles-34:28:4.summary: Because Ahab humbled himself, harm comes not in his days but his son's, the same pattern as Josiah.

2-chronicles-34:28:5.summary: The righteous man is taken from injustice and “his burial will be in peace.”
2-chronicles-34:28:5.why: Explains dying in peace before disaster.

2-chronicles-34:28:7.summary: Righteous men saved only themselves amid judgment; loose theme (truncated).

2-chronicles-34:28:8.summary: Hezekiah says “Let there be peace in my days,” judgment deferred past his reign.

2-chronicles-34:29:1.summary: Anointing Jesus for burial has no link to Josiah gathering elders.

2-chronicles-34:29:2.summary: Samuel's vow to pray has no link to Josiah gathering the elders.

2-chronicles-34:29:3.summary: David's gifts for the temple share nothing with Josiah gathering elders (truncated).

2-chronicles-34:29:4.summary: Hezekiah, rulers and assembly took counsel together; general royal assembly theme.

2-chronicles-34:30:1.summary: Moses “took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people,” as Josiah does.
2-chronicles-34:30:1.why: Echo of the Sinai covenant reading.

2-chronicles-34:30:2.summary: Judging small and great alike shares only the phrase “small and great.”
2-chronicles-34:30:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-34:30:3.summary: The king's duty to read the law; loosely fits Josiah reading the book.
2-chronicles-34:30:3.why: The king's relation to the law.

2-chronicles-34:30:4.summary: A battle order about “the small or the great” shares only incidental words.

2-chronicles-34:30:5.summary: The words “written in the book read before the king” are this same book now read to all.

2-chronicles-34:30:6.summary: Josiah commands Passover “as written in this covenant book,” the same book read here.
2-chronicles-34:30:6.why: Next step from the covenant reading.

2-chronicles-34:30:7.summary: Jehoshaphat's Levites taught Judah with “a book of the Lord’s law”; general teaching theme.
2-chronicles-34:30:7.why: Earlier public instruction in the law.

2-chronicles-34:30:8.summary: Asa's assembly entered a covenant to seek the Lord, from younger to older, a similar covenant renewal.

2-chronicles-34:30:9.summary: Hilkiah found “a book of law in the Lord’s house,” the same book read here.

2-chronicles-34:30:10.summary: Esdras read the book of the law before all the people, a parallel public reading (truncated).
2-chronicles-34:30:10.why: Later public reading of the law.

2-chronicles-34:30:11.summary: Solomon addresses all Israel's assembly at the temple; general royal assembly theme (truncated).
2-chronicles-34:30:11.why: King leading the assembly at the temple.

2-chronicles-34:30:12.summary: The fathers did not remain in the covenant; general covenant theme.

2-chronicles-34:30:13.summary: Shaphan read the book before the king, who tore his garments; same book now read publicly.
2-chronicles-34:30:13.why: Earlier private reading of the same book.

2-chronicles-34:30:14.summary: Ecclesiastes teaching the people knowledge has no link to reading the covenant book.

2-chronicles-34:30:15.summary: “Small and great” in the grave is an incidental verbal match only.

2-chronicles-34:30:16.summary: Ecclesiastes as king in Jerusalem has no link to Josiah's covenant reading.

2-chronicles-34:31:0.summary: Jehoiada made a covenant between people and king to be the Lord's people, a parallel renewal.

2-chronicles-34:31:1.summary: Joash was “standing by the pillar,” the same royal position Josiah takes.
2-chronicles-34:31:1.why: Explains the king's place at the pillar.

2-chronicles-34:31:2.summary: Asa's covenant to seek the Lord “with all the heart and all the soul” matches this pledge.

2-chronicles-34:31:4.summary: Solomon stood on a bronze platform before the assembly; loose parallel of the king's standing place.

2-chronicles-34:31:5.summary: Hezekiah resolves to “establish a covenant” with the Lord, the same reforming act.
2-chronicles-34:31:5.why: Earlier king's covenant to avert wrath.

2-chronicles-34:31:6.summary: Moses read “the book of the covenant” and the people pledged obedience, the Sinai model for this covenant.

2-chronicles-34:31:7.summary: Hebrews contrasts the old covenant with a better one; general covenant theme (truncated).

2-chronicles-34:31:8.summary: Jehoiada made a covenant in the Lord's house; general covenant-making theme.

2-chronicles-34:31:9.summary: An “everlasting covenant” for returning exiles; general covenant theme.

2-chronicles-34:31:10.summary: Priests standing at their stations shares only the idea of standing.

2-chronicles-34:31:11.summary: Joshua made a covenant with the people before the God of Israel, a parallel covenant renewal.

2-chronicles-34:31:12.summary: Leaders establish and write down a pledge, a later covenant renewal parallel to Josiah's.

2-chronicles-34:31:13.summary: All Israel stands before the Lord to enter His covenant and its curses (truncated).

2-chronicles-34:31:14.summary: Love the Lord “with all your heart, and with all your soul” underlies this covenant pledge.

2-chronicles-34:31:15.summary: The ruler stands at the gate during worship; loose parallel of a ruler's position.

2-chronicles-34:31:16.summary: “I have sworn and established it: to keep Thy righteous judgments” mirrors the king establishing a covenant to keep God's ordinances.
2-chronicles-34:31:16.why: Personal vow echoing the royal covenant.

2-chronicles-34:31:17.summary: Bending the heart to perform God's ordinances; general devotion to testimonies and ordinances.

2-chronicles-34:31:18.summary: Love God “from your whole heart, with your whole soul,” the same wholehearted language of the covenant.
2-chronicles-34:31:18.why: Jesus affirms the same covenant ideal.

2-chronicles-34:31:19.summary: Judah swore an oath “with all their soul” and sought the Lord, a parallel covenant pledge under Asa.

2-chronicles-34:31:20.summary: Hezekiah sought God “with his whole soul” in the law and ordinances, the same devotion.

2-chronicles-34:31:21.summary: An oath to walk in the law given through Moses and keep all the commandments and judgments, a later covenant renewal.

2-chronicles-34:31:22.summary: “These are the words of the covenant” matches “the words of the covenant written in this book.”
2-chronicles-34:31:22.why: Identifies the covenant words in the book.

2-chronicles-34:31:23.summary: Sirach's praise of Josiah: “He directed his heart toward the Lord” amid lawlessness.

2-chronicles-34:32:0.summary: Asa told Judah to seek “their fathers’ God” and keep the law; general reform theme.

2-chronicles-34:32:1.summary: Bowing in worship after offerings has no specific link to making a covenant.

2-chronicles-34:32:2.summary: Advice about the king's word and God's oath shares only a loose oath idea.

2-chronicles-34:32:3.summary: Judah did not return “with her whole heart, but in falsehood,” questioning the depth of this covenant.

2-chronicles-34:32:4.summary: Abraham commanding his household to keep the Lord's ways; loose leader-directs-people theme.

2-chronicles-34:32:5.summary: Judah was given one heart to carry out the king's ordinance; loose parallel of the people following the king.
2-chronicles-34:32:5.why: People united under a reforming king.

2-chronicles-34:32:6.summary: Manasseh told Judah to serve the Lord; general royal reform theme.

2-chronicles-34:33:0.summary: Details Josiah's cleansing of high places, groves and idols, summarized here as removing abominations (truncated).

2-chronicles-34:33:1.summary: Israel “served the Lord all the days of Joshua,” as the people served throughout Josiah's days.
2-chronicles-34:33:1.why: Faithfulness tied to a leader's lifetime.

2-chronicles-34:33:2.summary: Solomon's high places for Chemosh and Astarte “the abomination” are the kind of abominations Josiah removed.

2-chronicles-34:33:3.summary: Judah did not return with her whole heart, suggesting the reform's limits.

2-chronicles-34:33:4.summary: Kings' detailed account of Josiah removing Baal vessels, groves and idolatrous priests (truncated).
2-chronicles-34:33:4.why: Fuller parallel account of the purge.

2-chronicles-34:33:5.summary: Judah's mercy passing like morning dew; loose theme of short-lived faithfulness.

2-chronicles-34:33:6.summary: Sirach says he “removed the abominations of lawlessness,” recalling Josiah's purge.

2-chronicles-34:2:8.summary: 1 Kings 14:8 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
2-chronicles-34:2:8.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
2-chronicles-34:2:8.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

2-chronicles-35:1:2.summary: Passover kept “on the fourteenth day of the first month,” the same date.
2-chronicles-35:1:2.why: Later Passover on the lawful date.

2-chronicles-35:1:6.summary: Passover in the first month on the fourteenth, the same prescribed date.
2-chronicles-35:1:6.why: Prophetic vision of the same feast date.

2-chronicles-35:1:1.summary: Law commanding Passover “on the fourteenth day of the first month,” which Josiah follows.

2-chronicles-35:1:4.summary: Command to sacrifice the Passover to the Lord at His chosen place (truncated).
2-chronicles-35:1:4.why: Legal basis for a central Passover.

2-chronicles-35:1:5.summary: Hezekiah's Passover in Jerusalem, the closest earlier royal Passover (truncated).

2-chronicles-35:2:0.summary: Hezekiah arranged the divisions of priests and Levites for the Lord's house, as Josiah stationed priests.

2-chronicles-35:2:1.summary: David urges building the sanctuary; general encouragement for temple work.

2-chronicles-35:2:3.summary: Hezekiah exhorts Levites to purify the house; general theme of restoring service (truncated).

2-chronicles-35:2:4.summary: Jehoiada established the divisions of priests and Levites over the Lord's house, parallel to stationing priests.

2-chronicles-35:2:5.summary: Priests keep the charges of the altar; general priestly duty theme.

2-chronicles-35:2:6.summary: “They stationed the priests in their divisions” over the service of God, closely paralleling this verse.

2-chronicles-35:2:7.summary: Priestly divisions serving by Sabbath under Jehoiada; general divisions theme.

2-chronicles-35:3:1.summary: Levites teaching the law; the Greek source calls the Levites “mighty,” not teachers, so the link is lost.
2-chronicles-35:3:1.why: Greek wording lacks the teaching link.

2-chronicles-35:3:2.summary: Priests guarding knowledge; the Greek source has no teaching role to connect.
2-chronicles-35:3:2.why: Greek wording lacks the teaching link.

2-chronicles-35:3:3.summary: Hezekiah encourages the Levites during a Passover festival; general parallel.

2-chronicles-35:3:4.summary: Levites declare God's law and serve at the altar; general Levitical role.

2-chronicles-35:3:5.summary: Ministers as servants of the people; loose echo of ministering to God's people.

2-chronicles-35:3:6.summary: Levites were brought near to minister in the Lord's tent and serve the congregation, as Josiah urges them to serve the people.

2-chronicles-35:3:7.summary: The ark was brought into Solomon's house, the place where it is now restored.

2-chronicles-35:3:8.summary: Holiness of the place where the ark entered; general ark theme.

2-chronicles-35:3:9.summary: Finding the law book has no specific link to placing the ark or Levite service.

2-chronicles-35:3:10.summary: Levites helped the people understand the law; Greek source lacks the teaching link, so only loosely related.

2-chronicles-35:3:11.summary: Levites given to perform works in the Tent; general Levitical role.

2-chronicles-35:3:12.summary: The sons of Kohath were to carry the holy things, the shoulder burden Josiah says is now over (truncated).
2-chronicles-35:3:12.why: Explains “nothing to lift upon your shoulders.”

2-chronicles-35:4:0.summary: Divisions set “following David’s ordinance” by Solomon, matching preparation by David's writing through Solomon.

2-chronicles-35:4:2.summary: Lists of priests and Levites by ancestral houses; general background (truncated).

2-chronicles-35:4:3.summary: Priests and Levites listed by families after the return; general background (truncated).

2-chronicles-35:4:4.summary: The sons of Aaron had divisions; general background to priestly courses.

2-chronicles-35:5:0.summary: Servants “who stand in the Lord’s house” shares the standing image only.
2-chronicles-35:5:0.why: Worship of those serving in the temple.

2-chronicles-35:5:1.summary: “You who stand in the Lord’s house” shares the image of standing to serve.

2-chronicles-35:5:2.summary: Priests in divisions and Levites in allotted groups over God's service, matching the divisions here.

2-chronicles-35:6:0.summary: Hezekiah's call to purify relies on a purification idea absent from this Greek-based verse.
2-chronicles-35:6:0.why: Greek wording lacks the purification link.

2-chronicles-35:6:1.summary: Levites purifying themselves; this verse speaks of preparing holy things, not purification.
2-chronicles-35:6:1.why: Greek wording lacks the purification link.

2-chronicles-35:6:2.summary: Christ's blood cleansing conscience has no link to preparing the Passover here.
2-chronicles-35:6:2.why: No real connection in the text.

2-chronicles-35:6:3.summary: Moses commanded to “slaughter the Passover,” the Lord's word through Moses that Josiah invokes.

2-chronicles-35:6:5.summary: Consecrating the congregation in Joel depends on purification wording not present here.
2-chronicles-35:6:5.why: No real link in the text.

2-chronicles-35:6:6.summary: Levites slaughtered the Passover for their brothers, as Josiah directs them to do for their brethren.
2-chronicles-35:6:6.why: Later Passover with same Levitical role.

2-chronicles-35:6:7.summary: Job purifying his sons has no link to the Passover preparations here.

2-chronicles-35:6:8.summary: Jacob's household purifying shares nothing with preparing the Passover in this Greek text.

2-chronicles-35:6:9.summary: Cleansing with hyssop in a penitential psalm has no link to this verse.

2-chronicles-35:6:10.summary: At Hezekiah's Passover, Levites sacrificed for others “according to the command of Moses” (truncated).

2-chronicles-35:6:11.summary: Levites helping priests skin burnt offerings is not linked to the Passover duties described here.

2-chronicles-35:6:12.summary: Preparing for Sinai by abstaining has no link to preparing the Passover.

2-chronicles-35:6:13.summary: Corpse-impurity law relies on purification wording absent from this verse (truncated).

2-chronicles-35:6:14.summary: Hezekiah's Passover was delayed because priests were not purified; loose Passover-preparation link.

2-chronicles-35:6:15.summary: Purifying the people before Sinai has no link to the Passover preparations here.

2-chronicles-35:7:0.summary: Solomon's vast royal offerings of cattle and sheep; general theme of royal sacrifice.

2-chronicles-35:7:1.summary: Hezekiah contributed calves and sheep to the assembly for the Passover festival, as Josiah gives here.

2-chronicles-35:7:2.summary: David gives gold and silver “acquired for myself” to God's house, a gift from royal property.

2-chronicles-35:7:3.summary: The ruler provides offerings at the festivals for the house of Israel, as Josiah supplies the Passover.
2-chronicles-35:7:3.why: Ruler's duty to provide festival offerings.

2-chronicles-35:7:4.summary: The Greek “the devout made wise plans” does not carry a generosity link.

2-chronicles-35:7:5.summary: Solomon's great seven-day feast with all Israel; general royal festival theme.

2-chronicles-35:7:6.summary: Hezekiah's portion “from his belongings” supplied offerings, as Josiah's came “from the king’s property.”

2-chronicles-35:8:0.summary: Hezekiah’s assembly brings counted calves and sheep to the Lord’s house, a similar tally of sacrificial animals at a reform festival, but a different occasion.
2-chronicles-35:8:0.why: Compares Josiah’s Passover gifts with Hezekiah’s offerings.

2-chronicles-35:8:1.summary: Only the words “priests” and “people” overlap; the arrest of the apostles has nothing to do with Passover contributions.

2-chronicles-35:8:2.summary: Gifts of livestock and goods for the temple project parallel giving for worship only in general terms.
2-chronicles-35:8:2.why: General theme of voluntary giving for God’s house.

2-chronicles-35:8:3.summary: Family leaders make freewill offerings for the house of God, echoing leaders giving generously, but for rebuilding, not Passover.
2-chronicles-35:8:3.why: Shows leaders setting an example in giving.

2-chronicles-35:8:4.summary: Mentions voluntary offerings of “people and priests” for God’s house, a general parallel to contributions for people and priests.
2-chronicles-35:8:4.why: Loose parallel of offerings for temple worship.

2-chronicles-35:8:5.summary: Paul’s principle of giving according to what one has is a general teaching on generosity, not tied to the Passover gifts.

2-chronicles-35:8:6.summary: Phinees as former leader of gatekeepers shares only the idea of a leader; nothing about contributions or Passover.

2-chronicles-35:8:7.summary: Ezra weighs out freewill offerings of silver and gold to priests for God’s house; shares leaders’ giving and priests, but not Passover (truncated range).
2-chronicles-35:8:7.why: General theme of offerings entrusted to priests.

2-chronicles-35:8:8.summary: Rulers of Israel give eagerly for the Lord’s house, with a “Jiiel” named among the givers, closely matching rulers’ contributions in the source.
2-chronicles-35:8:8.why: Models leaders’ generous giving for worship.

2-chronicles-35:8:9.summary: Early believers sharing possessions has no specific link to Josiah’s officials supplying Passover animals.
2-chronicles-35:8:9.why: Only a very general giving theme.

2-chronicles-35:8:10.summary: Zephaniah appointed priest-overseer in the Lord’s house shares only the office idea; no contributions or Passover.

2-chronicles-35:8:11.summary: Tyre’s daughters bringing gifts to a king is unrelated to Passover contributions.

2-chronicles-35:8:12.summary: Believers laying proceeds at the apostles’ feet has no specific tie to Passover animals given by rulers.

2-chronicles-35:8:13.summary: Giving freely “as he has decided in his heart” is a general principle; the source records contributions without that emphasis.

2-chronicles-35:8:14.summary: David and the people “offer eagerly” for the temple, a general parallel to leaders’ contributions for worship.
2-chronicles-35:8:14.why: Shows the spirit of willing offerings.

2-chronicles-35:8:15.summary: “Hilkiah the priest” finds the law book in the Lord’s house, the same Hilkiah who here gives Passover animals.
2-chronicles-35:8:15.why: Identifies Hilkiah and his role in Josiah’s reform.

2-chronicles-35:8:16.summary: Mentions “rulers of the holy things” among priestly houses, loosely echoing “rulers of God’s house”.

2-chronicles-35:8:17.summary: Heads of families give to the treasury for the work, a general parallel to leaders’ contributions.
2-chronicles-35:8:17.why: Another list of leaders’ gifts for worship.

2-chronicles-35:8:18.summary: The temple captain bringing the apostles shares no element with the Passover contributions.

2-chronicles-35:9:0.summary: Judah’s insincere return has no link to the Levite rulers supplying Passover animals.

2-chronicles-35:9:1.summary: Micah’s question about calves and thousands of rams contrasts lavish sacrifice with justice and mercy; the source only lists animals given.
2-chronicles-35:9:1.why: Reminds that sacrifice must accompany justice.

2-chronicles-35:9:2.summary: “Chonenias the Levite” oversees offerings under Hezekiah, the same name heading the Levite rulers here.

2-chronicles-35:9:3.summary: God rejects multitudes of burnt offerings of rams and lambs without righteousness; the source simply records generous offerings (truncated range).

2-chronicles-35:9:4.summary: God says obedience mattered more than burnt offerings; only a contrastive link to the list of Passover animals (truncated range).

2-chronicles-35:10:0.summary: At Hezekiah’s Passover priests and Levites “stood at their stations” by rule, matching the ordered stations here.
2-chronicles-35:10:0.why: Parallel arrangement at the earlier Passover.

2-chronicles-35:10:1.summary: After the exile priests are stationed “in their divisions” and Levites in groups for service, echoing this ordering.

2-chronicles-35:10:2.summary: Josiah’s command to stand by courses and divisions is the instruction this verse reports carried out.
2-chronicles-35:10:2.why: Shows the king’s command being obeyed.

2-chronicles-35:11:0.summary: Levites help priests “skin” the burnt offerings under Hezekiah, the same division of labor as here.

2-chronicles-35:11:1.summary: The law has priests pour the blood and the victim be “skinned”, the exact tasks performed at this Passover.
2-chronicles-35:11:1.why: Shows the rite follows the Mosaic law.

2-chronicles-35:11:3.summary: Hebrews speaks of blood for cleansing in the law; only a general link to the priests handling blood.

2-chronicles-35:11:4.summary: Under Hezekiah “the priests received the blood and poured it” on the altar, matching the priests’ blood rite here.

2-chronicles-35:11:5.summary: Levites may not approach the altar, which explains the distinct roles, but the source does not state this rule.
2-chronicles-35:11:5.why: Background to separate priest and Levite duties.

2-chronicles-35:11:6.summary: Priests alone keep the altar service; a background principle for priests handling blood.
2-chronicles-35:11:6.why: Explains why priests, not Levites, poured blood.

2-chronicles-35:12:0.summary: Laws on fat portions offered to the Lord give general background to preparing offerings “as written in the Book of Moses”.

2-chronicles-35:12:1.summary: Rules for removing fat and kidneys for the Lord loosely illustrate the offerings prepared by the law.

2-chronicles-35:12:2.summary: Aaron’s sons offer fat portions “upon the whole burnt offerings”, a general link to preparing burnt offerings.

2-chronicles-35:12:3.summary: The fat of the deliverance sacrifice belongs to the Lord; general legal background only.

2-chronicles-35:13:1.summary: Meat boiling in a “cauldron” and “bronze kettle” and meat to “roast” mirror roasting and boiling in bronze vessels here, though Eli’s sons abuse it.
2-chronicles-35:13:1.why: Contrasts proper and abusive handling of sacrifices.

2-chronicles-35:13:2.summary: Passover law says “boil it, and roast it” at the chosen place, the instructions followed at Josiah’s Passover.

2-chronicles-35:13:3.summary: Holy offerings “boiled in a bronze vessel” match boiling the holy things in bronze vessels.
2-chronicles-35:13:3.why: Law behind the bronze cooking vessels.

2-chronicles-35:13:4.summary: A lament about being poured out and melting has no link to cooking the Passover.

2-chronicles-35:13:5.summary: Only the “boiled” foreleg of a Nazirite offering overlaps with boiling holy things.

2-chronicles-35:13:6.summary: Jerusalem’s lament about fire sent into its bones has nothing to do with roasting the Passover.

2-chronicles-35:13:7.summary: Being fervent in spirit has no specific link to cooking and distributing the Passover.

2-chronicles-35:14:0.summary: Apostles delegate table-serving so they can keep to their ministry, loosely like Levites preparing so priests stay at the altar.
2-chronicles-35:14:0.why: Shared idea of dividing ministry tasks.

2-chronicles-35:15:0.summary: Lists the Levite “gatekeepers” and their posts at the king’s gate, the same office stationed at each gate here.

2-chronicles-35:15:1.summary: Gatekeeper divisions assigned by lot “for each gate” match the gatekeepers stationed at each gate.
2-chronicles-35:15:1.why: Shows the origin of gate assignments.

2-chronicles-35:15:3.summary: Levites stationed “according to the command of King David, Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet”, like singers by David’s and the king’s prophets’ commands.

2-chronicles-35:15:4.summary: Only the heading “for Asaph” connects; the psalm’s content about the defiled temple is unrelated.

2-chronicles-35:15:5.summary: David organizes gatekeepers and those praising with instruments, the two Levite groups named here.
2-chronicles-35:15:5.why: Davidic origin of singers and gatekeepers.

2-chronicles-35:15:6.summary: The Saints text shows only a cry to God, without any Asaph or Jeduthun heading, so no link appears.
2-chronicles-35:15:6.why: Greek-numbered text lacks the expected heading.

2-chronicles-35:15:7.summary: “Aiman” and “Idithon” (Heman, Jeduthun) lead praise with Idithon’s sons “at the gate”, matching the singers and gatekeepers here.

2-chronicles-35:15:8.summary: Only the heading “Of Asaph” links to Asaph’s sons; content is a teaching psalm.

2-chronicles-35:17:1.summary: The command to keep the feast of unleavened bread “for seven days” is what Israel observes here.
2-chronicles-35:17:1.why: Shows obedience to the festival law.

2-chronicles-35:17:4.summary: “Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days” matches the observance described.
2-chronicles-35:17:4.why: Legal basis of the seven-day feast.

2-chronicles-35:17:6.summary: Under Hezekiah “the sons of Israel present” kept “the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days”, nearly identical wording.

2-chronicles-35:17:2.summary: Passover followed by the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days, the exact sequence observed here.

2-chronicles-35:17:3.summary: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread” is the law Israel keeps here.

2-chronicles-35:17:5.summary: The unleavened bread days ending in a feast on the seventh day define the seven-day observance kept here.

2-chronicles-35:17:7.summary: The Lord’s Passover followed by seven days of unleavened bread matches the observance (truncated range).

2-chronicles-35:17:8.summary: Paul applies Passover and unleavened bread to Christ and sincerity, a typological rather than historical link.

2-chronicles-35:17:9.summary: “Unleavened bread with it for seven days” after the Passover sacrifice is the observance described.
2-chronicles-35:17:9.why: Explains the feast’s remembrance of Egypt.

2-chronicles-35:18:0.summary: Hezekiah calls all Israel to Passover because many had not kept it “according to the writing”, background to the unmatched Passover.
2-chronicles-35:18:0.why: Context for the rarity of such Passovers.

2-chronicles-35:18:2.summary: “Since the days of Solomon … there had been no such festival” uses the same no-equal formula for Hezekiah’s feast.

2-chronicles-35:20:2.summary: “Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, who was beside the Euphrates River at Carchemish” names the same campaign.
2-chronicles-35:20:2.why: Locates Neco’s expedition and its outcome.

2-chronicles-35:20:0.summary: The Greek-based text names “Chalanneh” and Babylon, not Carchemish, so the expected place link is absent.
2-chronicles-35:20:0.why: Greek wording drops the place link.

2-chronicles-35:21:0.summary: A foreign king warns a Judean king to stay home rather than “engage in evil” and fall with Judah, like Neco’s warning.
2-chronicles-35:21:0.why: Parallel unheeded warning against needless war.

2-chronicles-35:21:1.summary: An Assyrian claims “The Lord said to me” to attack, as Neco claims God told him to hurry.

2-chronicles-35:21:2.summary: “What have I to do with you … the Lord has told him” closely echoes Neco’s idiom and appeal to God’s command.
2-chronicles-35:21:2.why: Same idiom of separation and divine instruction.

2-chronicles-35:21:3.summary: “What have we to do with Thee” shares only the idiom of separation, in a different setting.

2-chronicles-35:21:4.summary: Assyria claims it did not come “without the Lord” to make war, like Neco’s divine justification.

2-chronicles-35:21:5.summary: “What is this to Me and to you” shares the idiom only, in an unrelated context.

2-chronicles-35:22:0.summary: Kings fight “by Megiddo’s water”, the same battlefield as the “plain of Magedon”.

2-chronicles-35:22:1.summary: Ahab disguises himself for battle; the Saints text says Josiah “strengthened himself”, so the disguise link does not carry, leaving only a doomed king entering battle.
2-chronicles-35:22:1.why: Loose parallel of ill-fated royal battles.

2-chronicles-35:22:2.summary: The king of Israel “concealed himself” for battle; Saints’ Josiah “strengthened himself”, so only the fatal-battle pattern remains.
2-chronicles-35:22:2.why: Loose parallel to Ahab’s fatal battle.

2-chronicles-35:22:3.summary: Neco’s message is the very warning “through God’s mouth” Josiah refused to heed.

2-chronicles-35:22:4.summary: The Greek-based text has Jeroboam sending his wife to inquire, with no disguise or battle, so no link to Josiah.
2-chronicles-35:22:4.why: Greek text lacks the disguise motif.

2-chronicles-35:22:5.summary: Kings seek the Lord’s word before battle, contrasting Josiah’s failure to listen; only a general link.
2-chronicles-35:22:5.why: Contrast in seeking God before war.

2-chronicles-35:22:6.summary: Great mourning “in a plain” echoes Magedon’s plain, but the Greek text lacks Megiddo, so the allusion is faint.

2-chronicles-35:22:7.summary: “Harmagedon” takes its name from Megiddo, the “plain of Magedon” where Josiah fought.
2-chronicles-35:22:7.why: Connects Megiddo to the final battle.

2-chronicles-35:22:8.summary: Kings’ account: Josiah carried dead from “Mageddo” to Jerusalem, the same battle’s outcome.

2-chronicles-35:22:9.summary: Ahab shot in battle anticipates Josiah’s wounding in the next verse rather than this one.
2-chronicles-35:22:9.why: Pattern of kings struck by archers.

2-chronicles-35:22:10.summary: Leaders who “did not inquire of the Lord” parallel Josiah ignoring God’s word only in general.
2-chronicles-35:22:10.why: Danger of acting without God’s counsel.

2-chronicles-35:22:11.summary: A wounded king of Judah, Ahaziah, flees “to Megiddo and died there”, the same place of Josiah’s fatal battle.
2-chronicles-35:22:11.why: Megiddo as a place of royal death.

2-chronicles-35:23:0.summary: An archer hits the king, who says “take me out of the battle, for I am wounded”, nearly Josiah’s words.

2-chronicles-35:23:1.summary: Joram killed by an arrow shares only a king being shot.

2-chronicles-35:23:2.summary: God’s arrows in a poetic lament share only the image of arrows.

2-chronicles-35:23:3.summary: A king withdraws to be treated for battle wounds, a loose parallel to Josiah’s wounding.
2-chronicles-35:23:3.why: General motif of a wounded king.

2-chronicles-35:23:4.summary: Joseph harassed by “masters of arrows” is poetic and unrelated to Josiah’s battle.

2-chronicles-35:23:5.summary: A man drew his bow and struck the king, who says “take me out of the battle, for I am hurt”, matching Josiah’s plea.
2-chronicles-35:23:5.why: Close verbal parallel of royal battle death.

2-chronicles-35:24:0.summary: Great “mourning in Jerusalem” echoes Judah and Jerusalem mourning Josiah, but the Greek text lacks the Megiddo reference.

2-chronicles-35:24:2.summary: One fate befalls righteous and ungodly, a reflection fitting a righteous king’s death, but no specific link.

2-chronicles-35:24:3.summary: God’s judgments as a great deep has no specific tie to Josiah’s death and burial.

2-chronicles-35:24:4.summary: Righteous people suffering what the ungodly deserve loosely fits Josiah’s fate.
2-chronicles-35:24:4.why: Wisdom on the puzzle of suffering.

2-chronicles-35:24:5.summary: Huldah’s word that Josiah would be added “to your fathers” and his tomb is fulfilled in his burial with his fathers.
2-chronicles-35:24:5.why: Shows prophecy fulfilled in his death.

2-chronicles-35:24:6.summary: Only the phrase “his second chariot” is shared; Joseph’s honor is unrelated to Josiah’s death.

2-chronicles-35:25:0.summary: Jeremiah tells them not to lament “the dead” but the exile; the shown verse does not name Josiah.
2-chronicles-35:25:0.why: Jeremiah’s word on lamenting a dead king.

2-chronicles-35:25:1.summary: Lament over “the Lord’s anointed” seized may echo a fallen king but does not name Josiah.

2-chronicles-35:25:2.summary: Flute players and mourners show a culture of public lament, only generally like the laments for Josiah.

2-chronicles-35:25:3.summary: Cursing a day and subduing the sea creature has no link to laments for Josiah.

2-chronicles-35:25:4.summary: Jeremiah calls women who lament to raise a dirge, generally like the male and female lamenters here (truncated range).
2-chronicles-35:25:4.why: Shows the role of lament singers.

2-chronicles-35:25:5.summary: A call to cry out over shattered lovers has no specific link to Josiah’s lament.
2-chronicles-35:25:5.why: Only a general cry of grief.

2-chronicles-35:25:6.summary: “Mourners circled” at a death is a generic mourning image.

2-chronicles-35:26:0.summary: Hezekiah did what was good and right before the Lord, a general parallel to Josiah’s recorded deeds.

2-chronicles-35:27:0.summary: “The rest of the acts … written in the book” of the kings is the same regnal source formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:1.summary: “Written in the writing of the kings” repeats the source-citation formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:2.summary: Manasseh’s deeds “written in the accounts of the seers” uses the same citation formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:3.summary: “First and last … written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel” nearly matches word for word.

2-chronicles-35:27:4.summary: Amon’s deeds “written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah”, the same closing formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:5.summary: Hezekiah’s deeds “written … in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel”, the same book named.
2-chronicles-35:27:5.why: Same source cited for another king.

2-chronicles-35:27:6.summary: Jehoshaphat’s acts “first and last” written in a book of the kings repeats the formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:7.summary: “The rest of Hezekiah’s deeds … written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah” is the same formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:8.summary: Uzziah’s acts “first and last” were written down, the same summary formula.

2-chronicles-35:27:9.summary: Ahaz’s deeds “written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah”, the standard closing formula.

2-chronicles-36:1:0.summary: “Shallum son of Josiah, who reigned in place of his father Josiah” is Jehoahaz, made king here.

2-chronicles-36:1:1.summary: “The people of the land took” Uzziah and made him king in his father’s place, the same accession formula.
2-chronicles-36:1:1.why: Role of the people of the land in succession.

2-chronicles-36:1:2.summary: “The people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place”, the same group acting at Josiah’s accession.

2-chronicles-36:1:4.summary: Lists “Josiah’s sons”, including Salloum (Jehoahaz), the son anointed here.

2-chronicles-36:4:0.summary: Shallum son of Josiah “went out” and will die where deported, matching Joahaz taken to Egypt and dying there.

2-chronicles-36:4:1.summary: A lion cub caught and “led … with a muzzle to Egypt’s land” pictures Joahaz taken into Egypt.

2-chronicles-36:4:2.summary: “Joakim the second” among Josiah’s sons is Eliakim/Jehoiakim installed here.

2-chronicles-36:5:1.summary: Dated to “the beginning of the reign of King Jehoiakim son of Josiah”, the reign introduced here.

2-chronicles-36:5:2.summary: Shown verses condemn an unjust king building his house without righteousness; the king is not named in the shown truncated text.

2-chronicles-36:5:3.summary: King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah’s roll and receives judgment, illustrating the evil he did.

2-chronicles-36:5:4.summary: Only a date “in the days of Jehoiakim king of Judah” links to this reign.
2-chronicles-36:5:4.why: Places an oracle in his reign.

2-chronicles-36:5:5.summary: “King Jehoiakim” has the prophet Uriah killed, a concrete case of his evil.

2-chronicles-36:5:6.summary: Only the date “fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah” connects.

2-chronicles-36:6:0.summary: Manasseh “bound … in fetters” and brought “to Babylon” mirrors Jehoiakim bound in bronze fetters and taken to Babylon.

2-chronicles-36:6:2.summary: A second lion cub caged and brought “to Babylon’s king” pictures a Judean king taken to Babylon (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:6:3.summary: God raising the Chaldeans against Judah gives general background to Nebuchadnezzar’s attack (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:6:4.summary: The shown text describes the later deportation of the eighteen-year-old “Joakim” (Jechonias) to Babylon, not this king (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:6:5.summary: Kings closes Joakim’s reign with his acts recorded and his son reigning, the same king’s end.
2-chronicles-36:6:5.why: Compare Kings’ account of Jehoiakim’s end.

2-chronicles-36:6:6.summary: God bringing the northern clan against the land foretells Babylon’s attack in general terms.

2-chronicles-36:6:7.summary: “In his days Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon came up” against Joakim, the same event.

2-chronicles-36:7:0.summary: Babylon takes “treasures of the Lord’s house” and gold vessels, as Nebuchadnezzar carries off its vessels here.

2-chronicles-36:7:1.summary: A false promise to return “the vessels of the Lord’s house” refers to these vessels taken to Babylon.
2-chronicles-36:7:1.why: Later dispute over the stolen vessels.

2-chronicles-36:7:2.summary: False prophets claim “the vessels of the Lord’s house will return from Babylon”, referring to this plunder.

2-chronicles-36:7:3.summary: Vessels of God’s house “Nebuchadnezzar had brought from Jerusalem” are misused at Belshazzar’s feast.
2-chronicles-36:7:3.why: Later story of the same vessels.

2-chronicles-36:7:5.summary: Cyrus returns “the vessels of the Lord’s house that Nebuchadnezzar had taken … and placed in the house of his god”.

2-chronicles-36:8:1.summary: “Joakim’s sons: Jechonias his son” confirms the succession recorded here.

2-chronicles-36:8:2.summary: Jechoniah appears in Matthew’s genealogy at the deportation to Babylon.

2-chronicles-36:8:3.summary: “Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah” is the son who reigns here, judged by God.

2-chronicles-36:8:4.summary: Jeconiah “cast out and thrown into a land he did not know” describes the king who succeeds here.

2-chronicles-36:9:0.summary: Kings: he was “eighteen years old”, reigned “three months”, and did evil, the same reign (named Joakim in Saints).

2-chronicles-36:10:0.summary: Zedekiah reigned because “Nebuchadnezzar had made him king over Judah”, matching this verse.

2-chronicles-36:10:1.summary: Earlier removal of “the vessels of the Lord’s house to Babylon” parallels the desirable vessels taken here.

2-chronicles-36:10:2.summary: Remaining vessels Babylon’s king did not take “when he deported Jeconiah” refers directly to this event.

2-chronicles-36:10:3.summary: Dates by “King Jehoiakim’s captivity” in the Saints text; links to the king’s deportation only loosely given the name difference.

2-chronicles-36:10:4.summary: Nebuchadnezzar “deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim … to Babylon”, the event recorded here.

2-chronicles-36:10:5.summary: The deported king (called Joakim in Saints) is released in Babylon decades later.
2-chronicles-36:10:5.why: Later fate of the exiled king.

2-chronicles-36:10:6.summary: The “vessels of the living God’s house” misused in Babylon relate generally to the vessels taken.

2-chronicles-36:10:7.summary: “Vessels of God’s house that his father Nebuchadnezzar had brought from Jerusalem” are those carried to Babylon.
2-chronicles-36:10:7.why: Shows the plundered vessels in Babylon.

2-chronicles-36:10:8.summary: A king handed “into the hands of the Chaldeans” fits Jechonias’s fate, though the shown verse names no one.

2-chronicles-36:10:9.summary: Babylon’s king “will take her king and her rulers and bring them … in Babylon”, describing this deportation.

2-chronicles-36:10:10.summary: All the vessels of God’s house brought into Babylon completes the removal begun here.

2-chronicles-36:10:11.summary: Nabouchodonosor besieges Jerusalem, takes the king and the treasures of the Lord’s house, the same event (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:10:12.summary: “At the return of the year” matches “At the turn of the year” as a season idiom only.

2-chronicles-36:10:14.summary: Lists Sedekias among Josiah’s sons, making him Jechonias’s uncle (“his father’s brother”).

2-chronicles-36:10:15.summary: Nebuchadnezzar takes the king and “a portion of the Lord’s sacred vessels” to Babylon’s idol-temple, as here.
2-chronicles-36:10:15.why: Daniel’s account of the vessels’ removal.

2-chronicles-36:11:1.summary: “Zedekiah was twenty-one years old … and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem” is word for word the same.

2-chronicles-36:11:3.summary: Only a date in “the fourth year of Zedekiah” connects to his reign.

2-chronicles-36:12:0.summary: Amon “did not humble himself before the Lord”; the Saints source says Zedekiah “felt no shame”, so the wording link is only partial.

2-chronicles-36:12:1.summary: Zedekiah consults Jeremiah yet Jeremiah warns “you certainly will not listen”, showing his disregard (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:12:2.summary: “Neither he nor his servants … obeyed the Lord’s words, which He spoke through Jeremiah” states the same charge (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:12:3.summary: The shown verse only accuses Belshazzar of not blessing God; the humility link of the label is absent.
2-chronicles-36:12:3.why: Shown text lacks the intended link.

2-chronicles-36:12:4.summary: A call to humble oneself before the Lord contrasts with Zedekiah’s refusal, but the Saints source speaks of shame, not humility.

2-chronicles-36:12:5.summary: Manasseh’s prayer and “turning back” contrasts loosely with Zedekiah’s refusal.
2-chronicles-36:12:5.why: Example of a king who repented.

2-chronicles-36:12:6.summary: King Zedekiah sends to Jeremiah and receives the Lord’s word of judgment (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:12:7.summary: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God” contrasts generally with Zedekiah’s unrepentance.

2-chronicles-36:12:8.summary: Hezekiah and Jerusalem “humbled themselves” and averted wrath, contrasting with Zedekiah.
2-chronicles-36:12:8.why: Contrasting response of an earlier king.

2-chronicles-36:12:9.summary: Manasseh “humbled himself greatly” when afflicted, unlike Zedekiah.

2-chronicles-36:12:10.summary: The Lord’s word through Jeremiah “to Zedekiah king of Judah” about the city’s fall (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:12:11.summary: Pharaoh refuses to reverence God, a general parallel to a king defying God’s word.

2-chronicles-36:12:12.summary: Jeremiah speaks “to Zedekiah king of Judah”, urging submission to Babylon (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:12:13.summary: Josiah “did not listen to … words through God’s mouth”, as Zedekiah ignores “what came from the Lord’s mouth”.
2-chronicles-36:12:13.why: Two kings refusing the divine word.

2-chronicles-36:13:2.summary: “Do not harden your necks” and return to the Lord is the warning Zedekiah defies.

2-chronicles-36:13:3.summary: “Do not harden your hearts” echoes hardening generally.

2-chronicles-36:13:4.summary: Israel “stiffened their necks” and refused to listen, the same idiom of obstinacy.

2-chronicles-36:13:5.summary: Pharaoh’s refusal to let Israel go is a general parallel of obstinacy.

2-chronicles-36:13:6.summary: Saul violates Israel’s sworn oath to the Gibeonites, a loose parallel to Zedekiah breaking his oath.

2-chronicles-36:13:7.summary: Pharaoh’s heart “became heavy” and he did not listen, a general hardening parallel.

2-chronicles-36:13:8.summary: Warning against being “hardened by the deceit of sin” is a general echo.

2-chronicles-36:13:9.summary: Leaders “swore to them” in a covenant, a loose parallel on the binding force of oaths.

2-chronicles-36:13:10.summary: “Stubborn, your neck an iron sinew” is the same image as hardening his neck.
2-chronicles-36:13:10.why: Vivid image of a stiff neck.

2-chronicles-36:13:12.summary: Hoshea breaks faith with his Assyrian overlord and is imprisoned, loosely like Zedekiah breaking with Nebuchadnezzar.

2-chronicles-36:13:13.summary: Pharaoh “made his heart heavy”, a general parallel of hardening.

2-chronicles-36:13:14.summary: “Hardness and unrepentant heart” storing up wrath echoes refusing to return to the Lord generally.

2-chronicles-36:13:15.summary: They “stiffened their necks and did not listen” though urged to turn back, the same idiom and charge.

2-chronicles-36:13:16.summary: Leaders “sworn to them by the Lord” keep their oath, contrasting loosely with Zedekiah breaking an oath sworn by God.
2-chronicles-36:13:16.why: Oaths by God must be kept.

2-chronicles-36:14:0.summary: Israel’s leaders shedding blood is a general indictment of leaders, not of temple defilement.

2-chronicles-36:14:1.summary: Shame belongs to “our kings, rulers, and fathers” who sinned, a general confession.

2-chronicles-36:14:2.summary: “Her priests … profaned My holy things” and rulers are corrupt, matching priests and leaders defiling the Lord’s house.
2-chronicles-36:14:2.why: Prophetic indictment of priests and rulers.

2-chronicles-36:14:3.summary: Ahaz and Uriah the priest install a foreign altar in the Lord’s house, an example of foreign practices (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:14:4.summary: Jerusalem’s leaders and priests corrupt for gain, a general parallel to leaders’ unfaithfulness.

2-chronicles-36:14:5.summary: Confession that “our kings” offended and were handed to foreign kings, a general echo.

2-chronicles-36:14:6.summary: Ahaz acted “according to the abominations of the nations”, the same phrase as here.

2-chronicles-36:14:7.summary: Rulers mistreat Jeremiah, a general sign of leaders’ unfaithfulness.

2-chronicles-36:14:8.summary: The prosperous “broke the yoke” together, a general picture of leaders’ rebellion.

2-chronicles-36:14:9.summary: Kings, rulers, and fathers did not listen to the prophets, a general confession.

2-chronicles-36:14:10.summary: Leaders of Jacob’s house who hate good are condemned, a general indictment.

2-chronicles-36:14:11.summary: Manasseh builds altars “in the Lord’s house” and sets an image there, a concrete defilement of the temple (truncated range).
2-chronicles-36:14:11.why: Example of defiling the Lord’s house.

2-chronicles-36:14:12.summary: Manasseh led Judah to do evil “beyond all the nations”, echoing sin by the nations’ standards.

2-chronicles-36:14:13.summary: “Her priests profane holy things” and rulers are predatory, matching corrupt priests and leaders.

2-chronicles-36:14:14.summary: No one acts rightly among people, a general lament over corruption.

2-chronicles-36:14:15.summary: Rulers demand Jeremiah’s death, showing leaders’ hostility, not temple defilement.

2-chronicles-36:14:16.summary: Ezekiel sees “abominations and all the idols” within the temple courts, the defilement of the Lord’s house (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:15:2.summary: God spoke “rising early” and sent His prophets, the same idiom.

2-chronicles-36:15:0.summary: God spoke and called but they did not answer; the Saints text lacks “rising early”.

2-chronicles-36:15:1.summary: “I sent you My servants the prophets” urging repentance, the same sending of messengers.

2-chronicles-36:15:3.summary: “I sent you My servants the prophets at dawn”, matching rising early and sending.

2-chronicles-36:15:4.summary: Prophets “whom I send to you from early morning” is the same idiom.

2-chronicles-36:15:5.summary: God “grew weary over Israel’s distress”, a general sign of compassion like sparing His people.

2-chronicles-36:15:7.summary: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem that missed its visitation, a general parallel of God’s pity before judgment.

2-chronicles-36:15:8.summary: “He sent prophets to them to turn them back … but they did not listen” matches God’s sending of prophets.

2-chronicles-36:15:9.summary: The Lord warned Israel and Judah “through all His prophets”, the same pattern of warnings.

2-chronicles-36:15:10.summary: The Lord spoke against Manasseh’s people “but they did not listen”, a brief general parallel.

2-chronicles-36:15:11.summary: The Lord “pitied them” and was unwilling to destroy, like His sparing His people.

2-chronicles-36:15:12.summary: God’s heart turns within Him over Ephraim, a general picture of divine compassion.

2-chronicles-36:16:0.summary: The people say “Our prophets became wind” and deny coming evils, treating God’s words as nothing.

2-chronicles-36:16:1.summary: Men mock Jesus, saying “Prophesy!”, a general echo of mocking prophets.

2-chronicles-36:16:2.summary: Hezekiah’s runners were treated “with laughter and mockery”, the same scorn of God’s messengers.

2-chronicles-36:16:3.summary: Rejecting the message rejects God himself, a general principle behind despising God’s words.

2-chronicles-36:16:4.summary: Sudden destruction and “incurable crushing” echo “no healing” only in phrasing.

2-chronicles-36:16:5.summary: Lament over God’s wrath against His sheep relates generally to His anger rising.

2-chronicles-36:16:6.summary: King Zedekiah imprisons Jeremiah for prophesying, a concrete case of mistreating His prophets.
2-chronicles-36:16:6.why: Specific example of persecuting a prophet.

2-chronicles-36:16:7.summary: Because the fathers “provoked the God of heaven”, He gave them to Nabouchodonosor, the same cause and result.

2-chronicles-36:16:8.summary: The stiff-necked man suddenly burns and “there is no healing”, matching the phrase and its cause.

2-chronicles-36:16:9.summary: Wisdom kept calling, was ignored, and ruin came, the same pattern of rejected warnings and judgment (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:16:10.summary: Farmers beat and kill the owner’s repeatedly sent slaves, echoing God’s rejected messengers (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:16:11.summary: The psalmist is mocked, a general mockery theme only.

2-chronicles-36:16:12.summary: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” summarizes the treatment of prophets described here.

2-chronicles-36:16:13.summary: Herod mocks Jesus, a general parallel of mocking God’s messenger.

2-chronicles-36:16:14.summary: Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy pit, a concrete instance of mistreating the Lord’s prophet.
2-chronicles-36:16:14.why: Example of abuse of a prophet.

2-chronicles-36:16:15.summary: The Greek-based text reads “do not rejoice”, not “do not mock”, so the mocking link does not carry.
2-chronicles-36:16:15.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-36:16:16.summary: Jesus foretells being mocked and insulted, a general mockery theme.

2-chronicles-36:16:17.summary: Nations defile the temple and God’s anger blazes, related to the coming judgment rather than mocking prophets.

2-chronicles-36:16:18.summary: Athenians mocking the resurrection share only the word “mocked”.

2-chronicles-36:16:19.summary: Jeremiah says he became a laughingstock, “mocked” all day, a prophet personally scorned.

2-chronicles-36:16:20.summary: Soldiers mock Jesus, a general mockery parallel.

2-chronicles-36:16:21.summary: Pharisees “sneered” at Jesus’ teaching, a general parallel of sneering at God’s word.

2-chronicles-36:16:22.summary: The faithful “experienced mockery” and chains, generally like mistreated prophets.

2-chronicles-36:16:23.summary: Mocking the apostles as drunk shares only the verb “mocked”.

2-chronicles-36:16:24.summary: Warning to “scoffers” of coming judgment is a general parallel to mockers judged.

2-chronicles-36:16:25.summary: “They persecuted the prophets before you” recalls this persecution of God’s prophets.

2-chronicles-36:17:0.summary: A plea about houses of lawlessness has no specific link to the Chaldean slaughter.

2-chronicles-36:17:1.summary: Kings and sons “handed over into the hand of the kings of the nations—to the sword, captivity”, the same judgment.

2-chronicles-36:17:2.summary: “Do not spare … have no mercy”, killing old man, young man and maiden, beginning at the holy places, mirrors this slaughter.

2-chronicles-36:17:3.summary: The Lord acted because they sinned, a general explanation of the disaster.

2-chronicles-36:17:4.summary: God “brought all these great calamities” on the people, a general reference.
2-chronicles-36:17:4.why: God as author of the disaster.

2-chronicles-36:17:6.summary: Covenant curses for disobedience broadly anticipate this judgment (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:7.summary: God foretells forsaking His people for breaking His covenant, general background (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:8.summary: The covenant curse on those turning to other gods anticipates judgment in general (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:9.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem in Zedekiah’s reign and the city is breached, the same event (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:10.summary: The Lord “sent against him” Chaldean raiders because of His anger, as He brings the Chaldean king here.

2-chronicles-36:17:11.summary: The Lord brought Assyrian commanders against Manasseh, a general parallel of God bringing a foreign army.

2-chronicles-36:17:12.summary: Zechariah killed in the Lord’s house courtyard loosely echoes slaughter in the sanctuary.

2-chronicles-36:17:13.summary: “Young men fallen by the sword” matches the young men killed with the sword.

2-chronicles-36:17:14.summary: Covenant curses for disobedience broadly foretell defeat and exile (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:15.summary: The Song of Moses foretells God turning His face for idolatry, general background (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:16.summary: Jeremiah 52 narrates Zedekiah’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar’s siege and the city’s breach, the same events (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:17:17.summary: The Lord “brought” calamities because “we did not listen”, a general confession.

2-chronicles-36:17:18.summary: Widows and remnants given to the sword is a general picture of judgment.

2-chronicles-36:17:19.summary: Blood poured around Jerusalem and unburied dead is a general lament on the slaughter.

2-chronicles-36:17:20.summary: Warning that disobedient Israel “shall surely perish” on the land is general background.

2-chronicles-36:17:21.summary: Priest killed in “the Lord’s sanctuary”, “virgins and young men” lost, “slaughter without sparing”, closely match this verse.
2-chronicles-36:17:21.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-chronicles-36:17:22.summary: Galileans killed with their sacrifices shares only bloodshed near worship, not this event.

2-chronicles-36:18:0.summary: Earlier removal of “vessels of the Lord’s house to Babylon” leads to the total removal here.

2-chronicles-36:18:1.summary: “The desirable vessels of the Lord’s house” brought into Babylon precede this final plunder.

2-chronicles-36:18:2.summary: God’s words through prophets “overtook your fathers”, a general reflection on judgment fulfilled.

2-chronicles-36:18:3.summary: Hezekiah shows his treasures to Babylonian envoys, setting up Isaiah’s prophecy that they would go to Babylon (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:18:4.summary: The remaining vessels “will go into Babylon”, fulfilled when everything is brought there.

2-chronicles-36:18:5.summary: “They will take everything in your house … will reach Babylon” is fulfilled by this plunder.

2-chronicles-36:18:6.summary: Shown verse only says “they drank from them”; the vessels link depends on context not shown.

2-chronicles-36:18:7.summary: The Chaldeans carry the bronze, vessels and utensils of the Lord’s house to Babylon (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:19:0.summary: Nations “defiled Thy holy temple” and made Jerusalem a hut, lamenting this destruction.

2-chronicles-36:19:1.summary: False confidence in “The Lord’s temple” is a general prelude to its destruction.

2-chronicles-36:19:2.summary: Gold dimmed and holy stones poured out loosely evoke the destroyed beautiful articles.

2-chronicles-36:19:3.summary: Zion plowed and “the mountain of the house” a grove foretells the temple and city laid waste.

2-chronicles-36:19:4.summary: God will do “to this house … as I did to Shiloh”, foretelling the temple’s destruction.

2-chronicles-36:19:6.summary: “The house, our holy place … became fire-burned, and all the glorious things collapsed” mirrors the burning and destruction.

2-chronicles-36:19:7.summary: “He burned the Lord’s house” and pulled down “the whole wall of Jerusalem”, the same event.

2-chronicles-36:19:8.summary: Jesus foretells stones torn down, a later temple destruction, only thematically similar.

2-chronicles-36:19:9.summary: Solomon is warned that passers-by will be astonished at “this lofty house”, anticipating its destruction.

2-chronicles-36:19:10.summary: “They burned Thy sanctuary with fire” and tore it down, lamenting this same burning.
2-chronicles-36:19:10.why: Psalm lament over the destroyed sanctuary.

2-chronicles-36:19:11.summary: Jacob devoured and his place desolate is a general lament.

2-chronicles-36:19:12.summary: “They burned the chosen city of the sanctuary” recalls this burning of Jerusalem and the temple.

2-chronicles-36:20:1.summary: Cyrus king of the Persians ends the exile and sends the people back, the end of servitude noted here (truncated range).

2-chronicles-36:20:3.summary: “In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians” the exile ends, completing this verse’s timeframe.

2-chronicles-36:20:4.summary: “You shall serve your enemies” for disobedience is fulfilled as the survivors become slaves in Babylon.

2-chronicles-36:21:0.summary: Jeremiah’s word that “seventy years” would be fulfilled for Babylon is the very prophecy the source says was fulfilled.
2-chronicles-36:21:0.why: Shows the prophecy behind the seventy years.

2-chronicles-36:21:3.summary: Daniel reads Jeremiah’s prophecy of Jerusalem’s desolation lasting “seventy years,” the same reckoning the Chronicler cites.
2-chronicles-36:21:3.why: Another reader of the same Jeremiah prophecy.

2-chronicles-36:21:4.summary: The angel laments Jerusalem’s neglect in the “seventieth year,” echoing the seventy years of desolation.
2-chronicles-36:21:4.why: Shows the seventy-year period nearing its end.

2-chronicles-36:21:5.summary: Leviticus warns that the land “shall receive its Sabbaths when it is desolated,” the curse the source says was fulfilled.
2-chronicles-36:21:5.why: Gives the Torah basis for the land’s Sabbaths.

2-chronicles-36:21:6.summary: The law of the land’s seventh-year “Sabbath” explains what Sabbaths the desolate land was making up.
2-chronicles-36:21:6.why: Explains the land-Sabbath law being enforced.

2-chronicles-36:21:7.summary: Jeremiah threatens to make the house like Shiloh and the city a curse; general doom, no seventy years or Sabbaths.
2-chronicles-36:21:7.why: Background to Jeremiah’s warnings of ruin.

2-chronicles-36:21:8.summary: Jeremiah foretells the land laid “waste” and made a ruin by the northern clan; the shown verse lacks the seventy years.

2-chronicles-36:21:9.summary: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah to submit his neck; only loosely related to the fulfilled word of desolation.
2-chronicles-36:21:9.why: Shows Jeremiah’s warning to the last king.

2-chronicles-36:21:10.summary: Zechariah says the prophets’ words overtook the fathers, a general reflection on fulfilled prophetic warnings.
2-chronicles-36:21:10.why: Reflects on prophecy fulfilled in exile.

2-chronicles-36:22:3.summary: The preceding verse speaks of “the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth” and seventy years, which this verse says was fulfilled.
2-chronicles-36:22:3.why: Immediate context of the fulfilled prophecy.

2-chronicles-36:22:9.summary: Both are dated “in the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians.”
2-chronicles-36:22:9.why: Places Daniel’s vision at the same moment.

2-chronicles-36:22:0.summary: Jeremiah predicts judgment on Babylon “when the seventy years are fulfilled,” the turning point that brings Cyrus.
2-chronicles-36:22:0.why: The prophecy whose fulfillment is noted.

2-chronicles-36:22:4.summary: Isaiah names “Cyrus” as the Lord’s anointed who will see Jerusalem rebuilt and the holy house founded.
2-chronicles-36:22:4.why: Prophecy naming Cyrus as God’s instrument.

2-chronicles-36:22:5.summary: God “rousing the Medes” against Babylon parallels His stirring a foreign king, but the people and purpose differ.

2-chronicles-36:22:6.summary: Jeremiah promises the desolate land will again hear joy and exiles return; restoration theme, not the Cyrus decree itself.

2-chronicles-36:22:7.summary: Ezra continues the same account: those “whose spirit God had stirred” go up to build the Lord’s house.
2-chronicles-36:22:7.why: Parallel narrative of the Cyrus decree.

2-chronicles-36:22:8.summary: Jeremiah promises good things and the return of exiles; general restoration theme.

2-chronicles-36:22:10.summary: “The Lord stirred up the spirit” of Zerubbabel and the people, the same divine stirring for temple work.
2-chronicles-36:22:10.why: Same idiom of God stirring for rebuilding.

2-chronicles-36:22:11.summary: God “stirred up the spirit” of Assyrian kings to deport Israel, a mirror use of the same idiom for a foreign king.
2-chronicles-36:22:11.why: Contrasting use: God stirs kings to exile and to restore.

2-chronicles-36:22:12.summary: The Lord “raised up an adversary” against Solomon; only a loose parallel to God stirring a ruler.

2-chronicles-36:22:13.summary: David speaks of God “stirring” Saul against him; shared idea of divine stirring only.

2-chronicles-36:22:14.summary: Hezekiah’s decree for a “proclamation” throughout Israel resembles Cyrus’s proclamation in form only.

2-chronicles-36:22:15.summary: A proclamation in Judah and Jerusalem for temple offerings; similar form but different occasion.
2-chronicles-36:22:15.why: Similar royal proclamation for the temple.

2-chronicles-36:22:16.summary: The Lord “raised up an adversary” against Solomon; only a loose parallel to God stirring Cyrus.

2-chronicles-36:22:18.summary: “The Lord stirred up” foreigners against Joram, the same idiom used here for judgment rather than restoration.

2-chronicles-36:22:19.summary: “The One who promised is faithful” matches the general theme of God fulfilling His word.

2-chronicles-36:22:20.summary: God summoning armies to destroy the world has no specific link to Cyrus’s decree to rebuild.

2-chronicles-36:23:0.summary: Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar that “the Lord of heaven has given you” the kingdom, as Cyrus says of “the God of heaven.”
2-chronicles-36:23:0.why: Foreign kings receive rule from heaven’s God.

2-chronicles-36:23:1.summary: Zechariah calls exiles to flee Babylon and escape to Zion, matching Cyrus’s invitation to “go up.”
2-chronicles-36:23:1.why: Prophetic call to return from exile.

2-chronicles-36:23:3.summary: God “humbles this one and raises that one,” a general principle of God granting rule.

2-chronicles-36:23:4.summary: God “transfers kings and appoints them,” general sovereignty over rulers.

2-chronicles-36:23:5.summary: Daniel tells Belshazzar God “gave you your kingdom”; similar idea, different king and outcome.
2-chronicles-36:23:5.why: Contrasting response of a foreign king.

2-chronicles-36:23:7.summary: “If God is for us” shares only a vague idea with “His God shall be with him.”

2-chronicles-36:23:8.summary: Artaxerxes’ decree lets anyone of Israel who wishes “go to Jerusalem,” echoing Cyrus’s permission to go up.
2-chronicles-36:23:8.why: Later Persian decree with same permission.

2-chronicles-36:23:10.summary: David’s “Who is eager…for the Lord?” resembles “Who among you…?” as a call to temple work.

2-chronicles-36:23:11.summary: David’s charge to build, “the Lord be with you,” echoes the blessing on those going to build.
